editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Those who praise Pythagoras of Samos report this of him: that he was not yet an Ionian, but had once been Euphorbus at Troy; that he had come to life again after dying, and had died as the songs of Homer tell; that he refused to wear clothing made from dead animals, and kept himself pure of all food that comes from living things, and of sacrifice. For he would not stain the altars with blood; rather the honey-cake and frankincense and the singing of a hymn—these were what came to the gods from this man—and he knew that the gods welcome such offerings more than the hecatombs and the knife laid upon the sacrificial basket. For he was in fellowship with the gods, and learned from them in what way they take pleasure in men and in what way they are displeased; and from them too he spoke of nature. The rest of mankind, he said, only guess at the divine and hold opinions about it that are inconsistent with one another; but to him Apollo himself had come, acknowledging that it was he in person, and Athena and the Muses and other gods had been with him, though they had not acknowledged themselves, gods whose forms and names men did not yet know. And whatever Pythagoras declared, his disciples held to be law, and they honoured him as one who had come from Zeus; and silence concerning the divine was a practice among them. For they heard many divine and secret things, which it would have been hard for them to keep had they not first learned that to be silent is also a form of speech. They say too that Empedocles of Acragas trod this same path of wisdom. For the lines "Farewell; I go among you as a god immortal, no longer mortal," and "For once I have already been a girl and a boy," and the ox at Olympia, which he is said to have made of pastry and offered in sacrifice—these would be the words of one who approved the way of Pythagoras. They record many other things about those who pursued wisdom in the manner of Pythagoras; but it is not fitting for me to touch on these now, since I am hastening toward the work I have set myself to complete.

From there they set out about the time of summer, themselves riding, with their guide; and there was a keeper for the camels. The supplies, of all they needed, were abundant, since the king had given them; and the country through which they travelled fared well, and the villages received them with attentions; for the leading camel bore upon its forehead a golden frontlet, that those who met them might know the king was sending one of his friends.

Concerning the Hyphasis, and how far it runs across India, and what marvel attaches to it, these are the things one ought to know. Its springs gush up out of a plain, navigable from the very source; but as the river goes on it becomes impassable even to boats. For sharp ridges of rock rise up alternately out of the water, around which the current is forced to wind, and this makes the river unnavigable. In breadth it is the equal of the Ister, which is held to be the greatest of the rivers that flow through Europe. Trees grow along its banks much like those of the Ister, and from these trees there is also distilled a kind of myrrh, which the Indians use as a marriage unguent; and unless those who gather for the wedding sprinkle the bridal pair with this myrrh, the union is thought incomplete and not joined in a way pleasing to Aphrodite. They say that both the grove about the river and the peacock-fish, which this river alone breeds, are sacred to this goddess. They have named them after the bird, since their crests are dark blue, their scales spotted, and their tails golden, and they unfold them whenever they please. There is also in this river a certain creature resembling a white worm. From this, by melting it down, they make an oil, and from this oil there comes forth a fire which nothing can contain except glass. This creature may be caught only by the king, and it is used for the taking of walls. For whenever the fat touches the battlements, it calls up a fire too strong for any of the extinguishers that men have devised against incendiaries.

When they saw the man come forward into Ephesus in Ionia, not even the craftsmen kept to their trades any longer, but followed him — one admiring his wisdom, another his appearance, another his manner of life, another his bearing, and some all together. Reports about him came in too: some from the oracle at Colophon, singing of him as a sharer in its own wisdom, and plainly wise, and the like; some from Didyma; some from the temple about Pergamum, for the god bade many of those who sought health to resort to Apollonius, since this both he himself wished and seemed good to the Fates. Embassies came to him also from the cities, holding him a guest-friend and a counsellor of life and of the founding of altars and images; and he set each of these right, in some things writing to them, in others saying that he would come. And when Smyrna too sent an embassy, but did not say what it needed, only entreating him to come, he asked the envoy what they needed of him, and he said, "to see him and to be seen.

As for the Pillars, which they say Heracles fixed as the boundaries of the earth, I leave aside the fabulous parts and will set out rather what is worth hearing and worth telling. The headlands of Europe and Libya, holding between them a strait of sixty stades, carry the Ocean into the inner seas; and the headland of Libya, whose name is Abinna, lions range over about the ridges of the mountains that look out beyond it, where it borders on the Gaetulians and the Tingae, both of them savage Libyan peoples. As one sails in along the Ocean it extends for nine hundred stades as far as the mouths of the Salex; but beyond that no one could reckon how far, for after this river Libya is without life and inhabited by men no longer. The headland of Europe, which is called Calpis, lies on the right of the entrance, six hundred stades in length, and ends at the ancient Gadeira.

Ethiopia covers the western horn of all the land that lies beneath the sun, as the Indians cover the eastern; and meeting Egypt at Meroe, and skirting some part of unrecorded Libya, it ends at the sea which the poets call Ocean, naming thus all that goes round the earth. It gives the river Nile to Egypt, which, beginning at the Cataracts, leads down from the Ethiopians all the Egypt that it floods. In size this country is not worthy to be compared with India — nor indeed is any other of the continents famous among men; but even if we should join all Egypt to Ethiopia, and let us suppose the river too to do this, the two together, great as the sum is, are still not commensurate with the land of the Indians. Yet the rivers of both are alike, to one who reckons the Indus and the Nile; for they water their continents in the season of the year when the earth desires it, and alone of rivers they produce the crocodile and the hippopotamus, and the rites of worship over them are equal, for much of what is said of the Indians is consecrated to the Nile too. The likeness of the continents is confirmed by the spices in them, and confirmed too by the lions and the elephant, which in each is caught and made to serve. They feed beasts also of a kind found nowhere else, and black men, which other continents do not, and there are nations of Pygmies among them, and of men who bark in different ways, and other marvels of the kind. The griffins of the Indians and the ants of the Ethiopians, though unlike in form, yet have, they say, like purposes; for in each they are sung of as guardians of gold, cherishing the gold-bearing soil of the continents. But no more of these things; let the discourse go on its own way, and let us hold to our man.

I am aware that tyrannies are the finest touchstone of men who pursue philosophy, and I grant that we may examine how each man has shown himself, more or less, to be a man than another. But my argument bears upon this: in the time when Domitian held tyranny, accusations and indictments hemmed our man about. How they began, and from what source, and what the name of each was, I shall set out presently. Since, however, it is necessary to tell what he said, and as what kind of man he left the trial—having convicted the tyrant rather than been convicted himself—it seems best to me, before all this, to go through whatever I have found worth relating of the deeds of wise men against tyrants, and to set these beside the deeds of Apollonius; for so, I suppose, one ought to seek the truth.

Let us go into the court to hear the man make his defence against the charge; for the sun is already rising, and the entrance to it is opened to men of repute. And those who dwell with the emperor say that he had not even touched food, for he was poring, I think, over the matters of the trial; and he held a book ready in his hand, partly in anger, partly less so. One must figure him as one vexed at the laws, since they have brought courts into being.

For Apollonius practised a discipline akin to theirs, and approached wisdom in a more divine way than Pythagoras, and rose above tyrannies; and though he lived in times neither very ancient nor yet recent, men do not yet know him for the true wisdom which he practised both philosophically and soundly. One praises this in the man, another that; and some, because he consorted with the magi of Babylon and the Brahmans of India and the Naked Sages of Egypt, take him for a magician and slander him as one whose wisdom was gained by sorcery—judging him wrongly. For Empedocles and Pythagoras himself and Democritus, though they kept company with magi and said many supernatural things, were not yet drawn down into the craft; and Plato, who travelled to Egypt and blended much of the teaching of the prophets and priests there into his own discourses, and like a painter laid colours upon outlines already sketched, was never thought to practise magic, although he was envied for his wisdom beyond all other men. Nor would foreseeing and foreknowing many things lay Apollonius open to the charge of this craft; or else Socrates too will stand accused for what he foreknew from his divine sign, and Anaxagoras for what he foretold. And who does not know that Anaxagoras, when there was the least likelihood of rain at Olympia, came into the stadium under a sheepskin in expectation of a downpour; and that he foretold a house would fall, and did not lie, for it fell; and that he prophesied night would come out of day, and that stones would be cast down from heaven about Aegospotami, and was proved true? Yet men set these things down to the wisdom of Anaxagoras, while they take from Apollonius the power of foreknowing through wisdom, and say he did these things by the art of the magician. It seems to me, then, that I should not overlook the ignorance of the many, but should give an exact account of the man—both in the times at which he said or did anything, and in the modes of wisdom by which he came near to being thought a divine and supernatural being. I have gathered my material partly from the cities that loved him, partly from the temples whose ordinances, already grown lax, he restored, partly from what others said of him, and partly from his own letters. For he wrote letters to kings, sophists, philosophers, to the men of Elis and Delphi, to Indians and Egyptians, on the subject of the gods, of customs, of conduct, of laws; and wherever anything was amiss, he set it right. But the more precise details I gathered in this way.

As they approached the Caucasus, they say they perceived the earth to be more fragrant. Let us make this mountain the beginning of the Taurus, which goes through Armenia and Cilicia as far as the Pamphylians and Mycale; and Mycale, ending at the sea which the Carians inhabit, would be reckoned the limit of the Caucasus, but not, as some say, its beginning. For the height of Mycale is not yet great, while the summits of the Caucasus rise so high that the sun is cleft about them. With another arm of Taurus it embraces also all the Scythia bordering on India, along the Maeotis and the left side of the Pontus, a length of about twenty thousand stadia; so great a measure of the earth does the elbow of the Caucasus span. As for what is said of the Taurus in our own land, that it travels beyond Armenia—long disbelieved, it is now at last confirmed by the leopards, which I know are caught in the spice-bearing region of Pamphylia. For they delight in spices, and drawing the scents from afar, they come from Armenia through the mountains toward the gum of the storax, whenever the winds blow from it and the trees grow full of juice. And they say that a leopard was once caught in Pamphylia wearing a torque around its neck, of gold, on which was inscribed in Armenian letters: "KING ARSACES TO THE NYSIAN GOD." For the king of Armenia at that time was Arsaces, who, I suppose, when he saw the leopard, dedicated it to Dionysus for the size of the beast. For Dionysus is named Nysian, from Nysa in India, by the Indians and by all the peoples toward the sunrise. This leopard had been for some time subject to a man, and had endured a hand to stroke and caress it; but when spring drove it to frenzy—the season when even leopards are weak before the passions of love—it bounded off to the mountains in longing for the males, just as it was in its adornment, and was caught about the lower Taurus, drawn by the perfume. The Caucasus bounds India and Media, and reaches down to the Red Sea with another arm.

They say too that wild asses are caught in these marshes, and that these beasts have a single horn upon the forehead, with which they fight after the manner of bulls and not without spirit; and that the Indians make a drinking-cup of this horn. For whoever drinks from it that day will fall into no sickness, nor feel pain if wounded; he may pass through fire, and is proof against all the poisons that men drink to do harm. This cup belongs to kings, and to the king alone the hunting of the beast is reserved. Apollonius said that he had seen the creature and admired its nature; and when Damis asked him whether he accepted the story about the cup, he said: "I will accept it, if I learn that the king of these Indians here is immortal. For a man who can offer to me, or to anyone, a draught so free of sickness and so wholesome — why should he not rather pour it out for himself, and drink daily from this horn even to drunkenness? For no one, I imagine, would find fault with him for being drunk on that.

Apollonius said: "I will come; but grant, O Muses, that we may love one another too." His first discourse, then, he delivered to the Ephesians from the steps of the temple, not after the manner of the Socratics, but leading them away from other things and turning their zeal from them, and counselling them to give their minds to philosophy alone, and to fill Ephesus with earnestness rather than with the idleness and arrogance he found there. For they were given over to dancers and devoted to Pyrrhic measures; all was full of flutes, full of effeminate men, full of din. And though the Ephesians turned to him, he did not think fit to overlook these things, but rooted them out and made the multitude ashamed of them.

As for the turnings of the Ocean, I myself saw them among the Celts, of the kind that are reported; and considering on many grounds the cause by which so boundless a sea both advances and is drawn back, I think Apollonius observed how the matter truly stands. For in one of his letters to the Indians he says that the Ocean, driven by winds beneath its surface from many chasms which the earth provides under it and around it, moves outward and again withdraws, whenever the breath sinks back, as in a man's breathing. He confirms this also from those who lie sick at Gadeira: for during the time that the water is at the flood, the souls do not leave those who are dying — which would not happen unless a breath were also advancing upon the land. And what they say is seen of the moon as it is born, grows full, and wanes, this I know of the Ocean, for it makes equal the measures of the moon, diminishing with her and growing full along with her.

For when he came to the borders of the Ethiopians and the Egyptians — they call the place Sycaminus — he met with uncoined gold and linen and ivory and roots and myrrh and spices, all lying unguarded at a parting of the ways. What this means I will explain, for the custom holds even to our own day among us. The Ethiopians bring to market the things which Ethiopia gives, and the Egyptians take all of it up and bring to the same place an Egyptian market of equal worth, buying what they have not with what they have. The people who dwell on the borders of the continents are not yet black, but of one colour with their neighbours, for some are less black than the Ethiopians, others more so than the Egyptians. Apollonius, then, understanding the manner of the market, said: "Our worthy Greeks, unless an obol breed an obol and they raise the price of their wares by selling dear or locking them up, say they cannot live: one pleading a daughter coming of age for marriage, another a son now passing into manhood, another a contribution to a club, another that he is building a house, another that he would be ashamed to be thought a worse man of business than his father. But it would be well if wealth were held in dishonour and equality flourished, and the black iron lay idle, men being of one mind, and all the earth seemed one."

Zeno of Elea, then—he who is held to have been the founder of dialectic—when he was bringing down the tyranny of Nearchus the Mysian, was caught and put to the rack. He kept silence about his own fellow-conspirators, but those who were firmly the tyrant's men he slandered as not being firm, so that some of them died as though on true charges, while he set the affairs of the Mysians free, overthrowing the tyranny by turning it against itself. Plato says that he himself took up the struggle for the freedom of the Sicilians, sharing this design with Dion. Phyton, when he was driven out of Rhegium, took refuge with Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily; but being judged worthy of greater honour than befits an exile, he understood that the tyrant was also in love with Rhegium, and when he wrote of this to the Rhegians he was caught. The tyrant then bound him alive to one of his siege-engines and brought him up to the walls, so that the Rhegians might not strike the engine out of sparing for Phyton; but Phyton shouted to them to strike, for they were the mark of their own freedom. Heracleides and Python, who killed Cotys the Thracian, were both young men, but by their admiration of the discussions of the Academy they became wise and so free men. And who does not know the deeds of Callisthenes of Olynthus? On the same day he both praised and reviled the Macedonians, when they were at the height of their power, and so died with a name for giving offence. Diogenes of Sinope and Crates of Thebes—the one, coming straight from Chaeronea, rebuked Philip on behalf of the Athenians; saying that he was a Heracleides, he destroyed with arguments those who had taken up arms on Philip's behalf; the other, when Alexander said that he would rebuild Thebes for his sake, declared that he had no need of a fatherland that someone, grown strong with arms, might raze again. And many such things might be told; but the argument does not allow length to one who is bound also to contradict these examples—not as though they were not noble, or not held in account by all, but as being less than the deeds

We shall also meet the man as one who held that he would converse rather than run a contest for his life; and this we may infer from what passed before the court. For going forward he asked the clerk by whom he was being led, whither they were going; and when the clerk said that he was leading him to the court, "And before whom," he said, "shall I plead?" "Before your own accuser," he said, "and the emperor will judge." "And for me and the emperor," he said, "who will be judge? For I shall show that he wrongs philosophy." "And what account," he said, "does an emperor make of philosophy, even if he should chance to wrong her?" "But philosophy makes great account of an emperor," he said, "that he may rule fitly." The clerk, praising this—for indeed he was moderately disposed toward Apollonius, as he showed even at the outset—said, "By how much water will you measure out your speech? For this I must know before the trial." "If the trial allows me to say all that it demands," he said, "the Tiber itself would not be measured out in time; but if I am to answer only what I am asked, then the questioner is the measure of the answerer." "You have practised opposite virtues," he said, "professing both brevity and length on the same matters." "Not opposite," he said, "but alike; for he who is master of one would fall short in nothing of the other. And a due proportion compounded of both I would not call a third virtue, but the first virtue of speech; and I count silence in a court a fourth virtue too." "A profitless one, at least," he said, "to yourself and to anyone about to be in danger." "And yet it greatly profited Socrates the Athenian," he said, "when he avoided the indictment." "And how did it profit him, since, because he kept silence, he was put to death?" "He was not put to death," he said; "the Athenians only thought so."

There was a man named Damis, not without wisdom, who once dwelt in ancient Nineveh. This man joined Apollonius in the study of philosophy, and has written an account of his travels, which he says he shared, and of his maxims and discourses, and of all that he said by way of prophecy. And a kinsman of Damis brought the tablets of these memoirs, hitherto unknown, to the knowledge of the empress Julia. Since I belonged to her circle—for she esteemed and welcomed all rhetorical discourse—she commanded me to recast these compositions and to attend to their style; for the writer of Nineveh had told his story clearly, but not gracefully. I came also upon a book by Maximus of Aegae, which had gathered all that Apollonius did at Aegae; and a will too was written by Apollonius, from which one may learn that he became one who exalted philosophy toward the divine. For no heed should be paid to Moeragenes, who composed four books about Apollonius and yet was ignorant of much concerning the man. How I gathered together these scattered materials, and how I took pains to compose them, I have now said. May this work bring honour to the man to whom it is dedicated, and benefit to those who love learning; for they may indeed learn what they do not yet know.

The barbarians tell tales about the mountain, which the Greeks too sing of regarding it: that Prometheus was bound there for his love of mankind, and that a second Heracles—for they do not mean the Theban; he would not have endured this—shot the bird which Prometheus fed with his entrails. Some say he was bound in a cave, which is in fact shown at the foot of the mountain, and Damis says that bonds are fastened to the rocks, the material of which it is not easy to make out; others say he was bound on the summit of the mountain. The summit is double-peaked, and they say that his hands were bound to these peaks, which are no less than a stadium apart, so great is the distance. The bird, the eagle, those who dwell about the Caucasus reckon their enemy, and the nests which the eagles build upon the crags they burn, hurling fire-bearing darts, and they set traps against them, saying that they take vengeance for Prometheus; so far are they mastered by the myth.

Here too they say they met with a woman who was black from the head to the breasts, but from the breasts to the feet all white; and that the others fled from her as from some terror, but that Apollonius took the woman by the hand and understood what she was. For such a woman is consecrated to Aphrodite among the Indians, and a dappled woman is born to the goddess, just as the bull Apis is born to the Egyptians.

His other discourses he held about the groves in the covered walks. Once, when he was discoursing of fellowship and teaching that men should feed one another and be fed by one another, sparrows sat silent upon the trees, but one of them, flying up, cried out, seeming to urge something on the rest; and they, when they heard it, themselves screamed and flew up, led by the one. Apollonius held to his discourse, knowing whither the sparrows flew, but not interpreting it to the multitude. But when all looked up at them, and some foolishly thought it a portent, Apollonius turned aside from his discourse and said: "A boy has slipped while carrying grain in a bowl, and having gathered it up carelessly has gone off, leaving much of it scattered in such-and-such an alley; and this sparrow, who chanced to be by, has come as a herald to the rest of the windfall, and is making them his messmates." Most of the hearers ran off at a run to this place, and Apollonius went through to those who remained the discourse on fellowship he had begun; and when they came back shouting and full of wonder, he said: "You see how the sparrows care for one another and rejoice in fellowship; but we will not have it so. Nay, if we see a man sharing with others, we count him a prodigal and a wanton and the like, and those fed by him we call parasites and flatterers. And what is left for us but to shut ourselves up, like fatted fowl, and gorge ourselves in the dark, until we burst with growing fat?

Day succeeds night and night day; among the Celts as the darkness or the light gradually retires, as it does here, but about Gadeira and the Pillars they are said to fall upon the eyes all at once, like flashes of lightning. They say too that the Isles of the Blest are bounded by the Libyan limit, where it rises toward the uninhabited headland.

Discoursing thus, and making the occasions, as he was wont, his counsellors of what to discuss, he proceeded toward the statue of Memnon; and there led them an Egyptian youth, of whom Damis writes as follows. Timasion was the youth's name; he was just passing out of boyhood and was still strong in the bloom of youth. While he was living soberly, a stepmother in love with him beset him and made his father harsh toward him, contriving nothing of the sort that Phaedra did, but slandering him as effeminate and rejoicing more in lovers than in women. So he left Naucratis — for these things happened there — and lived about Memphis, and had got himself a private boat and acted as skipper on the Nile. Seeing Apollonius sailing up as he himself sailed down, he understood that the crew was of wise men, judging by the cloaks and the books over which they were busy, and he begged to be given a share in the voyage, since he loved wisdom. And Apollonius said, "The young man is sober, gentlemen, and let him be granted what he asks," and he went through the story of the stepmother to those of his companions who were near, in a lowered tone, while the youth was still sailing up to them. When the ships drew together, Timasion crossed over, and after saying something to his own helmsman about the cargo, addressed the men. So Apollonius, bidding him sit down before his eyes, said, "Egyptian youth — for you seem to be one of the natives — tell me what evil or what good you have done, that for the one you may obtain release from me on account of your age, and for the other, being praised, may join in philosophy with me and these men." But seeing Timasion blush and shift the impulse of his mouth toward speaking or not, he pressed his question again and again, as though he had no foreknowledge of him. Taking courage, Timasion said: "O gods, what shall I call myself? For I am not bad, yet whether I ought to be reckoned good I do not know, for not to do wrong is not yet a matter for praise." And Apollonius said, "Well done, young man! You talk to me as if from India, for this is the view of the divine Iarchas too. But say how you came to think this, and from what; for you seem to be one who has guarded against doing some wrong." And when he began to say that his stepmother had set herself upon him, while he had withdrawn from her love, there was an outcry, since Apollonius had foretold it as by a divine power; but Timasion broke in and said, "My good men, what has come over you? For the things said are as far from wonder, I think, as from laughter." And Damis said, "It was something else we wondered at, which you do not yet know. And you, young man, we praise, because you think you have done nothing brilliant." "Do you sacrifice to Aphrodite, young man?" asked Apollonius; and Timasion said, "Yes, by Zeus, every day, for I hold the goddess great in human and divine affairs." So Apollonius, overjoyed, said: "Let us vote, gentlemen, that he be crowned for self-control even above Hippolytus the son of Theseus; for Hippolytus outraged Aphrodite, and perhaps for this reason was not even mastered by the pleasures of love, nor did any love revel about him, but he was of a more rustic and unsoftened lot; whereas this youth, though he says he is subject to the goddess, was nowise moved toward the woman in love, but went away in fear of the goddess herself, if he did not guard against an evil love. And the very thing of being at variance with any one of the gods, as Hippolytus was with Aphrodite, I do not count self-control; for it is more sober to speak well of all the gods, and that too at Athens, where altars are set up even to unknown divinities." So much earnest care did he bestow on Timasion. Yet he called him Hippolytus for the eyes with which he looked upon his stepmother. He seemed too to take care of his body and to have laid hold of gymnastics gracefully.

of Apollonius, even if they appear the finest among others. The deed of the Eleatic, then, and that of the men who slew Cotys, are not yet worth much account; for to enslave Thracians and Getae is easy, but to set them free is folly, since they do not even rejoice in freedom, holding it, I suppose, no disgrace to be slaves. As for Plato—that he fared in no wise wisely in setting Sicily to rights rather than Athens, or that he was fittingly sold when he both failed and made others fail—I do not speak, out of regard for those who hear such things grudgingly. The deeds of the Rhegian against Dionysius were daring, for Dionysius held Sicily insecurely; yet since he would certainly have died at that man's hands, even had he not been struck by the Rhegians, he did nothing wonderful, I think, in choosing rather a death for the freedom of others than one for his own slavery. Callisthenes could not even now escape the appearance of being a base man; for in praising and reviling the same men he either reviled those he thought worthy of praise, or praised those whom he ought to have been seen reviling—and besides, the man who sets himself to abuse good men cannot escape seeming a slanderer, while he who flatters the wicked with praise will himself take upon him the blame for the wrongs they do, since the wicked are made worse by being praised. Diogenes, had he said these things to Philip before Chaeronea, might have kept the man pure of his arms against the Athenians; but coming upon the deeds already done he reproached, yet did not set them right. And Crates might even be charged by a man who loves his city with not having joined Alexander in the counsel he used for rebuilding Thebes. But Apollonius—neither fearing for an endangered fatherland, nor despairing of his life, nor drawn into senseless words, nor on behalf of Mysians or Getae, nor against a man who ruled a single island or no great country, but against him under whom were the sea and the whole earth—against this man, since he tyrannized harshly, set himself in array on behalf of the gain of the ruled. He had used this same purpose against Nero too; though one may regard

Thus was he prepared against all that came from the tyrant. But as he stood before the court, another clerk came up and said, "Tyanean, enter naked." "Are we to bathe, then," he said, "or to plead?" "It is not about your dress," he said, "that this is ordered; but the emperor forbids you to bring in either amulet or book or any written thing at all." "Nor a cane," he said, "against those who foolishly persuade him to such things?" The accuser cried out, "Sire, the sorcerer threatens me with blows; for it was I who persuaded you to this." "Then you," he said, "are the greater sorcerer; for what I have not yet persuaded the emperor of—that I am no sorcerer—you say you have persuaded him that I am." While the accuser was reviling thus, there was present one of the freedmen of Euphrates, who was said to have been sent by Euphrates as a messenger of Apollonius's discourses in Ionia, together with money that was given to the accuser.

Apollonius, then, had for his native city Tyana, a Greek city in the nation of the Cappadocians; his father bore the same name; the family was ancient and traced back to the founders of the city; his wealth surpassed that of the people there, and the country was rich. While his mother was carrying him, an apparition came to her—Proteus, the Egyptian divinity who changes his shape in Homer. She, in no way afraid, asked him what she would bring forth. "Me," he said. "And who are you?" she asked. "Proteus," he answered, "the Egyptian god." Now what manner of being Proteus was in wisdom, why should I explain to those who have heard the poets—how he was of many forms and ever changing and beyond capture, and seemed to know and to foreknow all things? And one must keep Proteus in mind, especially when the story as it goes on shows the man to have foreknown more than Proteus did, and to have risen above many things baffling and impossible, at the very moment when he seemed most caught.

Having passed the Caucasus, they say they saw men four cubits tall, who were already turning black, and others five cubits tall when they had come beyond the river Indus. On the journey as far as this river they found the following things worth recounting. They were travelling in bright moonlight when an apparition of an empusa fell upon them, becoming now one thing, now another, and then nothing at all. But Apollonius understood what it was, and himself reviled the empusa, and ordered those about him to do the same, for this was the remedy against such an assault; and the apparition fled away shrieking, as ghosts do.

From there, they say, they crossed the spur of the Caucasus that stretches down to the Red Sea, and it was thickly overgrown with groves of fragrant trees. The crests of the mountain bear cinnamon, which resembles young vine-shoots, and the goat is the test of this spice; for if a man holds out cinnamon to a goat, it will whimper towards his hand like a dog, and follow him as he goes, pressing its nose against it; and if the goatherd drags it away, it will lament as if torn from the lotus. On the cliffs of the mountain there grow tall frankincense-trees and many other kinds, and the pepper-trees, whose cultivators are the apes. Nor shall I pass over what the pepper-tree resembles, nor the manner of its cultivation, which I will set forth. The pepper-tree resembles the agnus castus of the Greeks in other respects and especially in the cluster of its fruit; but it grows on sheer crags inaccessible to men, where it is said that a community of apes dwells in the recesses of the mountain and in whatever is hollow of it. These apes the Indians count of great worth, since they harvest the pepper for them; and so they keep the lions off them with dogs and weapons. For a lion attacks an ape, when he is sick, for the sake of a remedy — for the flesh of the apes checks his disease — and when he is old, for the sake of food; for being now past their prime for the hunting of deer and boar, they devour the apes, using upon this the strength that is left them. But the men do not look on idly; rather, holding these beasts to be their benefactors, they take up arms against the lions on their behalf. For the way they deal with the pepper-trees is this. The Indians go up to the lower trees, cut off the fruit, and make little threshing-floors about the trees, into which they heap the pepper as though casting it away — as though it were some worthless thing of no concern to men. The apes, watching this from above and from their inaccessible heights, when night comes imitate the work of the Indians: they strip off the clusters from the trees and carry them, casting them down, into the floors; and at daybreak the Indians take up heaps of the spice without having toiled at all, but at their ease and asleep.

When a plague was creeping upon Ephesus, but the disease had not yet swollen up, Apollonius perceived its onset, and perceiving it he foretold it often in his discourses, crying, "O earth, remain as you are," and uttering such things with a threat: "Save these, and you shall not pass this way here." But they paid no heed, and thought such things mere marvel-mongering, the more so as he went about all the temples and seemed to turn it aside and pray it away. And since they were senseless in their suffering, he thought he need no longer help them, but went round the rest of Ionia, setting right the affairs of each people, and ever speaking something for the safety of those present.

Gadeira lies at the very limit of Europe, and its people are extravagant in matters of religion. They have set up an altar to Old Age, and they alone of men sing a paean to Death; and there are altars there to Poverty and to Art, and to the Egyptian Heracles, and others to the Theban. For the one, they say, drove his cattle to the neighbouring Erytheia, when he took Geryon and his cattle; while the other by his wisdom measured out the whole earth to its limit. Moreover they say that the people of Gadeira are Greek and are educated in our own manner. They cherish the Athenians above all the Greeks, and sacrifice to Menestheus the Athenian; and admiring Themistocles, the hero of the sea-fight, for his wisdom and his courage, they have set up a bronze statue of him deep in thought and, as it were, declaring an oracle.

Under this guide they say they came to the precinct of Memnon. Concerning Memnon Damis writes as follows. He was the son of Dawn, and died not at Troy, since he never came to Troy, but ended his life in Ethiopia, having reigned over the Ethiopians for five generations. And they, being the longest-lived of men, lament Memnon as one cut off very young, and weep over him all that men weep over the untimely dead. The place in which the statue stands resembles, they say, an ancient market-place, such as are left, in cities once inhabited, of the broken stumps of columns and the traces of walls and seats and door-posts and images of Hermes, some destroyed by hands, some by time. The statue is turned toward the sunbeam, beardless still, of black stone, with both feet set together after the manner of the statuary in the time of Daedalus, and the hands pressed straight upon the seat; for it is seated as if in the act of rising up. This posture, and the expression of the eyes, and all that they sing of the mouth as about to speak, they say wins less wonder at other times, for it does not yet appear to be alive; but when the beam strikes the statue — and this happens at the rising of the sun — they could not hold back their amazement: for the moment the beam came upon its mouth it spoke; and its eyes seemed to stand bright toward the light, as the eyes of men do who love the sun. Then they understood, they say, that it seems to rise up before the Sun, like those who do honour to the higher power standing upright. So having sacrificed to the Ethiopian Sun and to Memnon of the Dawn — for so the priests instructed, naming the one from burning and warming, the other from his mother — they went on by camels to the dwellings of the Naked Sages.

those acts as skirmishings, since he did not come to close grips, but by strengthening Vindex and by terrifying Tigellinus made the tyranny more rotten; and here some boastful argument springs up, that there was nothing noble in attacking a Nero who lived the life of some lyre-girl or flute-girl. But of Domitian what will they say? His body was strong; pleasures from instruments and from clashing sounds, which wear away the spirited part, he rejected, but the griefs of others, and whatever a man might lament, he drew toward his own delight. Mistrust he called the people's safeguard against tyrants, and the tyrant's against all men; and night he held it fitting for a king to make an end of all business and a beginning of murders—whence the Senate was shorn of its most distinguished members, and philosophy so cowered that some, casting off their dress, fled away into the western land of the Celts, others into the deserts of Libya and Scythia, and some were carried off into arguments that counselled wrongdoing. But he—just as Sophocles has made Teiresias speak of himself to Oedipus, "For I do not live as a slave to you, but to Loxias"—having so made wisdom his mistress, was free of Domitian's current, prophesying to himself the words of Teiresias and Sophocles, fearing nothing of his own, but pitying those whom others were destroying. Hence he gathered against the tyrant such youth as the Senate held, and such understanding as was seen in some of them, going about among the nations and discoursing philosophy to the governors, that the strength of tyrants was not immortal, and that by the very seeming terrible they are the more easily caught. He related to them also the Attic Panathenaea, in which Harmodius and Aristogeiton are sung, and the deed from Phyle, which overthrew thirty tyrants at once; and he set forth the ancestral history of the Romans themselves, how they too, being of old a free people, used to thrust out tyrannies with arms.

Such was the skirmishing before the trial; and these were the things in it. The court had been adorned as for a gathering to hear a festal oration; and all the men of mark shared in it, the emperor making it a contest to convict him before as many as possible upon the charge concerning the men. But Apollonius so far overlooked the emperor as not even to glance at him; and when the accuser reproached him with this contempt and bade him look toward the god of all men, Apollonius lifted his eyes to the roof, showing that he was looking toward Zeus, and holding the man who was impiously flattered to be baser than the flatterer. The accuser cried out such things as these: "Measure now, sire, the water; for if you allow him length of speech, he will choke us. And I have here a book in which the charges are set down on which he must speak; let him defend himself against them one by one."

He is said to have been born in a meadow, beside which a temple has now been built to him. And let no one be ignorant of the manner of his birth. As his mother neared the hour of her delivery, a dream came to her, bidding her walk into the meadow and gather flowers. And when she came, her maids gave their attention to the flowers, scattered over the meadow, while she herself was carried off to sleep, lying down upon the grass. Swans, then, that the meadow fed, formed a chorus around her as she slept, and raising their wings, as is their way, they all sang out together—for there was a breath of the west wind too in the meadow—and she started up at the song and gave birth; for any shock is enough to bring on a birth, even before its time. The people of the country say that at the very moment he was born a thunderbolt, which seemed about to fall to earth, rose up into the upper air and vanished aloft; whereby the gods, I think, were revealing and foreshowing how this man would be conspicuous and above all things on earth, near to the gods, and all that he became.

As they crossed a summit of the mountain and walked along it, since it was steep, Apollonius asked Damis thus: "Tell me," he said, "where were we yesterday?" "In the plain," he said. "And today, Damis, where are we?" "In the Caucasus," he said, "unless I have forgotten myself." "When, then, were you the more below?" he asked again. And he said: "This is not even worth asking; for yesterday we were travelling through the hollow of the earth, but today we are near to heaven." "Do you think, then, Damis," he said, "that yesterday's journey was below, and today's above?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "unless I am mad." "In what, then, do you suppose the roads differ from one another, or what more do you have today than yesterday?" "Because yesterday," he said, "I walked where many do, but today where few do." "Why, Damis," he said, "is it not possible, by turning aside from the highroads in a city, to walk among few men?" "I did not say that," he said, "but that yesterday we were carried through villages and men, while today we ascend some untrodden and divine region; for you hear from the guide that the barbarians make it the dwelling of the gods"; and at the same time he looked up to the summit of the mountain. But Apollonius, leading him back to what he had asked at first, said: "Can you say, then, Damis, what you have understood of the divine by walking near to heaven?" "Nothing," he said. "And yet you ought," he said, "standing upon so great and divine an engine, to bring forth now clearer opinions about heaven and about the sun and the moon, which perhaps you think you could touch with a rod, standing so close to this heaven." "What I knew yesterday about the divine," he said, "I know today also, and no other opinion about it has yet fallen upon me." "So then, Damis," he said, "you happen to be below still, and have gained nothing from the height, and you are as far from heaven as you were yesterday. And I had good reason to ask you what I did at the beginning; for you thought you were being asked ridiculous questions." "But indeed," he said, "I thought I would come down wiser, Apollonius, having heard that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae observed the things in heaven from Mimas in Ionia, and Thales of Miletus from the neighbouring Mycale; and some are said to have used Pangaeus as an observatory, and others Athos. But I, having gone up to a greater height than these, shall come down no wiser than myself." "Nor did they," he said; "for such lookout-points show heaven bluer and the stars larger and the sun rising out of night—things already plain even to shepherds and goatherds; but in what way the divine cares for the human race, and how it rejoices to be served by it, and what virtue is, and what justice and temperance, neither Athos will reveal to those who climb it, nor the Olympus admired by the poets, unless the soul beholds these things—the soul which, if it lay hold of them pure and undefiled, would, I should say, dart up far higher than this Caucasus."

When they had passed over the mountain, they say they saw a smooth plain cut up with trenches full of water. Some of these ran crosswise, others straight, drawn off from the river Ganges; and they served both as boundaries of the land and as channels for the plains, whenever the earth was thirsty. They say that this land is the best in India and the largest of all the territories there, fifteen days' journey in length to the Ganges, and eighteen from the sea to the mountain of the apes, along which it lies. The whole country is level, black, and fruitful of all things. For in it one may see ears of grain standing as tall as reeds, and beans three times the size of the Egyptian, with sesame and millet of vast growth. Here too they say grows the coconut, many of which are dedicated in the temples in these parts as a marvel. The vines grow small, like those of the Lydians and Maeonians, but their wine is drinkable and fragrant from the very vintage. Here too they say they met a tree resembling the laurel, on which grows a calyx like a great pomegranate, and within the calyx is set an apple, dark blue like the cup of the hyacinth, and the sweetest of all the fruits the seasons bring.

As he came to Smyrna, the Ionians met him, for they happened to be sacrificing at the Panionia; and reading too an Ionian decree in which they begged him to share their assembly, and lighting on a name least Ionian — for one Lucullus was inscribed at the head of the resolution — he sent a letter to their council making a rebuke about this barbarism; for he found Fabricius too and other such names among those who had voted. How vigorously he rebuked them, the letter about this shows.

They say too that they saw there trees of a kind found nowhere else on earth, called the trees of Geryon. There are two of them, and they grow from the mound which stands over Geryon, of a form between the pine and the fir, but of a different kind, and they drip with blood, just as the poplar of the Heliades drips with gold. The island on which the temple stands is just the size of the temple, and there is nothing rocky about it, but it is like a smoothed starting-line. In the temple both the Heracleses are honoured, they say, but there are no images of them; only altars — two of bronze and without inscription for the Egyptian, and one of stone for the Theban — on which they say are carved the hydras and the mares of Diomedes and the twelve labours of Heracles. The golden olive of Pygmalion is also dedicated there in the Heracleion, worthy of wonder, they say, both for its branch, which it resembles, but to be wondered at still more for its fruit, for it teems with emerald. They say too that the golden belt of Teucer son of Telamon is shown there; but how he came to sail to the Ocean, or for what purpose, neither does Damis himself say he could make out, nor that he heard it from them. As for the pillars in the temple, they are made of gold and silver fused into a single colour, more than a cubit in height and of square workmanship, like anvils; and their tops are inscribed with letters neither Egyptian nor Indian, nor of any kind one could interpret. So Apollonius, since the priests told him nothing, said: "The Egyptian Heracles does not allow me to keep silent about what I know. These pillars are the bonds of earth and Ocean, and he inscribed them in the house of the Fates, that no strife might arise among the elements, nor that they should dishonour the friendship which they have toward one another."

Meeting a man dressed in the fashion of the Memphites, and rather wandering than walking with purpose, those about Damis asked who he was and why he roamed; and Timasion said: "Ask me, not him, for he would not tell you his own suffering, out of shame at the misfortune he is under; but I, since I know the man and pity him, will tell all about him. He killed a Memphite unwillingly; and the laws of Memphis bid him who flees on a charge of involuntary homicide — and he must flee — be with the Naked Sages, and when he has washed himself of the blood, go back to his home now pure, after first going to the tomb of the slain man and slaughtering there something of no great size. In the time before he meets the Naked Sages he must wander about these borders, until they take pity on him as a suppliant." So Apollonius asked Timasion how the Naked Sages were minded toward that fugitive, and he said, "I do not know; for this is the seventh month he has been a suppliant here, and there is yet no release." "You do not speak of wise men," said Apollonius, "if they do not purify him, nor know that Philiscus, whom this man killed, traced his descent to Thamus the Egyptian, who once ravaged the country of the Naked Sages." So Timasion, marvelling, said, "How do you mean?" "As it is, my young man," he said, "and as it was done. For Thamus, once plotting revolution against the Memphites, was checked and held back by the Naked Sages; but failing in his attempt, he laid waste all the land which these men cultivate, for he was strong as a brigand about Memphis. Of him I see Philiscus, whom this man killed, to be the thirteenth descendant, and plainly accursed to those whose land Thamus then ravaged. And where is the wisdom — if this man, whom one ought to crown even had he killed with forethought, they do not purify for an involuntary homicide, and one done on their own behalf?" The youth, then, struck with amazement, said, "Stranger, who are you?" And Apollonius said, "He whom you would find among the Naked Sages. But since it is not yet holy for me to address the man who is in blood, bid him take heart, young man, as one who will at once be pure, if he goes where I am lodging." And when he came, Apollonius performed all that Empedocles and Pythagoras hold lawful for purifications, and bade him go to his home as now pure of the charge.

When a tragic actor came to Ephesus to perform the drama of Ino, and the governor of Asia was listening—a man who, though young, was conspicuous among those of consular rank, yet held over-timid views on these matters—the actor was already reaching the iambic lines in which Euripides says that tyrants, who have grown great over a long time, are caught by small means; and Apollonius leapt up and cried: "But this coward understands neither Euripides nor me."

The emperor, praising this as the best of counsel, ordered the man to make his defence according to the informer's plan; and passing over the other charges as not worthy to bring a man into argument, he questioned him about four, which he thought hard and difficult to answer, thus: "What was it, Apollonius, that you learned, that you do not wear the same dress as all men, but one peculiar and special?" "Because," he said, "the earth that nourishes me also clothes me, and I do not trouble the wretched animals." Again he asked, "On what account do men name you a god?" "Because," he said, "every man held good is honoured with the title of god." (Whence this argument was reasoned out by the man, I have shown in the discourses about the Indians.) Third he asked about the plague at Ephesus: "For from what source," he said, "or by reckoning what did you foretell to the Ephesians that they would fall sick?" "By using, sire," he said, "a lighter diet, I was the first to perceive the danger; and if you wish, I will tell the causes of plagues too." But the emperor, fearing, I think, lest he should ascribe to such sicknesses his own injustice and impure marriages and the things he did against reason, said, "I have no need of such an answer." But when he brought the fourth question to bear upon the men, he did not set out at once, but, after a long pause, and much reflection, and like one dizzy, he asked not according to the expectation of all; for they thought that, leaping out of his pretence, he would not even spare to name the men, and would cry out cruel things about the sacrifice. But he did not so; rather, slinking up to the question, "Tell me," he said, "having gone forth from the house on such a day and journeyed into the country, for whom did you sacrifice the boy?" And Apollonius, as though chiding a stripling, said, "Speak fair words; for if I went forth from the house, I was in the country; and if so, I also sacrificed; and if I sacrificed, I also ate. But let those of credit say these things." When the man had said this, and a praise was raised greater than the imperial court allowed, the emperor, thinking that those present bore witness with him, and being affected by the answers, since they were vigorous and full of sense, said, "I release you from the charges; but you will wait until we are together in private." But Apollonius, recovering himself, said, "I thank you, sire; but through these accursed men the cities have perished, the islands are full of exiles, the mainland of lamentation, the armies of cowardice, the Senate of suspicion. Give me too a place, if you will; if not, send one to take my body, for my soul you cannot; nay, you will not even take my body, for you shall not kill me, since I am not fated to die." And saying this he vanished from the court, ordering well the present moment, with regard to matters about which the tyrant plainly meant to question him not simply, but at leisure and out of his abundance—for he prided himself, I suppose, on not having killed him—and foreseeing how not to be drawn into such things. And this he held it best to attain, if he were not unknown in his nature, but known to be such as could never be caught against his will. For the fear about the men was now well with him; for those concerning whom the tyrant did not even set out to ask anything, how could he plausibly have killed them on charges not credited in the court? Such I have found to be the things of the trial.

There is near Tyana a water of Zeus the God of Oaths, as they call it—they name it Asbamaean—of which a spring rises up cold, and yet it bubbles like a heated cauldron. To those who keep their oaths this water is kind and sweet, but on those who swear falsely justice follows hard upon their heels; for it strikes their eyes and hands and feet, and they are seized with dropsy and wasting, and they cannot even depart, but are held there on the spot and lament beside the water, confessing the oaths they have broken. Now the people of the country say that Apollonius was the son of Zeus, but the man himself calls himself the son of Apollonius.

Having crossed the mountain, they came upon men already riding on elephants. These are men midway between the Caucasus and the river Cophen, leading a savage life, and they are horsemen of this herd; and some were leading camels, which the Indians use for racing, and which travel a thousand stadia in a day without ever bending a knee. One of the Indians, then, riding up on such a camel, asked the guide where they were going; and when he heard the purpose of the journey, he reported it to the nomads, who shouted as though pleased, and bade them come near, and when they had come, offered them wine, which they contrive from the date-palms, and honey from the same plant, and slices of lions and leopards, whose skins too were freshly flayed. These the travellers received, all but the meat, and went on toward the dawn.

As they came down the mountain, they say they fell in with a hunt of dragons, of which I must speak. For it would be quite absurd, when much has been said about the hare and how it is caught and may be caught, by those who give their minds to such things, that we should pass over an account of a noble and divine hunt, which was not omitted even by the man for whose sake I have written these things. For all the land of India is girdled with dragons of measureless length; the marshes are full of them, the mountains are full of them, and no hill is without one. Those of the marshes are sluggish and thirty cubits long, and have no upraised crest, but are like the female dragons, sufficiently black on the back and less scaly than the rest. And Homer has touched on these creatures more wisely than the common run of poets; for he called the dragon that dwelt at Aulis beside the spring "blood-red on the back," whereas the other poets say that the one of like kind in the grove of Nemea had a crest also, which we should not find among the marsh-dragons.

Coming forward another day among the Ionians, he asked, "What is this mixing-bowl?" And they said, "The Panionian." So drawing from it and pouring a libation, he said: "O gods, leaders of the Ionians, grant to this fair colony to use the sea in safety, and that no evil revel come upon the land from it, nor Aegaeon the earth-shaker ever shake the cities." Such things he prophesied, foreseeing, I think, what befell in later times about Smyrna and Miletus and Chios and Samos and many of the Ionian cities.

They say too that he sailed up the river Baetis, which best of all shows the nature of the Ocean. For when the sea is at the flood, the river runs back toward its sources, the breath, it seems, driving it back from the sea. The land of Baetica, after which this river is named, they say is the best of all countries, for it is well provided with cities and pastures, and the river is led through to all the towns; it is full of every kind of husbandry and of seasons such as the autumnal and mystic seasons of Attica.

Setting out thence at sunrise, they came before noon to the place of meditation of the Naked Sages. These Naked Sages, they say, dwell upon a hill of moderate height, a little from the bank of the Nile; in wisdom they fall short of the Indians more than they surpass the Egyptians, and they are clad naked, in the same way as those who take the sun at Athens. There are a few trees in the district, and a grove not large, into which they gather for common business; their sanctuaries are not set in one place, as those of the Indians, but one is here and another there over the hill, accounted worthy of reverence, as the Egyptian accounts say. They worship the Nile above all, for they hold this river to be earth and water. They themselves have no need of hut or house, living in the open air and under the very sky; but for the strangers they had built a portico large enough, of the same length as those of the Eleans, under which the athlete awaits the noonday proclamation.

When word came, moreover, that Domitian had made a brilliant purification of the Hearth of the Romans, having killed three of the Vestals on the charge of breaking the girdle and of not keeping themselves pure of marriage—they who ought chastely to have served the Trojan Athena and the fire there—he said: "Would that you too, O Sun, might be purified of the unjust murders of which the whole world is now full." And he did not say this in private, like cowards, but in the throng and to all men he proclaimed it and made his prayer.

Since a speech too was composed by him, as for one who would deliver his defence by the water-clock, but the tyrant cut him short into the questions I have related, let the speech also be recorded. For I am not unaware that those who praise the buffoonish styles will slander it, as being less chastened than they themselves say it should be, and as overdoing it both in words and in sentiments; yet, as I reflect upon the man, it does not seem to me that the wise man would soundly play his own character if he practised balanced clauses and antitheses, and made his tongue clatter like a castanet. For such things suit rhetoricians, and not even they need them; for cleverness in courts, if open, may slander a man as one plotting against the jurors, but if hidden, may go off victorious; for to escape the notice of the judges that one is clever is the truer cleverness. But a wise man making his defence—for the wise man will not accuse those he is strong enough to reprove—needs a character other than that of the men of the courts; and a speech composed indeed, but not seeming so; and let it be somewhat solemn, not far from the bearing of one who overlooks his peril; and let pity be absent from the speaker—for he who will not consent even to entreat, what could he say toward pity? Such will the speech seem to those who hear me and the man not softly; for it was composed by him thus:

As he advanced to the age for letters, he showed strength of memory and force of application; his speech was Attic, nor was his accent corrupted by the dialect of the nation; and all eyes were turned upon him, for he was conspicuous in beauty. When he was fourteen, his father took him to Tarsus, to Euthydemus from Phoenicia. Now Euthydemus was a good rhetorician and undertook his education; but the boy, while he kept to his teacher, thought the temper of the city strange and unfavourable for the study of philosophy. For nowhere do men cling more to luxury; mockers and insolent men are they all, and the people of Tarsus give more thought to fine linen than to wisdom; and the river Cydnus flows through the city, beside which they sit like waterfowl. Hence the words "Cease being drunk on your water" are spoken by Apollonius to them in a letter. So he removed his teacher, having asked his father's leave, to Aegae nearby, where there was quiet suited to one who would philosophize, and pursuits more fitting for a young man, and a temple of Asclepius, and Asclepius himself manifest to men. There the followers of Plato and of Chrysippus and the men of the Peripatos joined him in the study of philosophy, and he gave ear also to the doctrines of Epicurus, for he did not despise these either; but the doctrines of Pythagoras he grasped with a certain ineffable wisdom. For his teacher in the doctrines of Pythagoras was not very earnest, nor did he practise philosophy with energy, being a slave to his belly and to sexual pleasure, and modelled upon Epicurus. This was Euxenus of Heraclea in Pontus, who knew the opinions of Pythagoras as birds know what they learn from men; for the "Good morning" and "Fare well" and "Zeus be gracious" and the like the birds pronounce without knowing what they say, and without any goodwill toward men, but having their tongues merely trained. But Apollonius, like young eagles which while their wings are still soft fly beside their parents, being trained by them in flight, but when they are able to soar, fly above their parents—especially if they perceive them to be gluttonous and flying near the ground for the sake of carrion—so too Apollonius, while still a boy, attended Euxenus and was led by him along the path of discourse; but when he reached his sixteenth year, he set out upon the life of Pythagoras, having been winged toward it by some higher power. Yet he did not cease to love Euxenus, but having asked of his father a country house for him, in which there were gentle gardens and springs, he said: "Live in your own way, but I shall live the way of Pythagoras."

As they were taking their morning meal beside a spring of water, Damis, pouring out some of the wine from the Indians, said: "Here is to you, Apollonius, in the name of Zeus the Saviour, for you drink but seldom. For you will not, I suppose, refuse this too, as you do that from the vines"; and at the same time he poured a libation, since he had mentioned Zeus. Apollonius, laughing, said: "Do we not also abstain from money, Damis?" "By Zeus," he said, "as you have shown in many places." "Then," he said, "shall we abstain from a gold or silver drachma, and not be overcome by such coinage, although we see not private men only but kings gaping after it, yet if someone gives us bronze for silver, or gilt and debased metal, shall we take it, since it is not that for which the many long? And indeed there is also among the Indians coinage of orichalc and black bronze, with which, I suppose, all who come to the dwellings of the Indians must buy everything. What then? If the good nomads had offered us money, would you, Damis, seeing me refuse, have admonished me and taught me that money is that which the Romans stamp, or the king of the Medes, while this is some other stuff dressed up by the Indians? And if you had persuaded me of this, what would you have thought me? A counterfeit, surely, and one who had thrown away philosophy more shamefully than worthless soldiers throw away their shields. And yet, when a shield is thrown away, another could be got for the man who threw it, none worse than the first, as Archilochus thinks; but how is philosophy to be recovered by one who has dishonoured and cast it away? And now Dionysus would forgive a man overcome by no wine; but if I should choose the date-wine before the wine of the grape, he will be displeased, I know well, and will say his own gift has been outraged. We are not far from the god, for you hear from the guide that the mountain Nysa is near, on which Dionysus does many wonderful things, I suppose. And indeed drunkenness, Damis, comes upon men not from grapes alone, but the date-wine too maddens them in like manner; at any rate we have already met many of the Indians held by this wine, some of whom dance till they fall, others sing while they nod off, like our own people leaving a drinking-party by night and out of season. That you too think this drink a wine you show, by pouring a libation of it to Zeus and praying over it all that one prays over wine. And I have said these things to you, Damis, on my own behalf; for I would not lead you away from drinking, nor these attendants, and I would even allow you to eat meat; for to abstain from these things I see leads to nothing for you, but for me to what I have agreed upon for philosophy from my boyhood." Damis and his company accepted this argument and were glad to feast well, thinking they would travel the more easily if they lived more plentifully.

But those that haunt the foothills and the ridges go down into the plains to hunt, and they surpass the marsh-dragons in every way; for they grow to a greater length and move swifter than the swiftest rivers, and nothing escapes them. These have a crest also, moderate while they are young, but growing and rising high as they reach their full size, when they become red and saw-backed. These too grow beards, and lift their necks aloft, and their scales glitter like silver, while the pupils of their eyes are a fiery stone; and their strength, they say, is irresistible for many hidden things. The plain-dragon becomes a prize to the hunters whenever it draws down one of the elephants; for this destroys both beasts together. And to those who take dragons there come as gain the eyes, the skin, and the teeth. In other respects these teeth are like those of the largest swine, but slenderer and twisted, and unworn at the point, like the teeth of great fishes.

Seeing the Smyrnaeans earnest about all kinds of discourse, he strengthened them and made them more earnest, and bade them take pride in themselves rather than in the beauty of their city; for though it was the fairest of cities under the sun, and made the sea its own, and held the springs of the west wind, yet it was sweeter for it to be crowned with men than with porticoes and paintings and gold more than is needed. For buildings, he said, remain in the same place and are nowhere seen but in that part of the earth where they are; but good men are seen everywhere and speak everywhere, and make the city from which they spring as great as the land they can travel over. He said that cities so fair were like the statue of Zeus wrought by Pheidias at Olympia, for it sits — so it seemed good to the craftsman — but that men who come to all places are in nothing unlike the Homeric Zeus, whom Homer wrought in many forms, more wonderfully put together than the ivory one; for the one is seen on earth, but the other is conceived in heaven in all its parts.

Damis says that there were many discussions between him and Apollonius concerning what they met with there, but that the following are worth recording. As they were once sitting in the Heracleion, Menippus laughed aloud — for he had been reminded of Nero — and said: "What are we to make of the noble fellow? In which of the games has he been crowned, and do not the best of the Greeks resort to the festivals with their whole heart in laughter?" Apollonius said: "As I heard from Telesinus, the worthy Nero is afraid of the whips of the Eleans. For when his flatterers urged him to win the Olympia and to have Rome proclaimed, he said, 'If only the Eleans do not begrudge it, for they are said to use the whip and to think themselves above me'; and many other things still more foolish than these he uttered. As for me, I say that Nero will win at Olympia — for who is so bold as to set himself against him? — but that he will not win the Olympia, since they are not even held at the right season. For though the Olympia belonged of ancestral right to last year, Nero ordered the Eleans to postpone them to the time of his own visit, that they might sacrifice to him rather than to Zeus. He has proclaimed a tragedy and a citharody for men who have neither theatre nor stage for such things, but only a natural stadium and everything in the open; and he wins prizes for things that ought to be hidden away. Having thrown off the garb of Augustus and of Julius, he now reclothes himself in that of Amoebeus and Terpnus — what will you say to that? And while he perfects the parts of Creon and Oedipus so exactly that he fears to make some slip about a door or a robe or a sceptre, yet of his own self and of the Romans he falls so far away that, instead of making laws, he sings songs, and goes round begging outside the doors within which a king ought to sit and transact business on behalf of land and sea. There are many tragic heroes, Menippus, among whom Nero enrols himself. And what then? If one of them, after playing Oenomaus or Cresphontes, should leave the theatre so full of his mask that he wished to rule over others and thought himself a tyrant, what would you call such a man? Would he not need hellebore and a draught of the drug that purges the wits? But if the very man who holds the throne brings his own affairs round to the level of tragic actors and stage-artists, softening his voice and fearing the Elean or the Delphian judge — or not fearing him, but acting his own art so badly that he does not think he will be whipped by those whom he is appointed to rule — what will you say of the wretched men who live under such a piece of filth? And whom, Menippus, do you think the Greeks the worse off for: Xerxes burning their cities, or Nero singing? For if you would consider the market they bring to his songs, and how they are driven out of their houses, and how they are not allowed to keep a single article of value, whether vessel or slave; and how grievously they suffer in respect of their wives and children, while Nero culls from every house the pleasures that are spoken of with shame; and how many lawsuits will spring up — leave the others aside and consider those concerning his theatres and songs: 'You did not come to hear Nero,' or, 'You were present, but listened carelessly; you laughed, you did not applaud, you did not sacrifice for the sake of his voice, that it might go the brighter to Pytho' — many a spectator's Iliad of woes will you think there is among the Greeks. As for the cutting of the Isthmus, whether it will be cut or not — and it is being cut now, they say — I learned long ago, the god having revealed it." Then Damis broke in and said: "But to me, Apollonius, this work of the cutting seems to outdo all that Nero has done, for the conception, you see, is a great one." "It seems so to me too, Damis," he said, "but its incompleteness disgraces him, as one who sings without finishing and digs without finishing. When I read the deeds of Xerxes I praise the man, not because he bridged the Hellespont, but because he crossed it; whereas Nero I see neither sailing through the Isthmus nor reaching the end of his digging; and I think too that he will withdraw from Greece full of fear — unless the truth has perished."

Here Damis records a deed of Euphrates, which let us think not childish, but less honourable than befits philosophy. For since he often heard Apollonius wishing to match Indian wisdom against Egyptian, he sent to the Naked Sages Thrasybulus of Naucratis to slander the man. He said that he came for their company, but that the Tyanean too would come; and that this would give them no small contest, since he thought himself above the wise men of the Indians, whom he extolled in every discourse, and had got together countless refutations against them; and that he yielded nothing either to sun or sky or earth, for he himself moved and bore and rearranged these things wherever he wished.

When Domitian, having killed Sabinus, one of his own kinsmen, was taking Julia to wife—Julia being the wife of the man slain, and Domitian's niece, one of the daughters of Titus—Ephesus was sacrificing for the marriage; and Apollonius, standing over the rites, said: "O night of the Danaids of old, how singular you were!" And in Rome itself things were brought about for him in this fashion.

The contest is for great things, both for you, sire, and for me; for you are in danger over things in which no autocrat should ever be—if you shall seem to have slandered philosophy by no just trial—and I over things in which not even Socrates ever was at Athens, whom those who drew up the indictment held to deem the divinities new, but neither called nor thought a daemon. Since, then, the danger has come so hard upon each of us, I will not shrink from counselling you too in whatever I have persuaded myself of. For when the accuser set us into this contest, there came over the many an untrue opinion about me and about you. For they thought that you, taking anger as your counsellor in the hearing, would even kill me—whatever 'to kill' may be—and that I would remove myself from the court by whatever ways there are of escaping; and there were, sire, ten thousand of them. But hearing this, I did not come to a prejudgement, nor did I condemn your hearing as not holding the straight course; rather, agreeing with the laws, I stand under the argument. Of this I become a counsellor to you too; for it is just not to prejudge, nor to sit persuaded that I have done you some evil; nor, while concerning the Armenian and the Babylonian and all who rule there—men who have horse in plenty and every kind of archery and a golden land and a throng of men, as I know—you would laugh to hear that you would suffer anything from them which should take this rule from you—to believe of a wise and naked man that he has a weapon against the Roman autocrat, and to accept this from an Egyptian informer saying things which you never heard even from Athena, whom you say foresees for you; unless, by Zeus, flattery and false accusation have now so increased among these accursed men, that they say the gods are fit counsellors to you in small things—such as ophthalmias, and not running a fever, and not having some swelling of the inwards—touching you and tending you like physicians wherever you are ill, but in the danger to your rule and your person they neither counsel whom you must guard against, nor teach what weapon there will be for you against them when they come; rather, the informers are to you the aegis of Athena and the hand of Zeus, professing to know about you what not even the gods know, watching for you while you wake and sleeping for you—if indeed these men sleep—pouring evils upon evils, as the saying is, and forever composing these Iliads. And as for their keeping horses, and being wheeled out into the marketplace on chariots of white horses, and their gluttony in silver and gold, and the favourites bought for two and three myriads, and their adultery while they go unnoticed, and their marrying the women they have adulterously taken whenever they are caught with them, and those who applaud them for their fine victories, whenever a philosopher or a consul, doing no wrong, is caught by these men and destroyed by you—let it be granted to the luxury of the accursed, and to there being for them no longer any fear of laws or of eyes.
