But to think so far above men as to wish to foreknow what is the gods'—this I neither praise, and hearing it I dread; and if you should accept it, they will perhaps write against you too as slandering the opinion about the divine; for there is hope that such indictments will be composed against you as well, when none is left for the informers. And I understand that I rebuke rather than defend; but let this be said by me on behalf of the laws, which, if you do not hold to be your rulers, you will not rule. Who, then, will be my advocate as I plead? For if I should call upon Zeus, under whom I know I have lived, they will say that I practise sorcery and bring heaven down to earth. Let us discourse, then, about this with a man whom the many say is dead, but I deny it; and this man is your father, to whom I am worth as much as he is to you; for he made you, but by me he was made. He, sire, will be my helper in the defence, knowing my affairs far better than you. For he came to Egypt when he was not yet autocrat, to sacrifice to the gods in Egypt and to confer with me about the rule; and meeting me with my hair long and dressed as I am, he asked not a single thing about my appearance, holding all in me to be well; and confessing that he had come for my sake, he went off praising me, having said what he would say to no other and heard what he would hear from no other. And the resolve with which he used to grasp at rule was strengthened in him above all by me, having now been shifted by others not unfit, yet not so as to please you; for those who persuaded him not to rule were, I suppose, also taking from you the holding of this after him; but when I counselled him not to think himself unworthy of a rule that came knocking at his door, and to make you its heirs, he said his judgement was well, and was himself raised up great and raised you up. And if he had thought me a sorcerer, he would not have joined me in fellowship of his cares; for he did not come and discourse such things as, "Compel the Fates, or Zeus, to declare me tyrant," or "work me portents in the sky, showing the sun rising from the west and setting where it begins." For he would not have thought me fit to rule, either holding me capable of such things, or hunting by tricks a rule that ought to be won by virtues. And besides, I discoursed with him publicly, in a temple; but the meetings of sorcerers shun the temples of the gods, for these are hateful to those about the art; and putting forward night and all that is lightless as their cover, they do not allow the foolish even to have eyes or ears. He discoursed with me in private too, yet Euphrates and Dion were present all the same—the one most hostile to me, the other most familiar; for may I never cease to write Dion among my friends. Who, then, among wise men, or those who lay claim to wisdom, would come to the arguments of sorcerers? And who would not equally guard against appearing base both among friends and among enemies? And the arguments were opposed to sorcerers; for you, perhaps, hold that your father, longing for kingship, trusted to sorcerers rather than to himself, and sought from me a constraint upon the gods to attain it; but he thought he had it even before he came to Egypt, and afterward discoursed with me of greater things—of laws and of just wealth, and how the gods are to be served, and what goods come from them to those who rule by the laws; which he longed to learn. To all of which the sorcerers are a thing opposed; for if these things have force, there will be no such art. And it befits, sire, to have considered this too: of all the arts among men, each does one thing, but all for money's sake—some for small, some for great, some for what they will be fed by; and not the mechanical only, but the others too are alike wise and half-wise, except true philosophy. I call wise poetry, music, astronomy, the sophists, and those of the orators who are not of the marketplace; and half-wise painting, sculpture, statuary, pilots, husbandmen, if they follow the seasons; for these arts too fall not far short of wisdom. But there is a sort, sire, of false-wise and beggars—do not take it for divination, for that is worth much, if it tell true, though whether it is an art I do not yet know—but I say the sorcerers are false-wise; for that things which are not, are, and that things which are, are disbelieved—all this I ascribe to the opinion of the deceived, for the cleverness of the art lies upon the folly of those deceived and sacrificing; and the art is wholly money-loving, for what they trick out, this is found by them for a wage, and they hunt for excesses of money, drawing on those who are in love with anything, as men able to do all. What wealth, then, sire, have you seen about me, that you think I practise false-wisdom, and that too when your father held me above money? And that I speak the truth, where is the letter of the noble and divine man, who in it sings of me, among other things, that I am poor? "The autocrat Vespasian to Apollonius the philosopher, greeting. If all, Apollonius, wished to philosophize as you do, philosophy and poverty would fare very happily—philosophy keeping herself unbribed, poverty self-chosen. Farewell." Let your father defend me by this, defining for me the unbribedness of philosophy and the self-choosing of poverty; for he remembered, I suppose, the things in Egypt too, when Euphrates and many of those who profess philosophy approached him and asked for money not even covertly, but I not only did not approach for money, but thrust those others away as unsound; and I was set against money while still a stripling. My patrimony, at least—and it was a brilliant estate—having looked on it for a single day, I gave up to my brothers and friends and to the poor of my kin, practising, as it were from the very Hearth, to need nothing. Let Babylon be set aside, and the parts of India beyond the Caucasus and the river Hyphasis, through which I journeyed like myself; but of things here, and of my not looking to silver, I make this Egyptian a witness; for saying that dreadful things have been done and counselled by me, he has not said for how much money I did these crimes, nor what gain I had in mind; rather, I seem to him so senseless as to practise sorcery, yet—what others do for much money—I myself to do wrong not even for money, proclaiming, I suppose, a market of this sort: "Come, you fools, for I practise sorcery, and not even for money, but free of charge; and you will gain, each of you, the going off with what he loves, but I dangers and indictments." But that we may not go into senseless arguments, let us ask the accuser on which charge he must speak first. And yet why ask? For he went through the matter of my dress at the beginning of his speech, and—by Zeus—of what I eat and do not eat. Defend yourself on these things, divine Pythagoras; for we are tried for things which you discovered and I approve. The earth, sire, grows all things for men; and to those who wish to keep peace with the animals there is need of nothing, for some things they reap of her, and others they sow while she nurses them, as it suits the seasons; but some, as though deaf to the earth, have whetted the knife against the animals for the sake of dress and food. The Indian Brahmans then themselves did not approve this, and taught the Naked Sages of the Egyptians not to approve it; and from this Pythagoras took it—the first of the Greeks to mingle with the Egyptians—and gave back to the earth what was ensouled, but ate what she herself grows, saying it was undefiled, for it is fit to nourish body and mind; but the dress that the many wear from dead skins he said was not pure, and clad himself in linen, and on the same reasoning plaited his sandal of papyrus; and he reaped of his being pure many fruits, but first the perceiving of his own soul. For having lived in the times when Troy fought for Helen, and being the fairest of the sons of Panthus and most fairly dressed, he died so young as even to furnish Homer a lament; and passing into more bodies, by the ordinance of Adrasteia, which the soul changes about, he came back again into the form of a man, and was born to Mnesarchides the Samian, wise out of a barbarian, and Ionian out of a Trojan, and so far immortal as not even to have forgotten that he was Euphorbus. The forefather of my own wisdom I have named, and that I am not its discoverer, but hold it as an inheritance from another. And I do not condemn those who fare delicately for the sake of the phoenix-bird, nor for the one from the Phasis or the Paeonians, which those who indulge the belly in all things fatten for their feasts; nor have I ever indicted anyone over the fish which they buy at a higher price than the brilliant once bought their horses branded with the koppa; nor have I begrudged anyone purple, or any Pamphylian or soft garment; but for asphodel, O gods, and dried fruits and pure simple fare I am under indictment, and not even my dress is inviolate, but the accuser strips even that from me as worth much to sorcerers. And yet, take away the argument about ensouled and unensouled things, by which one seems pure or not, and how is linen better than wool? The one was shorn from the gentlest of animals, and one cared for by the gods, who do not disdain to be shepherds, and—by Zeus—who once held it worthy even of a golden form, whether gods or stories. But flax is sown as it chances, and there is no tale of gold about it; yet all the same, since it was not plucked from anything ensouled, it seems pure to the Indians, pure to the Egyptians, and to me and Pythagoras it has become, for this reason, the dress of those who discourse, pray, and sacrifice. And it is pure too to sleep the night beneath it; for dreams come truer to those who live as I do. Let us defend ourselves also about the hair we once had, since an indictment has been found even about neglect; and let it be judged not by the Egyptian, but by the blond and well-combed striplings, who kindle the lovers and the courtesans they revel after, and let them hold themselves happy and enviable for their hair and the perfume that drips from it, and me wholly devoid of love-charm and a lover of not loving. For this will be said to them: O wretches, do not falsely accuse the discovery of the Dorians; for wearing the hair long comes from the Lacedaemonians, practised by them in the times when they were most warlike, and Leonidas was king of Sparta wearing his hair long, for the sake of manliness and of appearing solemn to friends and terrible to foes; and so Sparta wears her hair long for him no less than for Lycurgus and Iphitus. But of a wise man's hair let the iron be sparing; for it is not lawful to bring it where are all the springs of the senses and all the voices, whence prayers come forth and reason, the interpreter of wisdom. For Empedocles, fastening a fillet of the most purple about his hair, swept through the streets of the Greeks composing hymns that he would be a god out of a man; but I, using neglected hair and not yet having needed such hymns over it, am led to indictments and courts. And what shall I say of Empedocles? That he sang of himself, or of the happiness of the men of his day, among whom these things were not falsely accused? Let us discourse no further about the hair, for it has been cut, and envy has forestalled the accusation; on account of which one must defend oneself about the other charge, which is grave, and such, sire, as to furnish fear not to you alone but to Zeus. For he says that men hold me a god, and publicly proclaim this, thunderstruck by me; and yet, even before the charge, he ought to have shown what I discoursed, what so marvellous thing I said or did, that I drew men to pray to me. For I never discoursed among the Greeks—though I knew them—either into what my soul has changed or will change, nor did I send forth such opinions about myself, nor did I go off into oracles and chanting of prophecies, as is the way of those who invoke gods; nor do I know any city in which it was resolved that men should gather to sacrifice to Apollonius. And yet I was worth much to each, in whatever they asked of me; and they asked such things as these: that the sick not be sick; that they be holier in initiation, holier in sacrifice; that insolence be cut out; that the laws be strong. And my wage for these things was that they should appear better than themselves; and I was doing you a favour in this. For as the herdsmen of oxen render their not being unruly a favour to the owners of the oxen, and the keepers of flocks fatten them to the profit of those who possess them, and the keepers of bees take away their diseases, that the swarm may not perish for its master—so I too, stopping civic faults, was setting the cities right for you; so that even if they held me a god, the deceit held profit for you, for they listened to me, I suppose, with eagerness, fearing to do what does not seem good to a god. But it was not this they thought, rather that there is a certain kinship of man to god, through which alone of animals he knows the gods, and philosophizes about his own nature and how he shares in the divine. He says, then, that the very form is like to god, as statuary interprets and colours; and he is persuaded that the virtues come to him from god, and that those who share them are nigh to gods and divine. And let us not call the Athenians the teachers of this thought, since they first set up the titles 'the just,' 'the Olympians,' and such names—titles, as is likely, more divine than to lie upon a man—but Apollo at Pytho. For Lycurgus from Sparta came to his temple when his laws, by which Lacedaemon is ordered, had just been written; and Apollo, addressing him, tests the opinion about him, saying at the beginning of the oracle that he is at a loss whether to call him god or man; but going on he declares and votes him this title, as to a good man. And no contest or danger came upon Lycurgus from this among the Lacedaemonians, as immortalizing him, since he did not rebuke the Pythian for addressing him so, but they agreed with the oracle, being persuaded, I suppose, of these things even before the oracle. And the affairs of the Indians and Egyptians are these: the Egyptians in other matters falsely accuse the Indians and slander their opinions on affairs, but the argument which is spoken about the Demiurge of all they so praise as even to teach it to others, though it is the Indians'. The argument knows a god as Demiurge of the generation and being of all things, and the cause of his conceiving this is that he is good. Since, then, these things are akin, I hold to the argument and say that good men have something of god. And let the cosmos that lies under god the Demiurge be reckoned the things in heaven and all the things in sea and earth, of which the share is equal to men, except for fortune. But there is also a certain cosmos upon a good man, not exceeding the measures of wisdom—which you yourself, sire, will say has need of a man likened to god. And what is the form of this cosmos? Souls that are disorderly seize more madly upon every form; their laws are stale to them, and temperance nowhere, and the honours of the gods dishonoured; they are in love with chatter and luxury, from which springs idleness, an evil counsellor of every work. And drunken souls leap upon many things, but nothing checks this skipping, not even if they drank all the drinks that, like mandragora, are held sleep-bringing. But there is need of a man who will care for the cosmos about them—a god come of wisdom. For he is enough to lead them away from loves, toward which they are carried more savagely than their wonted company, and from money-loving, through which they say they have not yet all, since they do not also hold their mouth under the inflowing wealth. For to keep them from laying hands on murders is perhaps not impossible to such a man, but to wash them clean is possible neither to me nor to the god the Demiurge of all. Let there be, sire, an accusation about Ephesus too, since it was saved, and let the Egyptian judge me, as is fit for the indictment. For the accusation is, I suppose, of this sort: among the Scythians or Celts, who dwell by the river Ister or the Rhine, a city has been founded no smaller than Ephesus in Ionia; this city, being a base of barbarians who do not hearken to you, a plague was about to destroy, and Apollonius healed it. There is some defence even to this for a wise man, if the emperor should wish to take what is opposed to him by arms and not by diseases—for may no city ever be wiped out, neither for you, sire, nor for me, nor may I see by the temples a disease through which the sick will lie within them. But let the affairs of barbarians not be in earnest, nor let us rank in health those who are most hostile and not in treaty with our race. But who will take from Ephesus its being saved—a city which had the beginnings of its race from the purest Attica, which has advanced beyond all that are Ionian and Lydian, which has gone forward to the sea because it overtops the land on which it was founded, which is full of philosophic and rhetorical reflections, by which the city is strong not in horse but in myriads of men, praising wisdom? What wise man do you think would forsake the contest for such a city, when he reflects on Democritus, who once freed the Abderites of a plague, and bethinks himself of Sophocles the Athenian, who is said even to have charmed winds that blew out of season, and has heard the deeds of Empedocles, who held back the rush of a cloud bursting upon the Acragantines? The accuser cuts me off—for you too, sire, hear it, I suppose—and says that it is not because I became the cause of safety to the Ephesians that I am indicted, but because I foretold that the sickness would fall upon them; for this, he says, is beyond wisdom and portentous, and I could not have reached such truth unless I were a sorcerer and ineffable. What then will Socrates say here, about what he said he learned from his daemonic sign? What Thales and Anaxagoras, the two Ionians, the one foretelling the abundance of olives, the other many of the heavenly phenomena—did they foretell these by sorcery? And indeed these men too were brought before courts on other charges, and nowhere among the charges is it said that they were sorcerers because they foreknow. For this seemed ridiculous, and not even in Thessaly was it credible to say against wise men—where the little women had an ill name for drawing down the moon. Whence, then, did I perceive the sickness about Ephesus? You heard the accuser too say that I do not live as the rest; and about my own food, that it is light and pleasanter than another's Sybaris, it was said at the beginning. This, sire, keeps my senses in a certain ineffable clearness and allows nothing turbid to be about them, and lets me see through, as in the gleam of a mirror, all things coming to be and to come. For the wise man will not wait for the earth to exhale or the air to grow corrupt, if the danger flows from above, but will understand these things even while they are at the doors, later than the gods, but quicker than the many; for the gods perceive things to come, men things coming to be, and wise men things drawing near. But the causes of plagues, sire, ask in private, for they are too wise to be told to the many. Does living so, then, work only fineness of the senses, or also strength toward the greatest and most marvellous things? One may observe what I say from other things, but not least from what was done in Ephesus about that sickness; for the form of the plague—it was likened to a beggarly old man—I both saw and, seeing, seized, not stopping the disease but rooting it out; and to whom I prayed, the temple shows which I founded in Ephesus for this—for it is of Heracles Averter—for I chose him as fellow-worker, since, being wise and brave, he once cleansed Elis of a plague by washing away the exhalations which the earth furnished under the tyranny of Augeas. Who, then, sire, do you think, ambitious to appear a sorcerer, would ascribe to a god what he himself had wrought? What admirers of his art would he win by yielding to a god the being marvelled at? And who, being a sorcerer, would pray to Heracles? For such things the wretches ascribe to pits and to the gods below, from whom Heracles must be set apart, for he is pure and kindly to men. I prayed to him once in the Peloponnese too, for there was there a certain phantom of a lamia about Corinth, feeding on the fair among the young, and he joined me in the contest, asking for no marvellous gifts, but honey-cake and frankincense, and the doing of something for the saving of men; for this, even under Eurystheus, he held a wage for his labours. Be not vexed, sire, to hear of Heracles; for Athena cared for him, since he was good and saving to men. But since you bid me defend the sacrifice—for you signify this with your hand too—hear a true defence: I, who do all for the saving of men, have never yet sacrificed for them, nor would I sacrifice anything, nor would I touch rites in which there is blood, nor would I pray looking toward a knife or a sacrifice such as he says. You have not caught a Scythian, sire, nor one from somewhere unmingled, nor have I ever mixed with Massagetae or Tauri, since I would have changed even those from the custom of human sacrifice; but to what folly should I be driven, that I, discoursing most of all about divination and where it is strong or not, and having perceived best of men that the gods reveal their counsels to holy and wise men even without divining, should lay hands on bloodshed and on entrails unsacrificed by me and unblessed? For at these the very voice of the daemonic would have left me, as not being pure. And indeed, if one took away the pollution of the sacrifice and examined the accuser against what he said a little before, he himself frees me of the charge; for him whom he says I foretold the sickness to the Ephesians without needing any sacrifice—what need had I of victims for things which it was given me to know even without sacrificing? And what need of divination about things of which I myself, and another, was persuaded? For if I am tried about Nerva and his party, I will say again what I said before, when you charged this: I hold Nerva worthy of all rule and of every word of good omen that comes; but no good contestant in cares, for his body is dissolved by sickness, through which his judgement too is full of weariness and not even sufficient for affairs at home. He praises you, at least, in body and praises you in judgement, likely, I think, suffering somewhat, for human nature is indeed more ready to praise the things in which it is not itself strong. And Nerva has felt something kindly toward me too; I have never known him laugh in my presence, nor play any of the usual jests among friends; but like striplings toward their fathers and teachers, he speaks cautiously all that is before me, and still blushes; and knowing that I praise gentleness, he so practises it overmuch that he appears even to me lowlier than is fitting. How, then, would anyone hold it credible that Nerva desired rule, who is content to rule his own house, or that he discoursed with me of great things, who took no courage even about small ones, or that he joined judgement with me about things which, if he considered mine, he would join with no other? Or how am I still wise to interpret a man's judgement, trusting divination but distrusting wisdom? And Orfitus and Rufus, the just and temperate but sluggish men, as I well know—if they say they were slandered as tyrant-mongers, I do not know whether they err more about these or about Nerva; but if as having become counsellors, is Nerva more credible to attempt rule, or these to counsel it? But surely the man who judges these things ought to have reflected on this too: what did my helping those who came to innovation mean for me? For he does not say that money came to me from them, nor that I did this lifted up by gifts; but let us consider whether, needing great things, I deferred their benefactions to the time when I thought they would rule, in which it would be open to me to ask great things and to be held worthy of greater. How, then, will this be plain? Reflect, sire, on yourself and on those who ruled before you—your brother, I suppose, and your father, and Nero—under whom they ruled; for it is chiefly under these emperors that I have lived in public view, spending the rest of the time among the Indians. Of these eight-and-thirty years—for so long is the span down to you—I have never frequented imperial doors except in Egypt, your father's, since he was not yet emperor and confessed that he came for my sake; nor have I discoursed anything servile to emperors or about emperors to peoples, nor have I made myself brilliant by letters, either by emperors writing to me or by myself showing that I write; nor have I betrayed myself, flattering emperors for the sake of gifts. If, then, you should ask me, having reflected on the rich and the poor, to which of these nations I enrol myself, I will say the richest; for to need nothing is, for me, Lydia and all the Pactolus. How, then, would I either have deferred the gifts of those who were not yet emperors to the time when I thought they would rule—I who did not even choose those from you, whom I held to rule securely—or have devised changes of kingdoms, who did not use even those established for the sake of being honoured? And how much accrues to a philosopher who flatters the powerful, the case of Euphrates shows; for to him from this—why do I say money? They are very springs of wealth; and now at the tables he bargains, a huckster, an under-huckster, a tax-gatherer, an obol-weigher, becoming all the things sold and selling; and he is forever stamped at the doors of the powerful and stands before them longer than the doormen, and has often been shut out even by the doormen, like the greedy among dogs; and never having laid out a drachma even to a philosopher, he fortifies his own wealth against others, feeding this Egyptian here with money and whetting against me a tongue that deserves to be cut out. Euphrates, then, I leave to you; for you, if you do not praise flatterers, will find the man worse than I describe. But hear the rest of the defence. What is it, and about what? A certain lament for an Arcadian boy was sung, sire, in the accusation: that he was cut up by me by night—but whether he speaks of a dream, I do not yet know—and that this boy was of good parents and of the form that the fair Arcadians have in their roughness. They say that this boy, supplicating and lamenting, was slaughtered, and that I, dipping my hands in the boy's blood, prayed to the gods for truth. Thus far they try me, but what follows touches the gods; for they say that the gods heard me praying thus, and gave favourable victims and did not kill me for my impiety. As for the hearing being impure, what, sire, should I say? But about what I must defend myself—who is this Arcadian? For if he is not nameless in his fathers, nor servile in form, it is time for you to ask what was the name of his parents, of what house he was, what city in Arcadia reared him, from what altars he was led here to be sacrificed. He does not say this, though he is clever at not telling the truth. So then he tries me about a slave. For one who has no name himself, nor any of those he was born of, no city, no estate—must we not, O gods, rank this one among slaves? For all is nameless. Who, then, is the trader of the slave? Who bought him from the Arcadians? For if the race of these is fit for the slaughtering divination, it is likely the boy was bought for much money, and that someone sailed to the Peloponnese, that the Arcadian might be brought up to us from there; for Pontic or Lydian or Phrygian slaves one might buy even here, of whom one may meet whole herds coming hither; for these nations, and all the barbarians, having all time hearkened to others, do not yet think it shameful to be slaves. The Phrygians, at least, hold it native to sell their own, and not to be concerned when they are enslaved; but the Greeks are still lovers of freedom, and a Greek man will not sell even a slave beyond the borders; whence neither slave-dealers nor slave-traders may go among them, and to Arcadia still less, for besides their being free above all Greeks they have need also of a throng of slaves. And Arcadia is rich in crops and grassy and wooded, not only the heights but all that is underfoot. They have need, then, of many husbandmen, of many goatherds, swineherds and shepherds and oxherds, some over oxen, some over horses; and the country needs many woodcutters, and they are trained in this from childhood. And even if the affairs of the Arcadians were not such, but they could, like others, sell their own slaves besides, what did being from Arcadia contribute to the much-talked-of wisdom, that the slaughtered one be Arcadian? For the Arcadians are not the wisest of the Greeks, that they should show in the rational parts of their entrails something more than another man; rather, they are the most rustic of men and swinish, both in other things and in stuffing themselves on acorns. I have perhaps defended myself more rhetorically than my manner, interpreting the ways of the Arcadians and passing in my argument into the Peloponnese. For what is the defence proper to me? I did not sacrifice, I do not sacrifice, I do not touch blood, not even if it be of an altar; for Pythagoras knew it so, and those from him likewise, and in Egypt the Naked Sages and the wise of the Indians, from whom the principles of wisdom came even to those about Pythagoras. Sacrificing by these rules, they do not seem to wrong the gods, but the gods grant them to grow old whole in body and free of disease, and to seem ever wiser, and to be tyrannized over by none and to need nothing. And it is not unfitting, I think, that they should ask good things for pure offerings. For I think the gods too, having the same mind as I about sacrifices, grow the incense-bearing things of the earth in a pure part of the world, that from them we may sacrifice without bearing iron in temples, nor sprinkling blood on altars. But I, as it seems, forgetting myself and the gods, sacrificed in a way that neither I am wont to, nor any man would. Let the time too free me of the charge, which the accuser has named; for that day on which he says these things were done by me—if I was in the country, I sacrificed; and if I sacrificed, I also ate. Then, sire, you often ask whether I was not dwelling in Rome at the time? And you too, best of emperors, were dwelling there, but you would not say you sacrificed such things; and the informer too, but he will not confess to doing the deeds of murderers, though he lived in Rome; and myriads of men, whom it were better to drive out as aliens than to bring under indictments in which being here will be a proof of crimes. And yet to have come to Rome rather acquits one of seeming to innovate; for to live in a city in which all are eyes, all ears, of things that are and are not, does not allow a man to lay hands on innovation, at least if he is not over-eager to die, and brings the more cautious and temperate slowly even to what is permitted. What, then, informer, was I doing on that night? If you ask as you would ask yourself—since you too have come to ask—I was preparing contests and accusations against good men, to destroy those who did no wrong, and to persuade the emperor by not speaking the truth, that I might be in repute and this man defiled; but if you inquire as of a philosopher, I was praising the laughter of Democritus, with which he laughs at all human things; but if as of me, Philiscus of Melia, who had philosophized with me four years, was then sick, and I lodged with him, so grievously affected as even to die of the sickness. And yet I would have prayed for many love-charms for that man's soul, and—by Zeus—if there are any songs of Orpheus over the dead, I would not have been ignorant of those either; for I think I would even have gone beneath the earth for his sake, if these things were possible; so was I bound to him by all that he did philosophically and according to my mind. This you may hear, sire, even from Telesinus the consul, for he too was present with the Melian, tending him by night as much as I. And if you distrust Telesinus, since he is of the philosophers, I call the physicians as witnesses; and these are Seleucus of Cyzicus and Stratocles of Sidon. Ask these whether I speak the truth; and more than thirty disciples followed them, witnesses, I suppose, of the same things; for to summon hither the kinsmen of Philiscus you will perhaps think a delay of the trial, since they straightway departed Rome for the country of the Melians for the burial of the dead. Come, witnesses—for indeed you have been charged about this. WITNESSES. By how far, then, the indictment was composed apart from the truth, the testimony of the men shows clearly; for not in the suburbs but in the city, not outside the wall but in a house, not with Nerva but with Philiscus, not slaughtering but praying for a soul, not for kingship but for philosophy, not voting in a younger man in place of you, but saving a man like myself. What, then, has the Arcadian here? What the tales of victims? What the persuading of such things? For there will be sometime even what has not been, if it is judged as having been. But the incredibility of the sacrifice, sire, where will you rank it? For there were of old too good diviners by victims, and such as to name—Megistias from Acarnania, Aristander from Lycia, and Ambracia bore Silanus; and the Acarnanian sacrificed for Leonidas king of Sparta, the Lycian for Alexander the Macedonian, and Silanus for Cyrus who longed for kingship; and if anything in human entrails lay clearer or wiser or truer, the sacrifice was not difficult, with kings standing over it, who had many cup-bearers, many captives, and lawlessness without danger, and no fear of accusation if they slaughtered anyone; but, I think, it occurred to the men, as it does to me now in danger over such things, that the irrational animals, since they are slaughtered in ignorance of death, likely have nothing of the entrails troubled by their not understanding what they will suffer; but a man, always having in his soul some dread of death even when it is not yet at hand—how is it likely that, when it is already present and before his eyes, he should show anything on the entrails divinatory, or rightly sacrificed at all? That I conjecture these things rightly and according to nature, consider thus, sire. The liver, in which those clever at this say the tripod of their divination is, is composed of blood not pure; for all that is unmixed the heart holds, drawing it off through blood-bearing veins to all the body; and the gall, lying upon the liver, anger rouses, but fears draw down into the hollows of the liver. By the things that provoke, then, the gall, seething and not even bearable to its own vessel, is poured over upon the liver, where all the gall holds back the smooth and divinatory parts of the inward; but by the things that frighten, sinking together, it draws down with it the light in the smooth parts, for then even the pure part of the blood withdraws, by which the liver is spleen-like, running by nature beneath the membrane about it and floating upon the muddy part. What, then, sire, is the work of the bloodshed, if the sacred parts shall be unmarked? And human nature makes them unmarked, understanding death, and the very men who die; for the stout-hearted die with anger, the more faint-hearted with fear. Whence the art, among the barbarians not unskilled in it, praises the slaughtering of she-goats and lambs, since the animals are simple and not far from senseless, but does not hold cocks and swine and bulls worthy of its secrets, since these are spirited. I understand, sire, that I provoke the accuser, since I have made you a wiser hearer, and you seem to me even to attend to the argument; but if I should not state anything of it clearly, I grant you to ask me. I have said what is to be said against the Egyptian's indictment; and since, I think, the slanders of Euphrates too must not be overlooked, do you, sire, judge which of us philosophizes the more. For he contends not to speak the truth about me, but I deem it unworthy; and he holds you a master, but I a ruler; and he gives you a sword against me, but I a word. But the things over which he has slandered me are the arguments I made in Ionia, and he says they were spoken by me not to your advantage. And yet what was said was about the Fates and Necessity; and the affairs of kings became my example of the argument, since your affairs seem the greatest of human things; and I philosophized about the strength of the Fates, and that the things they spin are so unalterable that, even if they should vote a kingship to another which already belonged to him, and he should kill this man, lest the rule should ever be taken from him by him, yet the dead man would come back to life for the things resolved by the Fates. For we bring in the excesses of arguments for the sake of those who disbelieve the plausible, just as if I should say this too: he to whom it is fated to be a carpenter, this man, even if his hands be cut off, will be a carpenter; and he to whom it is to win a victory at Olympia in the race, this man, even if his leg be maimed, will not miss the victory; and he to whom the Fates nodded the mastery in archery, this man, even if he lose his eyes, will not fall from the mark. And the affairs of kings I spoke of, looking, I suppose, to the Acrisii and the Laii and Astyages the Mede and many others who seemed to set their affairs well at the start, of whom some, thinking to kill their sons, some their grandsons, were stripped by them of their kingship, when they sprang up out of obscurity with destiny. And if I delighted in flattery, I would say that I had your own affairs in mind too, when you were shut up here by Vitellius, and the temple of Zeus was being burned about the brows of the city, and he said his own affairs would lie well if you did not escape him—and yet you were quite a stripling and he was not yet what he became—but all the same, since the Fates resolved otherwise, he perished by his own counsels, and you now hold what was his. But since I am vexed by the harmony of flattery, for it seems to me to be of the ill-rhythmed and ill-sounding, let this string be cut for me, and think I have had nothing of yours in mind, but have discoursed only the things about the Fates and Necessity; for these he says were spoken by me against you. And yet this argument even the many of the gods endure, nor is even Zeus vexed to hear it, when the poets in the Lycian tales sing to him "Ah me, that Sarpedon..." and such things, in which he says he yields his son to the Fates; and again in the Weighing of Souls, when they say that he honoured Minos the brother of Sarpedon, when he died, with a golden sceptre, and set him to judge in the marketplace of Aidoneus, yet did not beg him off from the Fates. But you, sire, on what account are you vexed at the argument, when the gods endure it, for whom things are forever fixed, and do not kill the poets for it? For it befits to follow the Fates and not to be harsh at the changes of affairs, and not to distrust Sophocles, who says best of men: "For the gods alone there is no old age, nor ever to die; but all else all-mastering time confounds." For human prosperities go in a circle, and the length of bliss, sire, is for a day; this man holds my things, another his, and so-and-so, holding the things of so-and-so, holds them not. Reflecting on these things, sire, cease exiles, cease bloodshed, and use philosophy for what you will, for the true philosophy is unaffected; but take away the tears of men, since now an echo, a myriad from the sea, far more from the mainlands, comes of men lamenting, each what is worthy of his lament. And the things that spring from these, more than can be numbered, are fastened upon the tongues of the informers, who slander all to you and you, sire, to all.

When Euxenus, supposing that he was laying hold of some great purpose, asked him where he would begin, "Where the physicians do," he said; "for they too, by purging the bowels, keep some from falling ill at all, and cure others." And having said this, he renounced the eating of living things, as neither pure and as dulling the mind, and ate dried fruits and vegetables, saying that all things the earth herself gives are pure. Wine too he said was a pure drink, coming to men from a plant so kindly to them, but that it was opposed to the right constitution of the mind, troubling the ether within the soul. After this purification of his body, he made bare feet his adornment, and clothed himself in linen, refusing what comes from animals; he let his hair grow long, and lived in the temple. Those about the temple were amazed at him, and Asclepius once said to the priest that he rejoiced to heal the sick with Apollonius as his witness; and on account of this fame the Cilicians themselves and those round about flocked to Aegae to see him. And the Cilician saying, "Where are you running? To see the youth?"—this was spoken about him, and gained the honour of a proverb.

Having crossed the river Cophen—themselves on boats, but the camels through the water on foot, for the river was not yet large—they came into the country ruled by the king, in which the mountain Nysa is planted, rising to a sharp summit like Tmolus in Lydia, and one may climb it, for it has been made passable by cultivation. Having gone up, they say they came upon a temple of Dionysus, which Dionysus is said to have planted for himself with laurels set in a circle, enclosing just so much ground as suffices for a temple of moderate size; and he set ivy and vines about the laurels, and set up within an image of himself, knowing that in time the trees would grow together and provide a roof of themselves—which is now so joined that the temple is neither rained upon nor pierced by wind. Sickles and baskets and presses and the implements of presses are dedicated to Dionysus, of gold and silver, as to one who treads the grapes. The image is likened to an Indian youth, and is carved of white stone. When Dionysus celebrates his rites and shakes Nysa, the cities below the mountain hear him and are stirred up together with him.

The mountain-dragons have scales that gleam like gold, and they are longer than those of the plain; they have beards like clusters, golden also, and their brows overhang more than those of the plain-dragons, and beneath the brow lies an eye terrible and fierce in its gaze. They carry a sound like the clash of bronze when they move along the ground, and from their crests, which are flame-coloured, there flashes a fire brighter than a torch. These take elephants also, and are themselves caught by the Indians in this way. Upon a scarlet cloak they weave golden letters, and lay it before the dragon's lair, having charmed the letters with a spell that brings sleep, by which the eyes of the dragon, otherwise unblinking, are overcome; and they chant over it much of their secret wisdom, by which it is drawn on, and stretching its neck out of the lair it falls asleep upon the letters. Then the Indians, falling upon it as it lies, drive their axes into it, and cutting off the head carry off the stones within it. In the heads of the mountain-dragons, they say, there lie hidden stones of flowery hue, flashing back all colours, and of unspeakable power, like the ring which they say came to Gyges. But often the Indian, axe and skill and all, is seized by the dragon and carried off into its lair, all but shaking the mountain. These dragons are also said to dwell in the mountains about the Red Sea; and a terrible hissing is heard from them, and when they go down to the sea they swim far out into the deep. As to the length of years of this creature, it is impossible to know and incredible to tell. So much I know about dragons.

Moreover he reasoned with the Smyrnaeans about how cities might be safely governed, seeing them at variance with one another and not agreed in their counsels; for he said that the city which is to be rightly governed needs a discord of concord. This being thought said unconvincingly and not in due sequence, Apollonius, understanding that the multitude did not follow the argument, said: "White and black could never become the same, nor could the bitter be soundly blended with the sweet; but concord may quarrel for the safety of cities. And what I mean, let us take to be this: let that faction which leads to swords and to stoning one another be far from a city which needs the rearing of children and laws and men by whom words and deeds are wrought; but the rivalry of citizens with one another for the common good, and how one might speak a better counsel than another, and one preside over an office better than another, and one go on an embassy, and another build something more splendid than his fellow-magistrate — this, I think, is good strife and faction with one another for the common good. For each to pursue a different thing and bring it to the city's benefit seemed to the Lacedaemonians of old a foolish thing, since they laboured at war and all were strong for it and laid hold of this alone; but to me it seems best that each should do what he knows and what he can. For if one be admired for leadership of the people, another for wisdom, another for enriching the common store, another for being honest, another for being grave and unforgiving to wrongdoers, another for keeping his hands clean, the city will be well established, or rather will stand firm.

When afterwards one of those who run the swift courses came to Gadeira and bade them sacrifice for the good news, singing of Nero as thrice victor at Olympia, the people of Gadeira understood about the victory and that there was some famous contest in Arcadia, since, as I said, they are eager for the affairs of the Greeks; but the cities neighbouring Gadeira knew neither what the Olympia were, nor what a contest or games might be, nor for what they were to sacrifice, but were carried off into absurd notions, thinking these things a victory of war and that Nero had taken captive certain Olympian men; for they had never been spectators of tragedy or citharody.

Having put together such things, the Naucratite departed; and they, holding this to be true, did not refuse him their company when he came, but pretended to be busy about great matters and engaged with them, and said they would come to discourse with him too, if they had leisure and learned what he wished and what he had come desiring. And the man who came from them bade them lodge in the portico; but Apollonius said, "Of a roof speak nothing, for the sky here allows all men to live naked" — taunting them as being naked not from endurance but from necessity — "but what I wish, and for what I have come, the others I do not wonder at for not yet knowing, but the Indians did not ask me these things."

It seemed that Nerva was suited to the rule which, after Domitian, he took up soberly; and the same opinion was held of Orfitus and Rufus. These men Domitian, saying that they were plotting against him, shut up in islands—two of them—while to Nerva he assigned Tarentum to dwell in. Now Apollonius, being a friend to them, during all the time that Titus ruled, both together with his father and after his father, was forever sending these men letters about temperance, attaching them to the emperors as good men; but under Domitian, since he was harsh, he detached the men from him and strengthened them for the freedom of all. Counsels by letter, however, he thought not safe for them, for many of the powerful were betrayed even by slaves and friends and wives, and no house then kept a secret. So, taking aside at different times the most discreet of his own companions, he would say: "I make you the bearer of a brilliant secret; you must go to Rome, to such a one, and speak with him, and become, for the persuading of the man, all that I myself would be." But when he heard that they had fled—after showing some impulse against the tyrant, but falling away through hesitation from what they had purposed—he was discoursing about the Fates and Necessity in the grove of Smyrna,

Thus were the things from preparation with the man; but at the end of the speech I found the last words of the former speech, "for you shall not kill me, since I am not fated to die," and the things before this still, from which this comes. And when he left the court in a daemonic manner, and not easy to tell, the tyrant did not suffer what the many thought; for they thought that he would cry out cruel things about this and make a pursuit of the man, and proclaim through all his realm that he was nowhere to be approached; but he did none of these things, either contending against the opinion of the many, or understanding at last that nothing was sufficient against the man. But whether he overlooked it, let us reckon from what follows; for he would appear rather confounded than contemptuous.

It is right not to pass over even what happened in the temple, when one is telling the life of a man who was held in account even by the gods. For a young Assyrian came to Asclepius, and lived in luxury though sick, and spent his life in drink; or rather he was dying, for he was held by dropsy, and taking pleasure in drunkenness he neglected dryness. He was therefore neglected by Asclepius for this reason, and not even in a dream did the god visit him. When he complained of this, the god stood over him and said, "If you talk with Apollonius, you will be the better for it." So he came to Apollonius and said: "What good might I gain from your wisdom? For Asclepius bids me be with you." "That," said he, "which will be worth much to you as things now stand. For you want health, I suppose?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "the health which Asclepius promises but does not give." "Hush," he said; "for to those who are willing he gives it; but you do things contrary to your disease. For you give yourself to luxury, and you heap rich food upon bowels that are moist and corrupted, and you pour mud upon water." This, I think, he prophesied more clearly than the wisdom of Heraclitus; for Heraclitus said that one suffering from this affliction needed someone to make drought out of flood—words neither easy to understand nor plain—whereas Apollonius brought the youth back to health by interpreting the wise saying clearly.

Greeks dispute with Indians about this Dionysus, and Indians among themselves. For we say that the Theban marched against the Indians, both campaigning and reveling, using as evidence, among other things, the dedication at Pytho, which the treasuries there hold laid away. It is a disc of Indian silver, on which is inscribed: "DIONYSUS, SON OF SEMELE AND ZEUS, FROM THE INDIANS TO APOLLO OF DELPHI." But the Indians about the Caucasus and the river Cophen say that he came among them as an Assyrian stranger who knew the affairs of the Theban; while those who dwell in the land between the Indus and the Hydraotes, and the country beyond, which ends at the river Ganges, say that Dionysus was the son of the river Indus, and that the Theban, coming to him, took the thyrsus and gave him to the rites, and saying that he was the son of Zeus and had lived in his father's thigh until his birth, found from him a mountain Merus, on which Nysa borders, and planted Nysa for Dionysus, bringing from Thebes the slip of the vine—where Alexander too performed the rites. But the inhabitants of Nysa say that Alexander did not go up the mountain, but set out to, since he was ambitious and fond of antiquities; yet fearing that, if the Macedonians came among the vines, which they had not seen for a long time, they might be carried back into longing for home or take up some craving for wine, being now accustomed to water, he passed Nysa by, praying to Dionysus and sacrificing at the foot of the mountain. I know that in writing this I please some not at all, since those who served with Alexander did not record even these things truthfully; but I at least need the truth, which, had they too praised it, they would not have taken from Alexander this praise either. For greater, I think, than his going up the mountain and reveling, as they say, is this—that for the endurance of his army he did not even ascend.

The city beneath the mountain, which is very great, they say is called Paraca, and in the midst of it are dedicated very many heads of dragons, since the Indians of that place train themselves in this hunting from their youth. They are said also to understand the speech and counsels of animals, by feeding, some on the heart, some on the liver, of a dragon. As they went on, they say they heard a flute, as of some herdsman ordering his flock; and it was white deer being pastured, which the Indians milk, holding the milk from them to be very nourishing.

As he was going through this, he saw a ship of the three-masted kind sailing out, and the sailors each doing his part differently to put her to sea. So turning to those present he said: "Do you see the ship's company, how some have boarded the boats, being rowers, some haul up and stow the anchors, some spread the sails to the wind, some keep look-out from stern and prow? If one of these should fail in his own work, or handle the seamanship ignorantly, they will sail badly and will themselves seem the storm; but if they vie with one another and contend that no one shall seem worse than his fellow, fair are the havens for this ship, and all is full of calm and good sailing, and their good counsel will seem the very Poseidon of safety.

The people who dwell at Hippola — and this too is a city of Baetica — Damis says suffered a strange thing at the hands of a tragic actor, which is worth recording. For when the cities were sacrificing frequently for the victories, since the Pythian successes too were now being announced, a tragic actor of the kind not thought worthy to contend against Nero went round the western cities collecting money; and plying his art he was held in repute among the less barbarous, first for the very reason that he came among men who had never yet heard tragedy, and then because he claimed to render Nero's melodies exactly. But when he entered Hippola he seemed terrible to them even during the time he was silent upon the stage; and the people, seeing him walk grandly, and gape so wide, and stand upon buskins so high, and the monstrous robes about him, were not without fear of his appearance; and when, raising his voice, he uttered a loud cry, most of them took to flight, as though smitten by a daemon. Such are the manners of the barbarians there, and so primitive.

So Apollonius, reclining under one of the trees, conversed with his companions on whatever they asked; but Damis, taking Timasion aside, asked him privately: "These Naked Sages, my good fellow — for you have, as is likely, kept company with them — how wise are they?" "In many great things," he said. "And yet," said Damis, "their behaviour toward us is not wise, my noble friend; for not to come to terms with such a man about wisdom, but to use arrogance toward him — I do not know what to call it, but conceit, my comrade." "Conceit? Which I never before saw about them, though I have now twice come here; for they were always moderate and good toward those who mingled with them. Lately, indeed — and it is perhaps fifty days ago — Thrasybulus was staying here, doing nothing brilliant in philosophy, and they received him gladly, since he had enrolled himself with Euphrates." And Damis said, "What do you say, young man? You have seen Thrasybulus the Naucratite in this place?" "Yes," he said, "and besides, I brought him down from here in my own ship." "I have the whole of it, by Athena!" cried Damis, crying out and indignant; "for it seems some villainy has been wrought." So Timasion broke in: "The man, when I asked him yesterday who he was, did not yet think me worthy of the secret; but you, if these are not mysteries, tell me who he is, for perhaps I too might contribute something to the hunt for what is sought." And when he heard from Damis that he was the Tyanean, "You have got the matter," he said; "for Thrasybulus, as he sailed down the Nile with me, when I asked him why he went up there, told me, to his own no good wisdom, that he had filled these Naked Sages with suspicions against Apollonius, so that he should be looked down on when he came; and from what he is at variance with him I do not know, but to fall to slandering I hold both womanish and uneducated. I will learn how they are disposed by addressing the men, for they are my friends." And Timasion came back about evening, saying nothing to Apollonius except that he had addressed them, but privately reporting to Damis that they would come on the morrow, full of what they had heard from Thrasybulus.

in which the Meles flows; and knowing that Nerva would soon hold rule, he was carrying through his argument, that not even tyrants are able to do violence to the things that come from the Fates. A bronze image of Domitian had been set up by the Meles, and turning the bystanders toward it he said: "Fool, how greatly you go astray concerning the Fates and Necessity! For the man fated to be tyrant after you—even if you kill him, he will come back to life." This came to Domitian through the slanders of Euphrates; and for which of the men he uttered it as oracle, no one understood. But the tyrant, taking his own fear for good ground, set out to kill the men; and that he might not be seen acting beyond reason, he summoned Apollonius to defend himself concerning the secrets shared with them. For if Apollonius came and were condemned, Domitian would not seem to have killed men untried, but men convicted in him; or if by some cleverness Apollonius slipped away from public view, then the men would the sooner perish, as having been condemned even by their partner in the charge.

For he was hearing another trial after that one—it was a city contending against a man over a will, I think—and there escaped him not only the names of the litigants, but even the sense of the suit; for his questions were senseless, and his answers not even on the matter of the trial; which strongly convicted the tyrant of being dismayed and at a loss, chiefly because he had been persuaded by his flatterers that nothing could escape him.

Seeing once a great quantity of blood upon the altar, and the sacrificial victims laid out upon it—Egyptian oxen and great swine that had been slaughtered, some of them being flayed, others cut up—and two golden vessels dedicated, set with stones of the most Indian and marvellous kind, he came to the priest and said: "What is this? For someone is making a splendid gift to the god." "You will wonder the more," said the priest, "that this man, who has never yet supplicated here, nor stayed the time that others stay, nor yet gained health from the god, nor even has what he came to ask for—for he seems to have arrived only yesterday—yet sacrifices thus lavishly. He says he will sacrifice still more and dedicate still more, if Asclepius receives him. He is among the very richest; for in Cilicia at least he possesses more substance than all the Cilicians together; and he supplicates the god to give him back one of his eyes, which has fallen out." But Apollonius, as he was wont to do when grown old, fixing his eyes upon the ground, asked, "What is his name?" And when he heard it, he said: "It seems to me, priest, that we should not receive this man in the temple, for he comes here defiled, and has met with his affliction for no good reason; and the very fact of sacrificing lavishly before obtaining anything from the god is the act not of one who sacrifices, but of one who begs pardon for wretched and cruel deeds." So spoke Apollonius. And Asclepius, standing over the priest by night, said: "Let so-and-so depart, keeping his own goods; for he deserves not even to keep his other eye." So the priest, inquiring about the man, found that this Cilician had a wife who had a daughter by a former marriage; and he was in love with the girl and lived shamelessly with her, nor did he even take care to hide it. For the mother, coming upon them in bed, put out both the girl's eyes and one of his, driving the pins of her brooches into them.

The rock Aornus, not far distant from Nysa, Damis says he did not see, for it lay off the road and the guide feared to turn aside anywhere from the straight way; but he heard that it was taken by Alexander, and that it is called Aornus, not because it rises fifteen stadia—for the sacred birds fly even above this—but because they say there is on the summit of the rock a cleft which draws down the birds that fly over it, as may be seen at Athens in the vestibule of the Parthenon, and in many places in the land of the Phrygians and Lydians; on account of which the rock both is called and is Aornus.

From there, journeying four days through a happy and well-tilled country, they say they came near to the tower of the sages. Their guide bade the camel kneel, and leapt down from it, full of fear and sweat. Apollonius understood where he had come, and laughing at the Indian's terror said, as it seems to me: "This man, even if after measuring out some great stretch of sea he had put into a long-sought harbour, would still be vexed at the land and afraid of being in port." And saying this he bade his camel kneel — for by now he was used to such things. But what so frightened the guide was the coming near to the sages; for the Indians fear these men more than their own king, since the king himself, under whom the country lies, asks these men about all that he must say and do, as those who send to an oracle of a god; and they signify what is better for him to do, and what is not better they forbid and warn against.

With such discourses he held Smyrna together. But when the disease fell upon the Ephesians and nothing availed against it, they sent an embassy to Apollonius, making him the physician of their suffering. He did not think the journey should be put off, but saying "Let us go," he was in Ephesus — doing, I think, what Pythagoras did, being at once in Thurii and Metapontum. So gathering the Ephesians, he said: "Take courage; for today I will stay the disease." And saying this he led men of every age to the theatre, where the statue of the Averter is set up. There seemed to be an old beggar there, blinking his eyes by craft, and he carried a wallet with a crust of bread in it, and was clad in rags and squalid of face. So setting the Ephesians round him, Apollonius said: "Pelt this enemy of the gods, gathering as many stones as you can." The Ephesians wondered what he meant, and thought it dreadful to kill a stranger so wretchedly off — for he kept entreating them and saying many things to move their pity — but Apollonius pressed on, urging the Ephesians to drive him hard and not let up. And when some began with a few shots at him, and the man who seemed to blink looked up of a sudden and showed eyes full of fire, the Ephesians understood that it was a demon, and stoned him so that they heaped a cairn of stones over him. After a little while Apollonius bade them take away the stones and learn the beast they had killed. So when what seemed to have been pelted was uncovered, the man had vanished, but a dog appeared, in form like a Molossian, but in size like the largest lion, crushed by the stones and foaming at the mouth like a mad thing. So the statue of the Averter, which is Heracles, is set up about the place where the phantom was pelted.

The governor of Baetica was eager to come to a meeting with Apollonius, but he said that his company would seem unpleasant to those who were not philosophers; yet the man pressed his request. And since he was said to be a worthy man and at variance with the mimes of Nero, Apollonius wrote him a letter that he should come to Gadeira; and laying aside the pomp of his office he came with a few of those most attached to him. When they had greeted one another and had sent away those present, what they discussed no one knows; but Damis conjectures that they came to an agreement against Nero. For after they had conferred privately for three days, the one departed embracing Apollonius, and the other said, "Farewell, and remember Vindex." What was this? Against Nero, while he sang in Achaea, the western peoples are said to have been stirred up by Vindex, a man fit to cut the strings which Nero so ignorantly twanged; for he addressed to the camps over which he was set a speech against him such as one might breathe forth against a tyrant out of a most noble philosophy: he said that Nero was anything rather than a player of the lyre, and a player of the lyre rather than a king; and he charged him with madness and avarice and cruelty and every kind of wantonness, but the cruellest of his deeds he did not lay to his charge — that he had justly killed his own mother, since she had borne such a son. Knowing then that this would be so, Apollonius set the neighbouring governor in array with Vindex, all but taking up arms himself on behalf of Rome.

That evening, then, they were busy with moderate matters not worthy of record, and slept where they had supped; but at daybreak Apollonius, after worshipping the Sun as was his wont, was standing fixed in some thought, when Nilus, who was the youngest of the Naked Sages, ran up to him and said, "We have come to you." "Naturally," said Apollonius, "for I too have come a road to you, the road from the sea here." And saying this he followed Nilus. Having addressed them and been addressed — for they met one another about the portico — he said, "Where shall we sit together?" "Here," said Thespesion, pointing to the grove. Now Thespesion was the eldest of the Naked Sages, and led them all; and the rest followed the eldest with an orderly and leisurely walk, as the Hellanodicae follow theirs. When they had sat down, as it chanced — for this they no longer did in order — they all looked to Thespesion as the host of the discourse, and he began thus: "They say you have visited Pytho and Olympia, Apollonius — for Stratocles of Pharos reported this here, saying he had met you there — and that Pytho escorts those who come to her with flute and song and harping, and thinks fit to offer comedies and tragedies, and then provides the bare contest late after these; whereas Olympia removes such things as unfitting and not good there, and provides for those who come to her naked athletes, this being the ordinance of Heracles. Think these things here to be over against Indian wisdom in this way: for they, as if calling men to Pytho, court the people with varied allurements, but we, as in Olympia, are naked. The earth here spreads nothing beneath us, nor gives us milk, as to Bacchants, or wine, nor does the air bear us aloft; but spreading the earth itself beneath us we live, sharing with it its natural gifts, that it may give them gladly and not be tortured against its will. And that we are not unable to work wonders" — he pointed to a tree, an elm it was, the third from that under which they conversed — "bid the wise Apollonius be addressed by it." And it addressed him, as it was bidden, the tree did, and the voice was articulate and feminine. He did these things to point against the Indians, thinking to turn Apollonius from his opinion of them, since he was always going through every saying and deed of the Indians. And Thespesion added this too: that it is enough for the wise man to be pure of food that has breath in it, and of desire, which comes in through the eyes, and of envy, which comes as a teacher of injustice to the hand and the mind; and that truth has no need of wonder-working and forced art. "For consider Apollo," he said, "the Delphian, who holds the centre of Greece for the utterance of oracles. There, then, as you yourself surely know, he who wants the voice asks a short question, and Apollo, without any prodigy, says what he knows; and yet it would have been easy for him to shake all Parnassus, and to turn the springs of Castalia into wine by changing them, and to refuse Cephisus to be a river; but he, boasting in none of these things, declares the bare truth itself. Let us think that not even the gold or the offerings that seem splendid come to him by his own will, nor that Apollo rejoices in his temple, even though it should be shown twice as great as it now is; for this god once dwelt in a humble roof too, and a little hut was put together for him, into which, they say, the bees contributed wax and the birds feathers. For simplicity is a teacher of wisdom, a teacher of truth, which if you praise you will seem truly wise, forgetting the fables among the Indians. For 'do this' or 'do not do this,' 'I know' or 'I do not know,' 'this thing rather than that' — what need have these of din? What need of thundering, or rather of being thunderstruck? You have seen in the writings of painting the Heracles of Prodicus, how Heracles is a youth, not yet in the choice of his life, and Vice and Virtue, taking hold of him, lead him to themselves: the one decked out in gold and necklaces and a sea-purple robe, with the bloom of the cheek and the braidings of the hair and the painting of the eyes, and she has a golden sandal too, for she is painted exulting in this; while the other is like one worn with toil, of harsh aspect, having made squalor her ornament, unshod is Virtue and plain in dress, and would have appeared naked, had she not known what is seemly in women. Think then of yourself too, Apollonius, as standing midway between Indian and our own wisdom, and hearing the one say that she will spread flowers for you to sleep on, and, by Zeus, give you milk to drink and feed you on honeycombs, and that you shall have nectar from her and wings whenever you wish, and she will wheel in tripods as you drink and golden thrones, and you shall toil at nothing, but all things will come to you of themselves; and the other say that you must lie on the ground in squalor, and appear naked, as we do, toiling, and hold nothing dear or sweet that came to you without labour, and be neither a boaster nor a hunter of conceit, and abstain even from dreams that rise from the earth. If then you choose according to Heracles, and use an adamantine resolve, not dishonouring truth nor declining the simplicity that is according to nature, you will say that you have taken many lions, and cut off many hydras, and Geryones and Nessuses and all his labours; but if you welcome the way of the mountebanks, you will flatter eyes and ears, and you will seem no wiser than another, and you will become the prize of a Naked Egyptian sage."

While Domitian was purposing this, and was already writing to the governor of Asia that Apollonius should be seized and brought up, the Tyanean foresaw it all, divinely and as was his custom; and saying to his companions that he had need of a secret journey, he put some in mind of the ancient Abaris, and that he had set out upon some such undertaking. But he, not revealing his own mind even to Damis, sailed with him to Achaea; and landing at Corinth and doing for the Sun about midday all that he was wont to do, he set out at evening for the land of the Sicilians and the Italians. Meeting a fair wind and a smooth current that ran beneath the sea, he came to Dicaearchia on the fifth day. There he fell in with Demetrius, who was held the boldest of the philosophers, since he was living not far from Rome; and Demetrius understood that he had withdrawn himself from the tyrant. But, for the sake of conversation, Apollonius said: "I have caught you living delicately, and in the most blessed dwelling-place of happy Italy—if indeed it is happy—where they say that Odysseus too, abiding with Calypso, forgot the smoke of Ithaca and his home." Demetrius embraced him, and with some words of good omen said: "O gods, what will philosophy suffer, being endangered in such a man as this?" "And in what danger is it?" said Apollonius. "In the very things," he said, "that you have come foreknowing; for if I am ignorant of your mind, I do not even know my own. But let us not talk here; let us go where our converse will be ours alone, and let Damis be present too—Damis, whom I, by Heracles, hold the Iolaus of your labours."

Having so disposed the tyrant and shown to be a plaything of his own philosophy the man terrible to all Greeks and barbarians, he left the court before noon, and about late afternoon appeared at Dicaearchia to Demetrius and Damis; and this was indeed the meaning of his charging Damis not to wait for the defence, but to go on foot to Dicaearchia. For he did not foretell what he had resolved, but bade the man most fit to him do the things that followed upon his resolves.

That in sacrificing or dedicating one should not exceed due measure, he taught in this way. When many had once gathered in the temple, just after the Cilician had been driven out, he asked the priest thus: "Are the gods just?" "Most just," he said. "And are they intelligent?" "And what," said he, "is more intelligent than the divine?" "Do they know the affairs of men, or are they without experience of them?" "Why, this," said he, "is the chief respect in which the gods surpass men: that men, through weakness, do not even know their own affairs, while it belongs to the gods to know both theirs and ours." "All most excellent, priest," said he, "and most true. Since, then, they know all things, it seems to me that the man who comes to the house of a god, conscious of good deeds in himself, should pray such a prayer as this: 'O gods, give me what is owed me.' For surely, priest, to the holy what is owed is good things, and to the base the opposite; and the gods, acting well, send away whomever they find sound and unwounded by vice, crowning him, not with golden crowns, but with all good things; but whomever they see branded and corrupt, they leave to justice, being angry with them only so far as that they dared to enter even temples while unclean." And glancing at the same time toward Asclepius, "You play the philosopher, Asclepius," he said, "in your ineffable wisdom that is akin to yourself, by not allowing the base to come here, not though they should bring you all the treasures of India and Sardis. For it is not in honour of the divine that they offer and dedicate these things, but to purchase justice, which you do not grant them, being most just." Many such things he discoursed in the temple while still in his youth. And these too belong to his time at Aegae.

As they rode toward the Indus, they came upon a boy of about thirteen years riding on an elephant and striking the beast. When they marveled, "What is the work, Damis," he said, "of a good horseman?" "What else," he said, "than, having seated himself upon the horse, to govern it and turn it with the bridle and chastise it when it grows disorderly, and to foresee that the horse does not fall into a pit or trench or chasm, when it goes through marsh or mud?" "And shall we require nothing else, Damis," he said, "of the good horseman?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said: "to give the horse rein when it leaps up an incline, but, when it goes down a slope, not to give way to it, but to pull it back; and to stroke its ears or mane; and not always to use the whip seems to me the mark of a wise horseman, and I would praise one who rides thus." "And what does the war-horse and battle-charger require?" "The same things, Apollonius," he said, "and besides these, the casting of weapons and the guarding against them, the charge and the retreat and the rallying of comrades against the enemy, and not letting the horse be terrified when a shield clangs or helmets flash or there is a shout of men singing the paean and raising the war-cry—all this, I think, belongs to the wisdom of horsemanship." "What then," he said, "will you say of this horseman upon the elephant?" "Far more marvelous, Apollonius," he said; "for that one so young should be set over so great a beast and steer it with the hooked staff which you see him drive into the elephant like an anchor, and should fear neither the look of the beast nor its height nor its great strength, seems to me a thing more than human; and I would not have believed it, by Athena, had I heard it from another." "What, then," he said, "if someone wished to sell us the boy, would you buy him, Damis?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "with all that I have. For to lord it, like one who has seized a citadel, over the greatest of beasts the earth feeds, seems to me the mark of a free and brilliant nature." "And what use will you make of the boy," he said, "if you do not also buy the elephant?" "I will set him over my house," he said, "and my servants, and he will rule them far better than I." "And are you not fit," he said, "to rule your own?" "In the same way as you, Apollonius," he said; "for I too have left my affairs and go about, like you, in love of learning and despising the things abroad." "But if you bought the boy, Damis, and you had two horses, one a racer, the other a war-horse, would you set him upon the horses?" "Upon the racer," he said, "perhaps I would, since I see others doing so; but the battle-horse and the horse in arms, how should this boy mount it? For he could not carry the shield horsemen need, nor breastplate nor helmet; and how should he wield a spear, who could not yet brandish the shaft of a dart or arrow, seeming still to lisp at warlike things?" "Then it is something else, Damis," he said, "that drives and directs this elephant, and not this driver, whom you all but worship in your amazement." And when he said, "What could this be, Apollonius? For I see nothing upon the beast except the boy," "This beast," he said, "is teachable beyond all others, and once it has been compelled to live under a man, it endures everything from the man and practices conformity with him, and rejoices to feed from his hand, like little dogs, and fawns on him with its trunk as he approaches, and lets him thrust his head into its throat and gapes as long as the man wishes, as we saw among the nomads. But by night it is said to lament its slavery—not, by Zeus, with the shriek it commonly utters, but with a piteous and pitiable wailing; and if a man come upon it while it bewails these things, the elephant checks its lament, as though ashamed. So it rules itself, Damis, and the persuasion of its nature leads it rather than the man set over it and directing it."

As they were about to halt in the village near by — it is not yet a stade distant from the hill of the sages — they say they saw a youth running towards them, the blackest of all the Indians, with a crescent gleaming faintly between his brows. This same thing I hear told in later times of Memnon, the foster-child of Herodes the sophist; he was of Ethiopian stock, and in his boyhood this gleam was thought to shine, but as he grew to manhood it faded and vanished together with his youthful bloom. The Indian, they say, carried a golden anchor, which the Indians use as a herald's wand, signifying that he can stay all things.
