Having purged the Ephesians of the disease and having had enough of the affairs of Ionia, he set out for Greece. So going to Pergamum and delighting in the temple of Asclepius, and suggesting to the suppliants of the god what they should do to win favourable dreams, and healing many, he came to the Troad; and filled with all the ancient lore concerning them, he visited the tombs of the Achaeans, and saying much over them, and offering many bloodless and pure sacrifices, he bade his companions go to the ship, but he himself said he would pass the night on the mound of Achilles. His companions tried to frighten him from it — for by now the Dioscoridae and the Phaedimi and all such company were with Apollonius — saying that Achilles still appeared terrible; for this even those in Ilium were persuaded of him. "And yet," he said, "I know well that Achilles delights in meetings; for he greeted Nestor from Pylos warmly, since he always told him something useful, and he honoured Phoenix his fosterer and attendant and the like, since Phoenix passed his time with him in discourse; and he looked most gently on Priam, though most hostile to him, when he heard him speak; and meeting Odysseus in their quarrel, he showed himself so moderate that he seemed to Odysseus fair rather than terrible. The shield and the helmet that nod, as they say, terribly, are, I think, for the Trojans, since he remembers what he suffered from them when they broke faith with him over the marriage; but I have nothing to do with Ilium, and I shall discourse with him more gracefully than his companions of old; and if he kills me, as you say, I shall lie with Memnon, I suppose, and Cycnus, and perhaps Troy will bury me in a hollow grave, like Hector." Such things he said to his companions, half in play, half in earnest, and went up the mound alone, while they went to the ship, evening being now come.

As things were aflame about the west, they turned thence toward Libya and the Tyrrhenians, going partly on foot and partly by ship, and put in at Sicily, where Lilybaeum is. Sailing on past Messene and the strait, where the Tyrrhenian sea, meeting the Adriatic, makes the Charybdis dangerous, they say they heard that Nero had fled, that Vindex was dead, and that some men from Rome itself, and others from wherever it might be among the nations, were laying hold of the empire. When his companions asked him to what these things would come and to whom the empire would belong, he said, "To many Thebans." For he likened the power which Vitellius and Galba and Otho used for a short time to the Thebans, who for a very brief time were brought into the affairs of the Greeks.

When he had said this, all turned to Apollonius — those about himself knowing that he would reply, those about Thespesion wondering what he would say against it. He, praising Thespesion for his fluency and force, said, "Do you add anything?" "No, by Zeus," he said, "for I have spoken." And when he asked again whether any other of the Egyptians would, "Of all of them," he said, "you have heard through me." So pausing a little and fixing his eyes on what had been said, Apollonius spoke thus: "The choice of Heracles, which Prodicus says he made as a youth, is soundly stated by you, and in accordance with the mind of philosophy, you wise men of Egypt; but it does not concern me at all. For I have not come to make you counsellors of my life, having long ago chosen what seemed best to me; and being the eldest of you except Thespesion, I myself might more reasonably have counselled you on the choice of wisdom, had I met you not yet having chosen. Yet, old as I am and come so far in wisdom, I shall not hesitate to use you as reckoners of my own resolve, teaching you that I rightly chose these things, than which nothing better has yet come into my mind. For having perceived something great in Pythagoras, and that by a wisdom unspeakable he knew not only who he himself was but who he had been, and that he came pure to the altars, and used a belly undefiled by the eating of things that breathe, and a body pure of all garments made of dead creatures, and that he was the first of men to restrain his tongue, finding the rule of silence under the device of an 'ox upon it,' and that he established all the rest of his philosophy as oracular and true — I ran to his doctrines, not choosing one wisdom out of two, as you, best Thespesion, counsel. For philosophy, setting before me her own doctrines, all that they are, and throwing about them an order suited to each, bade me look upon them and choose soundly. The grace of all of them was august and divine, and a man might have shut his eyes before some of them out of amazement; but my eye stood firm toward all of them, for they encouraged me, drawing me on and proclaiming what they would give. And when one of them said that she would pour over me, without my toiling, a great swarm of pleasures, and another that she would give me rest after toil, and another that she would mingle good cheer with the toil — everywhere pleasures showed through, and the reins of the belly were loosed, and a hand ready toward wealth, and no bridle of the eyes, but loves and longings and such passions were allowed; one of them boasted that she could restrain such things, but she was bold and abusive and with elbows thrust against everything — I saw a form of wisdom unspeakable, by which even Pythagoras was once mastered, and which stood not among the many, but apart from them and silent. Understanding that I did not consent to the others, but that I did not yet know hers, she said, 'My young man, I am unpleasant and full of toils; for if any one come to my ways, he must of his own choice take away from his table all that has life, and forget wine, and not muddy the bowl of wisdom which stands in souls free of wine; nor shall a cloak warm him, nor wool sheared from a living creature; sandals of papyrus I give them, and to sleep where they may; and if I perceive them mastered by the pleasures of love, there are pits for me, down which justice, the attendant of wisdom, bears and thrusts them; and so harsh am I to those who choose my ways that I hold even bonds upon their tongues. But what shall be yours if you endure these things, learn from me. Self-control and justice straightway, and to think no man enviable, and to be terrible to tyrants rather than to lie beneath them, and to appear sweeter to the gods, sacrificing little, than those who pour out before them the blood of bulls; and being pure I will give you foreknowledge too, and so fill your eyes with light that you may discern a god and know a hero and convict shadowy phantoms when they belie the forms of men.' This is the choice of life I made, you wise men of Egypt, which choosing soundly and according to Pythagoras I neither deceived nor was deceived; for I became what the true philosopher should, and of all that she said she would give to one who pursued philosophy, I have all. For I made a study of the origin of the art and whence its principles came, and it seemed to me to belong to men of surpassing endowment who had searched out divine things best, and the soul, of which the immortal and unbegotten are the springs of generation. Now to the Athenians this argument seemed not at all suited; for the argument of Plato, which he there divinely and most wisely uttered about the soul, they themselves slandered, admitting opinions about the soul contrary to this and untrue. So one had to consider what city, what nation of men there was, among whom — not this man yes, that man no — every age should speak the same about the soul. And I, my youth so leading me, and my not yet understanding, looked to you, since you were said to know things prodigiously; and I went through these matters to my own teacher. But he, checking me, said: 'If you happened to be one of those who love, or of an age for loving, and then, meeting a fair youth and admiring him for his bloom, you sought too whose son he was — and his father were a breeder of horses and a general, and his grandfathers furnishers of choruses, and you called him the son of some captain of a trireme or phylarch — do you think you would win the favourite by these names, or that he might find you unpleasant for naming the youth not from his father but from an alien and bastard stock? So, loving wisdom which the Indians found, you name it not from its natural fathers but from those by adoption, and you give the Egyptians something greater than if, as they themselves sing, the Nile should rise for them mingled with honey.' This turned me to the Indians rather than to you, when I had reflected about them that such men are finer in understanding, dwelling among purer beams, and truer in their opinions about nature and the gods, as being near the gods and dwelling at the springs of the life-giving and warm substance; and when I met them I felt toward the profession of the men something like what the Athenians are said to have felt toward the wisdom of Aeschylus. For he became a poet of tragedy, and seeing the art unfurnished and not yet adorned — if he had only contracted the choruses, which were drawn out at length, or invented the dialogues of the actors, doing away with the length of the monologues, or devised the dying behind the scenes, so as not to slay in open view — even this would not have been divorced from wisdom, and he might be thought to have given an idea to another less skilful in poetry. But he, considering himself, that he should speak worthily of making tragedy, and considering the art too, that it was naturally suited to grandeur rather than to the abased and underfoot, laid hold of costume modelled on the forms of the heroes, and set the actors upon buskins, that they might walk evenly with the heroes; and first he adorned them with robes such as it befits heroes and heroines to wear; whence the Athenians held him the father of tragedy, and called him even when dead to the Dionysia, for by their decree the plays of Aeschylus were produced again, and he won the victory anew. And yet of a well-furnished tragedy the grace is small, for it delights in a little part of the day, like the season of the Dionysia; but of philosophy, when it is composed as Pythagoras judged right and held divine, as before Pythagoras the Indians did, the grace is not for a short time, but for boundless and more than number. So I think I have felt nothing unreasonable in being mastered by a well-furnished philosophy, which the Indians, arraying it for what is fitting, wheel out upon a lofty and divine machine. That I admired them with justice, and with justice hold them wise and blessed, it is now time to learn. I saw men dwelling upon the earth and not upon it, and walled without walls, and possessing nothing yet possessing the things of all. And if I touch on riddles, the wisdom of Pythagoras allows this, for he handed down riddling too, having found silence a teacher of speech. Of this wisdom you yourselves were once the counsellors of Pythagoras, in the time when you praised the things of the Indians, being yourselves of old Indians. But when, out of shame at the reason for which you came here from the wraths of the earth, you wished to seem other men rather than Ethiopians come from the Indians, everything was done by you toward this end; whence you were stripped of the equipment that came from there, as though stripping off with it the being Ethiopians, and you voted to worship the gods after the Egyptian rather than your own fashion, and fell to discourses not fitting about the Indians, as though you yourselves were not slandered by the very thing from which you have come to be slandered. Nor have you yet refashioned this, you who even today have made a display of it, abusive and iambic, saying that the Indians practise nothing good but astonishments and seductions, some for the eyes, some for the ears; and not yet knowing my wisdom, you appear insensible of the opinion held of it. For myself I will say nothing — may I be what the Indians hold me — but the Indians I do not allow you to touch. But if there is in you any sound wisdom of the Himeraean man, who, singing of Helen contrary to his former tale, called it a palinode — 'this story is not true' — it is now time for you too to say so, taking up a better opinion of them than that which now stands by you. And if you are unmusical even toward a palinode, yet you ought at least to spare men whom the gods, thinking them worthy of their own possessions, do not think themselves unworthy of what those men have got. You went through, Thespesion, an account of Pytho too, as giving her oracles simply and without furnishing, and your example of the argument was the temple put together of wax and feathers. To me, however, not even these seem unfurnished; for the line 'bring feathers, you birds, and wax, you bees' belongs to one furnishing a house and the form of a house; and he, I think, thinking these small things and beneath his wisdom, needed another temple and another, and now great ones and a hundred feet long, and on one of them he is said to have hung golden Sirens too, holding a certain persuasion of the Sirens; and he gathered the most esteemed offerings into Pytho for ornament's sake, and neither drove away statuary, which brought him colossi to the temple, some of gods, some of men, some of horses and bulls and other creatures, nor Glaucus coming with his stand, nor the captured citadel of Ilium which Polygnotus paints there. For surely he did not think the Lydian gold an ornament of Pytho, but brought that in on behalf of the Greeks, showing them, I think, the wealth of the barbarians, that they might long for that rather than for sacking one another's goods; but the Greek manner, suited to his own wisdom, he furnished, and with it adorned Pytho. And I think that for ornament's sake too he set his oracles into metre. For had he not been making this display, he would have made his answers thus: 'Do this' or 'do not do this,' and 'go' or 'do not go,' and 'make allies' or 'do not' — for these are brief, or, as you say, naked; but that he might appear grand of speech and pleasanter to those who ask, he fitted on poetry, and does not think there is anything he does not know, but says he knows even the sand, how much it is, having numbered it, and that he has comprehended all the measures of the sea. Or do you set down these things too as wonder-mongering, because Apollo declares them haughtily and with a right pride? But, that you may not be vexed, Thespesion, at the saying — old women with sieves hung on them go to shepherds, and at times to herdsmen, healing the sick of the flocks by divination, as they say, and they think fit to be called wise and wiser than the plain seers. This is what you too seem to me beside the wisdom of the Indians; for they are divine and adorned after the Pythian manner, but you — yet nothing shall be said further, for fair speech is dear to me, and dear to the Indians, which I would welcome as at once the attendant and the leader of my tongue, hunting what is possible to me with praise and love of them, but what is not within my reach, leaving it untouched by blame. But you, hearing in Homer's Cyclopeia how the earth feasts the wildest and most lawless, unsown and unploughed, rejoice in the tale; and if certain Edonians or Lydians keep Bacchic revel, you do not disbelieve that it will give them springs of milk and wine and make them drink of these; yet from the Bacchants of all wisdom will you take away gifts coming of themselves from the earth? Tripods of themselves come to the banquets of the gods too, and Ares, ignorant and hostile as he is, has not yet been painted as charging Hephaestus over them, nor is there any record that the gods ever heard such a charge: 'You do wrong, Hephaestus, in adorning the banquet of the gods and setting marvels about it.' Nor was he ever blamed for the golden handmaidens, as corrupting the materials, because he made the gold to breathe; for every art will care for ornament, since the very existence of the arts was found out for ornament's sake. And to go unshod, and the cloak, and to have a wallet hung on one — this is a device of ornament; for even being naked, as you are, though it resembles an unfurnished and plain attire, is studied for ornament's sake, and is not even free of what is called conceit in another. As for the ancestral customs of the Sun and the Indians, and the manner in which he rejoices to be worshipped, let them hold their own law; for the gods below welcome trenches and the rites done in the hollow earth, but of the Sun the air is the chariot, and those who would fittingly sing him must rise from the earth and soar aloft with the god. This all men wish, but the Indians alone can do."

Having said this, he led them to the country place of the elder Cicero, which is near the town. When they had seated themselves under a plane-tree, the cicadas, as the breeze played softly under them, were at their songs; and Demetrius, looking up at them, said: "O blessed and truly wise, how the Muses have taught you a song not yet brought to trials or slanders, and have made you stronger than the belly, and have settled you, away from human envy, in these trees, on which, happy beings, you sing the happiness that is yours and the Muses'." Apollonius understood whither this tended, and finding fault with the words as feebler than his profession, said: "When you wished to deliver a praise of cicadas, you did not deliver it openly, but cowered here, as though there were a public law laid down that no one should praise cicadas." "It was not for praise," he said, "that I spoke thus, but to show that to these their music-halls are left free, but to us not even to mutter is allowed; rather, wisdom has been found to be an indictment. And while the charge of Anytus and Meletus says, 'Socrates does wrong by corrupting the young and bringing in strange divinities,' against us they write thus: 'So-and-so does wrong by being wise and just, by understanding the gods, by understanding men, and by knowing much concerning the laws.' And you—by how much you are the wisest of us, by so much the wiser an accusation has been found against you; for Domitian wishes you to share in the charges on which Nerva and his fellows are in exile." "And they are in exile—but on what charge?" "On the greatest of present charges, as it seems to the prosecutor; for he says he has caught them leaping at his own rule, and that you stirred the men to this, having, I suppose, cut up a boy." "What," he said, "as though the rule were dissolved by a eunuch?" "It is not this," he said, "that we are falsely accused of; they say that you sacrificed a boy for the sake of the divination which the fresh entrails reveal; and there is added to the indictment something about your dress and your way of life, and the fact that there are those by whom you are worshipped. I heard this from Telesinus, a man dear to both you and me." "A godsend," he said, "if we shall meet Telesinus; for you mean, I suppose, the philosopher who held consular office under Nero." "Him I mean," he said. "But how should you come together with him? For tyrannies are more suspicious toward all men of repute, if they enter into common talk with men in such a charge as you now bear; and besides, Telesinus withdrew himself even by the edict that has now been proclaimed against all philosophy, choosing rather to flee as a philosopher than to remain as a consular." "Let the man not run risk on my account," said Apollonius, "for he runs risk enough on behalf of philosophy. But tell me this, Demetrius: what do you think I should best say or do to dispose of my own fear?" "Do not jest," he said, "nor say that you fear what you dread; for if you held these things fearful, you would have gone off in flight from the argument about them." "And would you," he said, "have fled, if you were in the danger I am in?"

Now Damis had arrived the day before and met with Demetrius about the things before the trial; and Demetrius was more cautiously disposed than befits one who hears about Apollonius, by what he had heard; and again the next day he was asking about the same things, walking with him along the sea where are the tales about Calypso; for they despaired, as of one who would not come, since the affairs of the tyranny were grievous to all, but they honoured what he had ordered because of the man's nature. Giving up, then, they sat down in the nymphaeum where is the jar—it is of white stone, holding a spring of water that neither overflows the mouth nor, if one bales it out, falls short. Having discoursed about the nature of the water, not very earnestly because of their despondency over the man, they led the argument back to the things before the trial.

There was a governor of the Cilicians, an insolent man and corrupt in matters of love. Word of the beauty of Apollonius came to him; and he, bidding farewell to the business he was engaged in—he was holding an assize at Tarsus—set out for Aegae, saying that he himself was ill and had need of Asclepius. And coming to Apollonius as he walked apart, he said, "Commend me to the god." But he replied: "And what need have you of one to commend you, if you are a good man? For the gods welcome the worthy even without those who introduce them." "Because, by Zeus, Apollonius," he said, "the god has made you his guest-friend, but not me yet." "Why, nobility of character was my introducer," he said, "which I use as far as a young man can; and I am a servant and companion of Asclepius. If you too care for nobility, go boldly to the god and pray for whatever you wish." "By Zeus," he said, "I will, if I may first pray to you." "And what will you pray to me for?" "What one should pray to the beautiful for: we pray them to share their beauty and not to grudge their bloom." He said this with affected softness, making his eyes melt, and writhing himself, and in short all that such wanton and notorious men do. But Apollonius, looking at him fiercely and with a glare, said, "You are mad, you abomination." And when the man not only took this with anger, but even threatened to cut off his head, Apollonius, laughing, cried out, "O the day of so-and-so!" And it was the third day from that on which executioners killed that insolent man along the road, on the charge that with Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, he had been plotting revolt against the Romans. These things and many such are recorded by Maximus of Aegae, who was even thought worthy of imperial letters, being held in high repute for his eloquence.

Coming to the Indus, they say they saw a herd of elephants crossing the river, and heard the following about the beast: that some of them are marsh-dwellers, others mountain-dwellers, and a third kind, the plain-dwellers, and they are caught for the use of war. For they fight equipped with towers such as receive ten or fifteen of the Indians together, from which the Indians shoot arrows and hurl javelins, as though casting from gates. And the beast itself counts its trunk a hand and uses it for hurling. As much as the Libyan elephant is larger than a Nisaean horse, by so much are the Indian larger than those of Libya. As to the age of the animal, and that they are very long-lived, others too have spoken; but these men say they came upon an elephant at Taxila, the greatest city in India, which the natives anoint with myrrh and bind with fillets. For it was one of those that had fought against Alexander on the side of Porus, and which, because it had fought eagerly, Alexander dedicated to the Sun. There were upon it spirals of gold about its tusks—or horns—and Greek letters upon them, saying: "ALEXANDER, SON OF ZEUS, TO THE SUN, AJAX." For he set this name on the elephant, deeming a great beast worthy of a great name. And the natives reckoned it three hundred and fifty years since the battle, not yet saying how old it was when it fought.

Running up to Apollonius, he addressed him in the Greek tongue; and this seemed no great marvel, since all in the village also spoke Greek. But the words "Hail, So-and-so" — addressing him by name — astonished the rest, and gave the man confidence as to the purpose of his coming. For looking at Damis he said: "We have come, in plain truth, to men who are wise; for they seem to have foreknowledge." And at once he asked the Indian what he ought to do, longing now for the meeting. The Indian said: "These must halt here, but you must come as you are; for they themselves command it.

Apollonius, coming about dawn, said: "Where is Antisthenes the Parian?" Now this man had been with him in Ilium for seven days already. When Antisthenes answered, he said: "Have you anything to do, young man, with Troy?" "Very much," he said; "for I am of old Trojan stock." "And a son of Priam too?" "By Zeus," he said; "for from this I think I am noble and of noble line." "With reason, then," he said, "Achilles forbids me to keep company with you; for when he bade me go on an embassy to the Thessalians concerning the charges he brings against them, and I asked what else besides this I might do to please him, he said, 'Do not make the youth from Paros a companion in your wisdom; for he is sufficiently a son of Priam, and does not cease hymning Hector.'

That he foreknew such things by a divine impulse, and that those who think the man a wizard reason unsoundly, the things already told make plain; but let us consider this also. Wizards — and I hold them the most wretched of men — some by torturing phantoms, some by barbarous sacrifices, some by some incantation or anointing, claim to alter what is fated; and many of them, brought to trial on such charges, have admitted that they are skilled in these things. But he followed what came from the Fates, and foretold that these things must come to pass; and he foreknew, not by wizardry, but from what the gods revealed. And when among the Indians he saw the tripods and the cup-bearers and all the things that came in of themselves, as I have told, he neither asked how they were contrived, nor desired to learn it, but praised them, while not thinking it right to emulate them.

Damis says he breathed again when he heard these things; for by the words of Apollonius the Egyptians were so affected that Thespesion, though black, was plainly seen to blush, and there appeared in the rest too a kind of astonishment at the things they heard from him as he discoursed forcibly and with fluency; and the youngest of the Egyptians, whose name was Nilus, even leaped up in wonder, and crossing over to Apollonius joined hands with him and begged him to tell the conversations he had had with the Indians. And Apollonius said, "To you I would grudge no discourse, since you are, as I see, a lover of hearing and welcome all wisdom; but to Thespesion, and any other who holds the things of the Indians nonsense, I would not pour out the discourses from there." Whereupon Thespesion said, "But if you were a merchant or skipper and brought us some cargo from there, would you, because it came from India, think fit to dispose of it untested, giving neither taste nor sample of it?" And Apollonius, taking him up, said, "I would furnish it to those who wished. But if someone, coming to the sea just as the ship had put in, abused the cargo and slandered it as coming from a land that bears nothing sound, and rebuked me for not having sailed for serious freight, and persuaded the rest to think so too — do you think anyone, having put into such a harbour, would cast an anchor or a cable, rather than shake out his sails and lift his ship into the open sea, entrusting his goods to the winds more gladly than to surly and inhospitable manners?" "But I," said Nilus, "lay hold of the cables, and entreat you, skipper, to share with me the cargo you bring; and I would gladly embark with you in the ship, a supercargo and mindful of your freight."

"No, by Athena," he said, "if anyone were giving judgement; but where there is no trial, and where, even if I made my defence, no one would hear—or would hear, yet would kill me though I did no wrong—you would never have allowed me to choose so cold and servile a death in place of the one that befits philosophy. And to philosophy, I think, it befits to die either freeing a city, or defending one's parents and children and brothers and the rest of one's kin, or contending for friends, who to wise men are more to be chosen than kinsmen, or than those purchased through love. But to die not for true charges, but for trumped-up ones, and to furnish the tyrant occasion to seem wise—this is far heavier than if a man, like Ixion (as they say), were bent upon a wheel in mid-air. For you, I think, the very coming here will be the beginning of a contest; for you add it to a sound mind, and to the fact that you would not have ventured the road hither if you had done any wrong; but to Domitian you will not seem so—rather, that having some secret strength you are boldly confident. For that he summoned you, yet not ten days have passed, as they say, and you have already arrived for the trial, not even having heard that you are to be tried—this will give point to the accusation, for you would appear to have foreknown it; and the argument about the boy will gain force. And take care lest the matter of the Fates and Necessity, on which they say you discoursed in Ionia, come upon you, and lest, fate wishing something out of the way, you, being constrained, go toward it unaware—for it is ever the wiser course to be on guard. If you have not forgotten what passed under Nero, you know my part, I suppose, and that I am no slave toward death. But those things had some ease in them; for Nero's lyre seemed to knock away from him the bearing proper to royalty, yet otherwise it fitted not unpleasantly, since through it he often granted truces and held back from murders—me at any rate he did not kill, though I was drawing the sword upon myself, because of those words of yours and mine which I went through at the bath; and the cause of his not killing me was that his voice was then at its prime, and that he was, as he thought, laying hold of brilliant melody. But now—by what fine voice, by what lyre shall we sacrifice? For all things are unmusical and full of gall, and he could be charmed neither by himself nor by others. And yet Pindar, praising the lyre, says that it charms even the spirit of Ares and holds him from war; but this man, though he established a musical contest here and crowns the victors in public, has killed some even of them—men who, they say, sang and played at a musical contest for the last time. You must take counsel also for the men's sake, for you will destroy them too, either by seeming bold, or by saying what you will not persuade. But your safety is at your very feet: of these ships—many, as you see, there are—some will set sail for Libya, some for Egypt, some for Phoenicia and Cyprus, some straight for Sardo, some beyond Sardo; embark on one and make your way to whatever of these nations you will; for tyrannies are less harsh to men in the public eye, if they perceive that such men approve of not living in the public eye."

When Damis had lamented and said something of this sort, "Shall we then ever, O gods, see the noble and good comrade?" Apollonius, hearing—for indeed he chanced to be already standing by the nymphaeum—said, "You shall see; or rather, you have seen." "Alive?" said Demetrius; "but if dead, we have not yet ceased weeping over you." Apollonius then, stretching out his hand, said, "Take hold of me; and if I escape you, I am a phantom come to you from Persephone, such as the gods below show to the more despondent in their mourning; but if I endure your touch, persuade Damis too that I am alive and have not cast off my body." They were no longer able to disbelieve, but rising up they hung upon the man and embraced him, and asked about the defence; for Demetrius held that he had not even made his defence, since he would have perished though doing no wrong, but Damis that he had defended himself—more quickly perhaps, for he did not think it was on that very day. But Apollonius said, "I have made my defence, men, and we are victors; and the matters of the defence came to me today, not long before this hour, for it was already advancing toward noon." "How then," said Demetrius, "did you accomplish so great a journey in a little of the day?" And Apollonius said, "Think anything you like, except a ram and wings of joined wax, and ascribe the procession to a god." "Everywhere," said Demetrius, "I hold that a god foresees your deeds and words, from whom your affairs are so; but the defence, what it was, and what the accusation held, and the character of the judge, and what he asked, and to what you assented or did not—tell all together, that I may tell each to Telesinus, for he will not cease asking about your affairs, who even some fifteen days ago, drinking with me at Antium, fell asleep at the table, and, his cup half-full, seemed in a dream that fire, spreading like a sea over the earth, took off some of the men, while others slipped away in time; for indeed it flowed like water; and that you, not as the many suffered, but swam through it when it parted. And upon this dream he poured libation to the gods of good omen and bade me take courage about you." And Apollonius said, "I do not wonder that Telesinus sleeps over me, for indeed he has long watched over me; but about the trial you shall hear, yet not here, for it is now late afternoon enough and it is time to go to the town, and the talk on the road is pleasanter as it escorts men walking. Let us go, then, talking about what you ask; and I will tell what was done today in the court. For the things before the trial you both know, the one being present, the other having heard, I think, of this man—not once, by Zeus, but again and again, if I do not forget Demetrius; but what you do not yet know, I will go through, threading it from the prophecy and the entering naked." And he went through his own speeches, and at the end of all the "for you shall not kill me," and the leaving of the trial, how he left.

When he heard that his father was dead, he ran to Tyana, and buried him with his own hands beside the tomb of his mother—she too had died not long before—and the property, which was splendid, he divided with his brother, who was dissolute and a lover of drink. His brother was in his twenty-third year and of an age not to be under guardians, while he himself was twenty, and the laws still subjected him to guardians. So, having stayed again at Aegae and made the temple both a Lyceum and an Academy—for it rang with every kind of philosophy—he returned to Tyana, now a man and master of his own affairs. And when someone said to him that it became him to bring his brother to his senses and to change his way of life, "This will seem rash," he said; "for how should I, a young man, bring an elder to his senses? But as far as I can, I will heal him of these afflictions." So he gives him half of his own portion, saying that his brother needed more, and he himself little; and gaining ascendancy over him and drawing him wisely toward obedience to one who corrects, he said: "Our father, who taught and admonished us, has departed; you alone are left to me, and I, I suppose, to you. So if I should err in anything, be my counsellor and heal my failings; and if you yourself should err in anything, bear with me as I teach you." And thus, as those who soothe horses hard to rein and not easily led bring them to obedience, so he brought his brother to compliance and reformed him of his faults, which were many; for he was a slave to dice and wine, and would go revelling after courtesans, vain of the hair which he tended even with dyes, swaggering and walking with his head in the air. When matters between him and his brother were well, he turned now to his other kinsmen, and won over those of them who were in need with the rest of his substance, leaving little for himself; whereupon he said that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, who left his property to herds and flocks, philosophized for sheep rather than for men, and that Crates of Thebes, who threw his substance into the sea, was of use neither to men nor to sheep. And since Pythagoras was praised for the saying that a man should go to no woman but his own, "That," he said, "was laid down by Pythagoras for others; but I, for my part, would neither marry nor ever come to the embrace of love"—surpassing even the saying of Sophocles. For Sophocles said that in reaching old age he had escaped a raging and savage master; but Apollonius, through virtue and self-control, was not overcome by it even in his youth, but, though young and strong of body, mastered it and lorded it over the raging thing. Yet nevertheless some slander him in matters of love, alleging that he committed an error of passion, and on that account spent a year abroad among the nation of the Scythians—a man who never went to the Scythians nor was ever carried away into the passions of love. Indeed not even Euphrates ever slandered the man in matters of love, although he forged false writings against him, as we shall show in our account of Euphrates; for Euphrates was at variance with Apollonius, since the latter checked him in everything he did for the sake of money, and drew him away from money-making and from trafficking in wisdom. But let these things be deferred by me to their proper time.

Juba, who once ruled the Libyan nation, says that Libyan horsemen on elephants once joined battle with one another—some having a tower carved on the tusks, others nothing—and that, night overtaking the battle, the marked ones were defeated and fled to Mount Atlas, and that he himself, four hundred years later, caught one of those that had escaped, and the mark was on it, hollow and not yet worn away by time. This Juba holds the tusks to be horns, because they grow from the same place as the temples, and are not whetted on anything else, and remain as they grew and do not, like teeth, fall out and grow again. But I do not accept the argument. For horns, if not all, at least those of stags, fall out and grow again; whereas of teeth those of men will all fall out and grow again, but in no other animal would a tusk or canine fall out of itself, nor grow again once fallen, since nature has set them in the jaws for the sake of a weapon. And besides, horns trace a circular line at the root each year, as goats and flocks and oxen show, but a tusk grows smooth, and unless something maims it, remains ever such, for it partakes of stony matter and substance. And again, the bearing of horns belongs only to cloven-hoofed animals, but this beast is five-toed and many-cleft at the base, which, because it is not bound up by hooves, stands as in something soft. To all horned creatures nature sets bones beneath, hollow and porous, and makes the horn grow about them from without, but the elephant's she shows solid and uniform; and when split open a thin pipe runs through the middle, as in teeth. The tusks of the marsh-elephants are livid and loose and awkward to work, for in many places caverns lurk in them, and in many places nodules stand up that do not yield to the craftsman's art; those of the mountain-elephants are smaller than these, but sufficiently white and with nothing hard to work in them; but the best are the tusks of the plain-elephants, for they are largest and whitest and pleasant to split open, and become whatever the hand wishes. And if one must record the dispositions of elephants too, the Indians hold those caught in the marshes to be witless and light, those from the mountains malicious and treacherous, and, unless they need something, not to be trusted by men; but the plain-elephants are said to be good-natured and docile and lovers of imitation; at any rate they draw, and dance, and sway to the flute, and leap from the ground.

The word "they themselves" seemed at once Pythagorean to Apollonius, and he followed gladly. The hill on which the sages have their dwelling is, they say, in height the equal of the Acropolis of the Athenians, and it rises straight up from the plain; and a natural rock, equally well-formed, fortifies it, running round it in a circle, on which in many places one may see cloven footprints, and the marks of beards and faces, and here and there backs, as of men who had slipped off. For when Dionysus, together with Heracles, made trial of the place, they say he bade the Pans assail it, as being mighty against earthquakes; but the sages thunderstruck them, and they fell, one this way, one that, and the rocks were as it were stamped with the figures of their failure. About the hill they say they saw a cloud, in which the Indians dwell, visible and invisible, and whatever else they will. Whether there were other gates to the hill, they could not tell; for the cloud about it allowed it to appear neither unbarred nor barred.

So Antisthenes went off unwillingly. And when day came, and the wind blew up from the land, and the ship was about to weigh anchor, more others flocked to her, small as she was, wishing to sail with Apollonius; for it was now late autumn and the sea less sure. So all, holding the man mightier than storm and fire and the hardest of things, wished to embark with him, and begged him to give them a share in the voyage. And since the company was many times the ship's measure, looking out for another and larger ship — for there were many about the Aianteum — he said, "Let us embark here, for it is good to be saved with the more." So rounding the Trojan headland, he bade the pilot put in to the Aeolian land, which lies opposite Lesbos, and make his moorings rather towards Methymna. "For there somewhere," Achilles says, "Palamedes lies, where there is also a statue of him a cubit high, in a form older than Palamedes." And as he went out of the ship he said: "Let us care, O men of Greece, for a good man, through whom is all wisdom; for we should become better than the Achaeans themselves, if we honour for his virtue one whom they slew by no justice." So they leapt from the ship, and he came upon the tomb and found the statue buried beside it. On the base of the statue was inscribed, TO THE DIVINE PALAMEDES. So setting it up — as I too saw — and building a shrine about it large enough for the worshippers of Enodia to feast some ten messmates in it, he made this prayer: "Palamedes, forget the wrath you once wrathed among the Achaeans, and grant that men may become many and wise. Yes, Palamedes, through whom are words, through whom are the Muses, through whom am I.

When they had come to Syracuse, a woman of no obscure family gave birth to a monster, such as no midwife ever delivered: for the infant had three heads, each on its own neck, but all the parts below them belonged to a single body. The cruder interpreters said that Sicily — for it is Trinacria — would perish, unless it should come to agreement and breathe as one; for many of its cities were in faction against themselves and against one another, and ordered life was absent from the island. Others said that Typho, who is many-headed, was threatening Sicily with fresh troubles. But Apollonius said, "Go, Damis, and look at it, whether it is so put together." For it was exposed in public to those who understand portents; and when Damis reported that it was three-headed and male, Apollonius gathered his companions and said: "Three are the emperors of the Romans, whom I lately called Thebans; and none of them will bring his rule to completion, but some, prevailing at Rome itself, and one in the regions bordering on Rome, will perish, casting off the mask sooner than the tyrants of the tragedies." And the saying at once came to light: for Galba died at Rome itself after laying hold of the empire; Vitellius too died after dreaming of empire; and Otho, dying among the western Gauls, did not even obtain a splendid tomb, but lies like a private man; and fortune flew through all this in a single year.

Wishing to break off such talk, Thespesion said: "I am glad, Apollonius, that you are vexed at what you heard; for you may pardon us too for being vexed at the things by which you slandered the wisdom here, before you had even come to a trial of it." He, struck for a moment by the saying, because he had not yet heard about Thrasybulus and Euphrates, but conjecturing, as was his wont, what had happened, said: "The Indians, Thespesion, would not have suffered this, nor would they have given heed to Euphrates letting down such things, for they are wise to foreknow. As for me, I have no private quarrel with Euphrates; but by drawing him away from money and from praising gain got from anything, I seemed to him to give counsel neither suitable nor possible to him; and he counts this a reproach, and never ceases putting together something against me. But since he seemed to you plausible in slandering my character, consider that he slandered you before me; for to me the dangers about him who is to be slandered seem no small thing, for he will be hated, no doubt, though doing no wrong; but neither do those who will listen to the slanders seem free of dangers, if first they are caught honouring falsehood and thinking it worthy of what truth is, and then lightness and easy leading — to be mastered by which is shameful even for a youth — and they will seem envious, making envy their teacher of unjust hearing, and themselves more liable to the slanders which they hold true against others; for the natures of men are more ready to do what they do not disbelieve. May such a man never be a tyrant, nor preside over a people, for under him democracy too will be a tyranny; nor judge a cause, for he will discern nothing aright; nor command a ship, for the ship will be in mutiny; nor lead an army, for the enemy will fare well; nor practise philosophy in such a state, for he will not form opinions toward the truth. And of you Euphrates has taken away even the being wise; for those whom he has led on by falsehood, how could they think themselves worthy of a wisdom from which they have fallen away by being persuaded of things not plausible?" Soothing him, Thespesion said, "Enough of Euphrates and of mean-spirited words; for we might even be reconcilers between you and him, thinking it wise to arbitrate among wise men." "And between me and you," he said, "who will reconcile me? For one slandered must surely be set at war on behalf of the truth." "Let it be so," said Apollonius, "and let us lay hold of earnest things, for this will reconcile us better."

Damis, overcome by the words of Demetrius, said: "Be then a friend at hand to the man, and you may do him some great good; for my word is of small weight, if I should counsel him not to tumble onto upright swords, nor to fling himself against a tyranny held no easier than any. Indeed, of this very journey hither, had I not chanced upon you, I did not even know the meaning; for I follow him faster than a man follows himself, yet if you should ask me whither I sail or for what, I am ridiculous in my voyage, measuring out the Sicilian seas and the Tyrrhenian gulfs, but not knowing for what. And if I ran the risk on a forewarning, I could say to those who ask, that Apollonius is in love with death, and I sail as a rival lover; but since I know nothing, it is now my part to speak of what I do know, and I will speak of it for the man's sake. For if I should die, philosophy will not yet suffer terribly, since I am like a baggage-carrier of a noble soldier, accounted worthy of mention because I follow such a man; but if there shall be someone who kills this man—and tyrannies are well supplied to compose some things and to exalt others—a trophy, I think, will stand against philosophy, fallen in the person of the best of men that ever practised it; and there will be many an Anytus and Meletus against us, indictments now from this quarter, now from that, against those who have associated with Apollonius—how this one laughed as he attacked the tyranny, how that one urged him on as he spoke, how another gave him leave to speak, how another went off with praise of what he heard. But I say that one should die for philosophy as for temples and walls and tombs; for the safety of such things many famous men have welcomed death; but that philosophy should perish—may neither I die for that, nor anyone who loves both her and Apollonius."

Then Demetrius cried out, "I thought you had come saved, but these things are the beginning of dangers for you; for he will seize you when you are denounced and barred from all retreat." But Apollonius, declaring himself strong against the fear of Demetrius, said, "If you too were so easy to catch as he! But how his affairs now stand, I know; for being ever a hearer of flattering words, he has now heard rebuking ones, and the natures of tyrants are torn by such things and grow bilious about them. But I need rest, not having yet bent my knee from the contest." And Damis said, "I, Demetrius, was so disposed toward this man's affairs as even to lead him away from this road on which he has come, and you too, I suppose, counselled this, that he might not go into dangers willing and grievous; but when he chanced to be bound, as it seemed to me, and I held his affairs hopeless, and he said that it lay with himself to be loosed, and, freeing his leg of the bond, showed it—then first I understood the man, that he was divine and stronger than our wisdom; whence, if I should meet even harder things than these, I should fear nothing under him, even in danger. But since evening is near, let us go to the lodging and take care of the man." And Apollonius said, "I need only sleep; the rest I hold in equal account, whether any of it be present or absent." After this, having prayed to Apollo and again to the Sun, he went into the house where Demetrius dwelt, and washing his feet and bidding Damis and his company dine, since they seemed to him to have eaten nothing, he cast himself on the couch, and, chanting over his sleep the verse of Homer, slept, as one who held the present matters not worth pondering.

When Euxenus once asked Apollonius why he did not write, though he held noble opinions and used a style of approved and elevated expression, "Because," he said, "I have not yet kept silence." And from then on he resolved that he must keep silence, and he held his tongue; but his eyes and his mind read much, and stored up much in memory. Indeed, when he reached a hundred years of age, he was stronger in memory than Simonides; and a certain hymn of his to Memory was sung, in which he says that all things are withered by time, but that time itself is ageless and immortal through memory. Yet he was not without grace in company during the time he kept silent; but in answer to what was said his eyes too would make some sign, and his hand, and the nod of his head; nor did he appear unsmiling or sullen, for he kept his love of companions and his kindliness. This way of life, he says, was the most laborious he ever undertook, practised through five whole years; for though he had much to say, he had to say it not; though he heard much that angered him, he had to hear it not; and often, when moved to rebuke many, he had to say to himself, "Endure, my heart and tongue," and when discourses jarred upon him, he had to put off his refutations for the time.

When Apollonius saw the elephants crossing the Indus—there were, I think, thirty of them—and using as their guide the smallest among them, and the larger ones taking up their own young upon the projections of their tusks and binding them fast with their trunks, "These things, Damis," he said, "they do of themselves, with no one ordering them, through intelligence and wisdom; and you see how, like baggage-carriers, they have taken up their young and bound them and lead them?" "I see, Apollonius," he said, "how wisely and intelligently they do it." "What, then, is the meaning of that foolish speculation among those who quibble whether or not goodwill toward offspring is natural? For this even the elephants now proclaim, that it comes to them from nature; for they have surely not learned it from men, as they have other things, since they have not yet lived with men, but, possessing by nature the love of what they have begotten, they care for them and rear their young. And do not speak of the elephants, Damis; for this animal I rank second to man in intelligence and counsel. Rather I consider the bears—how, though they are the fiercest of beasts, they do everything for their cubs; and the wolves—how, ever bent upon plunder, the female guards what she has borne, while the male, for the safety of the whelps, brings her food; and the leopards likewise, which through their heat delight to become mothers, for then they wish to lord it over the males and rule the house, and the males endure everything from them, overcome by the young. There is a story too about lionesses, that they take leopards for lovers and receive them upon the lions' beds in the plains, but when the time of birth comes, they flee up to the mountains and the haunts of the leopards, for they bear spotted young, and so they hide them and suckle them in winding thickets, pretending to spend the day at hunting. For if the lions detect this, they tear the cubs to pieces and rend the litter as bastard. You have surely met one of the lions in Homer too, how he glares terribly for the sake of his cubs and braces himself to enter battle. And they say the tigress, fiercest of beasts in this country and about the Red Sea, rushes upon the ships to demand back her cubs, and if she recovers them goes off rejoicing, but if they sail away she howls beside the sea and sometimes dies. And who does not know about the birds? How eagles and storks would not build a nest before first fitting into it, the one the eagle-stone, the other the lychnis-stone, for the sake of egg-bearing and that snakes may not draw near them. And if we look at the creatures in the sea, we would not wonder that the dolphins, being good-natured, love their young; but the whales and seals and the viviparous tribes—how shall we not wonder, when a seal, which I saw at Aegae shut up for shows, so mourned its cub which died, that it had borne in its pen, that it would not take food for three days, though it is the greediest of beasts; and the whale takes up its young into the cavities of its throat, when something larger than itself pursues it? And a viper was once seen licking and tending the snakes she had borne, with her tongue thrust out. For let us not accept, Damis, the foolish story that vipers are born without a mother; for neither nature has allowed this, nor experience." Damis, taking up the word, said: "Do you allow me, then, to praise Euripides for that iambic line in which he has made Andromache say, 'For all men, then, their children are their soul'?" "I allow it," he said, "for it is wisely and divinely said; but it would have been far wiser and truer if it had been sung of all living things." "You seem, Apollonius," he said, "to be re-writing the line, that we may sing it thus: 'For all living things, then, their children are their soul.'" "And I follow you," he said, "for it is better."

He himself went up by the southern side of the hill, following the Indian; and first he saw a well four fathoms deep, from which a light, of the deepest blue, was sent up to the mouth; and when the noonday sun stood over it, the light was drawn up from the ray and rose, presenting the appearance of a warm rainbow. He learned afterwards about the well, that the earth beneath it was of red arsenic, and that they held the water to be sacred, and no one drank of it or drew it up, but it was reckoned an oath by all the Indians round about. Near it was a crater of fire, from which there rose a leaden-coloured flame, but no smoke darted from it, nor any odour; nor did this crater ever overflow, but it gave forth just so much as not to brim over the pit. Here the Indians purify themselves of their involuntary offences, and so the sages call the well the "well of testing," and the fire the "fire of pardon." And they say they saw two jars of black stone, of the rains and of the winds. The jar of the rains, if India is oppressed by drought, when opened sends up clouds and waters all the earth; but if the rains are excessive, it checks them by being shut. The jar of the winds does the same, I think, as the bag of Aeolus; for opening the jar a little they let one of the winds blow forth in its season, and from this the earth is strengthened. They say also that they came upon statues of gods; and if of Indian or Egyptian gods, no marvel; but the most ancient of the Greek images, that of Athena Polias, and of Apollo of Delos, and of Dionysus of the Marsh, and of Apollo of Amyclae, and all that are thus ancient — these the Indians set up and worship after Greek usage; and they say they dwell in the very midst of India. And they make the hill the navel of this height, and upon it perform the rites of fire, which they say they themselves draw from the sun's rays; to this they also sing a hymn the whole day long, at noon.

He came also to the shrine of Orpheus, putting in at Lesbos. They say that there once Orpheus delighted in divination, until Apollo took it in charge himself. For when men no longer went to Gryneium for oracles, nor to Clarus, nor to where the Apolline tripod is, but Orpheus alone gave oracles — his head having lately come from Thrace — the god stood over him as he prophesied and said: "Cease from what is mine; for I have endured enough of you even singing.

Passing on to Catana, where the mountain Aetna is, they say they heard the people of Catana, who believe that Typho is bound there and that the fire rises from him which makes Aetna smoke; but they themselves came to more credible accounts, befitting men who practise philosophy. Apollonius began with them thus, asking his companions: "Is there such a thing as mythology?" "Yes, by Zeus," said Menippus, "such as the poets praise." "And what do you think of Aesop?" "A teller of myths," he said, "and altogether a maker of fables." "And which of the myths are wise?" "Those of the poets," he said, "since they are sung as having happened." "And what of those of Aesop?" "Frogs," he said, "and asses, and trifles fit for old women and children to chew over." "And yet," said Apollonius, "to me the myths of Aesop seem the more suited to wisdom. For those concerning the heroes, on which all poetry depends, also corrupt their hearers, since the poets recount monstrous loves and marriages of brothers and slanders against the gods and the eating of children and base knaveries and lawsuits; and the air of their having happened draws on the lover and the jealous man and him who desires to be rich or to be a tyrant to do the very things the myths describe. But Aesop, out of wisdom, first of all did not set himself in the common ranks of those who sing such tales, but took a road of his own; then, like those who give a good feast on humbler dishes, from small matters he teaches great ones; and having set forth his story, he adds to it the 'do this' or 'do not do this.' Then he laid hold of truthfulness more than the poets do; for they force their own tales to appear plausible, whereas he, by announcing a tale that is false, as everyone knows, speaks truth by the very fact that he does not profess to speak of true things. And the poet, after telling his own tale, leaves it to the sound-minded hearer to examine whether it happened; whereas Aesop, after telling a false tale and adding an admonition, as he does, shows that he has used falsehood for the usefulness of the hearing. There is charm too in his making the dumb creatures pleasanter to men and worthy of their attention; for having from childhood kept company with these tales and been brought up by them out of infancy, we take up opinions about each of the animals — that some are royal, some simple, some clever, some guileless. And the poet, after saying 'many are the shapes of the divine powers' or some such thing, performs his dance and departs; but Aesop, after delivering his tale as an oracle, brings his discourse to a close in the end he had proposed.

Nilus, longing for the man's discourse, said: "And indeed it befits you to begin the earnest talk, going through for us the journey you made to the nation of the Indians, and the earnest pursuits there, which surely you carried on for brilliant ends." "And I," said Thespesion, "long to hear also about the wisdom of Phraotes; for you are said to bring from the Indians images of his words too." So Apollonius, making the things at Babylon the beginning of his discourse, went through everything, and they listened gladly, subjecting themselves to the discourse. And when it was noon, they broke off the conference, for at this hour the Naked Sages too betake themselves to the sacred rites.

To this Apollonius said that Damis, having spoken cautiously about present things, deserved pardon; for being an Assyrian and dwelling near the Medes, where men do reverence to tyrannies, he gives no great thought to freedom. "But you, Demetrius—I do not know how you will defend yourself to philosophy, laying before me fears of which, even if any seemed true, one ought rather to lead a man away than to settle him deeper into fearing, who did not even dread the things he was likely to suffer. Let the wise man die for the things you named; yet a man might die for these even if he were not wise. For to die for freedom is enjoined by law; to die for one's kin or friends or loved ones, nature has appointed; and nature and law enslave all men—nature even the willing, law the unwilling. But it is more proper to the wise to die for the things they have practised; for those things which, though no law commanded and no nature bred them, they have themselves trained in by strength and daring—for these, if anyone would do them away, let fire come upon the wise man, let the axe come, for none of these will conquer him, nor will it drive him round to any falsehood, but he will hold fast all that he knows, no less than what he has been initiated into. I know more than other men, since I know all things; but of what I know, some I know for the earnest, some for the wise, some for myself, some for the gods, and for tyrants nothing. That I have not come for senseless ends, one may consider: for concerning my own body I run no risk at all, nor could I die at the tyranny's hands, not even if I myself should wish it; but I understand that I run risk concerning the men, of whom the tyrant makes me either the beginning or the addition; and I am all that he wishes. But if I betrayed them, either by delaying or by playing the coward toward the charge, what should I seem to earnest men? Who would not justly kill me, as trifling with men to whom the things I asked from the gods had been entrusted? That I could not escape seeming a traitor, I wish to make plain. The characters of tyrannies are twofold: some kill men untried, others bring them before courts. The former resemble the hot and ready among beasts, the latter the softer and more sluggish. That both are harsh is clear to all who take for example, of the headlong and untried sort, Nero, and of the lurking sort, Tiberius; for the one destroyed men who did not even suspect it, the other men who had long been afraid. But I hold those tyrannies the harsher which make a pretence of judging and of voting something as if from the laws; for they do nothing according to them, yet they vote the very things that men who have judged nothing vote, giving the name of law to that which dwells upon anger; and the dying of men condemned takes from the wretched even the pity of the many, which one ought, like a burial-gift, to bring to those who have departed unjustly. The form of this tyranny I see to be judicial, but it seems to me to end in the untried; for those whom it has condemned before judging, it brings to trial as though not yet judged, and the man caught by the vote in the trial plainly says he has perished at the hands of one who did not judge by the laws, while the man who forsakes the trial—how could he escape having voted against himself? But for me, now that such men lie in my hands, to flee my own struggle and theirs—where on earth will it leave me to seem clean? For grant that you have said these things, and that I, persuaded as though they were rightly said, have obeyed, and that the men have been slaughtered: what prayer for fair sailing is left to such a man? Whither will he put in? To whom will he go? For he must, I think, depart from all the earth the Romans rule, and come to men who are friendly and not dwelling in the open. Such would be Phraotes and the Babylonian and the divine Iarchas and the noble Thespesion. If, then, I were to set out for the Ethiopians, what, my excellent friend, should I say to Thespesion? For if I hid these things, I should seem a lover of falsehood—nay rather a slave; and if I went to report them, I should need some such words as these: 'Thespesion, Euphrates slandered me to you for things I am not conscious of in myself; for he called me a boaster and a portent and an insulter of wisdom, of all that is Indian. But I—I am not these things, but a traitor of my own friends, and a slayer, and faithless, and such things am I; and a crown of virtue, if any, I come to be crowned with, since I have so destroyed the greatest of the houses in Rome that they shall not even be inhabited again.' You blush, Demetrius, hearing this—I see it. What then, if you should call to mind Phraotes too, and me fleeing to that man among the Indians—how should I look at him? What should I say of the things I fled? That I came noble and good before, and not faint-hearted toward death on behalf of friends; but that, when I had been with him, I cast this most divine of human things, dishonoured, to you? And Iarchas will not even ask me anything as I come, but, just as Aeolus once bade Odysseus depart from the island in dishonour, since he had used ill the gift of fair sailing, so he too, I suppose, will drive me from the hill, saying that I have done ill toward the cup of Tantalus; for they wish that he who has bent over it should share dangers with his friends too. I know how clever you are, Demetrius, to cut short all arguments, and so I think you will say to me some such thing as this: 'But do not go to these men; go to men with whom you have not yet mingled, and the flight will lie well with you, for among those who do not know you, you will more easily escape notice.' But let this argument too be tested, where it stands as to plausibility; for I think thus about it: I hold that the wise man does nothing privately or by himself, nor would even purpose anything so without witness as not to have himself at least present to himself. And whether the saying at Pytho is Apollo's own, or some man's who soundly came to know himself and therefore made it a maxim for all, the wise man, it seems to me, knowing himself and having his own mind as a comrade, would neither cower at any of the things the many cower at, nor would dare any of those things which others lay hold of not without shame; for being slaves of tyrannies, they have at times set out to betray even their dearest to them, fearing things not fearful, and not fearing the things one ought to fear. But wisdom does not allow this; for besides the Pythian inscription, it praises also the saying of Euripides, who holds that the disease which destroys men is understanding, when they reflect that they have done evil deeds. For this it was, I suppose, that pictured for Orestes the shapes of the Eumenides, when he raged over his mother; for the mind is lord of what is to be done, but understanding is lord of what has seemed good to the mind. If, then, the mind chooses good things, understanding sends the man at once into all temples, all streets, all sacred precincts, all the haunts of men, applauding and singing; and it will chant over him even as he sleeps, setting beside him a chorus of good omen out of the people of dreams. But if the mind's purpose slips into base things, understanding does not allow the man to send a straight glance to any human being, nor a free word from his tongue; it drives him from temples and from prayer, nor does it suffer him to lift his hand to the images, but checks him as he lifts it, as the laws check those who raise their hands against others; and it sets such men apart from every company, and frightens them as they sleep; and what they see by day, and what they think they hear or say, it makes for them dreamlike and empty as wind, while the dim and phantom-like flutterings it makes for them, by their fear, true now and plausible. That understanding, then, will convict me, coming as I do to men who know me and to men who do not, if I should turn traitor to the men, has, I think, been clearly shown me, and as truth makes manifest. But I will not betray even myself; I will contend against the tyrant, adding the word of noble Homer: 'Enyalius is shared in common.'"

About dawn, when Demetrius asked him whither on earth he would turn, and seemed to have his ears dinned by the thought of horsemen whom he supposed already pressing upon Apollonius through the tyrant's anger, "He will pursue," he said, "neither me nor any other; and for me the voyage will be to Greece." "A slippery one," he said; "for the place is most conspicuous; and one whom you could not escape even in obscurity, how should you escape notice in the open?" "I have no need to escape notice," he said; "for if, as you think, all the earth is the tyrant's, better are those who die in the open than those who live in obscurity." And to Damis: "Do you perceive a ship setting out for Sicily?" "I perceive it," he said; "for we are lodging by the sea, and the herald is near the doors, and the ship is already getting under way; I infer it from the shout of those aboard and from what they do about the weighing of the anchors." "Let us embark on this ship, Damis," he said, "to sail now to Sicily, and thence to the Peloponnese." "It seems good to me," he said;

He passed the years of his silence partly among the Pamphylians, partly in Cilicia; and walking through nations so given to luxury, he nowhere spoke, nor was he induced to mutter a word. Whenever he came upon a city in faction—and many were in faction over spectacles of no serious worth—coming forward and showing himself, and indicating by his hand and his face something of a rebuke to come, he would put an end to all disorder, and they would fall silent as in the mysteries. Now to restrain those who have rushed into faction over dancers and horses is no great matter, for those who behave disorderly over such things, if they look upon a man of worth, blush and check themselves and very readily come to their senses; but a city pressed by famine is not easily turned aside by a soothing and persuasive speech and stopped from its anger. Yet for Apollonius even silence sufficed with men so disposed. For he came to Aspendus in Pamphylia—this city stands upon the river Eurymedon, the third among those in that region—and bitter vetches were on sale, and people were feeding on whatever was necessary for food; for the powerful had shut up the grain and were holding it, to be sold dear from the country. Thereupon men of every age were roused against the magistrate, and were laying hold of fire to use against him, although he was clinging to the imperial statues, which were then more dreaded and more inviolable even than the Zeus at Olympia, being those of Tiberius, under whom a man is said to have been judged impious for having beaten his own slave who was carrying a silver drachma stamped with the image of Tiberius. So Apollonius, coming up to the magistrate, asked him by a sign what this meant; and when he said that he had done no wrong, but was being wronged together with the people, and that, unless he were granted a hearing, he would perish along with the people, Apollonius turned to those standing around and signed that they should hear him; and they not only kept silence, struck with awe of him, but even laid the fire upon the altars there. Then the magistrate, taking courage, said: "So-and-so and so-and-so," naming several, "are the cause of the famine that has set in; for they have taken away the grain and are guarding it, one in one part of the country, another in another." And when the Aspendians urged one another to go off to the farms, Apollonius signed to them not to do this, but rather to summon those who were at fault and to obtain the grain from them with their consent. And when they came, he came near to breaking into speech against them, moved by the tears of the multitude—for children too had flocked together and women, and the aged were lamenting as though they would die at once of famine—but honouring the rule of his silence, he wrote a rebuke on a tablet and gave it to the magistrate to read aloud. The rebuke ran thus: "Apollonius to the grain-dealers of Aspendus. The earth is the mother of all, for she is just; but you, being unjust, have made her the mother of yourselves alone; and if you do not cease, I will not suffer you to stand upon her." Frightened by this, they filled the market with grain, and the city came back to life.

"But tell me this: did we not say at the beginning of our discourse that there is wisdom about the elephants and intelligence in what they do?" "And with good reason, Damis," he said, "we said it; for if intelligence did not govern this beast, neither would it survive, nor the nations in which it lives." "Why then," he said, "do they make the crossing so foolishly and not to their own advantage? For the smallest leads, as you see, and one a little larger follows him, then another beyond this, and all the largest behind. They ought, surely, to travel the opposite way and make the largest a wall and a defence for themselves." "But, Damis," he said, "first, they seem to be fleeing a pursuit of men, whom indeed we shall meet following their track; and against pursuers one must rather have the rear fenced, as in wars; and reckon this most skilful in tactics of the beasts. Next, as to the crossing: if the largest of them crossed first, they would give no token whether all the rest would cross the water; for to the tallest the passage is easy and ready, but to the others hard and impassable if they do not rise above the stream; whereas, when the smallest has crossed, it now interprets to the rest that it is safe. And besides, the larger ones entering first would make the river deeper for the small, for the mud necessarily sinks into hollows through the weight of the beast and the thickness of its feet, while the smaller ones would do no harm to the passage of the larger, sinking less into the holes."

What manner of men these sages are, and how they dwell upon the hill, the man himself sets forth. For in one of his discourses to the Egyptians he says: "I saw Indians, Brahmans, dwelling upon the earth and not upon it, walled without walls, and possessing nothing yet possessing all things." This he wrote rather riddlingly; but Damis says that they sleep upon the ground, and strew beneath them such grasses as they themselves choose; and that he saw them walking on air, two cubits above the ground — not for the sake of working wonders, for these men disdain such ambition, but because, in whatever they do together with the Sun as they rise from the earth, they reckon they are doing what is acceptable to the god. The fire which they draw from the ray, although it is bodily, they neither burn upon an altar nor keep in furnaces, but, like the beams that are reflected from sun and water, so it is seen aloft and quivering in the upper air. By day they pray to the Sun on behalf of the seasons over which he presides, that they may come in due time to the earth and that India may prosper; but by night they beseech the ray not to take it amiss that it is night, but to remain as it was led down by them. Such is the meaning of Apollonius' saying that the Brahmans are upon the earth and not upon the earth. The phrase "walled without walls" signifies the air under which they live; for though they seem to lodge in the open, they raise a shadow over themselves, and are not wetted when it rains, and are in the sunshine whenever they will. The phrase "possessing nothing, having all things" Damis explains thus: all the springs that leap up from the earth for the Bacchants, whenever Dionysus shakes them and the earth, come also to these Indians as they feast and give feasts; so that, reasonably, Apollonius says that those who provide what they wish without preparation, but on the spur of the moment, possess what they do not possess. They let their hair grow, as the Lacedaemonians did of old, and the Thurians and Tarentines and Melians, and all who held Laconian ways in honour; they bind on a white turban, walk barefoot, and shape their dress much like the workman's tunic. The material of their dress is a wool of native growth which the earth itself brings forth, white like that of Pamphylia, but softer in its bearing, and a fat like oil drips from it. This they make into sacred raiment; and if anyone but these Indians tries to draw it up, the earth will not let go the wool. As for the power of the ring and the staff, both of which they wear, all things are within their power, but two are honoured in silence as unspeakable.

As they sailed after this over the Euboean sea, which Homer too thinks one of the hard and ill-charted, the sea appeared smooth and fairer than the season warranted, and there was talk about islands, since they fell in with many famous ones, and about shipbuilding and steering, fitting for sailors. But when Damis kept disparaging some of the topics, cutting others short, and not letting others be asked, Apollonius understood that he wished to be earnest about another subject, and said: "What ails you, Damis, that you break up the questions? For it is not seasickness or being ill from the voyage that turns you from the discourse, since the sea, you see, has put itself beneath the ship and bears us along. Why then are you vexed?" "Because," he said, "while a great theme lies in the midst, which it were more fitting to ask about, we ask about stale and ancient things." "And what," he said, "might this theme be, for which you hold the rest superfluous?" "Having met Achilles, Apollonius," he said, "and heard perhaps many things not yet known to us, you do not tell these, nor sketch for us the form of Achilles, but sail round the islands and build ships in your talk." "If I shall not seem to boast," he said, "all shall be told.

"And to me, Menippus, my mother, when I was a mere infant, taught a myth too about the wisdom of Aesop: that Aesop was once a shepherd, and pastured his flock by a temple of Hermes, and was in love with wisdom and prayed to him for it. And many others too came to Hermes asking the same — one bringing gold, another silver, another an ivory herald's wand, another kindling some such bright offering; but Aesop was so circumstanced as to have none of such things, and was sparing even of what he had: he poured a libation of milk to him, as much as a ewe gives when milked, and brought a honeycomb to the altar, as much as would fill his hand, and thought to feast him with myrtle-berries too, setting beside them a very few roses or violets.
