'For what need is there, Hermes,' he said, 'to weave garlands and neglect the sheep?' And when on the appointed day they came for the distribution of wisdom, Hermes, being eloquent and a god of gain, said: 'Take you philosophy' — to him who had dedicated the most — 'and you, go to the ways of orators' — to the one who had given the second offering — 'and for you there is a place in astronomy, and for you to be a musician, for you to be a poet of heroic measure, and for you of iambic.' But when, eloquent as he was, he had unwittingly used up all the parts of philosophy and had failed to notice that Aesop had fallen out of the reckoning, he remembered the Seasons, by whom he himself had been reared on the heights of Olympus — how, when he was still in swaddling-clothes, they had told him a myth about the cow, the tale which the cow told the man on behalf of herself and of the earth, and how it set him in love with the cattle of Apollo — and from this source he gave mythology to Aesop, as the last thing left in the house of wisdom: 'Take what I learned first.' Thus from this the many shapes of his art came to Aesop, and such was the issue of the matter of mythology. Yet perhaps I have done a foolish thing.

As Apollonius and those about him were supping, Nilus stood by them with vegetables and bread and sweetmeats, carrying some himself and others through others, and very wittily said: "The wise men send these gifts of hospitality to you and to me; for I too will sup with you, not uninvited, as they say, but inviting myself." "A pleasant gift of hospitality you bring, young man," said Apollonius, "yourself and your own character, for you seem to philosophize without guile and to welcome the things of the Indians and of Pythagoras. Recline here, then, and sup with us." "I am reclining," he said, "but there will not be food enough to fill me." "You seem to be a hearty eater," he said, "and a terrible feeder." "Most terrible indeed," he said; "for after you have set before me so great and so splendid a feast, I am not yet filled, and after a little I come back to feed again; what will you call me but insatiable and dreadfully a glutton?" "Eat your fill," he said; "and as for openings of discourse, hand over some yourself, and I will give others."

By these words Damis says that he himself was so disposed as to recover impulse and courage, and that Demetrius did not despair of the man, but praising him and agreeing with what he said, called the blessing of the gods upon him for that for which he was in danger, and upon philosophy herself, for whose sake he endured these things; and he offered to lead them to where he chanced to be lodging. But Apollonius declined this, saying that it was now late afternoon, and that about the lighting of the lamps the ships must set out for the Roman harbour, for this was the custom for these vessels. "We will dine together," he said, "when my affairs go well; for now some charge might be got up against you, as having dined with the emperor's enemy; and do not even come with us to the harbour, lest your having shared talk with me also slander you for secret counsels." Demetrius gave way; and embracing them he went off, turning about and wiping away his tears. But Apollonius, looking at Damis, said: "If you are stout-hearted, and have the courage that I have, let us both go to the ship; but if you are faint-hearted, it is time for you to remain here, for you will be with Demetrius this while—a man dear to both you and me." Damis took him up: "And what should I think myself," he said, "if, after such things as you have discoursed today about friends and the sharing of dangers that come upon them, I, deaf to the argument, should flee you and abandon your peril—I, who have never before seemed base on your behalf?" "You speak rightly," he said, "and let us go—I as I am, but you must change yourself into a more common guise, and neither wear your hair as you do now, but exchange this linen for that cloak there, and put off this footwear. Why this is my wish, I must explain. It is better to endure more before the trial; for I do not wish you to share these things with me, being seized, and you would be seized if your dress were brought into suspicion. Rather, follow me and be present at what I do as one not practising philosophy, but otherwise a friend of mine." This was the reason for Damis's changing the Pythagorean dress; for he says that he gave it up not as being base, nor out of any change of mind, but in praise of the art he assumed for the advantage of the moment.

"and let us sail." And greeting Demetrius, who was despondent over them, and exhorting him to take courage as a man for men, they sailed for Sicily with a fair wind, and, passing Messene, came to Tauromenium on the third day. After this, carried to Syracuse, they put out for the Peloponnese about the beginning of autumn, and crossing the open sea came in six days to the mouths of the Alpheus, from which this river pours, fit to drink, into the Adriatic and Sicilian sea. Disembarking, then, from the ship, and holding it of great worth to come to Olympia, they lodged in the temple of Zeus, never going off beyond Scillus; and when a rumour, thronging and intense, seized the Greek world that the man was alive and had come to Olympia, at first the report seemed not strong, for besides their having no human hope of him, since they had heard he was bound, they were not unacquainted with the tales that he had died burned, or had been dragged living, hooks fastened into his collar-bones, or had been thrust into a pit, or into the depths; but when it was believed that he had come, not for any Olympiad did Greece gather so uplifted as for him then. Elis and Sparta came from near at hand, Corinth from the bounds of the Isthmus, and the Athenians, though outside the Peloponnese, were not behind the cities that are at the doors of Pisa; the most distinguished of the Athenians themselves marching to the temple, and the youth from all the earth that frequents Athens. And indeed some from Megara dwelt at Olympia then, and many from Boeotia, and from Argos, and whatever was of repute among the Phocians and Thessalians; some who had already been with Apollonius to recover wisdom, since they thought to hear more and more marvellous things, and some unacquainted with him, holding it a terrible thing to seem to have been deaf to such a man. To those who asked in what manner he escaped the tyrant, he thought he need say nothing vulgar, but said only that he had made his defence and was saved; but when many came from Italy who proclaimed the things in the court, Greece was not far from doing him reverence, holding him a divine man chiefly for this very reason, that he set up no boast about these things.

He visited also great Antioch, when he had ceased from his silence, and entered the temple of Daphnaean Apollo, to which the Assyrians attach the Arcadian myth. For they say that the Daphne, daughter of Ladon, was transformed there, and a river Ladon flows for them, and a laurel tree is honoured among them—the one, that is, that took the maiden's place; and cypresses of immense height stand around the temple in a circle, and the place sends forth springs in plenty and at rest, in which they say Apollo bathes. There the earth has sent up a shoot of cypress, over Cyparissus, they say, an Assyrian youth; and the beauty of the plant confirms the transformation. Perhaps I seem to handle the matter too youthfully in telling such tales; but it is not for the sake of myth-telling that I do so. What, then, does my account intend? Apollonius, seeing that the temple was graceful but held no seriousness in it, only men half-barbarous and without culture, "Apollo," he said, "change these voiceless men into trees, that as cypresses at least they may make a sound." And surveying the springs, that they kept calm and that none of them murmured, "The voicelessness here," he said, "does not allow even the springs to speak." And looking toward the Ladon, "It was not your daughter alone who was transformed," he said, "but you too, by being thought a barbarian instead of a Greek and an Arcadian." When he resolved to discourse, he avoided the frequented and disorderly places, saying that he needed not men but real men, and he resorted to the more solemn places, and dwelt in those temples that were not closed. At sunrise he performed by himself certain rites, which he revealed only to those trained in silence for four years; and the time after that, if the city were Greek and the rites familiar, he would gather the priests and discourse about the gods and correct them, if anywhere they departed from established usage; but if the rites were barbarous and peculiar, he would learn who had founded them and on what occasion they were founded, and having inquired in what way these things were performed, and having suggested any wiser practice than what was done, he would go to his disciples and bid them ask what they wished. For he said that those who philosophize in this way should at dawn's beginning be in fellowship with the gods, as the day advances about the gods, and the time after that hold their converse on human affairs. And when he had told his companions all they asked, and had had enough of such converse, he would rise to the public discourse to all, not before midday, but when the day stood most fully fixed. And having discoursed as long as he thought sufficient, he would anoint himself, and after rubbing himself, throw himself into cold water, calling the baths "the old age of men." When Antioch was shut out from its baths for great offences, he said, "The emperor has granted you, evil as you are, to live more years." And when the Ephesians wished to stone their magistrate for not heating the baths, "You blame your magistrate," he said, "because you bathe badly; but I blame you because you bathe at all."

And I found in the writings of Juba that they help one another in the hunt and stand before the one that gives out, and if they rescue him, smear the gum of aloe upon his wounds, standing about him like physicians. Many such things were the subject of their philosophizing, taking as starting-points whatever was worth discourse.

As Apollonius drew near, the other sages welcomed him, greeting him with their hands; but Iarchas sat upon a high seat — it was of black bronze, adorned with golden figures, while the seats of the others were of bronze too, but plain and less high, for they sat below Iarchas. When he saw Apollonius, he greeted him in the Greek tongue and asked for the Indian's letter. When Apollonius marvelled at his foreknowledge, he said that one letter, a delta, was wanting in the epistle, which had been passed over in the writing; and so it proved. When he had read the letter, he said: "What do you think of us, Apollonius?" "What," he said, "but as the very distance I have come for your sake shows — a journey such as none of the men of my country has yet made?" "And what do you suppose we know more than you do?" "I," he said, "hold your knowledge to be wiser and far more divine; and if I find among you nothing beyond what I know, then at least I shall have learned that there is nothing more for me to learn." The Indian answered: "Others ask those who come to them whence they come and on what errand; but with us the first proof of wisdom is not to be ignorant of him who has come. Test this first." And saying this he recounted Apollonius' lineage on his father's and mother's side, and all that had passed at Aegae, and how Damis had come to him, and whatever they had been earnest about on the road, or had seen of another's earnestness; all this the Indian set forth without drawing breath and clearly, as though he had shared their journey. When Apollonius was astonished and asked whence he knew it, the Indian said: "You too have come a partaker of this wisdom, but not yet of all of it." "Will you then teach me," he said, "all the wisdom?" "Yes, and ungrudgingly," he said; "for this is wiser than to grudge and hide what is worth earnest study. And besides, Apollonius, I see you full of Memory, which we love above all the gods." "Have you then seen," he said, "what my nature is?" "We," he said, "Apollonius, see all the forms of the soul, tracing them out by countless signs. But since noon is near, and we must prepare what is fitting for the gods, let us now perform this; and afterwards let us discourse on whatever you wish, and be present at all that is done." "By Zeus," said Apollonius, "I should wrong the Caucasus and the Indus, which I have crossed to come to you, if I did not fill myself with all that you do.

The others too begged for this discourse and were eager to hear it. "Well," he said, "it was not by digging a trench, like Odysseus, nor by drawing up souls with the blood of lambs, that I came to converse with Achilles, but by praying such a prayer as the Indians say is made to heroes. 'O Achilles,' I said, 'most men say you are dead, but I do not grant the saying, nor does Pythagoras, the ancestor of my wisdom. If then we speak truly, show us your form; for you would greatly profit my eyes, if you would use them as witnesses of your being.' At this there was a slight earthquake about the mound, and a youth five cubits high rose up, Thessalian in his cloak; but his form was not that of a braggart, as Achilles seems to some, and though terrible to behold he did not lose his brightness, and his beauty seems to me not yet to have found a praiser worthy of it, though Homer said much of it; rather it is unspeakable and is undone by him who hymns it rather than sung in its own likeness. Seen at first, as I said, he grew greater and double and more than that; at least he appeared to me twelve cubits high, when he came to his fullest, and his beauty grew ever with his height. His hair, he said, he had never cut, but kept it unshorn for the Spercheius, for the Spercheius was the first river he used; but his beard had its first growth. Addressing me gladly, he said: 'I have met you, having long needed such a man. For the Thessalians have now for a long time left off their offerings to me, and I do not yet think fit to be wrathful — for if I were wrathful they would perish more than the Greeks here once did — but I use mild counsel, that they outrage not their customs, nor be convicted of being worse than these Trojans here, who, though robbed by me of so many men, sacrifice to me publicly and offer first-fruits of the season, and laying a suppliant's bough beg for a truce, which I will not grant; for the perjuries they swore against me will not let Ilium ever recover its ancient form, nor reach the bloom that has come to many of the ruined cities, but its dwellers shall be no better than if they were taken yesterday. That I may not show the affairs of the Thessalians the like, go on an embassy to their council concerning what I have said.' 'I will go on the embassy,' I said, 'for the purpose of the embassy was that they should not perish. But I, Achilles, have a request of you.' 'I understand,' he said; 'for you are plainly about to ask concerning the Trojan affairs. Ask five questions, such as you yourself wish and the Fates allow.' So I asked first whether, according to the poets' tale, he had met with burial. 'I lie,' he said, 'as was sweetest to me and to Patroclus, for we came together very young, and one golden urn holds us both as we lie, as one. As for the dirges of the Muses and Nereids, which they say were made over me, the Muses never came here at all, but the Nereids still come.' After this I asked whether Polyxena was slain over him. He said this was true, but that she was not slain by the Achaeans, but came of her own will to the tomb, and counting her love and his worthy of great things, fell upon an upright sword. Third I asked: 'Did Helen, Achilles, come to Troy, or did Homer think fit to suppose this?' 'For a long time,' he said, 'we were deceived, going on embassies to the Trojans and making our battles for her, as though she were in Ilium; but she dwelt in Egypt, in the house of Proteus, having been carried off by Paris. And when this was believed, we fought thenceforth for Troy itself, that we might not depart in shame.' I touched on a fourth question too, and said I marvelled that Greece had borne so many and such men together as Homer arrays against Troy. And Achilles said: 'Not even the barbarians fell much short of us, so did all the earth blossom with virtue.' Fifth I asked: 'Why did Homer not know Palamedes, or knowing him, leave him out of the tale about you?' 'If Palamedes,' he said, 'did not come to Troy, neither did Troy exist; but since a man most wise and most warlike died, as Odysseus thought good, Homer does not bring him into his poems, that he might not sing the disgraces of Odysseus.' And lamenting over him as greatest and fairest and youngest and most warlike, surpassing all in temperance, and contributing much to the Muses, 'But you, Apollonius,' he said — 'for the wise have fitting dealings with the wise — care for his tomb and take up the statue of Palamedes that is meanly cast aside; it lies in Aeolis over against Methymna in Lesbos.' Saying this, and at the end the matter of the youth from Paros, he departed with a moderate flash of lightning; for indeed the cocks were already taking up their song.

"For having intended to turn you to accounts more in keeping with nature and more true than those which most men sing about Aetna, I have myself been carried off into the praise of myths. Yet the digression has not been graceless; for the myth which we set aside is not of the tales of Aesop, but of the more theatrical kind, which the poets harp upon. For they say that some Typho or Enceladus is bound beneath the mountain, and that, dying hard, he breathes out this fire; but I say that giants did exist, and that in many parts of the earth bodies of this kind are revealed when their tombs are broken open — yet that they did not come to battle with the gods, but perhaps outraged their temples and shrines; while to say that they leapt up against heaven and would not allow the gods to be in it is madness to say and madness to think. Nor let that account, though it seems more reverent, be honoured: that Hephaestus busies himself with smith-work in Aetna, and that some anvil is struck there by him; for there are many other mountains in many parts of the earth that are on fire, and we should never have done in ascribing to them giants and Hephaestuses.

When they had supped, Nilus said: "Up to now I served as a soldier together with the Naked Sages, ranging myself with them as with light-armed troops or slingers; but now I will be a man-at-arms, and your shield shall adorn me." "But I think, Egyptian," he said, "you will incur blame from Thespesion and the rest, for going over to our ways more readily than the choice of a life allows, and without even staying for a fuller test of us." "Perhaps," he said; "but if there is to be blame for choosing, there may also be blame for not choosing, and they will be the more open to blame for choosing what I have chosen; for that men older and at once wiser have not long ago chosen what I now choose would be a juster charge against them, that having such advantage they did not choose the better thing to follow." "You have spoken no ignoble word, my young man; but take care lest, by the very fact of their being so wise and of such age, they appear to have chosen those things rightly and to decline these with reasonable argument, while you seem to lay hold of a bolder word, setting yourself up rather than following them." Turning about, the Egyptian said, against the opinion of Apollonius: "What it is reasonable for a young man to share with his elders I have not neglected; for when I thought there was about these men a wisdom belonging to no other men, I attached myself to them. The occasion of my impulse was this. My father once sailed of his own will to the Red Sea, commanding the ship which the Egyptians send to the nation of the Indians; and mingling with the Indians of the coast, he brought back tales about the wise men there, near to those you have gone through to us. Hearing from him too some such tale as this — that the Indians are the wisest of men, and the Ethiopians colonists of the Indians, and that these inherit their wisdom from their fathers and look to their home — when I became a youth I gave up my patrimony to those who wished it, and naked I came to these Naked Sages, to learn the things of the Indians, or at least things akin to them; and they seemed to me wise indeed, but not in that way. And when I asked them why they did not practise the philosophy of the Indians, they fell to slanders like those uttered today against you, and enrolled me, young as I still am, as you see, in their own community, fearing, I think, lest, leaping away from them, I should sail to the Red Sea, as my father once did — which, by the gods, I would not have given up; for I would have gone on even to the hill of the wise men, had not some god sent you here as a helper to me, that without sailing the Red Sea or risking the voyage to the Gulf-dwellers I might taste of Indian wisdom — not making today my choice of a life, but having long ago chosen it, while not having what I thought I should have. For what is strange if, having failed of something, a man returns to what he was hunting? And if I should bring these men over to this too, and become to them a counsellor of what I have persuaded myself, what bold thing, tell me, should I be doing? For neither is youth to be driven off from thinking out something better even than old age; and whoever becomes to another a counsellor of a wisdom which he has himself chosen, surely escapes the charge of persuading what he is not persuaded of; and whoever, receiving the goods that come from fortune, uses them alone, wrongs the goods, for he takes from them the appearing sweeter to more men."

Sailing from Dicaearchia, on the third day they put in at the mouths of the Tiber, from which the voyage up to Rome is of measured length. The imperial sword was then in the hands of Aelian; and this man had long admired Apollonius, having once been with him in Egypt, and openly he said nothing on his behalf to Domitian, for the office did not allow it—how could he praise to him a man held to be hateful to the emperor, or excuse him as a friend of his own?—but with all the secret arts by which one may defend a man, he used them all on his behalf. Even during the time before Apollonius arrived, while he was being slandered, Aelian said: "Sire, the sophists are a light-tongued tribe, and their art is a thing of boasting; and since they reap no good from being alive, they crave death, and do not wait for its coming of itself, but draw death upon themselves, challenging those who hold swords. This, I think, Nero too reflected on, that he might not be led by Demetrius to kill him; for when he perceived that the man courted death, he remitted death to him not out of pardon, but out of contempt for the killing. And Musonius the Tyrrhenian, who opposed the rule in many things, he confined to the island called Gyara; and so much weaker are the Greeks than these sophists, that then they sailed there to be with him, and now they sail to see the spring; for on that island, which was waterless before, a spring became Musonius's discovery, which the Greeks celebrate as they do the horse's spring on Helicon."

When a young man of those who had come from Athens said that Athena was very kindly to the emperor, "Cease," he said, "at Olympia to applaud these things and to slander the goddess to her father." But when the young man pressed his vexation and said that the goddess did rightly, since the emperor too held office under her name at Athens, "Would," he said—silencing him with the former of his answers, that he knew ill about the gods if he held them kindly to tyrants, and with the next, that the Athenians' voting was not consistent with their decrees for Harmodius and Aristogeiton, if, while thinking to honour those men in the marketplace for what they did at the Panathenaea, they should henceforth grant to tyrants

He cultivated a style of discourse that was not dithyrambic nor inflamed with poetic words, nor again over-refined and excessively Attic; for he thought it disagreeable to go beyond moderate Atticism. Nor did he give himself to subtle quibbling, nor draw out his discourses; nor did anyone hear him speak ironically or walking about among his hearers; but as though from a tripod, when he discoursed, he would say "I know," and "It seems to me," and "Where are you carrying yourselves?" and "You must know." And his opinions were brief and adamantine, his words proper and grafted to their subjects; and what he said had a ring, as of decrees pronounced from a sceptre. When one of the captious questioners asked him why he did not inquire, "Because," he said, "I inquired when I was a youth; but now I must not inquire, but teach what I have found." "How then, Apollonius," the man asked again, "will the wise man discourse?" "As a lawgiver," he said; "for the lawgiver must make into commands for the many those things of which he has persuaded himself." Thus did he pursue his work at Antioch, and turned to himself men most devoid of culture.

The things said by Nearchus and Pythagoras about the river Acesines—that it flows into the Indus and breeds serpents seventy cubits long—they say are such as has been told; and let my account be reserved for the dragons, whose hunting Damis describes. Having come to the Indus and being at the crossing of the river, they asked the Babylonian whether he knew anything of the river, inquiring about the passage; but he said he had not yet sailed it, nor knew from where it was navigable. "Why then," they said, "did you not hire a guide?" "Because there is one who will guide us," he said, and at the same time showed a certain letter that would accomplish this—at which they say Vardanes was admired for his humanity and care. For he had sent this letter to the satrap over the Indus, though he was not subject to his rule, reminding him of a kindness, and saying that he would not demand any return for it—for it was not in his character to ask back a favour—but that for receiving Apollonius and sending him where he wished he would feel gratitude. He had also given gold to the guide, that, if he perceived Apollonius in need, he might give it and not look to another's hand. When the Indian received the letter, he said he was held worthy of great things and would show no less ambition about the man than if the king of the Indians had written on his behalf; and he gave him the satrapal ship to embark on, and other boats on which the camels were carried, and a guide for all the country which the Hydraotes bounds, and wrote to his own king not to fall short of Vardanes himself in regard to a man who was both Greek and divine.

"Fill yourself," he said, "and let us go." So they came to a certain spring of water, which Damis says, on seeing it later, was like the Dirce in Boeotia. First they stripped, then anointed their heads with an amber-like drug, which so warmed the Indians that their bodies steamed and the sweat poured down in streams, as from those who bathe in fire; then they threw themselves into the water, and having so bathed they walked to the temple crowned and full of the hymn. Standing round in the figure of a chorus, with Iarchas as their leader, they struck the earth with their upright staves, and it, swelling up like a wave, lifted them two cubits into the air. And they sang a song like the paean of Sophocles which is sung to Asclepius at Athens. When they had come down to the ground, Iarchas called the youth who bore the anchor and said: "Take care of Apollonius' companions." And he, having gone and returned far swifter than the swift among birds, said: "I have taken care." So when they had performed most of the rites, they rested upon their seats; and Iarchas said to the youth: "Bring out for the wise Apollonius the throne of Phraotes, that he may sit upon it and discourse.

Such were the events on the ship. Sailing into the Piraeus about the season of the Mysteries, when the Athenians are at their most crowded among the Greeks, he hastened up from the ship to the city; and as he went he met many of the philosophers going down to Phalerum, some of whom were warming themselves naked, for the autumn is sunny for the Athenians, others studying out of books, others practising from memory, others disputing. No one passed him by, but all, judging that it was Apollonius, turned to walk with him and greeted him gladly; and ten young men, meeting him together, said, lifting their hands to the Acropolis, "By Athena yonder, we were just now walking to the Piraeus, to sail to Ionia to you." And he welcomed them, and said he rejoiced with them that they studied philosophy.

"What then is the cause of such mountains? Earth that yields a mixture of bitumen and sulphur smoulders of itself by nature, but does not yet give out fire; but if it happens to be full of caverns and a breath runs beneath it, it now raises a beacon-flame. And the flame, when it gets the upper hand, like water, flows off the mountains and is poured out over the plains, and a mass of fire moves toward the sea, making outfalls such as rivers do. As for the Region of the Pious, around whom the fire flowed, let some account of it be given here too; but let us hold that for those who do holy deeds all the earth is a safe place, and the sea easy to traverse, not only for those who sail but for those who try to swim." For he always brought his discourses to rest in profitable precepts.

When Nilus had spoken such things, and so boyishly, Apollonius took him up and said: "Will you not first discuss with me about a fee, since you love my wisdom?" "Let us discuss," said Nilus, "and ask what you will." "I ask you," he said, "to keep what you yourself have chosen, but not to trouble the Naked Sages by counselling things you will not persuade." "I will obey," he said, "and let the fee be agreed." Thus they made their compact in earnest. And when Nilus afterward asked him how long he would spend among the Naked Sages, "As long," he said, "as the wisdom of these men is worth to one who consorts with them; and then we will make the road to the Cataracts for the sake of the springs; for it is delightful not only to see the beginnings of the Nile, but also to hear it roaring."

With these things Aelian put off the emperor before Apollonius arrived; but when he had come, he set to wiser stratagems. He ordered that he be seized and brought up to him; and when the framer of the accusation reviled Apollonius as a sorcerer and one mighty in his art, Aelian said: "Keep yourself and his case for the imperial court." But Apollonius said: "If I am a sorcerer, how am I being tried? And if I am being tried, how am I a sorcerer?—unless indeed he says that the power of false accusation is so strong as not to be overcome even by sorcerers." When the accuser wished to say something still more ignorant, Aelian cut him off and said: "Leave me the time before the trial; for I will make trial of the sophist's mind in private and not before you, and if he admits that he does wrong, the arguments in court will be cut short for him and you will depart in peace; but if he denies it, the emperor will judge." Then, going forward into the secret court, in which great matters are both examined and kept silent, he said: "Withdraw from here, and let no one listen, for this is the emperor's pleasure."

to rule over them as elected." When Damis counselled him about money, since very little of their provision was left them, "Tomorrow," he said, "I will see to this." And going the next day into the temple, "Give me, priest," he said, "a thousand drachmas from the moneys of Zeus, if you do not think he will be very angry." And the priest said, "He will not be angry about these things, but rather if you do not take more."

After this, taking thought for himself of a greater journey, he conceived a desire for the Indian nation and the wise men in it, who are said to be the Brahmans and the Hyrcanians, saying that it befitted a young man to travel abroad and to be carried beyond his own borders. He counted it a windfall too to visit the magi who dwell in Babylon and Susa, for he might learn their teaching also by using the road. And he disclosed his purpose to his disciples, who were seven. When they tried to advise him otherwise, in case he might somehow be drawn from this resolve, "I," he said, "have made the gods my counsellors, and have told you what I have decided; but I was making a test of you, whether you are strong for the same things as I. Since, then, you are soft, fare you well and study philosophy; but I must go where wisdom and my divine guide lead me." Having said this, he set out from Antioch with two attendants, who had belonged to his father—one a swift writer, the other a fair one.

Thus they crossed the Indus, about forty stadia, for so much of it is navigable; and about this river they write as follows. The Indus rises from the Caucasus, larger at its source than all the rivers of Asia, and as it advances it makes many of the navigable streams its own; and, doing the same as the Nile, it pours over the land of India and brings earth upon the earth and gives the Indians to sow after the Egyptian fashion. As for the snows of the Ethiopians and the mountains of the Cataracts, I do not think it right to contradict those who have spoken; yet I do not agree, reasoning about the Indus, that it does the same as the Nile, since the country above it is not snowed upon; and besides, I know that the god makes the Ethiopians and Indians the horns of the whole earth, blackening the one at the rising of the sun, the other at its setting—which could not happen to these men unless they were warmed even in winter. But a land which the sun heats the whole year through, how should one think it snowed upon? How could the snow become a supplier to the rivers there, enabling them to rise above their own measure? And if snow did come to such sun-scorched places, how could it be poured out into so vast a flood? How could it suffice for a river that floods—

When he had taken his seat, Iarchas said: "Ask what you will; for you have come to men who know all things." Apollonius asked whether they knew themselves also, supposing that, like the Greeks, he held self-knowledge to be hard. But the other, contrary to Apollonius' opinion, said: "We know all things, since first of all we know ourselves; for none of us would come to this philosophy who did not first know himself." Apollonius, remembering what he had heard from Phraotes, and how he who is to be a philosopher must first test himself before setting out, agreed with this saying, for of himself too he was persuaded of it. Then he asked again what they held themselves to be; and the other said "gods." When he asked why, "Because," he said, "we are good men." This seemed to Apollonius so full of good breeding that he spoke of it afterwards even to Domitian, in his defence of himself.

It was the day of the Epidauria. Now it is the custom of the Athenians to initiate at the Epidauria, after the proclamation and the victims, at a second sacrifice; and this they ordained on account of Asclepius, because they initiated him when he came late from Epidaurus for the Mysteries. But most of them, neglecting the initiation, were busy about Apollonius, and were more eager for this than to go away initiated; and he said he would be with them again, but bade them attend to the rites then, for he too was to be initiated. But the hierophant would not provide the rites, for he would never, he said, initiate a sorcerer, nor open Eleusis to a man not pure in things divine. Apollonius, in no way the less himself for this, said: "You have not yet named the greatest charge that might be brought against me, that, knowing more about the rite than you, I came nevertheless as if to be initiated by one wiser than myself." When those present praised him for answering so vigorously and like himself, the hierophant, since by excluding him he seemed to be doing what was not dear to the multitude, changed his tone and said, "Be initiated, for you seem to have come a wise man." But Apollonius said: "I will be initiated another time, and so-and-so will initiate me" — using foreknowledge of the hierophant who came after that one, and who four years later presided over the temple.

After he had spent in Sicily a time long enough for his purpose, he made his way to Greece about the rising of Arcturus. The voyage being without trouble, he put in at Leucas and said, "Let us leave this ship, for it is not well for her to sail to Achaea." No one heeded the saying except those who knew the man; but he himself, in a Leucadian ship, together with those who wished to sail with him, put in at Lechaeum, while the Syracusan ship sank as she was entering the Crisaean gulf.

Having discoursed thus, and recalling some Indian matters, they slept in the grass; and at daybreak, after praying as they were wont, they followed Nilus, who led them to Thespesion. Greeting one another and sitting down together in the grove, they laid hold of a discussion, and Apollonius began it. "How much worth it is not to hide wisdom, yesterday's discourses show; for the Indians having taught me all of their wisdom that I thought befitted me, I both remember my teachers and go about teaching what I heard from them. And I might be of profit to you too, if you would send me forth knowing your wisdom as well, for I would not cease going through your doctrines to the Greeks and writing them to the Indians."

When they were by themselves, he said: "I, Apollonius, was a stripling at the time when the emperor's father came to Egypt to sacrifice to the gods and to consult you about his own affairs; and the emperor was already leading me as a tribune, since I knew matters of war; and you were so kindly disposed toward me, that while the emperor was giving audience to the cities, you took me aside in private and bade me tell of what country I was, and what my name, and how I stood with my father; and you foretold me also this office, which to the many seems the greatest, and greater than all human things together, but to me appears a crowd and a wretchedness. For I am the guardian of a harsh tyranny, and if I fail it, I dread what comes from the gods. How I am well-disposed toward you, I have shown; for he who said—from what I have somewhere said—that you would never cease loving a man as long as the memory of those things remained: my willingness to question you in private about what the accuser has framed has become no mean device for my converse with you, that you may take heart at the things that lie with me, and may foreknow the things that lie with the emperor. What he will vote concerning you, I do not know; but he is disposed like those who desire to condemn, yet are ashamed to do so on charges not true, and he makes you a pretext for the destruction of men of consular rank; for he wishes what he ought not, but does it, setting it in order to the appearance of justice. I too, then, must have my fiction and my onset against you; for if he suspects me of slackening, I do not know which of us two will perish the sooner."

When a Thessalian man, whose name was Isagoras, was with him at Olympia, "Tell me, Isagoras," he said, "is there such a thing as a festival?" "By Zeus," he said, "the pleasantest and most god-beloved of human things." "And what is its matter?" he said; "as if I had asked about the matter of this statue, and you had answered that it was composed of gold and ivory." "And what matter, Apollonius," he said, "is there of the incorporeal?" "The greatest," he said, "and most various; for in it are sacred precincts and temples and racecourses and a theatre, I suppose, and nations of men, some from the neighbouring land, some from beyond the borders and beyond the sea. And indeed it is composed of very many arts and devices and of true wisdom and of poets and counsels and discourses and naked contest and music, as is ancestral at Pytho." "It seems, Apollonius," he said, "that the festival is not only corporeal, but of more marvellous matter than the cities; for it gathers and settles together the most earnest of the earnest and the most notable of the notable." "Shall we then, Isagoras," he said, "as some hold walls and ships, hold the men to be it, or shall we need another opinion of it?" "This opinion is complete, Tyanean," he said, "and it is just to follow it." "And yet incomplete," he said, "as I reflect about it in my own way; for it seems to me that ships need men and men ships, and that men would never even have conceived the sea if there had been no ship, and that walls save men and men walls; and that a festival, on the same reasoning, is both the gathering of the men and the very place into which they must gather, and so much the more as walls and ships would never even have come to be except through the hands of men, but these places, having been spoiled by human hands only in being deprived of their spontaneity, came of nature well-furnished and were held worthy of being frequented. For gymnasia and porticoes and fountains and houses were wrought by human art, like the walls and the ships; but this Alpheus and the hippodrome and the stadium and the groves came, I suppose, before men—the river fit to be drink and bath, the plain wide for the horses to contend in, the place for the athletes to roll in the dust and run, because it furnishes a certain limit, a hollow of a stadium's length, and the groves to crown the victors and to train the runners among the athletes. For these things, I suppose, when Heracles reflected and admired the self-grown nature of Olympia, the place seemed to him worthy of the things still earnestly practised here."

And he came to ancient Nineveh, in which an image is set up after a barbarian fashion. It is in fact Io, daughter of Inachus, and small horns, as though just beginning, push out from her temples. While he stayed there and understood more about the image than the priests and prophets, Damis of Nineveh came to him—he whom I said at the outset travelled abroad with Apollonius and became his fellow-traveller in all wisdom and preserved much concerning the man. This Damis, admiring him and emulous of his journey, said: "Let us go, Apollonius, you following god, and I following you; for you would find me of much worth. If I know nothing else, at least I have been to Babylon, and I know the cities, however many there are, having gone up there not long ago, and the villages, in which there is much good; and indeed the languages of the barbarians, however many there are—and there is one of the Armenians, another of the Medes and Persians, another of the Cadusians, and I have learned them all." "But I, my friend," he said, "understand them all, though I have learned none." When the man of Nineveh marvelled, "Do not marvel," he said, "if I know all the tongues of men; for I know even what men keep silent." Then the Assyrian, when he heard this, made obeisance to him and looked on him as a divine being, and stayed with him, increasing in wisdom and remembering whatever he learned. The Assyrian's speech was of moderate quality, for it had no eloquence, since he had been educated among barbarians; but to record a discussion or a conversation, and to model whatever he heard or saw, and to compose a memoir of such things, he was quite competent, and pursued this best of all men. At any rate the tablet "Of the Scraps from the Manger" had this meaning for Damis: Damis wished that nothing of Apollonius should be unknown, but that if he ever let fall a careless word, this too should be written down. And it is worth telling what he said to the man who found fault with this work of his. For when a lazy and malicious man disparaged him, saying that he recorded other things rightly—all the man's maxims and opinions—but that in collecting these things so trivial he did much like dogs who feed on the crumbs that fall from the feast, Damis replied: "If there are feasts of the gods and the gods feed, surely they have servants too, whose care it is that not even the crumbs of ambrosia should be lost." Such a companion and lover did he meet with, with whom he travelled the greater part of his life.

—Egypt? As they were carried down the Indus, they say they met many river-horses and many crocodiles, as do those who sail the Nile; and they say there are flowers on the Indus such as grow up on the Nile, and that the seasons in India are warm in winter and stifling in summer, and that for this the divinity has best contrived, for their country is often rained upon. They say too that they heard from the Indians that the king came to this river when the seasons made it rise, and sacrificed to it bulls and black horses—for the Indians set white below black in honour, because, I suppose, of their own colour—and, having sacrificed, they say he cast into the river a golden measure, fashioned like the one with which grain is measured out; and on what account the king does this the Indians could not guess, but they themselves conjecture that this measure is sunk either for abundance of crops, which the farmers measure out, or for the moderation of the stream, that it may not flood the land by coming in great volume.

Taking up the question again, he said: "And of the soul, what do you think?" "What," said the other, "Pythagoras delivered to you, and we to the Egyptians." "Would you then say," he asked, "as Pythagoras declared himself to have been Euphorbus, that you too, before coming into this body, were some Trojan or Achaean, or such a one?" The Indian said: "Troy perished by the Achaeans who sailed against it then, but you Greeks have been undone by the tales told about it. For thinking that those alone were men who fought against Troy, you neglect more men and more divine, whom both your land and that of the Egyptians and of the Indians have borne. Since, then, you ask me about my former body, tell me which of those who came against Troy, or in its defence, you hold most admirable." "I hold Achilles," he said, "the son of Peleus and Thetis; for he is hymned by Homer as the fairest and, beyond all the Achaeans, the greatest, and great deeds are known of him; and he counts as great the Ajaxes and Nireus, who after him are sung as fair and noble." "To him, Apollonius," he said, "look, and to my ancestor, or rather to my ancestral body; for this Pythagoras held to be Euphorbus.

Damis says the man held very many discussions at Athens, but did not write them all, only the necessary ones and those earnest about great matters. His first discourse, since he saw the Athenians fond of sacrifice, was about rites, and how one should sacrifice, or pour a libation, or pray, in a way proper to each of the gods, and at what hour of day and night; and there is a book of Apollonius to be met with, in which he teaches these things in his own words. He went through these things at Athens, first for the sake of his own wisdom and theirs, then refuting the hierophant for what he had said blasphemously and ignorantly; for who any longer thought that the philosopher was impure in things divine, who knows how the gods are to be served?

Initiated at Athens — and the hierophant who initiated him was the one whom he had himself foretold to the former one — he met also Demetrius the philosopher; for after the affair of Nero's bath and what he said about it, Demetrius lived at Athens so nobly that he did not even leave Greece during the time that Nero was committing his outrages about the games. Demetrius said that he had met Musonius too about the Isthmus, bound and ordered to dig; and that he himself spoke such words of comfort as were fitting, while the other clung to his mattock and struck the earth stoutly, and looking up said, "Do I grieve you, Demetrius, by digging the Isthmus for Greece? But if you had seen me playing the lyre, like Nero, what would you have felt?" And let the sayings of Musonius be passed over, many and more wonderful as they are, lest I should seem to presume upon the man who reported them carelessly.

"Ask," they said, "for an argument follows, no doubt, upon a question." And Apollonius said: "About the gods I will ask you first: what made you hand down to the men here strange and ridiculous forms of gods, except for a few? A few? Yes, very few that are wisely and godlikely set up; but the rest of your sanctuaries appear to be honours of dumb and inglorious animals rather than of gods." And Thespesion, taking it ill, said: "And the images among you, how do you say they are set up?" "As it is fairest and most god-loving," he said, "to fashion gods." "You mean, I suppose, the Zeus at Olympia," he said, "and the seat of Athena, and that of the Cnidian and that of the Argive goddess, and all such fair things full of grace." "Not only these," he said, "but I say outright that statuary among other peoples lays hold of what is fitting, while you laugh at the divine rather than reverence it." "Did your Phidias," he said, "and your Praxiteles go up to heaven and take a cast of the forms of the gods and so make their art, or was there something else that set them to fashioning?" "Something else," he said, "and a thing full of wisdom." "What kind?" he said; "for you could say nothing but imitation." "Imagination," he said, "wrought these, a craftsman wiser than imitation; for imitation will fashion what it has seen, but imagination what it has not seen too, for it will set it up with reference to the reality, and imitation is often baffled by amazement, but imagination by nothing, for it moves unbaffled toward what it has itself set up. He who would conceive a form of Zeus must see him along with heaven and the seasons and the stars, as Phidias then strove to do; and he who would fashion Athena must think of armies and counsel and arts and how she sprang from Zeus himself. But if you make a hawk or an owl or a wolf or a dog and bring it into the temples instead of Hermes and Athena and Apollo, the beasts and birds will seem enviable in their images, but the gods will stand far away from their own dignity." "You seem," he said, "to examine our ways without testing them; for it is wise, if anything is among the Egyptians, not to be bold toward the forms of the gods, but to make them symbolic and full of hidden meaning, for so they would appear the more august." Laughing, Apollonius said: "O men, great profit have you gained from the wisdom of the Egyptians and Ethiopians, if a dog and an ibis and a goat shall seem to you more august and more godlike — for this I hear from the wise Thespesion. But what is august or fearful in these? For perjurers and temple-robbers and ribald nations are likely to despise such sanctuaries rather than to fear them; and if these are more august for being hinted at, the gods in Egypt would have fared far more augustly, if no image of them had been set up at all, but you had used a different way of theology, wiser and more secret. For it was open to you to build temples for them and to mark out altars, and to lay down what one should sacrifice and what not, and when and how much and what saying or doing, but not to bring in an image, leaving the forms of the gods to those who enter the sanctuaries; for the mind sketches and shapes something better than craftsmanship. But you have taken from the gods both the being fairly seen and the being conceived." To this Thespesion said: "There was a certain Athenian, Socrates, foolish, like us, an old man, who held the dog and the goose and the plane-tree to be gods and swore by them." "Not foolish," he said, "but divine and truly wise; for he swore by these not as gods, but that he might not swear by gods."

To this Apollonius replied: "Since we discourse soundly, and you have said to me all that your heart holds, and it is just that I too should speak to you; and since you philosophize about your own affairs, as do those who have associated much with me, and—by Zeus—are so humanely disposed toward us as to think that you share my danger, I will tell you my own mind. For me it was possible to flee you all into many parts of the earth that do not hearken to you, and to come to men wise—and wiser than I—and to serve the gods with right reason, going among the ways of men dearer to the gods than those here, among whom there is neither information laid nor any indictment, for by the very fact of neither doing wrong nor suffering wrong they have no need of courts. But fearing to incur the charge of a traitor, if I myself should flee the defence, and the men who are in danger through me should perish, I have come to make my defence. Tell me, then, the things I must defend myself against."

Having discoursed forty days in Olympia and shown the greatest earnestness, he said, "I will discourse to you, men of Greece, in the cities, at festivals, in processions, in mysteries, in sacrifices, in libations—but they need a man of taste—but now I must go down to Lebadeia, since I have not yet met Trophonius, though I once visited the temple." And saying this he went off into Boeotia, none of his admirers being left behind. The mouth in Lebadeia is sacred to Trophonius the son of Apollo, and is enterable only by those who come about oracles; it is seen not in the temple, but a little above the temple on a hillock, and iron spits, set in a circle about it, close it; and the descent is such as draws a man down when he has seated himself. They who go down are sent clothed in white dress, carrying honey-cakes in their hands as soothings of the reptiles which assail those who descend. And the earth sends them up, some not far off, some very far; for they are sent up even beyond the Locrians and beyond the Phocians, but most about the bounds of the Boeotians. Going in, then, to the temple, he said, "I wish to go down for the sake of philosophy." The priests opposed him, and to the many said that they would never furnish the temple's test to a sorcerer, but to the man they pretended that the days were unlucky and not pure for the oracle. That day, then, he discoursed by the springs of Hercyna about the cause and manner of the oracle—for that alone gives its responses through the inquirer himself; and when evening came, going to the mouth with the young men who followed him, and pulling up four of the spits which hold the bars of the passage, he went underground in his very cloak, as if he had dressed himself for a discourse, doing things so dear to the god that Trophonius, appearing to the priests, rebuked them on behalf of the man, and bade all follow to Aulis, since there he would come up most marvellously of men. For he came up after seven days, more than any who had ever gone under the oracle, bearing a book most fit to the question. For he had gone down saying, "What, Trophonius, do you too hold the most perfect and purest philosophy?" And the book held the opinions of Pythagoras, as though the oracle too agreed with this wisdom.

As they passed into the country between the rivers, the customs-officer set over the Zeugma led them to the tariff-board and asked what they were taking out. And Apollonius said: "I am taking out temperance, justice, virtue, self-control, courage, discipline," stringing together in this way many such feminine nouns. The man, already eyeing his own profit, said, "Then register the slave-girls." "It is not lawful," he said; "for I am not taking out these as slave-girls, but as mistresses." Now the country between the rivers is formed by the Tigris and the Euphrates, which flow from Armenia and the foot of Taurus, and enclose a land in which there are cities, but for the most part villages, and Armenian and Arabian peoples, whom the rivers shut in; many of these are nomads and roam about, thinking themselves so much islanders that they say they go down to the sea when they walk to the rivers, and they make the circuit of the rivers the boundary of their land. For having rounded off the aforesaid land, the rivers run on to the same sea. There are those who say that the greater part of the Euphrates disappears into a marsh, and that this river ends in the earth. And some lay hold of a bolder account, saying that it flows beneath the earth and comes to light in Egypt and mingles with the Nile. For the sake of exactness, and that nothing written by Damis may be omitted by me, I should have liked to tell also of the things they took pains over in their journey through these barbarian lands; but the story drives us on to greater and more marvellous matters—not, however, so as to neglect these two: the courage with which Apollonius passed through barbarous and brigand nations, not yet under the Romans, and the wisdom by which, in the Arabian manner, he came to understand the language of animals. He learned this while travelling through these Arabians, who know it best of all men and practise it. For it is by now common among the Arabians to hear birds prophesying as oracles do; and this understanding they gain by feeding on the hearts, some say, or, as others say, the livers of serpents.

When they had crossed the river, the guide from the satrap led them straight to Taxila, where the Indian had his palace. They say the dress of those beyond the Indus is of native linen, and shoes of papyrus, and a cap when it rains; and the more distinguished among them are clothed in byssus, and the byssus, they say, grows from a tree like the white poplar at the base, with leaves resembling the willow. And Apollonius was pleased with the byssus, he says, since it resembles a grey philosopher's cloak. And from India byssus comes to Egypt for many of the temples. Taxila, they say, is in size like Nineveh, walled in moderate fashion like the Greek cities, and the palace of a man who then ruled the realm of Porus; and before the wall they say they saw a temple, not far short of a hundred feet, of shell-stone, and a shrine built within it, smaller than the temple, which was so large and pillared, yet worthy of wonder; for bronze tablets are fastened to each wall, painted with the deeds of Porus and Alexander. They are wrought in orichalc and silver and gold and black bronze—elephants, horses, soldiers, helmets, shields, but spears and arrows and swords all of iron; and as is the report of a celebrated painting—say, if it were a work of Zeuxis or Polygnotus or Euphranor, who loved shading and the breath of life and depth and relief—so, they say, it shines forth there too, and the metals are fused like colours. And the very spirit of the painting is pleasing; for Porus dedicated these after the death of the Macedonian, yet in them the Macedonian conquers and recovers Porus when wounded, and gives him back India, now become his own. And it is said too that Porus mourned Alexander when he died, and bewailed him as a noble and good king, and that, while Alexander lived, after his withdrawal from India, Porus neither said anything as a king, though he was permitted, nor gave commands to the Indians, but, like a satrap, was full of moderation and did everything to please him.

"There was a time," he said, "when Ethiopians dwelt here, a race of India, and Ethiopia did not yet exist, but Egypt was bounded beyond Meroe and the Cataracts — Egypt itself supplying both the springs of the Nile and ending where its mouths end. So long as the Ethiopians dwelt here, subject to king Ganges, the land nourished them sufficiently and the gods cared for them; but when they slew this king, they were thought unclean by the rest of the Indians, and the land would not suffer them to remain. For the seed they sowed in it, before it came to the ear, it destroyed; the births of the women it made imperfect; and it fed the flocks ill.

As he was discoursing about libation, there chanced to be present at his talk a youth of the luxurious sort, so reputed for wantonness that he had once become a song of the wagoners; his country was Corcyra, and he traced his descent to Alcinous the Phaeacian, the host of Odysseus. Apollonius was going through the matter of libation, and bade them not drink from a certain cup, but keep it for the gods undefiled and undrunk. And when he bade them also make ears for the cup and pour the libation by the ear, from which part men least drink, the youth poured over the discourse a broad and wanton laugh. But Apollonius, looking up at him, said: "It is not you who do this insolence, but the demon who drives you without your knowing it." And indeed the youth was unknowingly possessed; for he laughed at things at which no one else laughed, and changed to weeping without cause, and talked to himself and sang. Most thought it was his rioting youth that carried him into these things; but he was in truth playing the part of the demon, and seemed to be drunk in what he then ran riot. And as Apollonius looked at him, the phantom uttered cries of fear and wrath, such as come from those being burned and racked, and swore to keep away from the youth and to fall upon no man. But when Apollonius, like a master to a slave crafty, knavish, shameless, and the like, spoke to him with anger and bade him depart with a sign, the demon said, "I will throw down such-and-such a statue," pointing to one of those about the Royal Stoa, near which this was happening. And when the statue first stirred, then fell, who could write the uproar at this, and how they clapped for wonder? But the youth, as if waking from sleep, rubbed his eyes and looked at the sun's rays, and drew on himself the respect of all who had turned to him, and no longer appeared wanton, nor looked disorderly, but returned to his own nature, no less than if he had used a drug; and changing his soft mantles and fine robes and the rest of his Sybaritic ways, he came to love squalor and a coarse cloak, and stripped for the manners of Apollonius.

After Apollonius had wintered among all the Greek sanctuaries, he set out about spring on the road to Egypt, having much rebuked the cities and much advised them, and given praise to many — for he did not refrain from praise whenever anything was soundly done. Going down to the Piraeus, he found a ship lying at anchor under sail, about to put off for Ionia; but the merchant would not allow him to embark, for he was sailing her as his own private vessel. When Apollonius asked what the cargo was, he said, "I am carrying images of the gods to Ionia, some of gold and stone, some of ivory and gold." "To set them up, or what?" "To sell them," he said, "to those who wish to set them up." "Do you fear, then, my good man, lest we plunder the images in the ship?" "It is not that I fear," he said, "but that they should sail with many others and be filled with the company of common men and the kind of life there is on shipboard — that I think a dreadful thing." "And yet, my good fellow" — for you seem to me to be some Athenian — "into the ships which you used against the barbarians, filled though they were with the disorder of sailors, the gods embarked along with you and did not think themselves defiled by you; while you so ignorantly thrust philosophic men from your ship, men in whom the gods most delight — and this when you have made merchandise of the gods themselves? The ancient image-making did not do this, nor did men go round the cities selling the gods, but only bringing their own hands and their stone-cutting and ivory-working tools, and setting beside them the unworked material, they wrought their craft in the very temples; whereas you, like Hyrcanian and Scythian wares — far be it from me to say of what — leading the gods thus into harbours and market-places, think you do nothing impious? And some men too, like gleaners, fasten upon some image of Demeter or Dionysus and say they are fed by the gods whom they carry; but that the gods themselves should be fed, and not even have their fill of this, is a dreadful trafficking — and I would call it folly too, if you fear nothing from it." Having rebuked him thus, he sailed on another ship.

After this Thespesion, as though shifting from this argument, asked Apollonius about the Laconian scourge, and whether the Lacedaemonians are flogged in public. "With the strokes that come from men, Thespesion," he said, "especially the free and esteemed among them." "And the household slaves who do wrong, what do they do to them?" he said. "They no longer kill them," he said, "as Lycurgus once allowed, but the same scourge is used on them too." "And how does Greece judge of these things?" he said. "They gather," he said, "as to the Hyacinthia and the Gymnopaediae, to look on with pleasure and all eagerness." "Then are not the worthy Greeks ashamed," he said, "either to see men who once ruled them flogged in public, or to be ruled by men who are flogged in public? And how did you not set this right? For they say you took thought even for the Lacedaemonians." "What could be set right," he said, "I counselled, and they did it eagerly, for they are the most freedom-loving of the Greeks, and alone obedient to one who counsels well; but the custom of the scourging is done to the Scythian Artemis, the oracles, they say, enjoining this; and to oppose the gods is madness, I think." "You have spoken of the gods of the Greeks, Apollonius," he said, "as not wise, if they became counsellors of scourging to men who practise freedom." "Not of scourging," he said, "but of sprinkling the altar with the blood of men, since among the Scythians too they were held worthy of this; but the Lacedaemonians, contriving against the inexorable demand of the sacrifice, have come to a contest of endurance, from which it is possible neither to die and yet to offer first-fruits to the goddess of their own blood." "Why then," he said, "do they not sacrifice strangers to Artemis, as the Scythians once held right?" "Because," he said, "it is not according to the temper of any Greeks to practise barbarous customs." "And yet they would seem more humane in sacrificing one or two than in driving out strangers altogether." "Let us not lay hold of Lycurgus, Thespesion," he said; "for one must understand the man, and that his not allowing strangers to stay among them had not the meaning of inhospitality, but of keeping their practices sound, the men from outside not consorting with Sparta. But I would have held the Spartiates to be such men as they think fit to seem, had they kept their home ways while consorting with strangers; for they ought, I think, to win their virtues not by the absence of strangers but by being seen the same in their presence. But they, though they used expulsions of strangers, were corrupted in their practices, and seemed to do the very things like those of the Greeks whom they most hated. Their dealings about the sea, at any rate, and the later imposition of tributes, were counselled in a more Attic fashion, and the very things for which they thought they must war against the Athenians, these they came to do themselves, conquering the Athenians in war but worsted in what they thought right to practise. And the very bringing in of a deity from the Taurians and the Scythians was the work of men holding strange ways. And if these things were by oracles, what need of the scourge? Why fashion a slavish endurance? It were more Laconian, I think, toward strength against death, that a Spartiate youth should of his own will be sacrificed upon the altar. For this would have shown Sparta the braver, and turned Greece away from setting itself in rivalry against them. And if it was reasonable to spare the young for war, yet the law among the Scythians laid down for those of sixty years would have been more proper for the Lacedaemonians to practise than for the Scythians, if they praise death truly and not for boast's sake. These things I have said not against the Lacedaemonians but against you, Apollonius; for if we examine bitterly the ancient customs, more venerable than we can know, setting ourselves to convict the divine because it delights in them, many strange arguments will spring up out of such philosophy; for we might lay hold of the rite at Eleusis too, because this and not that, and of the rites the Samothracians perform, since this and not that is done by them, and of the Dionysia and the phallus and the form at Cyllene, and we should never have done playing the slanderer over everything. Let us go on, then, to whatever else you wish, honouring also the saying of Pythagoras, which is of our own country; for it is well, if not about all things, yet at least about such things, to keep silent." Apollonius took him up: "If you had wished, Thespesion, to take the argument in earnest, Lacedaemon would have seemed to you to say many noble things on behalf of what she practises soundly and beyond all the Greeks; but since you so decline it as to think it not even holy to speak of such things, let us go on to another argument of great worth, as I persuade myself; for I will ask something about justice."

"The kinds of the indictment," he said, "are various and many; for they slander your dress and the rest of your manner of life, and the fact that there are those by whom you are worshipped, and the oracle you once gave at Ephesus about the plague; and they say you have spoken against the emperor—some things secretly, some openly, and some as one who has heard the gods. The charge least credible to me—for I know that you do not even endure the blood of sacrifices—but most credible as it is slandered to the emperor, is this: they say that you went into the country to Nerva and cut up for him an Arcadian boy, sacrificing against the emperor, and that you raised him up by these rites; and that this was done by night, when the month was already waning. This accusation, since it is far the greater, let us hold none other beside it; for he who lays hold of your dress and your way of life and your foreknowledge tends, I suppose, to this very point, and says that these very things gave you both your lawlessness against him and your boldness for the sacrifice. You must therefore have your defence prepared concerning these matters; and let your speech not be one that despises the emperor." And Apollonius said: "Let your proof that I do not despise him be that I have come for the sake of defence; and if my affairs stood so boldly that I were lifted above tyrannies, yet I have submitted myself to you, being such as you are and loving me. For to seem base to an enemy is no terrible thing, since enemies hate not for what a man is publicly slandered for, but for what privately he has given offence in; but to take from a friend the charge of seeming base—this is heavier than all the enemy's charges together; for one could not escape being hateful to those friends as well, for the things for which one was base."

This book is set up at Antium and is held in earnest because of the affair; and Antium is of the Italians on the sea. These things, then, I grant may be heard even from the inhabitants of Lebadeia; but about this book let my opinion be declared, that it was conveyed later to the emperor Hadrian, when indeed some of Apollonius's letters too—not all of them—and that it remained at the palace in Antium, in which of the palaces about Italy he most rejoiced.

Having passed beyond Ctesiphon and come to the borders of Babylon, there was there a garrison set by the king, which one could not pass without being asked who he was and from what city, and on what errand he came. A satrap was set over this garrison, an "eye of the king," I suppose; for the Mede, having just come to power, did not allow himself to live without fear, but dreading both things that were and things that were not, he had fallen into terrors and alarms. So Apollonius and his company were brought before the satrap, who happened to have made himself a tent upon a covered carriage and to be driving out somewhere. And seeing a man full of squalor, he cried out like timid women and covered his face, and scarcely looking up at him, "From where," he asked, as though to a divinity, "have you been sent to us?" "By myself," he said, "in case you should somehow become real men, even against your will." Again he asked who he was that entered the king's country, and he said, "All the earth is mine, and it is permitted me to travel through it." "I will torture you," he said, "unless you tell." "Then, if with your own hands," he said, "may you yourself be tortured, for touching a man." When the eunuch was astonished at him, since he saw that he needed no interpreter, but understood the language without trouble and easily, "By the gods," he said, "who are you?"—now entreating, and changed in his tone. And Apollonius replied: "Since you have asked this moderately and not inhumanly, hear who I am. I am Apollonius of Tyana, and my road is to the king of the Indians, to inquire into the things there; but I should be glad to meet your king also, for those who have been with him say he is no mean man, if indeed this is Vardanes, who has now recovered the kingdom that was once lost to him." "He is the man, divine Apollonius," said he; "for we have long heard of you. And to a wise man he would yield even his golden throne, and would send each of you to the Indians upon a camel. And I make you my guest-friend, and give you of this money," showing him at the same time a treasure of gold, "as much as you wish to grasp, and not once, but ten times." When Apollonius declined the money, "Then take Babylonian wine," he said—"the king pours it for ten of us satraps—take an amphora, and roasted joints of pig and gazelle, and flour and loaves, and whatever you wish. For the road after this is for many stadia through villages not well supplied with food." And the eunuch, checking himself, said, "What, O gods, have I done! For hearing that the man neither feeds on animals nor drinks wine, I entertain him grossly and ignorantly." "But you may," he said, "entertain me lightly too, if you give bread and dried fruits." "I will give," he said, "leavened bread, and dates of the palm, amber-coloured and large; I will give also vegetables, all that the Tigris grows in its gardens." "But sweeter," said Apollonius, "are the wild and self-grown vegetables than those that are forced and cultivated." "Sweeter indeed," said the satrap; "but our land toward Babylon, being full of wormwood, grows them disagreeable and bitter." So at any rate he accepted the satrap's gift, and as he now departed, "My good man," he said, "do not only leave off well, but also begin well," gently admonishing him about his "I will torture you," and the words of barbarous bluster which he had heard at the outset.

The story does not let me pass over what they record about this Porus. When the Macedonian was at the crossing, and some advised him to make allies of the peoples beyond the Hyphasis and the Ganges—for he would never be drawn up in battle against all India in agreement—"If my subjects are such," he said, "that they cannot be kept safe without allies, it is better for me not to rule." And when someone reported to him that Alexander had captured King Darius, he said, "A king, but not a man." When the keeper had adorned the elephant on which he was to fight, and said, "This, O king, will carry you," he said, "Rather I will carry it, if I prove a man like myself." And when they proposed that he sacrifice the elephant to the river, that it might not receive the Macedonians' rafts nor be of easy passage to Alexander, he said, "It is not for men who bear arms to call down curses." And after the battle, when even to Alexander he seemed divine and beyond human nature, and one of his kinsmen said, "If you had made obeisance to him when he crossed, Porus, you would neither have been beaten in battle, nor would so many of the Indians have perished, nor would you yourself have been wounded," he said: "Hearing that Alexander was most ambitious, I understood that if I made obeisance he would count me a slave, but if I fought him, a king, and I chose to be admired rather than pitied; and I was not deceived; for by showing myself such as Alexander saw, I both lost and gained everything in a single day." Such is the account they give of this Indian; and they say he was the handsomest of the Indians, and as tall as none of the men after the Trojan heroes, and quite young when he warred against Alexander.

"And I should tell more of the man, were I not loath to set myself to my own praise; for I am he. This I made plain when I was four years old; for once, when Ganges had fixed seven adamantine swords in the earth, that no terror might come near the country, and the gods commanded those who came to sacrifice where these were fixed, but did not declare the place in which they had been set — I, a mere child, led the interpreters to a trench and bade them dig there, saying that the swords had been laid in that spot.

He is said to have rebuked the Athenians about the Dionysia, which they hold in the season of Anthesterion. For he thought they came together to the theatre to hear monodies and melodies and the parabases and rhythms of comedy and tragedy; but when he heard that to the flute's signal they danced with twistings, and in the midst of Orpheus' epic and theology acted now as Hours, now as Nymphs, now as Bacchae, he set himself to rebuke this, and said: "Cease to dance away the Salaminians and many other good men who lie dead. For if this dancing were Laconian, well done, soldiers; for you train yourselves for war, and I will dance with you. But if it is soft and bent on effeminacy, what shall I say of the trophies? For these stand not against Medes or Persians, but against yourselves, who set them up, should you fall short of those men. Whence come these saffron robes and purple and scarlet to you? For not even Acharnae was so arrayed, nor did Colonus ride so. And why do I say this? A woman admiral from Caria sailed against you with Xerxes, and there was nothing womanish about her, but a man's dress and arms; but you are softer than the women of Xerxes, arraying yourselves against yourselves — old men, young men, the company of ephebes, who once swore, going to the temple of Agraulus, to die for their country and to lay down their arms, but now perhaps will swear to play the Bacchant for their country and to take the thyrsus, wearing no helmet, but in a woman-mimicking shape, as Euripides says, shamefully conspicuous. And I hear you become winds too, and are said to wave your robes, billowing them aloft as drapery. But you should at least reverence these winds, who are your allies and have blown mightily for you, and not make Boreas, who is your kinsman and the most manly of all the winds, into a female; for Boreas would never have become the lover of Oreithyia, had he seen her dancing too.

When he had put in at Chios, without even setting foot on land he leapt across to the ship lying near — the ship was being announced for Rhodes — and his companions leapt across too, saying nothing, for their philosophy lay above all in following him in word and deed. Crossing with a favouring wind, he busied himself thus in Rhodes. As he came toward the statue of the Colossus, Damis asked him what he thought greater than that.
