And he said, "A man who pursues philosophy soundly and without guile." There was at that time staying in Rhodes a flute-player named Canus, who seemed to play the flute best of men. So calling him, Apollonius said, "What does the flute-player accomplish?" "Everything," he said, "that the hearer wishes." "And yet," he said, "many of those who hear wish rather to be rich than to hear the flute. Do you then make rich those whom you perceive to desire this?" "By no means," he said, "as I should wish." "What then? Do you make beautiful the young among your hearers? Since all those who are in their youth wish to seem fair." "Not this either," he said, "though there is the most of love in the flute." "What then is it," he said, "that you think the hearer wishes?" "What else," said Canus, "than that the grieving man should have his grief lulled to sleep by the flute, that the joyful should become more cheerful than himself, the lover warmer, and the lover of sacrifice more inspired and full of hymns?" "This then, Canus," he said, "does the flute itself accomplish, because it is composed of gold and orichalc and the shin-bone of deer — and some are of asses' bones — or is it something else that has this power?" "Something else, Apollonius," he said; "for music, and the modes, and the mingling and the ready variety of the playing, and the characters of the harmonies — these fit the hearers and make their souls such as they wish." "I understand, Canus," he said, "what your art accomplishes; for its variety and its reaching out to every mood, this you practise and supply to those who come to you. But to me the flute seems to need other things besides what you have said: good breath, good lip, and a deft hand in the player. There is good breath when the breath is clear and pure and the throat does not strike against it — for that is like an unmusical sound; good lip, when the lips, set against the flute's tongue, play without the face being puffed out; and the deft-handed player I hold of great worth, when neither the wrist gives out as it bends back, nor the fingers are slow to fly upon the notes — for the quick change from mode to mode belongs more to the deft-handed. If then you supply all these, play with confidence, Canus, for Euterpe will be with you."

"Let us lay hold of the argument," said Thespesion, "for it befits both the wise and the unwise. But, that we may not confound it by weaving in the opinions of the Indians, and go away with the argument unfinished, first tell us what the Indians held about justice; for it is likely you tested this there, and if the opinion be right, we shall agree; but if we say something wiser, do you agree, for this too is of justice." "Excellent, Thespesion," he said, "and most pleasing to me has been your speech; hear, then, what was discussed there. I went through with them how I had become helmsman of a great ship, in the time when my soul tended another body, and how I held myself most just, since, when brigands hired me to betray the ship by mooring it where they meant to lie in wait for it, on account of what it carried, I promised this, that they might not fall upon us, but sailed past them and rose above the place." "And did the Indians agree," said Thespesion, "that this was justice?" "They laughed at it," he said; "for justice, they said, is not the mere not doing wrong." "Soundly," he said, "did the Indians decide; for neither is it prudence not to think anything foolishly, nor courage not to leave one's post, nor temperance not to fall into the ways of adulterers, nor is it worthy of praise not to appear bad; for everything that stands equally distant from honour and from punishment is not yet virtue." "How then, Thespesion," he said, "shall we crown the just man, or for doing what?" "More completely and more fittingly," he said, "would you have been earnest about justice when the king, ruling so great and so happy a country, stood by while you philosophized, than about kingship, the most just of possessions." "If it had been Phraotes who came," he said, "you would rightly blame us for not being earnest about justice before him; but since you saw the man in the state I described yesterday, drunken and vexed at all philosophy, what need was there to give trouble? Why should they be ambitious before a man who held all things mere wantonness? But since justice must be tracked by wise men, as by us, rather than by kings and generals, let us go on to the simply just man. For what I thought myself, when I was on the ship, and what others are who do not lay hold of wrong, you say are not yet just, nor worthy of honour." "And reasonably," he said; "for never would a decree have been written among the Athenians or Lacedaemonians to crown So-and-so, because he is not of those who have prostituted themselves, or to make So-and-so a citizen, because he does not rob the temples. Who then is the just man, and the man doing what? For I know of no one crowned for justice, nor a decree written over a just man, that So-and-so ought to be crowned, since doing such a thing he appears just; for to one who considers the affair of Palamedes at Troy and of Socrates at Athens, justice will not seem even to fare well among men, for these men suffered most unjustly, being most just. Yet these perished on a reputation of wrongdoings, by a vote carried aside from the straight; but Aristides the son of Lysimachus justice itself once destroyed, and such a man on such a virtue went away into exile. And I know that justice will seem ridiculous, for, appointed by Zeus and the Fates to keep men from being wronged, she nowhere appoints herself to keep from being wronged herself. But the case of Aristides is enough for me to show who is the not-unjust man and who the just. For tell me, is not this that Aristides whom you who come from the Greeks say sailed to the islands about the tributes, fixed them in due measure, and came back in the same cloak?" "It is he," he said, "through whom love of poverty once flowered." "Suppose then," he said, "two demagogues at Athens praising Aristides just come from the allies, and one should propose to crown him because he has come back not rich nor having gathered any livelihood for himself, but poorest of the Athenians and poorer than himself; and the other should propose some such decree as this: 'Since Aristides, having fixed the tributes not above the power of the allies but as each has of land, took care both of their concord with the Athenians and that they should not seem to bear these things with vexation, be it resolved to crown him for justice' — do you not think that to the first decree he would himself object, as not worthy of the life he had lived, if he were honoured for what is mere not-wronging; but the second he might perhaps himself praise, as aiming at what he intended? For looking, I think, to the advantage both of the Athenians and the subjects, he took care of the due measure of the tributes; and this was shown the more after Aristides, for when the Athenians, transgressing the amounts he had fixed, imposed heavier ones on the islands, their naval power, by which most of all they were terrible, was torn apart, and that of the Lacedaemonians came forward to the sea, and none of their power held together, but all the subject states rushed to revolution and laid hold of escape. So that the just man, Apollonius, by the straight account, is not he who does no wrong, but he who himself does just things and sets others too to do no wrong; and from such justice will spring other virtues too, but especially the judicial and the legislative. For such a man will judge far more justly than those who swear over the cut victims, and will legislate, as the Solons and Lycurguses did, for to those men too justice was the beginning of writing laws."

It seemed to Aelian that he spoke well; and exhorting him to take heart, he laid hold of himself, so that the man should not be dismayed, "not even if a Gorgon's head were raised against him." So, calling those appointed to such tasks, he said: "I bid you keep this man fast, until the emperor learns that he has come and is saying what he has said." And he seemed like men very angry. Then, going into the palace, he did the things proper to his office. Here Damis records a deed both like and unlike that done in former times at Athens to Aristeides; for they drove out Aristeides with the ostracon on the score of his virtue, and as he was already outside the wall, one of the rustics came up to him and begged him to write something for him on the ostracon against Aristeides—the man knowing neither Aristeides nor even how to write, but only envy at justice; but here a tribune, of those who knew Apollonius very well, addressing him, asked insolently for what he was in danger; and when he said he did not know, "But I," he said, "know; for your being worshipped by men has slandered you as one held worthy of equal honour with the gods." "And who," said Apollonius, "is it that worshipped me?" "I," he said, "at Ephesus, while still a boy, when you healed us of the plague." "It was well done," he said, "both for you and for the city of the Ephesians that was saved." "For these things, then," he said, "I have also prepared a defence for you, which will free you of the charge; for let us go outside the wall, and if I strike off your neck with the sword, the charge is dissolved and you are acquitted; but if you confound me and I let go the sword, then you must needs be held divine and tried as though on true charges." So much more boorish was this man than the one who drove out Aristeides; and he said this chewing and with laughter, while Apollonius, as one who had not heard, talked with Damis about the Delta, where they say the Nile divides.

There came to him from Ionia too all his followers, whom Greece named the Apollonians, and mingling with those from the place they became a youth worthy to marvel at for their number and their impulse toward philosophy. For rhetoric lay neglected, and they paid small heed to those who beat together the art, holding the tongue alone its teacher; but all pressed toward his philosophy. And he, as they say the Gyges and the Croesuses furnish the doors of their treasuries unlocked, that those who need may bale them, so furnished his own wisdom to those who loved it, granting them to ask about everything.

When they had gone twenty stadia, they came upon a lioness that had been killed in the hunt; and the beast was large, larger than any I have seen, and the people who had flocked from the village were shouting, and, by Zeus, the hunters too, as though they saw some great wonder in it. And it was indeed a wonder; for when cut open she had eight whelps. Now as to the breeding of the lioness: lionesses are pregnant for six months, and give birth three times; the number of whelps at the first birth is three, at the second two, and when she comes to a third birth she brings forth a single whelp, large, I think, and fiercer in nature. For no heed should be paid to those who say that the whelps tear the wombs of lionesses and so come forth from the entrails. For nature, it seems, has made the offspring well-suited to the parent for the safety of the race. So Apollonius, gazing at the beast and considering it a long while, said: "Damis, the time of our stay with the king will be a year and eight months; for neither will he let us go sooner, nor would it be better for you to depart before this. One must reckon the whelps as months and the lioness as a year; for whole things must be compared with whole." "But what," said Damis, "will the sparrows in Homer say, which the serpent at Aulis devoured, eight of them, taking their mother as the ninth? Calchas, interpreting these, declared that Troy would be taken in nine years; so take care that, according to Homer and Calchas, our stay does not stretch to nine years." "Naturally, Damis," he said, "Homer likens the nestlings to years, for they had already come to be and exist; but I—how should I liken to years beasts that are unfinished and not yet born, and perhaps would never have been born? For things contrary to nature would never come to be, and, even if they do, they meet with swift destruction. But follow the argument, and let us go and pray to the gods who reveal these things."

During the time he stayed in the temple—and this became long, until it should be announced to the king that strangers had come—"Damis," said Apollonius, "is there such a thing as painting?" "If indeed," he said, "there is such a thing as truth." "And what does this art do?" "It mixes the colours," he said, "all that there are, the blue with the green and the white with the black and the red with the yellow." "And for what," he said, "does it mix these? For not for the sake of colour alone, like the encaustic painters." "For the sake of imitation," he said, "and of representing a dog and a horse and a man and a ship and all that the sun looks upon; and it represents even the sun himself, sometimes upon four horses, as he is said to appear here, sometimes again blazing across the heaven, when it sketches the ether and the house of the gods." "Then painting is imitation, Damis?" "What else?" he said; "for if it did not do this, it would seem ridiculous, making colours foolishly." "And the things seen in the heaven," he said, "when the clouds are torn apart from one another, the centaurs and stag-goats and, by Zeus, the wolves and the horses—what will you say? Are these not works of an imitative art?" "It seems so," he said. "Is god then a painter, Damis, and, leaving the winged chariot on which he travels ordering things divine and human, does he then sit down to play and to draw these things, like children in the sand?" Damis blushed, since the argument seemed to fall into such absurdity. But Apollonius, not despising him—for he was not harsh in his refutations—said: "But do you not wish to say this, Damis, that these things move through the heaven without meaning and at random, so far as god is concerned, but that we, having by nature the imitative faculty, give them form and shape?" "Let us rather think this, Apollonius," he said, "for it is more plausible and far better." "Then the imitative art is twofold, Damis, and let us hold one kind to be that which imitates with hand and mind, and this is painting, but the other kind to liken with the mind alone." "Not twofold," said Damis, "but we should hold the one more perfect, being painting, which can liken with both mind and hand, and the other a part of it, since it understands and imitates with the mind, even without being a painter, but could not use its hand to draw them." "Because, Damis," he said, "its hand is maimed by some blow or disease?" "No, by Zeus," he said, "but because it has handled neither pen nor any instrument nor colour, but is unskilled in drawing." "Then, Damis," he said, "we both agree that the imitative faculty comes to men from nature, but painting from art. And this would appear true of sculpture too. But painting itself you do not seem to me to think to be only that which is by colours; for one colour sufficed for the earlier painters, and as it advanced it took to four, then to more; but line too, and what is without colour, which is composed of shadow and light, it is right to call painting. For in these too likeness is seen, and form and mind and modesty and boldness, although these are bereft of colours, and show neither blood nor the bloom of any hair or beard, but, composed in a single mode, resemble the fair-skinned man and the white; and if we draw one of these Indians with a white line, he will surely seem black, for the snubness of the nose and the upright curls and the prominent jaw and the kind of startled look about the eyes blacken what is seen and sketch an Indian for those at least who do not look foolishly. Whence I would say that those who look at the works of painting need the imitative faculty too; for one would not praise a painted horse or bull unless he conceived the animal it is likened to, nor would one admire the Ajax of Timomachus, which is painted by him as maddened, unless he took up into his mind some image of Ajax, and how it was likely that he, having slain the cattle in Troy, sat down spent, taking counsel even to kill himself. But these contrivances of Porus, Damis, let us declare to be neither of the founder's art alone, since they are likened to paintings, nor of painting alone, since they were cast in bronze; but let us hold that one man, painter and founder, devised them, such as is shown in Homer of Hephaestus about the shield of Achilles. For these too are full of slayers and slain, and you would say the earth was bloodied, though it is of bronze."

"And do not yet marvel at me, if I have passed from one Indian into another. For this one" — and he pointed to a youth of some twenty years — "is by nature fitted for philosophy beyond all men, and is sound, as you see, and nobly built in body, and endures fire and every cutting; yet, being such, he is at enmity with philosophy." "What then," said Apollonius, "Iarchas, is the youth's affliction? For it is a strange thing you tell, if one so framed by nature does not embrace philosophy, nor love learning, and that too while living among you." "He does not live with us," he said, "but, like the lions, he has been caught against his will, and is shut in, but looks askance at us as we tame and stroke him. This youth, then, was Palamedes at Troy, and he had as his bitterest enemies Odysseus and Homer — the one who contrived against him the arts by which he was stoned to death, the other who did not deem him worthy even of a verse. And since neither did the wisdom he had profit him at all, nor did he meet with Homer as his praiser — by whom many even of the undistinguished were brought to fame — and since he was overcome by Odysseus though he did no wrong, he is set against philosophy and bewails his fate. And this is Palamedes, who writes also though he never learned letters.

He set right that too at Athens. The Athenians, coming together to the theatre beneath the Acropolis, gave their minds to the slaughter of men, and these things were pursued there more keenly than they now are in Corinth; for adulterers and harlots and burglars and cut-purses and kidnappers and such tribes were brought in, bought for great sums, and men armed them and bade them fight together. Apollonius laid hold of these things too, and when the Athenians called him to their assembly, he said he would not enter a place unclean and full of gore. He said this in a letter. And he said he marvelled how the goddess did not already leave the Acropolis too, when they poured out such blood for her. "For you seem to me," he said, "to be coming, when you celebrate the Panathenaea, no longer to slay oxen, but hecatombs of men, for the goddess. And you, Dionysus, after such blood do you frequent the theatre? And do the wise Athenians there pour libations to you? Depart, you too, Dionysus; Cithaeron is purer." Such are the most earnest of the things he philosophised at Athens then.

There was also a certain young man, newly rich and uneducated, who was building himself a house in Rhodes and bringing into it varied paintings and stones from all nations. So Apollonius asked him how much money he had spent on teachers and education; and he said, "Not even a drachma." "And on the house, how much?" "Twelve talents," he said, "and I would spend as much again." "And what," he said, "does the house mean for you?" "It will be a splendid way of living for the body," he said, "for there are running-tracks in it and groves, and I shall walk but a little to the market-place, and those who come in will address me with more pleasure, as though resorting to a temple." "And are men more to be envied," he said, "for themselves, or for the things about them?" "For their wealth," he said, "for money has the greatest power." "And of money, young man," he said, "which is the better guardian — the educated man or the uneducated?" And when he was silent, Apollonius said, "You seem to me, young man, not to possess the house, but the house to possess you. As for me, on entering a temple, I should far rather see in it, though small, an image of ivory and gold, than in a great one an image of clay and worthless."

So much, Damis says, they discussed about the just man, and Apollonius agreed with the argument, for it accorded with what was soundly said. And having philosophized about the soul too, that it is immortal, and about nature in terms near to the opinions of Plato, and having discoursed more about the laws among the Greeks, Apollonius said: "My journey here was for your sake and for the springs of the Nile, which, to one who goes forward only as far as Egypt, it is pardonable to be ignorant of, but to one who has gone on to Ethiopia, as I have, it would bring reproach to pass them by and not draw from them some discourses." "Go and prosper," he said, "and whatever is dear to you, pray for it at the springs, for they are divine. And you will make your guide, I think, the once Naucratite, now Memphite, Timasion, for he is acquainted with the springs and is so pure as to have no need of being sprinkled. But with you, Nilus, we wish to discuss something by ourselves." The meaning of the words was not hidden from Apollonius, for he understood that they were ill-disposed, since Nilus loved him; but withdrawing from the discourse, he went away to make ready, as if to set out at dawn. And not long after Nilus came, and reported nothing of what he had heard, but kept laughing to himself; and no one asked about the laughter, but they spared the secret.

When Aelian, calling him, bade him dwell in the free prison until the emperor should have leisure—"for he wishes to be with you in private first"—Apollonius left the court, and entering the prison said: "Let us talk, Damis, with those here; for what else should one do for the time during which the tyrant will discourse with me about his wants?" "They will think us babblers," he said, "if we drive them off from the defences they are preparing; and besides, it is out of place to walk among men so faint-hearted." "And yet these most of all," he said, "have need of one to talk with and to tend them; for if you should call to mind the verses of Homer in which Homer says that Helen poured the Egyptian drugs into the bowl, that the griefs of the soul might be steeped away, I think Helen, having learned Egyptian words, chanted them over the faint-hearted into the bowl, healing them by word mingled with wine." "It is likely," he said, "if indeed she came to Egypt and conversed with Proteus, or, as Homer thinks, was with Polydamna the wife of Thon. But for now let these men be put off, for I wish to ask you something." "I know what you will ask me," he said; "for you wish to hear from me the words that passed between me and the man, and what he said, and whether he was terrible or mild." And he went through them all. Damis, doing him reverence, said: "I do not disbelieve, then, that Leucothea once gave Odysseus her veil after the wreck of his ship, when, having fallen from it, he measured the sea with his own hands; for as we too have embarked on things desperate and dreadful, some god, I think, holds his hand over us, that we may not fall from all safety." Apollonius, rebuking the speech, said: "Whither will you stretch on, fearing these things, and not yet knowing that wisdom dismays all things that understand her, but is herself dismayed by nothing?" "But we," he said, "have come to one who understands nothing, and who not only is not dismayed at us, but does not even think there is anything that will dismay him." "Do you understand, then, Damis," he said, "that he is puffed up and senseless?" "I understand—how should I not?" he said. "Then by you too," he said, "the tyrant must be the more despised, by so much as you know him."

When some slandered him for shunning the visits of the governors and leading his hearers rather into quiet places, and one mocked him with driving his sheep elsewhere whenever he learned that the marketplace-men were approaching, "By Zeus," he said, "that the wolves may not fall upon the flock." And what did this mean for him? Seeing the marketplace-men gazed upon by the many and advancing from poverty to wealth, and so welcoming hatreds as to sell the very being hated, he led the young away from being with them, and rebuked rather bitterly those who had been with them, as one washing out a strange dye; for he was set against them at other times too, but by the prisons in Rome and the bound and the dying he was so disposed toward the art as to hold all these the work of the informers and of those puffed up with cleverness rather than of the tyrant.

As he advanced into the Cissian country and was now near Babylon, an apparition of a dream came to him, composed thus by the god who sent it. Fish, cast out of the sea, lay gasping on the land, uttering a lament like that of men, and bewailing that they had passed out of their proper element; and they besought a dolphin that swam by along the land to help them, being pitiable, like men in a foreign country weeping. Not at all dismayed by the dream, he reckoned up its meaning and how it stood; but wishing to disturb Damis—for he knew him to be among the more timid—he reported the vision to him, feigning fear, as though over the evil things he had seen. And Damis cried out as though he himself had seen these things, and tried to lead Apollonius back from going forward. "May we not too," he said, "like fish fallen out of our element, perish, and say many pitiable things in a foreign land, and falling perhaps into some helpless plight, supplicate some ruler or king, and he dishonour us, as the dolphins dishonour the fish." But Apollonius, laughing, said: "You do not yet philosophize, if you fear these things; but I will show you where the dream tends. The Eretrians inhabit this Cissian country, men who were once carried up from Euboea by Darius five hundred years ago; and they are said, just as the vision appeared, to have suffered the fate of fish in their capture; for they were all netted, as in a seine, and taken. The gods, then, seem to bid me go to them and take care of them, if I can. Perhaps too the souls of the Greeks, who drew the lot of dwelling here, are leading me to the benefit of their land. Let us go, then, turning aside from our road, asking only about the well beside which they dwell." This well is said to be a mixture of asphalt and oil and water; but when one draws it up and pours it out, these separate and are distinguished from one another. That he did go to Cissia he himself has acknowledged in what he writes to the sophist of Clazomenae; for he was so good and high-minded that, when he saw the Eretrians, he remembered the sophist and wrote to him both what he saw and what he did on their behalf; and throughout the whole letter he exhorts him to pity the Eretrians, and, whenever he should practise his discourse about them, not to refuse even to weep for them.

While the man was busy with such matters, there came to him from the king messengers and an interpreter, saying that the king made him his guest for three days, for it was not customary for strangers to stay longer in the city; and they led him to the palace. The city, as to its wall, I have described; and they say its alleys are laid out irregularly and in the Attic manner, and built with houses which, if one looked at them from outside, had a single story, but if one passed within, were underground, and presented below the earth as much as above.

As they were discoursing thus, a messenger came to Iarchas and said: "The king will come about the first watch of the afternoon to confer with you about his affairs." "Let him come," he said; "for he too would go away the better for knowing a Greek." And saying this he took up again the former discourse. So he asked Apollonius: "Would you tell of your first body, and who you were before the one you have now?" He said: "Since that was an inglorious thing, I remember little of it." Iarchas took him up: "Do you then think it inglorious to have been the pilot of an Egyptian ship? For I see that this is what you were." "True," he said, "Iarchas; for this is in plain truth what I was; but I hold it not only inglorious but base, and, though as worthy among men as ruling or commanding an army, ill spoken of by those who slander the sea. At any rate, the noblest of my deeds no one then thought worthy even of praise." "And what noble deed will you say you did, save the doubling of Malea and Sunium, when you reined in the ship as it ran wild, and clearly distinguished, at stern and prow, from what quarter the winds would break, and lifted the vessel over the reefs in the hollow of Euboea, where many headlands stand up?

He went on an embassy too to the Thessalians on behalf of Achilles, at the assemblies at Pylaea, where the Thessalians conduct the Amphictyonic business; and they, in fear, voted to restore the honours due to the tomb. And the monument of Leonidas the Spartan he all but embraced, in his admiration of the man. Walking to the mound on which the Lacedaemonians are said to have been buried under the arrows, he heard his companions disputing with one another what was the highest spot in Greece — Oeta, the mountain before their eyes, giving rise to the talk; and going up the hill he said: "I hold this to be the highest; for those who died here for freedom raised it level with Oeta and lifted it above many an Olympus. I admire these men, but the Acarnanian Megistias before them; for what he knew they would suffer, in this he desired to share with the men, not fearing to die, but fearing not to die with such men.

Seeing a young man, fat and proud of eating most of all men and drinking most wine, he said, "Are you then the man who stuffs himself?" "Yes," he said, "and I sacrifice for it." "And what have you got from this gluttony?" "To be wondered at and gazed upon; for perhaps you have heard of Heracles, how his eating was sung of like his labours." "That was because it was Heracles," he said; "but of you, you offscouring, what virtue is there? For the only way left for you to be gazed at is to burst."

So then, having supped and discoursed not about great things, they slept there; and at daybreak, after addressing the Naked Sages, they went on the road that stretches toward the mountains, keeping the Nile on the left, seeing these things worth recounting. The Cataracts are earthy mountains, like the Tmolus of the Lydians, and the Nile flows down from them, drawing the earth with it of which it makes Egypt. And the echo of the stream as it breaks down from the mountains and falls with a crash into the Nile seems hard and unbearable to hear, and many who have gone forward beyond the moderate distance have turned back, having lost their hearing.

As they were talking thus, a man came up—a Cilician, I think—and said: "I, sirs, am in danger for my wealth." And Apollonius said: "If you are rich from sources not lawful—such as robbery or poisons, those that are man-slaying, or by disturbing tombs, such as belong to the kings of old, which are full of gold and treasure—you ought not only to be tried, but to perish; for these things are wealth indeed, but ill-spoken-of and cruel. But if you are rich by inheritance, or by trade that is free and not huckstering, who is so harsh as to take from you, under the form of law, what you have lawfully gained?" "What I have," he said, "is from many kinsmen, and has come into my single house, mine; and I use it neither as another's, for it is mine, nor as mine alone, for it is common to me with good men. But the informers slander us as having gained our wealth to no good end for the tyranny; for if I attempted any innovation, it would be a provision for the road, they say, and for whomever I should attach myself to, my means would be no small weight. Charges have already been divined against us: that all wealth beyond measure breeds insolence; that he who is above the many sets his neck stiff and rouses his spirit, and will not be persuaded by the laws, and all but strikes on the cheek the governors who come to the provinces, making them slaves by money. I, when I was a stripling, before I had gained a substance of a hundred talents, held everything a thing to laugh at, and feared little for my possessions; but when five hundred talents came to me on a single day, by the death of my father's uncle to me, my mind so changed as horse-breakers change a horse from an untaught and unruly temper. As my wealth increased, bringing me gains by land and sea, I was so enslaved by the fear about it, that I had to bale out of my substance: part to the informers, whom one had to soften with this sop; part to the governors, that I might have strength against those who plotted against me; part to my kinsmen, that they might not envy my wealth; part to my slaves, that they might not grow worse, complaining of neglect; and there was pastured for me a brilliant herd of friends, who, foreseeing things for me, partly did them themselves and partly forewarned me. But for all that—having so fenced my wealth, having so safely walled it in—we are now in danger over it, and it is not yet clear even whether we shall stay unharmed in our body." And Apollonius said: "Take heart; for you have your wealth as a surety for your body; for through it you are bound, but it will release you when you are set free—not only from this prison, but from the tending of informers and slaves, to whom you were subject because of it."

About the time when he was earnest in Greece, such a sign held the heaven: a crown like a rainbow, going round the disk of the sun, dimmed its ray. That the sign bore toward innovation was plain to all; and the governor of Greece, calling him from Athens to Boeotia, said, "I hear, Apollonius, that you are wise in things daemonic." "If indeed you hear," he said, "that I am so in human things too." "I hear," he said, "and I agree." "Since, then," he said, "you agree, do not meddle with the counsels of the gods, for this human wisdom praises." But when he entreated Apollonius to say what he intended—for he feared lest all should pass into night—"Take courage," he said, "for there shall be some light out of this night."

In harmony with this, Damis too has written about the Eretrians. For they dwell in Media, not far distant from Babylon, a day's journey for a swift runner; and the country is without cities, for Cissia is all villages, and there is also in it a nomad people, who seldom dismount from their horses. The settlement of the Eretrians lies in the middle of the rest, and is surrounded by a ditch from the river, which they themselves are said to have thrown about the village, making it a wall against the barbarians in Cissia. The land is soaked with asphalt and bitter to plant; and the people there are very short-lived, for the asphaltic drink settles into many of their inward parts. They are fed by a hill on the borders of the village, which, rising above the corrupted ground, they sow and regard as land. They say that they heard from the natives that seven hundred and eighty of the Eretrians were taken—not all of them fighting men, for there was among them a part that was female and aged, and there was also, I think, a part that was children; for the greater part of Eretria had fled up to Caphereus and the highest point of Euboea. About four hundred men were carried up, and women perhaps ten; the rest, beginning from Ionia and Lydia, perished as they were driven up-country. Since the hill furnished them stone-quarrying, and some of them knew the arts of working stone, they built Greek temples and a market-place such as was fitting, and set up altars—two to Darius, one to Xerxes, and several to Daridaeus. They continued, down to Daridaeus, for eighty-eight years after their capture, writing in the Greek manner; and their ancient tombs are inscribed "so-and-so, son of so-and-so," and the letters are Greek, but, they say, of a kind they had not yet seen; and ships are carved on the tombs, according as each man lived in Euboea practising a seafaring or even a purple-dyeing trade; and they say there was an elegy to read, written on the monument of sailors and ship-owners: "We who once sailed the deep-flowing swell of the Aegean lie here in the midst of the Ecbatanian plain. Farewell, Eretria, once renowned, our fatherland; farewell, Athens, neighbour of Euboea; farewell, dear sea." The tombs, fallen to ruin, Damis says that Apollonius restored and closed up, and poured libations and brought to them all the customary offerings, except for slaughtering or burning any victim; and weeping and filled with emotion, he uttered these words in their midst: "Eretrians, carried hither by the lot of fortune, you at least, though far from your own land, are buried; but those who cast you down here perished about your island, unburied, in the tenth year after you; for the gods reveal the disaster in hollow Euboea." And Apollonius, at the end of his letter to the sophist, says: "I took care, Scopelianus, of your Eretrians while still a young man, and helped, as far as I could, both their dead and their living." And how did he care for the living? The barbarians who dwelt near the hill used, when the Eretrians had sown it, to plunder the produce, coming about the summer, and the Eretrians had to go hungry, working the land for others. So when he came to the king, he obtained for them that they alone should have the use of the hill.

They say they saw a temple of the Sun, to which the elephant Ajax was dedicated, and golden images of Alexander, and others of Porus, these of black bronze. As for the walls of the temple, gold gleams up from beneath the red stones, sending out a radiance like a sunbeam. The very seat is composed of pearl in the symbolic fashion which all the barbarians use for their temples.

Apollonius said: "Since you set me on the pilot's theme, hear what I think I then did soundly. The sea was once beset by Phoenician pirates, and they went round the cities learning who carried what. The pirates' agents, seeing the rich cargo of my ship, drew me aside and asked how large a share of the fare I would take. I said a thousand, since four of us were piloting the ship. 'And have you a house?' they asked. 'A poor hut,' I said, 'about the island of Pharos, where once Proteus dwelt.' 'Would you then,' they asked me, 'have land instead of sea, and a house instead of the hut, and ten times this fare, and escape the ten thousand evils which the swollen sea brings upon pilots?' 'I should wish it,' I said, 'but I do not think myself fit for piracy, now that I have grown wiser than I was and have been deemed worthy of crowns by my craft.' As they went on and said they would give me purses of ten thousand drachmas if I would become for them what they wished, I urged them to speak out, saying that I would fall in no way short of being wholly their man. So they said they were agents of pirates, and begged me not to deprive them of taking the ship, nor to sail out to the town when I should weigh anchor from there, but to bring to under the headland — for the pirate ships were lying in wait round about it. And they wished to swear to me that they would neither kill me themselves nor refuse to spare the death of any whom I should beg off. Now I did not think it safe for myself to reprove them, fearing that, falling into despair, they might attack the ship while she was on the high sea, and we should perish somewhere in the deep; so, promising to do their bidding, I said they must swear that they would in very truth keep faith. When they had sworn — for they were talking in a temple — 'Go,' I said, 'to the pirate craft, for we shall set out by night.' And I seemed the more convincing in still discussing the money, that it should be counted out to me good coin, and not before they had taken the ship. So they went off, but I put out to the open sea, doubling the headland." "And this," said Iarchas, "Apollonius, you hold to be a work of justice?" "Yes, and of humanity besides," he said; "for not to sell men's lives, nor to traffic away the merchants' goods, and to prove oneself, sailor though one is, stronger than money — this I think gathers up many virtues in one.

He visited all the Greek temples — the Dodonaean and the Pythian and the one at Abae — and went to those of Amphiaraus and Trophonius, and went up to the Museum on Helicon. As he frequented the temples and set them right, the priests went with him, his acquaintances followed, and mixing-bowls of discourse were set up, and the thirsty drew from them. And when the Olympic games were on, and the Eleans invited him to share the contest, he said: "You seem to me to disparage the renown of the Olympics in needing embassies to those who will come of their own accord." Coming to the Isthmus, when the sea about Lechaeum roared, he said: "This neck of land shall be cut, or rather shall not." And this too was a foretelling of the cutting through the Isthmus a little later, which seven years afterwards Nero purposed; for leaving his palace he came to Greece to submit himself to the heralds at the Olympic and Pythian games, and he won at the Isthmus too — his victories being for lyre-singing and heraldry — and he won the tragic prize at Olympia. Then he is said also to have laid hand to the new work at the Isthmus, making a circumnavigation and joining the Aegean to the Adriatic, that no ship need sail round Malea, and that most might be carried through the cut, shortening the long sea-passage. But where did Apollonius' oracle come out? The digging, beginning from Lechaeum, advanced perhaps four stades by continuous digging, but Nero is said to have stopped the cut — some say because the Egyptians who advised him on the seas said that the deep above Lechaeum, overflowing, would make Aegina vanish; others, because he feared changes in his rule. Such, then, was Apollonius' "the Isthmus shall be cut and shall not be cut.

Such were his doings in Rhodes; and now those in Alexandria, after he sailed in. Even while he was absent Alexandria loved and longed for Apollonius, as one man for another; and upper Egypt too, being full of theology, prayed that he would visit their lands. For since many came from there to Egypt and many mingled here from Egypt, Apollonius was sung of among them, and the ears of the Egyptians were pricked up toward him. As he advanced from the ship to the city, they looked upon him as upon a god, and gave way in the narrow streets, as to those who carry the holy things. As he was being escorted with more pomp than the governors of the nations, men were being led off to death, twelve in number, charged with brigandage; and looking at them he said, "Not all of them; for this man here has been falsely accused and will go free." And to the executioners by whom they were led he said, "I bid you slacken your pace and come more slowly to the pit, and to kill this man last, for he has no part in the charge; you would do a holier thing to spare these men a small part of a day — men whom it were better not to put to death at all." And meanwhile he lingered over what he was saying, drawing out a length not usual with him. What he intended by this was at once shown: for when eight had already had their heads cut off, a horseman riding to the pit cried out, "Spare Pharion! For he is no brigand, but accused himself falsely for fear of the rack, and when others were tortured he was acknowledged a good man." I pass over the leaping of Egypt for joy, and how they applauded at this — though they are in any case prone to wonder.

As Apollonius and those about him went forward, breast-like mountains appeared, bearing trees whose leaves and bark and tears the Ethiopians count as fruit. They saw also lions near the road, and leopards and other such beasts; but none of them attacked them, but leaped away from them, as though startled at the men. Deer too and gazelles and ostriches and wild asses were seen, many of these, but most of all the wild oxen and the goat-stags; and these beasts are compounded, the one of deer and bull, the other of the creatures from which it has taken its name. And they came upon bones of these and half-eaten bodies, for the lions, when they have gorged on the warm prey, disdain its remains, trusting, I think, that they will hunt again.

When another in his turn said that he was on trial because, while sacrificing at Tarentum, where he held office, he had not added to the public prayers that Domitian was the son of Athena, Apollonius said: "You thought, I suppose, that Athena could not bear a child, being a virgin for all time; but you did not know, it seems, that this goddess once bore a serpent to the Athenians."

After this, since he had had enough of the affairs of Greece, having spent two years in it, he sailed to Ionia with his fellowship following, and most of the time he philosophized about Smyrna and Ephesus, visiting the others too and seeming in no one of the cities unpleasant, but worthy to be longed for and a great gain to the discerning.

The things concerning this man at Babylon, and all that it is fitting to know about Babylon, I found to be as follows. Babylon is walled for four hundred and eighty stadia, so great is its circuit; and its wall is in height three half-plethra, and a little less than a plethron in breadth; it is cut by the river Euphrates with a resemblance of form, and a hidden bridge runs beneath it, joining unseen the palaces on either bank. For a woman named Medea, who once ruled there, is said to have bridged the river in a way no river was ever bridged before. For having heaped up beside the banks stones and bronze and asphalt and all that men have devised for underwater binding, she turned the stream into lakes; and then, when the river was already dry, she dug it out to a depth of two fathoms, fashioning a hollow tunnel, that it might come up, as out of the earth, into the palaces beside the banks; and she roofed it over to be level with the bed of the stream. The foundations stood firm, and the walls of the tunnel; but since the asphalt needed water to be turned to stone and to set, the Euphrates was let in upon the roof while it was still moist, and thus the bridge stood firm. As for the palaces, they are roofed with bronze and flash with light from it; the chambers and the men's halls and the porticoes are adorned, some with silver, some with golden hangings, some with gold itself, as with paintings; and the figures woven on the robes come to them from Greek stories—Andromedas and Amymones and Orpheus in many places. They take pleasure in Orpheus, honouring him perhaps for his tiara and trousers, but not for his music or the songs with which he charmed. Woven there too is Datis dragging Naxos out of the sea, and Artaphernes besieging Eretria, and of the deeds of Xerxes those he claimed as victories; for there are Athens taken, and Thermopylae, and things still more Median—rivers drawn off the land, and the bridge over the sea, and how Athos was cut through. They say too that they came upon a men's hall whose roof was carried up into the form of a dome, likened to a sort of heaven, and roofed over with sapphire stone—the stone is of the deepest blue and heavenly to look upon—and images of the gods they worship are set up aloft and appear golden, as out of the ether. There the king gives judgment; and four golden wrynecks hang from the roof, putting him in mind of Adrasteia and of not exalting himself above men. These the magi themselves say they tune, frequenting the palace, and they call them "the tongues of the gods."

About the palace, they say they saw no mass of buildings, nor spearmen nor guards, but, as about the houses of distinguished men, a few servants, and three, I think, or four who wished to converse with the king; and they admired this order more than the inflamed splendour at Babylon, and far more when they passed within; for the men's halls and the porticoes and the whole court, they say, were kept restrained.

The Indian laughed and said: "You seem to think that not doing wrong is justice; and this, I imagine, all Greeks think. For as I once heard from Egyptians who came here, governors come to you from Rome with the axe bared against you, not yet knowing whether they will rule worthy men or base; and you, if these do not sell their verdicts, call them just. This too I hear the slave-dealers do there: if they come bringing you Carian slaves and interpret their character to you, they make it the praise of the slaves that they do not steal. Such you deem worthy the rulers to whom you say you are subject, and brightening them with the praises you give to slaves, you send them off enviable, as you think. But your wisest poets do not grant you to be just and good even if you wish it. For Minos, who surpassed all men in cruelty and enslaved with his ships those upon the sea and in the sea, they honour with the sceptre of justice and set in Hades to judge the souls; while Tantalus, because he was good and shared with his friends the immortality given him by the gods, they shut off from drink and food, and there are some who even hang stones over him and heap terrible insults on a divine and good man — whom I should rather wish to have a lake of nectar welling round him, since he poured it out humanely and ungrudgingly." And as he said this he pointed to a statue on the left, on which was inscribed TANTALUS. The statue was four cubits high, and was like a man of fifty years, and was clothed in Argive fashion, but wore the cloak differently, like the Thessalians; and it held out a bowl sufficient for one thirsty man, in which a draught of pure liquor bubbled without overflowing the bowl. What they take it to be, and why they drink from it, I shall presently show. But one must hold that Tantalus did not sin with his tongue, but, because he shared the nectar with men, is driven by the poets, and is not at enmity with the gods; for if he were hateful to the gods, he would never have been judged good by the Indians, who are most dear to the gods and do nothing outside the divine.

There was philosophising at Corinth at that time one Demetrius, a man who had gathered up all the strength of the Cynic school, whom Favorinus later mentioned not ignobly in many of his discourses. Having felt towards Apollonius what they say Antisthenes felt towards the wisdom of Socrates, he followed him, eager to learn and attached to his words, and turned the more reputable of his own acquaintances towards Apollonius. Among these was Menippus the Lycian, twenty-five years old, of good judgment and well-built in body; indeed he was like a handsome and well-bred athlete in form. Most thought Menippus was loved by a foreign woman, and the woman seemed fair and sufficiently delicate and said she was rich; but none of this was really so, but only seemed so. For as he was walking alone on the road to Cenchreae, a phantom met him and became a woman, and clasped his hand, saying she had long loved him, and that she was a Phoenician and dwelt in a suburb of Corinth, naming the suburb, to which she said that if he came in the evening he should have her song and wine such as he had never drunk, and no rival should trouble him, and she would live, a fair woman, with a fair man. The young man was beguiled by this — for though strong in the rest of philosophy, he was overcome by love-matters — and went to her about evening, and thereafter frequented her like a beloved, not yet understanding that she was a phantom. But Apollonius, looking at Menippus like a sculptor, painted the young man and observed him, and judging him, said: "You who are fair and hunted by fair women are warming a serpent, and a serpent warms you." When Menippus marvelled, he said: "This woman is one you cannot marry. Why? Do you think she loves you?" "By Zeus," he said, "since she is disposed to me as one who loves." "And would you marry her?" he said. "For it would be a charming thing to marry one who loves." So he asked when the wedding was. "Soon," he said, "perhaps tomorrow." So Apollonius, watching for the time of the banquet, and standing over the guests as they had just come, said: "Where is the delicate woman, for whom you have come?" "Here," said Menippus, and rose blushing. "And the silver and gold and the rest with which the hall is adorned, to which of you does it belong?" "To the woman," he said; "for mine is only this," showing his cloak. And Apollonius said: "Have you seen the gardens of Tantalus, how they exist and do not exist?" "In Homer," they said; "for we have not gone down to Hades." "Take it that this adornment too is such, for it is not substance but the appearance of substance. And that you may know what I say, this good bride is one of the empusae, whom the many hold to be lamiae and bogies. These love, and they love sexual pleasure, but most of all they love human flesh, and they lure with their pleasures those they wish to devour." But the woman said, "Hush," and "Away," and seemed to loathe what she heard, and even mocked the philosophers as forever talking nonsense. But when the golden cups and the seeming silver were proved empty wind and all flew from their eyes, and the cup-bearers and cooks and all such attendance vanished, refuted by Apollonius, the phantom seemed to weep and begged him not to torture it, nor to compel it to confess what it was; but when he pressed and did not let up, it said it was an empusa, and was fattening Menippus with pleasures for the eating of his body; for it was wont to feed on fair and young bodies, since their blood is pure. This story, the best known of Apollonius', I have necessarily told at length; for many know it, since it happened in the heart of Greece, but they have received it only in summary, that he once caught a lamia in Corinth, while what she was doing, and that it was for Menippus, they do not yet know; but it has been told by Damis and from his account by me.

When he had gone up into the temple, the order about it and the account given of each thing seemed to him divine and composed according to wisdom; but the blood of bulls and the geese and all that was sacrificed — these things he did not approve, nor did he bring them to the feasts of the gods. When the priest asked him why he learned not to sacrifice thus, Apollonius said, "Do you rather answer me: why have you learned to sacrifice thus?" And when the priest said, "And who is so clever as to set right the customs of the Egyptians?" he said, "Every wise man, if he comes from the Indians." "And I shall roast a bull today," he said, "and do you share the smoke with us; for you will not grieve over your portion, if the gods too shall feast on it." When the figure of the victim was melting, he said, "Look at the sacred signs." "What signs?" said the Egyptian. "For I see nothing here." And Apollonius said, "Then the Iamidae, my good man, and the Telliadae and the Clytiadae, and the oracle of the Melampodidae, talked nonsense, saying so much about fire and gathering so many prophecies from it? Or do you hold the fire from pine and that from cedar prophetic and able to declare something, but the fire kindled from the richest and purest of tears not far more to be chosen? But if you were skilled in the wisdom of fire, you would see many things revealed even in the disk of the sun, when it rises."

Here dwell nomad Ethiopians, settled on wagons, and near these the hunters of elephants, who cut them up and make a market of them, whence they are named from the selling of elephants. The Nasamones and the Eaters of Men and the Pygmies and the Shadow-foots are nations of Ethiopians too, and these reach down to the Ethiopian Ocean, into which only those sail who are carried thither against their will.

Another was imprisoned on a charge of this sort: having a piece of land in Acarnania near the mouths of the Achelous, he was sailing round the Echinades in a little skiff; and having examined one of them, which now joined the mainland, he planted it with seasonable trees and sweet-wined vines, and made for himself a sufficient dwelling for his body upon it—for there was even water brought from the mainland enough for the island. From this an indictment arose: that this Acarnanian was not pure, but, conscious of unbearable deeds, withdrew and departed from the rest of the earth as defiled for him, and had chosen for himself the release of Alcmaeon the son of Amphiaraus—through which, after his mother, he dwelt at the mouths of the Achelous—if not for the like deeds, yet perhaps for cruel ones, and not far from those. But he said it was not so, but that out of love for a quiet life he had dwelt there, and that it had so fallen out to involve him in lawsuits, on account of which he was even imprisoned.

But the gods were now thrusting Domitian from his presidency over men. For he chanced to have killed Clemens, a man of consular rank, to whom he had given his own sister; and he had made a command about the third or fourth day after the murder that she too should go to a husband. Stephanus, then, a freedman of the woman, whom the form of the sign signified, whether reflecting on the dead man, or on all, set out, like the most freedom-loving of the Athenians, against the tyrant; and, slipping a sword under the forearm of his left arm and taking up his hand in bandages as though it were broken, he came up to him as he left the court and said, "I beg you, sire, alone, for great are the things you shall hear." And when the tyrant did not refuse the hearing, but took him aside into the men's hall where the palace is, he said, "Your most hostile Clemens has not died, as you think, but is where I know, and is arraying himself against you." When he had cried out greatly at what he heard, Stephanus, falling upon him as he was confounded, and drawing the sword from his arrayed hand, drove it through his thigh—not mortal to the immediate death, but not unseasonable to the death thereafter. And he, being otherwise strong in body, and about five-and-forty years of age, grappled with him though wounded, and throwing down Stephanus pressed upon him, digging out his eyes and crushing his cheeks with the base of a golden cup that lay there about the rites, and called also on Athena to help. The spearmen, then, understanding that he fared ill, came in together and killed the tyrant, who was already swooning.

About the magi Apollonius has said enough; for he was with them and learned some things, and went away having taught some things. But Damis does not know what discourses passed between the man and the magi, for he was forbidden to accompany him when he went to them. He says, however, that Apollonius visited the magi at midday and about midnight; and that he once asked, "What are the magi?" And he answered: "Wise men—but not in all things."

So Apollonius judged that the Indian was a philosopher, and bringing forward the interpreter, "I rejoice, O king," he said, "to see you a philosopher." "And I rejoice exceedingly," he said, "since you think so of me." "Is this the custom among you," he asked, "or did you establish your rule toward this moderation yourself?" "Temperately," he said, "I use what is temperately customary; I have most of men, but need little, for I consider most things to belong to my friends." "Happy in your treasure," he said, "if you value your friends above gold and silver, from whom many good things grow up for you." "And indeed," he said, "I share my wealth even with my enemies. For the barbarians always at variance with this land, who dwell nearby and make raids into my borders, I win over with this money, and by them my country is guarded, and they neither attack my territory themselves nor allow the barbarians who border them, harsh as they are, to do so." When Apollonius asked him whether Porus too paid them money, "Porus," he said, "loved war, but I love peace." By these words he wholly won Apollonius over, and Apollonius was so overcome by him that, once when rebuking Euphrates for not philosophizing, he said, "But let us at least respect the Indian Phraotes"—for this was the Indian's name. And when a satrap, since he had been held worthy of great honour from him, wished to bind upon him a turban adorned with golden gems, "I," he said, "even if I were of those who covet such things, would now refuse them and cast them from my head, having met Apollonius; and how should I now adorn myself with what I never before thought fit to be bound with, forgetting my guest and forgetting myself?" Apollonius asked him too about his diet, and he said: "Of wine I drink as much as I pour in libation to the Sun; what I take in the hunt, others eat, for it is enough for me to have had the exercise; but my food is vegetables and the pith of date-palms and the fruit of the palms and all the river grows in its gardens. And much grows for me from trees too, of which these hands are the farmers." Hearing this, Apollonius was overjoyed and kept looking at Damis.

As they were busy with this discourse, an uproar from the village fell upon them; for the king had arrived, decked out in Median fashion and full of pomp. Iarchas was vexed, and said: "If it were Phraotes who was halting here, you would see everything full of silence, as in a mystery." From this Apollonius understood that this king fell short of Phraotes not in a small degree but in all philosophy. And seeing the sages at ease and preparing nothing of what the king needed, who was coming after noon, he asked: "Where will the king lodge?" "Here," they said; "for the matters for which he comes we discuss by night, since the time is better for counsel." "And will a table be set for him on his arrival?" "By Zeus," they said, "a rich one, with all that is to be had here." "Do you then live richly?" he asked. "We," they said, "live frugally; for though we might eat more, we delight in little. But the king needs much, for he wishes it. Yet he will eat no living thing, for that is not lawful here, but sweetmeats and roots and the fruits of the season, all that India now has, and all that the coming seasons will give.

At that time too he was at variance with Bassus of Corinth; for this man was both thought and believed to be a parricide, and falsely laid claim to wisdom, and there was no bridle on his tongue. When Bassus reviled him, Apollonius checked him by what he wrote and what he said against him. For everything he said, as against a parricide, seemed true, since such a man would never fall to reviling, nor say what was not so.

With these words he checked the Egyptian as ignorant of divine things. And since Alexandria is devoted to horses and gathers to the hippodrome for that spectacle, while the people murder one another over it, he made a rebuke concerning this; and coming into the temple he said: "How long will you go on dying, not for children nor for sanctuaries, but so as to defile the temples by coming to them full of slaughter, and to perish within the walls? One horse, it seems, sacked Troy, which the Achaeans contrived in those days; but against you chariots and horses are yoked, through which you cannot live in good order. You perish, then, not at the hands of the sons of Atreus, nor of the sons of Aeacus, but at one another's — a thing not even the Trojans did in their drunkenness. At Olympia, where there are prizes for wrestling and boxing and the pancratium, no one ever died for the athletes, though pardon might exist if a man were over-zealous about his own kinsman; but here, over horses, you draw naked swords against one another, and stones are ready to be thrown. Fire upon such a city, where there is wailing and outrage of men slaying and slain, and the earth runs with blood! Have respect for the Nile, the common mixing-bowl of Egypt. But why do I mention the Nile to men who measure out the risings of blood rather than of water?" And he discoursed many other things in this rebuke, as Damis instructs us.

As the men were discoursing about the beasts and philosophizing about nature, which feeds one kind in one way and another in another, an echo struck upon them like thunder not yet harsh, but still hollow and within the cloud. And Timasion said, "Near is the cataract, men, the last for those who go down, the first for those who go up." And going forward about ten stades, they say they saw a river issuing from the mountain no less than the Marsyas and the Maeander at their first meeting; and praying to the Nile they went on, and saw beasts no longer — for these, being timid by nature, dwell rather near the calm waters than the violent and resounding — but they heard another cataract some fifteen stades on, now hard and unbearable to perceive, for it was twice the former and fell from higher mountains. Damis says that his own ears and those of one of the companions were so stunned that he himself turned back and begged Apollonius not to go forward, but that he held to the third cataract stoutly with Timasion and Nilus, and on his return reported about it as follows. Peaks hang over the Nile there, about eight stades in height, and the bank that lies over against the mountains is a brow of unspeakable rock; and the springs, hanging from the mountains, fall over onto the rocky bank, and pour thence into the Nile, surging and white. And the workings that come about them, being many times greater than the former, and the echo leaping from these to the mountains, make the study of the stream hard to hear. The road further on, leading to the first springs, they say is impossible to travel, and impossible even to think upon, for they tell many tales of spirits, such as Pindar too in his wisdom has hymned of the spirit whom he sets over these springs for the due measure of the Nile.

When more men within came to Apollonius, lamenting such things—for there were, I suppose, some fifty in that prison; and some of them were sick, some lay faint-hearted, some held out against death, some called upon their children and parents and their marriages—he said: "Damis, these men seem to me to need the drug I mentioned at the outset. Whether, then, it be Egyptian, or grow in all the earth, wisdom cutting its roots from her own gardens, let us add some of it to these wretched men, lest their own judgement destroy them before the event." "Let us add it," said Damis, "for they seem to need it." So Apollonius, calling them together, said: "Men who share this roof with me, I pity you, that you are destroyed by yourselves, not yet knowing whether the accusation will destroy you; for you seem to me, by killing yourselves before the death that, as you think, would be voted against you, to take courage at what you dread, and to dread what you should take courage at. Yet this is not fitting; rather, calling to mind the saying of Archilochus of Paros, who, naming endurance under griefs 'patience,' says that patience is the very discovery of the gods—you must bear up against these cruel things, as those who by skill rise above the surge, when the wave stands over the ship, and must not hold these things hard, to which you have come unwilling, and I willing. For if you agree with the charges, the day is more to be lamented on which your reasoning, setting out toward unjust and cruel deeds, undid you; but if neither you will say that you dwelt on the island in the Achelous for the reasons the accuser names, nor you that you set your wealth as a reserve against the kingship, nor you that you willingly took from the governor the seeming reverence due to Athena, nor each of you, who are in danger for the things for which you have come, will say that these are true—what means this lamentation over things that are not? For by so much as you call upon your nearest, by so much ought you the rather to be strong; for those things are the prizes, I suppose, of this patience. Or do you say that to be imprisoned here, and to live in prison, is terrible? Or is it the beginning of what you think you will suffer? Or is it of itself a punishment, even if you suffer nothing through it? But I, knowing human nature, will teach you an argument in no way like the food of physicians; for it both puts in strength and will not suffer a man to die. We men are in a prison this whole time which is called life; for this soul, bound into a perishable body, endures much, and is slave to all the things that come upon man. And those who first contrived houses seem to me not to have known that they were casting another prison about themselves; for indeed all those who dwell in palaces, safely furnished within them, we should hold rather bound than those whom they themselves will bind. And as I reflect, cities and walls seem to me to be common prisons, so that men are bound as they buy in the market, bound as they sit in assembly, and again as they watch the spectacles and send the processions. And the Scythians who wander in wagons are bound no less than we, for the Ister and the Thermodon and the Tanais set bounds to them—rivers not easy to cross unless they stand still from the frost—and they have houses upon their wagons, and they are carried, yet cowering within them. And, if the argument is not childish, they say that even Ocean was cast about the earth for the sake of binding. Come, poets—for these things are yours—and chant to these faint-hearted men, how Cronus was once bound by the counsels of Zeus, and Ares, the most warlike, was bound in heaven first by Hephaestus, and on earth by the sons of Aloeus. Reflecting on these things, and on many of the wise and blessed men whom wanton peoples bound and tyrannies insulted, let us accept these things too, that we may not fall short of those who accepted them." So did his words change the men in prison, that most of them touched food and departed from their tears, and came to the hope of suffering nothing at all, being with such a man.

These things were done in Rome, but were seen by Apollonius in Ephesus. For discoursing about the groves of the colonnades at noon, when indeed the things in the palace were happening, first he let his voice sink, as if afraid; then he interpreted more falteringly than was his power, like men who see something else amid their words; then he was silent, like those who have lost their argument; and looking terribly to the ground and advancing three or four of the steps, he cried, "Strike the tyrant, strike!"—not as one drawing the phantom of truth from some mirror, but as one seeing the very things and seeming to lay hold of what was being done. And Ephesus being dismayed—for all of it was present at his discourse—he paused as long as those who see, until something of the doubtful things should come to its end, and said, "Take courage, men, for the tyrant has been slaughtered today. Why do I say today? Just now, by Athena, just now, about the moment of the words at which I fell silent." Those in Ephesus held this madness, and wished it true but feared the danger of the hearing; "I do not wonder," he said, "at those who do not yet accept the argument, which not even all Rome yet knows. But behold, it knows; for it spreads abroad, and already myriads believe, and twice as many leap for joy, and twice as many again, and four times, and all the peoples there. This word will come hither too; and let your sacrificing upon it be deferred to the time when these things shall be reported; but I will go to pray to the gods for what I have seen."

But this was later. When he came to Babylon, the satrap set over the great gates, learning that he came for the sake of inquiry, held out to him a golden image of the king, which, unless one made obeisance to it, it was not lawful to pass within. For an ambassador coming from the ruler of the Romans is under no such necessity; but one who comes from barbarians, or who would explore the country, unless he first paid homage to the image, was held to be dishonoured and was turned back; and among the barbarians such silly matters are entrusted to a satrap. So when he saw the image, "Who is this?" he asked. And hearing that it was the king, he said: "This man whom you worship—if he should be praised by me and judged a true gentleman, will gain great things"; and saying this he went on through the gates. The satrap, marvelling at him, followed and, taking hold of the hand of Apollonius, asked through an interpreter his name and his house and his pursuit and on what errand he came; and writing these things down on a tablet, and his dress and his appearance, he bade him wait there, while he himself ran—

When they had discoursed sufficiently about the road to the Brahmans, he bade the guide from the Babylonian be entertained, as he was wont to entertain those who came from Babylon, and the guide from the satrap depart with provisions; and he himself, taking the hand of Apollonius and bidding the interpreter withdraw, said, "Would you make me your fellow-drinker?"—asking him in the Greek tongue. When Apollonius was amazed and said, "Why did you not speak so from the beginning?" he said: "I feared to seem rash by not knowing myself, nor that fortune makes me appear a barbarian; but overcome by you, since I see that you too are pleased with me, I could not hide myself; and how full I am of the Greek tongue I will show you in many ways." "Why then," he said, "did you not yourself invite me to the drinking-party, but bid me invite you?" "Because I hold you better than myself," he said, "for wisdom has the more kingly part." And at the same time he led both him and his company to where he was wont to bathe. The bath was a garden a stadium in length, in the midst of which a pool was dug to receive springs of fresh, cold water, and on either side were running-courses, in which he exercised himself with javelin and discus in the Greek manner; for his body was strong both by reason of his age—he was twenty-seven years old—and of this kind of training. When he had had enough, he leapt into the water and exercised himself in swimming. When they had bathed, they went to the common table garlanded, for this is the custom among the Indians whenever they drink at the king's table.

"But look," he said, "here he is." For the king was advancing, together with his brother and his son, flashing with gold and jewels. As Apollonius rose, Iarchas held him in his seat, for this was not their custom. Damis says he himself was not present at this, since on that day he was lodging in the village, but that having heard it from Apollonius he wrote it into his own account. He says, then, that while they sat, the king stretched out his hand to the men as if in prayer, and they nodded as though agreeing to what he asked, and he rejoiced greatly at the promise, as one who had come to a god. But the king's brother, and his son, a most beautiful youth, were regarded as no better than if they had been slaves of these attendants. After this the Indian rose and, uttering his voice, bade him touch food; and when the king accepted this most gladly, four Pythian tripods came forth of themselves, like those of Homer, advancing, and beneath them cup-bearers of black bronze, like the Ganymedes and Pelopses among the Greeks. The earth strewed beneath them grasses softer than couches. Sweetmeats and loaves and herbs and the ripe fruits of the season came in, all set out in order more pleasingly than if cooks had prepared them; and of the tripods two flowed with wine, while of the other two one gave a spring of hot water, the other of cold. The stones that come from India are among the Greeks set into necklaces and rings because of their smallness, but among the Indians they become wine-coolers and ice-pails because of their size, and bowls large enough to fill four thirsty men in the season of the year. The bronze cup-bearers, he says, drew wine and water in due measure, and passed the cups round, as at drinking-parties. And they reclined as at a common feast, yet not with the king set above the rest — that which among Greeks and Romans is of much account — but as it chanced, where each had a mind.

His doings at Olympia were these. As Apollonius was going up to Olympia, ambassadors of the Lacedaemonians met him, seeking his company; but there was nothing Laconian about them, and they were more delicate than themselves and full of Sybaris. Seeing men smooth-legged, sleek-haired, beardless, and even soft in their dress, he sent such a letter to the ephors that they made a public proclamation, removing the pitch-plasters from the baths and driving out the women who pluck the hair, and restoring all things to the ancient way; whence the wrestling-schools grew young again, and earnest endeavours, and the common messes returned, and Lacedaemon became like herself. Learning that they had set their house in order, he sent a letter from Olympia shorter than the Laconian scytale. It runs thus: "Apollonius to the ephors, greeting. It is for men not to err, but for the noble even to perceive their errors.

When Vespasian was meditating the imperial power about the nations bordering on Egypt, and was advancing upon Egypt, Dio and Euphrates — of whom a little later — bade men rejoice. For after the first emperor, by whom the affairs of the Romans were set in order, tyrannies so harsh prevailed for fifty years that not even Claudius, who ruled the middle thirteen of them, seemed good; though he came to power at fifty, when men's minds are most sound, and seemed to love all learning. Yet he too, at that age, suffered many childish things, and gave up his rule as a pasture to women, by whom he so carelessly died that, foreknowing as he did what he was to suffer, he did not guard even against what he had foreknown. Apollonius, like Euphrates and Dio, rejoiced at these things, but did not make a public exercise of them, holding such a manner of speech too rhetorical for all men; and as the emperor approached, the sacred things met him before the gates, and the revenues of Egypt and the nomes by which Egypt is divided, and the philosophers likewise and all wisdom. But Apollonius busied himself with none of these, but applied himself to the temple. When the emperor had spoken nobly and gently and gone through a discourse not long, he said, "Is the Tyanean staying here?" "Yes," they said, "and he has made us better." "How then might he meet with us?" he said; "for I greatly need the man." "He will meet you about the temple," said Dio; "for to me, when I came here, he agreed to this." "Let us go," said the king, "to pray to the gods and to be in the company of a noble man." From this arose a story that the empire entered his thoughts while he was besieging Solyma, and that he summoned Apollonius for counsel about it, but that Apollonius refused to come to a land which its inhabitants had defiled both by what they had done and by what they had suffered; and that therefore the emperor himself came to Egypt, having already won the empire, to discourse with the man on the matters I shall relate.

Having lodged after the cataracts in a not large village of Ethiopia, they were supping toward evening, mingling earnest with play, when they heard a sudden cry of the women in the village, calling to one another to seize and pursue, and summoning their own husbands too to share in the work; and the men, snatching up sticks and stones and whatever came to each one's hand, called out as though wronged in their marriages.
