For there was haunting the village, now for the tenth month, an apparition of a satyr, mad after the women, and it was said to have killed two of them, of whom it seemed most enamoured. So when his companions were dismayed, "Do not fear," said Apollonius, "for a certain satyr is rioting here." "Yes, by Zeus," said Nilus, "one whom we Naked Sages have long failed to turn from his leaping, though he has long been rioting." "But there is," he said, "a remedy against these riotous ones, which Midas once is said to have used; for this Midas had a share of the race of satyrs, as his ears showed, and one satyr, on the strength of the kinship, revelled against him, deriding the ears of Midas, and not only singing but also playing the flute at him; and Midas, I think, having heard from his mother that a satyr, when hunted by wine, falls into sleep and grows sober and is reconciled, mixed the spring that was about his palace with wine and let the satyr at it; and he drank and was caught. And that the tale lies not, let us go to the headman, and if the villagers have wine, let us mix it for the satyr, and he shall suffer the same as Midas's." This seemed good, and pouring four Egyptian amphoras into a trough from which the sheep in the village drank, he called the satyr, rebuking him in some unseen way; and the satyr was not yet seen, but the wine gave way, as if drunk; and when it was drunk up, "Let us make peace with the satyr," he said, "for he is asleep." And saying this he led the villagers to a cave of the Nymphs, not yet a plethron distant from the village, in which, pointing to him asleep, he bade them refrain from striking or abusing him, "for he has ceased from his follies." Such a deed of Apollonius — no, by Zeus, no by-work of his road, but a work of his passing through. And if anyone meets a letter of the man, in which, writing to a riotous youth, he says he sobered even a satyr-spirit in Ethiopia, he must remember this account. That satyrs exist and lay hold of love let us not disbelieve; for I know in Lemnos one of my own age, whose mother a satyr was said to visit, as was likely from this tale; for he seemed to wear a fawn-skin grown to him along the back, the foremost flaps of which, grasping the neck, were fastened about his breast. But no more of these things, for neither is experience to be disbelieved, nor am I.

On the next day he was discoursing, straining toward the same purpose, when there was sent in as a listener to his discourses one let down by Domitian. His appearance seemed downcast, as of one in some great danger, as he professed; and his tongue was not unstudied, like those of the informers who have gathered eight or ten phrases. But Apollonius, understanding the trick, discoursed of things that gave the man no opening; for he spoke to them of rivers and mountains, and went through beasts and trees, with which the others were entertained, but the man accomplished nothing. And when he tried to lead him into reviling the tyrant, "My good man," he said, "say what you will, for you shall not be slandered by me; but what I have to find fault with in the emperor, I will say to himself."

While these things were still disbelieved, the runners of the good news came, witnesses of the man's wisdom; for the slaughter of the tyrant, and the day that brought it, and the noontide, and the killers to whom the exhortation was given, were so as the gods revealed each of these to the man as he discoursed. Thirty days after this, when Nerva sent him word that he already held the rule of the Romans by the counsels of the gods and of him, and that he would more easily hold it if Apollonius came as his counsellor, he wrote to him at once this riddle: "We shall be together, sire, the longest time with one another, in which neither we shall rule another, nor another us"—understanding, perhaps, of himself that not long after he would depart from men, and of Nerva that he would rule a short time, for his kingship advanced to a year and four months, he seeming most temperate.

—in person to the men who are called the king's ears, and described Apollonius, declaring beforehand that he neither wished to make obeisance nor was at all like a man. They bade him bring the man, honouring him and doing nothing by way of insult; and when he came, the eldest of them asked him what he had learned that he should despise the king. "I have not yet despised him," he said. "But would you despise him?" he asked again. "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "if, on coming to know him, I do not find him a true gentleman." "And what gifts do you bring him?" And when he said "Courage and justice and the like," the man asked, "As to one who has them not?" "No, by Zeus," he said, "but as to one who is to learn to use them, if he has them." "And indeed," said the other, "by using these the king recovered the kingdom you see, which had been lost to him, and brought back this his house, not without labour, nor lightly." "And how many years is it now since he recovered his rule?" "We are entering the third," he said, "and now, I think, two months." Then Apollonius, raising up his thought, as was his way, said: "O bodyguard, or whatever it is right to call you, Darius, the father of Cyrus and Artaxerxes, who held this palace, they say, for sixty years, when he suspected the end of his life was near, is said to have sacrificed to Justice, and to have said, 'O mistress, whoever you are'—as though he had long desired justice, but did not yet know her, nor thought he possessed her; and he educated his two sons so ignorantly that they took up arms against one another, and one was wounded and the other killed by his brother. But you, perhaps, would have me believe that this man—who does not yet, it may be, even know how to sit upon the royal throne—has gathered together all the virtues at once, and you exalt him, bringing the gain, if he should grow better, to yourself, not to me." Then the barbarian, looking at the man beside him, said: "It is a godsend; some god leads this man here, for a good man consorting with a good man will show us our king far better and wiser and more agreeable; for these qualities are seen shining through the man." So they ran in, bearing the good news to all, that a man stood at the king's doors, wise and Greek and a good counsellor.

It is worth while not to omit the fashion of the drinking, clearly recorded by Damis. The king feasts upon a couch, and as many as five of his nearest kinsmen with him, while all the rest dine on seats. A table, like an altar, is built up in the midst, the height of a man's knee, embracing a circle such as a chorus of thirty men might form, on which laurels and other branches, like myrtle but bearing the perfume of the Indians, are strewn. There are laid out fish and birds, and whole lions and gazelles and swine and the loins of tigers; for the rest of the beast they refuse to eat, since they say that this animal, when first born, raises its forefeet to the rising Sun. And each guest rises and goes to the table, and taking up some of these things, or cutting off a portion, goes back to his own seat and fills himself, eating bread frequently between. When they have had enough, mixing-bowls of silver and gold are brought in, one sufficing for ten drinkers, from which they drink stooping down, as though being given to drink. And in the midst of the drinking they bring on perilous displays, not without their seriousness. For a boy, like the dancing-girls, was tossed lightly into the air, and an arrow was let fly upward together with him, and when he was high above the ground, the boy turned a somersault, lifting himself over the arrow; and had he failed in the somersault he was sure to be struck; for the archer, before letting fly, went round the drinkers showing the point and giving proof of the dart. And shooting through a sling, and shooting at a hair, and tracing the outline of one's own son with arrows as he stood against a board—these they practice over their cups and accomplish them even when drunk.

As the drinking went on, "I pledge you," said Iarchas, "O king, a Greek," pointing to Apollonius reclining below him, and signifying with his hand that he was noble and divine. The king said: "I heard that this man and those who lodge in the village belong to Phraotes." "Rightly and truly you heard," he said, "for he entertains him here too." "What is his pursuit?" he asked. "What else," he said, "but that of Phraotes?" "You have told me nothing strange," he said, "in saying that he embraces a pursuit which did not allow even him to become noble." Then Iarchas said: "Think more soberly, O king, of philosophy and of Phraotes; for while you were a youth, your youth allowed you such things, but now that you are passing into manhood, let us spare ourselves what is foolish and easy-going." But Apollonius, while Iarchas interpreted, said: "And you, O king — what has not being a philosopher given you?" "To me," he said, "all virtue, and to be one with the Sun." But the other, to curb his vanity, said: "If you were a philosopher, you would not think these things." "And you," said the king, "since you are a philosopher, my good man, what do you think of yourself?" "That I am held a good man," he said, "if I am a philosopher." Then stretching out his hand to heaven, "By the Sun," he said, "you have come full of Phraotes." But the other took this as a windfall and said: "My journey has not been in vain, if I have become full of Phraotes; and if you should meet him now, you would say he was full of me. He wished to write to you on my behalf, but since he said you were a good man, I begged off the trouble of the letter, seeing that no one wrote to him on my behalf either.

Looking at the statue at Olympia, he said: "Hail, good Zeus; for you are so good that you share even yourself with men." He explained too the bronze Milo and the meaning of the figure about him. For Milo seems to stand on a discus, both feet set together, and holds a pomegranate in his left hand, while of his right the fingers are straight and as it were thrust apart. The stories about Olympia and Arcadia tell that this athlete was immovable and was never forced from the spot on which he stood, and that the clenching of his fingers in holding the pomegranate showed this, and that they could not be parted from one another, even if one contended against a single one of them, since the joints were well fitted in the straight fingers; and the band which he wears they hold a symbol of temperance. Apollonius said this was wisely conceived, but that the truer account was wiser. "And that you may know the meaning of Milo: the Crotoniates made this athlete a priest of Hera. As to the headband, what need I explain further, having mentioned that he was a priest? The pomegranate alone of plants grows for Hera; and the discus beneath his feet — the priest, standing on a small shield, prays to Hera, and this the right hand signifies too. As for the work of the fingers and their not being parted, let it be set down to the ancient art of statuary.

For after sacrificing, and before he had yet dealt with the cities as their worth required, he addressed Apollonius, and as if praying to him said, "Make me king." And he said, "I have made you so; for when I prayed already for a king who should be just and noble and temperate, adorned with grey hairs and the father of true-born children, it was surely you that I asked from the gods." The king was overjoyed at this, for the crowd in the temple cried out, agreeing with the saying; and he said, "What did the rule of Nero seem to you?" And Apollonius said, "Nero knew, perhaps, how to tune a lyre, but he disgraced the empire by slackening and tightening it." "Do you bid the ruler, then, keep the mean?" "Not I," he said, "but God, who has defined equality as the mean. And good counsellors in these matters are these men too" — pointing to Dio and Euphrates, who had not yet come to disagreement with him. Then the king, raising his hands, said, "O Zeus, may I rule over the wise, and the wise over me." And turning to the Egyptians he said, "Draw from me as from the Nile."

When he came down from Ethiopia, the quarrel with Euphrates increased most of all then, out of the daily discussions; and he committed these to Menippus and Nilus, himself rebuking Euphrates but little, while of Nilus he took great care.

There were other episodes too in this prison—some contrived, some happening as they fell out, not yet great, nor worth my earnest care; but Damis, I think, that he might not leave any of them out, made mention of them. The matter worth telling is this: it was evening, and the man had now been confined five days, when one came into the prison, Greek in speech, and said: "Where is the Tyanean?" And taking him aside, "Tomorrow," he said, "the emperor will discourse with you"; and he hinted that he had heard this from Aelian. "I understand the secret," said Apollonius, "for only he knows it." "And to the keeper of the prison it has been ordered," he said, "to be everything you wish, friendly to you." "You do well," he said; "but I lead the same life here and outside; for I discourse on whatever comes to hand, and have need of nothing." "Not even of one to counsel you, Apollonius," he said, "how you shall discourse with the emperor?" "By Zeus, yes," he said, "if he persuade me not to flatter." "But what if he should persuade you not to despise and not to scorn the man?" he said. "He will counsel best," he said, "and as I have persuaded myself." "For these things I have come," he said, "and I rejoice to see you fitly prepared; but you must be prepared also against the emperor's voice and against the harshness of his countenance, for he speaks heavily even when he discourses mildly, and his brow lies over the look of his eye, and his cheek is full of gall—for this most of all it shows." "Let us not be dismayed at these things, Tyanean—they are rather of his nature and always the same." And Apollonius said: "Yet Odysseus, going into the cave of Polyphemus, neither having heard before how huge he was, nor what he feeds on, nor how his voice thunders, both took courage against him—though at first afraid—and left the cave a man indeed; but for me it is enough to come out, having saved myself and the companions for whom I am in danger." Having discoursed thus with the man who had come, and reported it to Damis, he slept.

But that he might not seem to neglect a good friend and ruler, he composed after this a letter to him, a counsel of imperial matters, and calling Damis said, "These things need you, for the secrets of the letter are written to the emperor, but are such as to be spoken either by me or through you." And late Damis says he understood the device; for the letter was excellently and on great matters composed by him, but might have been sent through another too. What, then, was the man's device? All the time he lived, he is said often to have uttered, "Live unnoticed; and if you cannot, depart life unnoticed." Drawing Damis, then, away from himself, that he might not put off his life before witnesses, he made the pretext of the letter and of his going up to Rome. And Damis says that he himself suffered something as he departed from him, not even knowing what was to come, but that the man, knowing well, said nothing to him, as those are wont who will see each other no more, but had so much over and above of being persuaded that he would forever be, that he charged him thus: "Damis, even when you philosophize by yourself, look to me."

When this was announced to the king, he happened to be sacrificing, with the magi present, for the sacred rites are performed by them; and calling one of them, he said: "The dream has come true that I was telling you today, of him who watched me in my sleep." Now such a dream had come to the king. He seemed to be Artaxerxes, the son of Xerxes, and to have changed into that man's form, and he was greatly afraid lest his affairs had now come to a change, interpreting in this way the change of form. But when he heard that the newcomer was a Greek and a wise man, Themistocles the Athenian came into his mind, who once, having come from the Greeks, consorted with Artaxerxes and made himself of much worth to him, and proved of great service. And holding out his right hand, "Call him," he said; "for it would be best to begin with him, sacrificing and praying together."

Damis and his company were amazed at these things as well-aimed, and admired the precision of the archery; but Apollonius—for he dined with the king, who shared his fare—gave less heed to these, and said to the king, "Tell me, O king, whence have you this command of the Greek tongue, and whence this philosophy about you here? For I do not suppose you trace it to teachers, since it is not likely there are any teachers of it among the Indians." The king, laughing, said: "The ancients used to ask those who sailed in whether they were pirates, so common did they reckon a thing, hard though it is; but you, it seems to me, ask those who come to you whether they are philosophers, so commonly do you think it lies even within the reach of any chance comer, though it is the most divine of human things. And that among you it is the same as piracy, I know; for they say there is none to be met with like you, but that the many, as though they had despoiled it from others, are clothed in it unfittingly and strut about trailing a borrowed garment. And, by Zeus, just as pirates live in luxury knowing they lie under justice, so they too, they say, give themselves to the belly and to love and to fine raiment. And the cause is this: you have laws, I suppose, that if a man debase the coinage he is put to death, and if one falsely register a child—or I know not what penalty there is for this; but those who counterfeit or debase philosophy, no law, I think, restrains among you, nor is any magistrate set over them.

Here the king's first drunken outburst ended; for hearing himself praised by Phraotes, he forgot his suspicion, and slackening his tone said: "Hail, good stranger." And Apollonius said: "And to you, O king; for you seem now to have arrived." "Who," said the king, "brought you to us?" "These gods," he said, "and wise men." "And concerning me," he said, "stranger, what report is there among the Greeks?" "As great," he said, "as the report of the Greeks here." "I," he said, "deem nothing among the Greeks worthy of report." "I will tell them this," he said, "and they will crown you at Olympia.

Being present at the games, he approved of the Eleans, how they cared for them and conducted them in order, and thought they were judged no less than the athletes who were to contend, and took thought to err in nothing willingly or unwillingly. When his companions asked him what Eleans he held to be concerning the management of the Olympics — whether wise — he said: "Wise I do not know, but sophists at least.

So Egypt revived in this way, men being already worn out by what oppressed them. And coming down from the temple he joined his hand to Apollonius, and leading him into the palace said, "Perhaps I seem childish to some in laying hold of empire about the sixtieth year of my life; so I will give a defence, that you may make my defence to others. For I have never, even as a youth, known myself overcome by wealth; and the offices and splendours that belong to the Roman empire I administered so temperately and moderately as to seem neither arrogant nor again cowed. Nor did I meditate any revolution even against Nero; but since he held the empire, even if not according to the laws, yet received it from a man who was emperor, I yielded to him for the sake of Claudius, who appointed me consul and a counsellor of his own. And by Athena, whenever I saw Nero behaving unseemly, the tears fell from me when I considered Claudius, by what a piece of filth the greatest of his possessions had been inherited. But seeing that not even when Nero was got out of the way did men's affairs change for the better, but that the empire fared so dishonourably as to lie at the mercy of Vitellius, I now go against it with confidence: first, because I wish to offer myself to men as one of much worth; and then, because the struggle will be against a man who is besotted. For Vitellius bathes in more perfume than I in water, and seems to me, even if struck with a sword, likely to give out perfume rather than blood; joining wine to wine he is mad; and he plays at dice, fearing lest the counters trip him up, yet over empire he flings the cast in sport; and lying beneath courtesans he assails married women, saying that love mixed with danger is the sweeter. I pass over his more wanton acts, that I may not speak such things before you. May I never look on while Romans are ruled by such a man, but, making the gods my leaders, may I become a man like myself. Therefore from you, Apollonius, I cast my cable; for they say you perceive most of what comes from the gods, and I make you a counsellor of cares on which land and sea depend, that if the signs from the gods appear favourable, I may do these things, but if they are adverse, and not for my good nor the Romans', I may not trouble the gods against their will."

When Titus had taken Solyma and all the neighbouring lands were full of corpses, the bordering nations would have crowned him; but he did not think himself worthy of this, for he himself had not done these things, but had lent his hands to a god who had shown his wrath. Apollonius praised this, for there appeared judgement in the man and understanding of human and divine things, and it was full of self-control not to be crowned for blood. So he put together a letter to him, of which he made Damis the bearer, and wrote thus: "Apollonius to Titus, general of the Romans, greeting. Since you would not be proclaimed for war, nor for hostile blood, I give you the crown of self-control, since you know for what one ought to be crowned. Farewell." Overjoyed at the letter, Titus said: "Both on my own behalf I am grateful to you, and on my father's, and I will remember these things; for I have taken Solyma, but you have taken me."

About dawn a clerk of the imperial trials came and said: "The emperor bids you, Apollonius, come to the court about the time when the market is full—not yet to make your defence, but he wishes to see you, whatever you are, and to be with you alone." "What then," he said, "do you discourse with me about these things? For are you not Apollonius?" "By Zeus," said the Tyanean, "I am." "To whom, then," he said, "shall I say this?" "To those who will lead me," he said; "for I must go forth as from a prison." "It has been ordered," he said, "to those others first; and I too will come at the proper time; but now I have come to give the order, for these things were ordered late in the evening."

The things recorded by Damis the Assyrian about Apollonius the Tyanean end in this discourse; for about the manner in which he died, if indeed he died, there are many accounts, but none is told by Damis. Yet I must not leave even this out; for the discourse, I suppose, ought to have its own end. Nor has anything been said by Damis about the man's age; but some say he came to eighty, some past ninety, some even beyond a hundred, whole in all his body and sound, and pleasanter than youth. For there is a certain bloom even about wrinkles, which flowered most about him, as the images of the man in the temple at Tyana show, and as the accounts that hymn the old age of Apollonius rather than the youth of Alcibiades of old.

So he entered, escorted by many—for they thought to do the king a favour by this too, having learned that he was pleased at his coming—but as he passed through the palace, he did not so much as glance at any of the things men wonder at, but, as though merely travelling, he went through them; and calling Damis, "You asked me the other day," he said, "what was the name of the Pamphylian woman who is said to have associated with Sappho and to have composed the hymns they sing to Artemis of Perga, in the Aeolian and Pamphylian manner." "I asked," he said, "but you did not tell me the name." "I did not, my good fellow," he said; "but I explained to you the modes of the hymns and the names, and how the Aeolian was carried over into the loftiest and most peculiar Pamphylian style; then we passed to another matter, and you no longer asked me about the name. Well, this wise woman is called Damophyle, and she is said, in the manner of Sappho, to have gained maiden disciples, and to have composed poems, some of them love-poems, others hymns. The hymns to Artemis are parodied by her and sung from the Sapphic measures." How far he was from being astonished at the king and his pomp, he made plain by not even thinking such things worthy of his eyes, but discoursing of other matters, and seeming to think that he saw those things too.

"But among us few lay hold of philosophy, and they are tested in this way. The young man, when he happens to have reached eighteen years—and this, I think, is the measure of an ephebe among you too—must go beyond the river Hyphasis to the men toward whom you have set out, having first declared publicly that he will philosophize, that it may be open to those who wish to bar him, if he comes not pure. And by pure I mean, first, what concerns his father and mother, that no reproach appear about them; then their parents, and a third generation upward, that there be no insolent or intemperate or unjustly money-getting man among them. And when no scar appears about these, nor any blemish at all, then they examine the young man himself and test him: first, whether he is of good memory; then, whether he is by nature modest and not feigning it; whether not given to drink, nor gluttonous, nor a braggart, nor a lover of laughter, nor rash, nor a railer; whether obedient to father, to mother, to teachers, to attendants; and above all, whether he is not corrupt in regard to his own youthful bloom. What concerns those who begot him and those who begot them is gathered from witnesses and from records that lie in public. For when an Indian dies, there comes to his doors a single magistrate appointed by the laws to write down how he lived; and if the magistrate lies or is deceived, the laws penalize him with this, that he shall hold no office again, as having falsified the life of a man. What concerns the ephebes themselves they learn by looking at them; for the eyes interpret much of human character, and much lies in the brows and cheeks to be judged and observed, from which wise and natural men, as in a mirror, behold the minds of men as images. For since philosophy is held in great honour here, and has this honour among the Indians, it is altogether necessary that those who go to it be thoroughly tested and subjected to countless proofs. That we do this under teachers, and that philosophizing comes to us as a matter of examination, I have said clearly; but my own case is thus.

And leaning towards Iarchas he said: "Let this man be drunk; but tell me why you do not deem these about him, his brother, as you say, and his son, worthy of a common table, nor of any other honour." "Because," he said, "they think they will one day be kings, and it is needful that they should be looked down upon, that they may learn not to look down on others." Seeing that the sages were eighteen, he asked Iarchas again what their being so many meant; "for the number," he said, "is not one of the squares, nor of those esteemed and honoured, like the ten, the twelve, the sixteen, and such." The Indian answered: "We are not slaves to number, nor is number our master, but we are esteemed by wisdom and virtue; and at one time we are more than now, at another fewer. My own grandfather, I hear, was reckoned among seventy wise men, being the youngest of them, but living to a hundred and thirty years was left alone here, since none of those others survived, nor was there then anywhere in India a philosophic or noble nature. The Egyptians wrote of him among the most fortunate, since he alone for four years presided over this throne, and he bade them cease to reproach the Indians with a scarcity of sages. And we, Apollonius, hearing the Egyptians tell of the Elean customs and of the Hellanodicae, who preside over the Olympics, being ten, do not praise the law laid down concerning them; for they leave the choice to the lot, which provides nothing, and even one of the meaner men might be chosen by the lot. But if they chose the men by merit or by vote, would they not err alike? For the number ten, being inexorable, would, if there were more just men, deprive some of being honoured for it; and if there were not ten just men, no one would seem to be just. So the Eleans would be far wiser to be at one time more, at another fewer in number, but the same in justice.

That he was at odds with those who thought they could write, and held ignorant those who laid hold of a subject too great for them, may be learned from this. A youth, conceited of his wisdom, meeting him about the temple, said: "Be eager with me tomorrow, for I shall read something." When Apollonius asked what he would read, "A discourse," he said, "I have composed to Zeus." And at the same time he showed it beneath his cloak, vaunting in the thickness of the book. "What then," he said, "will you praise of Zeus? The Zeus here, and that there is nothing on earth like it?" "That too," he said, "and many things before this and after it; for the seasons and the things on earth and above the earth, and that the winds and stars are all Zeus's." Apollonius said: "You seem to me to be a great encomiast." "For this reason," he said, "I have composed an encomium of gout too, and of being blind or deaf." "But do not banish dropsies or catarrhs from your wisdom," he said, "if you wish to praise such things; and you will be better still if you follow the dead and go through praises of the diseases by which they died, for fathers and children and the near of the dead will grieve less for them." And seeing the youth bridled by the discourse, the encomiast said: "O writer, will he praise better what he knows or what he does not know?" "What he knows," he said; "for how could one praise what one does not know?" "Have you then ever praised your own father?" "I wished to," he said, "but since he seems to me great and noble, the fairest of the men I know, able to govern a house and to use wisdom in all things, I left off the praise of him, that I might not shame my father with a meaner discourse." Apollonius, vexed — for this he felt towards vulgar men — said: "Then, you offscouring, do you think you could never praise your own father, whom you know as well as yourself, yet praising so easily the father of men and gods and the maker of all things about us and above us, you neither fear him whom you praise, nor understand that you are entering on a discourse too great for a man?

Apollonius, invoking the divine upon his words, said: "O Zeus of the Capitol — for I know you to be the arbiter of present affairs — guard yourself for this man, and this man for yourself; for it is fated that the temple which unjust hands burned yesterday should be raised again for you by this man." When the king marvelled at the saying, he said, "The events themselves will declare it; ask nothing of me, but carry through what you have rightly resolved." Now it had happened at Rome that Domitian, the son of Vespasian, had been drawn up against Vitellius on behalf of his father's empire; and being surrounded by a siege in the Capitol, he had escaped his besiegers, but the temple had been burned — and this appeared to Apollonius much sooner than if it had taken place in Egypt. After such conferences the one departed from the king, saying that the ancestral customs of the Indians did not allow him to do anything at noon other than what they do; while the other glowed yet more brightly and would not let affairs slip from him, but held to what he had heard as things secure and confirmed to him.

Proclaimed emperor in Rome and thought worthy of these honours, he was setting out to share the rule with his father, when, considering how much Apollonius would be worth to him even if they met for a little, he begged him to come to Tarsus; and embracing him when he came, he said: "My father wrote me everything in which he made you his counsellor, and here is the letter, in which you are written as his benefactor and all that we are; and I, though I am but thirty years old, am thought worthy of what my father was at sixty, and am called to rule before I know, perhaps, even how to be ruled; and I fear I am laying hold of greater things than I ought." So Apollonius, feeling his neck — for indeed he was as strong as those who train their bodies — said, "And who shall force a bull-neck so strong as this to bend beneath the yoke?" "He who reared me from a calf," said Titus, meaning his own father, and saying that he would be ruled by him alone, who from childhood had accustomed him to listen to him. "I am glad," said Apollonius, "first to see you prepared to follow your father, by whom even those who are not his children by nature are glad to be ruled, and to wait upon his doors, with whom you will be waited upon. When youth and age go together to rule, what lyre, what flute will sing so sweet and blended a harmony? For the older will accord with the younger, whence both age will have strength and youth will not be disorderly."

So he went off, and Apollonius, having rested himself on the couch, said: "I have need of sleep, Damis, for the night has been hard for me, wishing to recall the things I once heard from Phraotes." "And yet," he said, "you ought rather to be awake and to set yourself in order for the thing announced, since it is so great." "And how should I set myself in order," he said, "not even knowing what he will ask?" "Will you then improvise," he said, "about your life?" "By Zeus," he said, "Damis, for I use it itself as improvisation. But what I recalled of Phraotes I wish to go through with you, for it will seem useful to present matters, to you too. The lions which men tame, Phraotes bids one neither strike—for they bear malice if struck—nor fondle, for from this they grow arrogant; but rather, stroking them with a threat, to bring them into manageable tempers. This he said not of lions—for we were not earnest about the handling of beasts—but giving a rein for tyrants, by using which he held that one would not fall away from due measure." "This argument," he said, "is most well said toward the tempers of tyrants; but there is also in Aesop a certain lion, the one in the cave; and Aesop says that he was not sick, but seemed so, and laid hold of the beasts that came to him, but the fox said: 'What shall we make of this one, from whom no one comes back, nor is any footprint of those that go forth shown?'" And Apollonius said: "But I should have held the fox wiser, if, having gone in, she had not been caught, but had come out of the cave, showing her own footprints."

As for his death, some say he died in Ephesus, tended by two maidservants—for the freedmen of whom I spoke at the beginning were already dead—and that, having freed one, he was blamed by the other for not holding her worthy of the same, and that Apollonius said to her, "It befits you to be a slave to her, for this will be the beginning of good for you." After his death, then, the one was a slave to that woman, and she, on a small charge, sold her to a trader, from whom one bought her though she was not even comely; but he, being in love and a sufficient money-maker, both declared her wife and entered children by her on the registers. Others say he died in Lindus, going into the temple of Athena and vanishing within. And those in Crete tell a thing more marvellous than those in Lindus; for they say that Apollonius was living in Crete, marvelled at more than before, and came to the temple of Dictynna at an unseasonable hour. Now a guard of dogs is set over the temple, wardens of the wealth in it, and the Cretans hold them worthy to fall short of neither the bears nor the wild beasts there; but these neither barked when he came, but, approaching, fawned upon him as they would not even upon the very familiar. The keepers of the temple, then, seizing him as a sorcerer and a robber, bound him, saying that he had thrown some soothing to the dogs; but he, about the middle of the night, loosed himself, and calling those who had bound him, that he might not escape their notice, ran to the doors of the temple, which flew open; and when he had passed within, the doors came together as they had been closed, and there fell out a cry of maidens singing. And the song was: "Go from earth, go to heaven, go." Such as: Go up from the earth.

The king, seeing him approach from afar—for the courtyard of the temple had some length—talked with those near him, as though recognizing the man; and when he was already close, raising a great shout, "This," he said, "is Apollonius, whom my brother Megabates says he saw at Antioch, admired and worshipped by men of worth; and he painted him for me then just such as he comes now." And when Apollonius approached and greeted him, the king addressed him in the Greek tongue and bade him sacrifice with him; he was about to slay to the Sun a white horse of the finest Nisaean breed, adorned with trappings as for a procession. But Apollonius, taking up the word, said: "Do you, O king, sacrifice in your own way, but allow me to sacrifice in mine"; and taking up some frankincense, "O Sun," he said, "send me over so much of the earth as seems good to you and to me, and may I come to know good men, but may I neither learn to know base men, nor base men me." And saying this he cast the frankincense into the fire, and watched how it rose and where it grew turbid and in how many points it darted up, and touching the fire at times, where it appeared well-omened and pure, "Now, O king," he said, "sacrifice according to your own ancestral rites; for these are mine."

"I was born of a king for grandfather, who bore my own name, but of a private man for father. For my father, left quite young, had two of his kinsmen as guardians according to the laws of the Indians, who managed the kingdom for him not well, by the Sun, nor with measure, so that they seemed heavy to the subjects and the rule was ill spoken of. Some of the powerful, then, conspiring against them, set upon them at a festival and killed them as they sacrificed to the Indus, and themselves, leaping upon the rule, held the state. So the kinsmen, fearing for my father, not yet sixteen, sent him beyond the Hyphasis to the king there. He rules over more than I, and his country is by far more prosperous than this. And when the king wished to make him his son, my father declined, saying he would not strive against fortune which had taken the rule from him, but begged him to allow him to philosophize, going to the wise men; for so he could the more easily endure the troubles at home. And when the king wished to bring him back to his ancestral rule, he said, 'If you perceive me to be genuinely philosophizing, bring me back; but if not, let me remain as I am.' So the king himself, going to the wise men, said he would gain much from them if they took charge of the boy, who was already noble in nature; and they, seeing something more in him, welcomed the chance to impart to him their own wisdom, and eagerly taught him, since he was much given to learning. In the seventh year the king, falling sick—when indeed he died—sent for my father and declared him partner of the rule with his son, and promised him his daughter, who was of marriageable age; but my father, when he saw the king's son to be a slave to flatterers and wine and such evils, and full of suspicions toward himself, said: 'Keep these things and possess the whole rule; for it is foolish that one who could not gain even the kingdom that belonged to him should seem rashly to come to one that does not belong to him; but give me your sister, for this alone of yours is enough for me.' And having taken the marriage, he lived near the wise men in seven prosperous villages, which the king bestowed upon his sister as a dowry. Of this marriage, then, I was born, and my father, having taught me the lore of the Greeks, brought me to the wise men, perhaps before my time, for I was then twelve years old; and they reared me as their own child. For whomever they receive knowing the Greek tongue they love the more, as already akin to them in disposition.

While they were earnest about this, the king tried to break in, dividing them from all discourse and ever saying something witless and ignorant. So again he asked what they were earnest about, and Apollonius said: "We are discoursing of great things, and of those most esteemed among the Greeks; but you would think these small, for you say you are set against the affairs of the Greeks." "I am indeed set against them," he said, "yet I wish to hear all the same; for you seem to me to be speaking on behalf of the Athenians, the slaves of Xerxes." Apollonius said: "We are discoursing of other matters; but since you have made mention of the Athenians strangely and falsely, tell me this: have you slaves, O king?" "Twenty thousand," he said, "and I have bought not one of them, but they are all home-born." Again he asked, through Iarchas as interpreter, whether the king ran away from his own slaves, or the slaves from him; and the king, insulting him, said the question was slavish, "but nevertheless I answer: he who runs away is a slave and otherwise bad, but a master would not run from one whom he may rack and flog." "Then, O king," he said, "Xerxes is by your own showing declared to be a slave of the Athenians, and a bad slave, for he ran from them; since, beaten by them in the sea-fight at the straits, and fearing for his bridges over the Hellespont, he fled in a single ship." "And yet," said the king, "he burned Athens with his own hands." Apollonius said: "For this daring deed, O king, he paid such a penalty as no other man ever paid; for those whom he thought to have destroyed, from these he fled away. And I, when I consider Xerxes' purpose, by which he made his expedition, should hold him worthy to be reckoned by some, as he was, a Zeus; but for his flight I count him the most ill-fated of men. For had he died in the hands of the Greeks, what man would have been deemed worthy of more splendid words? What greater tomb would the Greeks have raised over him? What contest in arms, what contest in music, would not have been founded in his honour? For if Melicertes and Palaemon, who died still at the breast, and Pelops the Lydian incomer, who enslaved Arcadia and Argolis and all within the Isthmus, were raised by the Greeks to divine remembrance, what would not have befallen Xerxes at the hands of men who by nature love virtues and count it their own praise to praise those whom they conquer?

Apollonius' discourses at Olympia were about the most useful things — about wisdom and courage and temperance and, in a word, all the virtues; about these he discoursed from the steps of the temple, astonishing all not only by his thoughts but by the forms of his speech. The Lacedaemonians, standing round him, made him a guest-friend before Zeus, and a father of the young men at home, and a lawgiver of life, and a glory of the old. When a certain Corinthian asked him peevishly whether they would hold a Theophania for him too, "By the Twin Gods," he said, "they are ready." But Apollonius led them away from such things, that he might not be envied. When, crossing Taygetus, he saw Lacedaemon active and the customs of Lycurgus prospering, he thought it not unpleasant to meet too with the magistrates of the Lacedaemonians about what they wished to ask. So they asked, when he came, how the gods are to be served, and he said, "As masters." Again they asked, how the heroes; "As fathers." When they asked a third time, how men, he said, "That question is not Laconian." They asked too what he thought of their laws, and he said, "The best of teachers; but the teachers will be esteemed if the pupils are not idle." When they asked what counsel he gave about courage, "And what," he said, "will you use your courage for?

On the next day, about dawn, Apollonius came to the palace and asked the guards what the king was doing; and they said he had long been awake and was busy with letters. Hearing this he went away, saying to Damis, "The man will rule." Returning about sunrise he found Dio and Euphrates at the doors, and when they eagerly asked about the meeting he went through the defence which he had heard from the king, but kept silent about his own opinions. Being called in first, he said, "O king, Euphrates and Dio, long known to you, are at the doors, not careless of your affairs; call them in too to the common discussion, for they are wise men." "I keep my doors unbarred to wise men," he said, "and to you my very breast seems to be opened."

"And to me, Tyanean," he said, "about rule and kingship, what will you lay down?" "What you have persuaded yourself," he said; "for being subject to your father, it is plain that you will make yourself like him. And I would now tell you the saying of Archytas, for it is noble and worth learning. Archytas was a man of Tarentum, wise in the things of Pythagoras; he, writing about the rearing of children, says: 'Let the father be a pattern of virtue to his children'; for fathers too will walk the more strenuously toward the virtues, if their children are made like to them. And I will introduce to you Demetrius too, my own companion, who will be with you as much as you wish, teaching you what a good ruler ought to do." "And what, Apollonius," he said, "is the wisdom of this man?" "Frankness," he said, "and the speaking of truth and being dismayed by no one, for he is of the Cynic strength." And when Titus heard the word 'dog' with displeasure, "Yet in Homer," he said, "Telemachus, being young, seemed to need two dogs, and Homer sends them as attendants for the youth into the market-place of the Ithacans, though they were without speech; but you shall have a dog who, on your behalf against others and against yourself, if you should err, will bark wisely and not unreasonably." "Give me," he said, "the attendant dog, and I allow him even to bite, if he perceive me doing wrong." "A letter shall be written to him," he said, "for he philosophizes in Rome." "Let it be written," he said; "and I could wish someone would write to you too on my behalf, that you might become a companion of our road to Rome." "I will come," he said, "when it is better for us both."

Having said this, he snatched a very little sleep, only so much as came upon his eyes; and when day came, having prayed to the Sun, as is natural in a prison, he discoursed with those who came to him on whatever they asked; and so, when the market was full, the clerk came, bidding him be at the doors. "Let us not be summoned too late," he said. And saying "Let us go," he went forth with eagerness. As he went, four spearmen followed him, keeping farther off than those who accompany for the sake of guard; and Damis followed too, afraid, yet like one in thought. All men looked toward Apollonius, for his very dress drew their gaze, and the dismay about his form seemed divine; and the very fact that he came to be in danger on behalf of men made even those who had before maligned him friendly then. Standing by the palace and seeing some tended and some tending, as men went in and out with a clatter, he said: "This seems to me, Damis, like a bath; for I see those outside hastening in, and those inside out, and some resemble men who have bathed, others the unbathed." This saying I bid be kept inviolate, and not ascribed to this man or that, since it is so much Apollonius's that it is even written up for him in a letter. Seeing a very old man eager to rule, and for this very reason ruled and tending this emperor, he said: "Damis, not even Sophocles has yet persuaded the raging and savage master to depart." "Whom we ourselves too, Apollonius, have chosen," he said; "for it is for this that we stand at such doors." "You seem to me, Damis," he said, "to hold that Aeacus too, who is said to be in Hades, is the warden of these gates; for you are like a dead man." "Not a dead man," he said, "but one about to die." And Apollonius said: "You seem to me, Damis, to be ill-fitted toward death, though you have been with me a long time, philosophizing from a stripling; I thought you were prepared for it, and knew all my tactics; for as those who fight and bear arms need not courage only, but order too, that interprets the moments of battle, so those who pursue philosophy must take care for the moments in which they will die, that they may be borne to them not without order, nor death-courting, but with the best choice. That I have chosen to die best and at the moment befitting philosophy, if anyone should wish to kill me, I have defended both to others in your presence, and you yourself I have given up teaching."

About the soul, that it is immortal, he was still philosophizing, teaching that the argument about it is true, but not allowing men to meddle with such great things. For there came to Tyana a stripling bold in disputes and not agreeing with a true argument; and when Apollonius was now out of the world, and was marvelled at for his change, and none dared to gainsay that he was immortal, most of the discourses were about the soul—for there was there a youth in love with wisdom—but the stripling in no way agreed with the immortality of the soul, and said, "I, gentlemen, this tenth month now keep praying to Apollonius to reveal to me the argument about the soul; but he is so dead as not even to stand by me when I beg, nor to persuade me that he is immortal." Such things the stripling said then; but on the fifth day from that, having been earnest about the same things, he fell asleep where he was discoursing, and of the young men who were earnest with him some were at their books, some busy scratching geometric figures in the earth, when he, as though mad, leaping up half-asleep, streaming with much sweat, cried, "I believe you." And when those present asked what had befallen him, "Do you not see," he said, "Apollonius the wise, how he is present with us, listening to the argument, and chants marvellous things about the soul?" "And where is he?" they said; "for to us he appears nowhere, though we should wish this rather than to have the goods of all men." And the stripling said, "He seems to have come to discourse with me alone about the things I disbelieved; hear, then, what he chants over the argument: 'The soul is immortal, and not your possession, but Providence's, and after the body has withered, like a swift horse loosed from bonds, lightly leaping forth it mingles with the light air, having loathed its dreadful and much-suffering servitude. But what is this to you, who, when you are no longer, shall then seem to be? Or why, while you are among the living, do you search about these things?'" And this clear tripod of Apollonius stands about the secrets of the soul, that, of good cheer and knowing our own nature, we may go on to where the Fates appoint. Now to a tomb or false-tomb of the man I have nowhere come, though I have traversed most of the earth, however great it is; but everywhere to daemonic accounts of him, and there is a temple at Tyana wrought at imperial cost; for not even emperors held him unworthy of the honours of which they themselves were held worthy.

And he withdrew from the sacrifice, so as not to share in the blood. After the sacrifice he came up and said: "O king, do you know the whole Greek tongue, or a little of it, perhaps, for the sake of courtesy, and that you may not seem disagreeable if some Greek should come?" "The whole," he said, "as well as this native tongue; and say what you wish, for it is for this, I suppose, that you ask." "For this," he said, "then hear. The aim of my journey is the Indians; but I did not wish to pass even you by, both because I heard that you were a man such as I now see you already from the claw, and because I desired to behold the wisdom which is native and practised among you by the magi—whether they are wise in divine matters, as they are said to be. My own wisdom is that of Pythagoras of Samos, a man who taught me to serve the gods in this way, and to understand them whether seen or unseen, and to hold converse with the gods, and to be clothed in this earth-born wool—for it was not shorn from a sheep, but pure springs from pure things, the gift of water and earth, this linen; and the very letting-grow of my hair I practised from Pythagoras, and the keeping pure of animal food comes to me from his wisdom. A fellow-drinker, then, or partner in ease or luxury I could never be to you nor to any other; but of cares perplexing and hard to solve I could give solutions, knowing not only what should be done, but also foreknowing it." These things Damis says the man discoursed; but Apollonius has made them into a letter, and many others of the things he said in conversation he reshaped into letters.

"When my parents died not long after one another, they bade me go to the villages and take care of my own affairs, being nineteen years old. But the good uncle had already taken the villages from me, and did not even leave me the little plots my father had possessed, for he said they all belonged to his own rule, and that I should gain great things from him if he let me live. So, collecting a contribution from my mother's freedmen, I had four attendants. And as I was reading the play of the Heraclidae, someone stood by me bearing a letter from a man friendly to my father, who bade me cross the river Hydraotes and join him about the kingdom there, for I had many hopes of recovering it if I did not delay. The play, I think, some god brought to my mind, and I followed the omen; and having crossed the river, I heard that one of those who had usurped the rule was dead, and the other was being besieged in this very palace. So I went on in haste, crying out to those in the villages through which I passed, that I was the son of such a man and was going to my own rule; and they, rejoicing and greeting me, escorted me, thinking me like my grandfather; and they had daggers and bows, and we grew ever more numerous; and when I approached the gates, those within received me so gladly that, lighting torches from the altar of the Sun, they came before the gates and led me hither, hymning much my father and my grandfather; but the drone within, they shut round about with the wall, though I begged that he not die in such a fashion.

As Apollonius said this, the king was moved to tears, and said: "Dearest friend, what manner of men you show me the Greeks to be!" "Whence then, O king, were you so harsh towards them?" "They slander the Greek race, stranger," he said, "those who come here from Egypt, declaring themselves holy and wise and lawgivers of sacrifices and rites, all that the Greeks observe, but saying that the Greeks are nothing sound, but insolent, a rabble, full of all anarchy, tellers of tales and of marvels, and poor — yet showing this not as a thing of dignity but as an excuse for stealing. But now, hearing from you these things, and how ambitious and good they are, I make a truce henceforth with the Greeks, and grant them to be praised by me, and that I should pray for the Greeks all that I can, and that the Egyptians should be distrusted by me." And Iarchas said: "I too, O king, knew that your ears had been corrupted by these Egyptians, but I said nothing on behalf of the Greeks until you should meet with such a token. But since you have been made better by a wise man, let the loving-cup of Tantalus now be drunk by us, and let us sleep over the things for which we must be earnest by night; and of Greek discourses, which are the most numerous among men, I will fill you henceforth to your joy, whenever you come." And at once he led the way to his fellow-drinkers, being the first to stoop to the bowl, which gave drink enough to all, for the draught flowed ungrudgingly, as from welling springs; and Apollonius too drank, for this draught is found among the Indians as a pledge of friendship. And they make Tantalus its cup-bearer, since he was thought the most loving of men.

About this time there was a young Lacedaemonian charged among them with wronging the customs; for he was a descendant of Callicratidas, who was admiral at Arginusae, but he loved ship-owning and gave no heed to public affairs, but sailed off to Carthage and Sicily in ships he had built. Hearing that he was tried for this, Apollonius thought it dreadful to overlook the young man brought to trial, and said: "My good friend, why do you go about full of thought and brooding?" "A public suit," he said, "has been brought against me, since I am given to ship-owning and do not attend to public affairs." "Was your father a ship-owner, or your grandfather?" "Far from it," he said; "gymnasiarchs all, and ephors and patronomi; and Callicratidas my ancestor was one of the admirals." "Do you mean the one at Arginusae?" he said. "Him," he said, "who died in his admiralship." "Then did your ancestor's death not turn you against the sea?" "By Zeus, no," he said; "for I do not sail to fight a sea-battle." "And can you name a more wretched tribe than merchants and ship-owners? First they roam about, seeking a market in distress; then, mixing with brokers and hucksters, they sell and are sold, and pledging their own heads to unholy interest they hasten for the principal; and if they prosper, the ship sails well, and they make much of never having wrecked her, willingly or unwillingly; but if their trade does not meet their debts, they go over into the boats and dash the ships on the rocks, and most impiously call the destruction of others' livelihood the necessity of god, and rob even where they would not. And even if the seafaring and nautical tribe were not such, yet for a man who is a Spartiate and sprung of fathers who once dwelt in the heart of Sparta to lie in a hollow ship, forgetting Lycurgus and Iphitus but mindful of his cargo and the niceties of seamanship — from what shame is it free? For if from nothing else, he should at least consider Sparta herself, how, when she held to the land, she seemed to reach to heaven, but when she desired the sea, she was sunk and made to vanish, not only in the sea but on the land too." With these words he so mastered the young man that, bowing his head to the earth, he wept to hear how far he had fallen short of his fathers, and sold the ships by which he lived. And when Apollonius saw him restored and embracing the land, he led him to the ephors and begged him off the suit.

When they had been called in, he said, "Concerning my own purpose, gentlemen, I made my defence yesterday to the noble Apollonius." "We heard the defence," said Dio, "and it was sensible." "Today, then, dear Dio," he said, "let us philosophize together about what has been resolved, that I may do all as nobly as may be and for the salvation of men. For when I consider, first, Tiberius, how he turned the empire to inhumanity and cruelty; then Gaius after him, how, raving like a bacchant and aping the Lydian in his dress and winning wars that did not exist, he played the shameful bacchant over all the affairs of the Romans; then the worthy Claudius, how, overcome by women, he forgot to rule, and even to live, for he died at their hands, as they say; and as for Nero, why should I lay hold of him, when Apollonius has uttered a short and pithy saying about the slackening and tightening by which Nero disgraced the empire? And what should I say of the schemes of Galba, who died in the middle of the market-place, adopting as his own sons men who had sold themselves, Otho and Piso? And if we hand the empire to Vitellius, the most wanton of all, Nero will come to life again. Seeing then, gentlemen, that ruling has been brought into ill repute by the tyrannies I have named, I make you my counsellors how I might so dispose of it, now that it has already offended men." To this Apollonius said, "A flute-player of the most skilled used to send his pupils to the baser flute-players to learn how one ought not to play the flute. How one ought not to rule you have learned, O king, from these men who ruled badly; let us now be earnest about how one ought to rule."

Having sent away those present, Titus said: "We are by ourselves, Tyanean; for you allow me, I think, to ask about what is most serious to me?" "Ask," he said, "and the more eagerly, the greater the matter." "About my own soul," he said, "will my question be, and whom I should most guard against — unless I shall seem a coward in fearing these things already." "Cautious, rather," he said, "and on your guard, for of this one should most take forethought." And looking up to the sun he swore by it that he had himself been about to speak to Titus of these things even unasked, for the gods had revealed to him to foretell to him that while his father lived he should fear his father's bitterest enemies, but when he was dead, his own nearest kin. "And in what manner shall I die?" he said. "As Odysseus is said to," he said, "for they say that to him too death came from the sea." Damis interprets this thus: that he should guard against the spine of the trygon, with which they say Odysseus was struck; and that after holding the rule two years from his father, he died by the sea-hare; for this fish furnishes secret juices beyond all things on sea or land that slay men; and Nero put this hare into the dishes of his bitterest enemies, and Domitian put it into the dishes of his brother Titus, thinking it grievous not to rule with a brother, but to rule with a gentle and good one. Having discussed such things in private, they embraced one another in public; and as Titus went away, Apollonius said, "Conquer, O king, your enemies with arms, and your father with virtues."

So far for these things. But when the emperor had leisure, having thrust aside all that was at his feet, to come to talk with the man, the officers of such matters led him into the palace, not allowing Damis to follow him in. The emperor, wearing a wreath of olive, had just been sacrificing to Athena in the court of Adonis—and the court bloomed with gardens of flowers, such as the Assyrians make for Adonis, planting them under their own roofs for the mysteries. Being still by the rites, he turned about, and, dismayed by the form of the man, said: "Aelian, you have brought me a daemon." But Apollonius, not at all dismayed, and laying hold of what he had heard, said: "I thought, sire, that Athena had cared for you in the manner she once cared for Diomedes at Troy; for she took from the eyes of Diomedes the mist by which men see worse, and gave him to distinguish gods and men. But you the goddess has not yet purified with this purification, sire; though surely she ought, that you might see Athena herself better, and not rank men among the shapes of daemons." "And you, philosopher," he said, "when did you purify yourself of this mist?" "Long ago," he said, "and ever since I have practised philosophy." "How then," he said, "did you account men most hostile to me to be gods?" "And what war," he said, "is there for you with Iarchas, or with Phraotes among the Indians, whom alone of men I hold to be gods and worthy of this name?" "Do not lead me off to the Indians," he said; "but speak about your dearest Nerva and those who share his charge." "Shall I defend him," he said, "or—" "Do not defend him," he said; "for he is caught doing wrong; but teach me this—not that you yourself do wrong, sharing in such things with him." "If you wish to hear what I am conscious of," he said, "hear it; for why should I hide the truth?" The emperor thought he was to hear brilliant secrets, and that all things would tend to the destruction of the men; but Apollonius, seeing him uplifted by this opinion,

When the king said that he rejoiced and was more delighted at his coming than if he had added the wealth of the Persians and Indians to what he had, and that he made him his guest-friend and partner of the royal roof, "If I, O king," he said, "should ask you, on coming to my native city Tyana, to dwell where I dwell, would you have consented to dwell there?" "By Zeus, no," he said, "unless I were to dwell in a house large enough to receive splendidly my spearmen and my bodyguards and myself." "Then the same argument holds from me too," he said; "for if I dwell beyond my station, I shall live ill, since excess troubles the wise more than deficiency troubles you. Let me, then, be entertained by some private man who has as much as I, and I will be with you as much as you wish." The king consented, lest he should unawares do something disagreeable to him, and Apollonius lodged with a Babylonian who was good and otherwise noble. As he was now dining, a eunuch, one of those who carry messages, stood by, and greeting the man said: "The king presents you with ten gifts, and makes you master of naming them; but he asks you not to ask small things, for he wishes to display his magnanimity to you and to us." Praising the offer, "When, then, must I ask?" he inquired. "Tomorrow," he said; and at once he went round to all the king's friends and kinsmen, bidding them be present when the man should ask and be honoured. Damis says that he understood Apollonius would ask for nothing, having observed his character and knowing that he prayed to the gods such a prayer as this: "O gods, grant me to have little and to need nothing." Yet seeing him standing intent and like one in thought, he supposed that he would ask, but was testing within himself what he meant to ask. And Apollonius, now in the evening, said: "Damis, I am considering with myself why ever the barbarians think eunuchs chaste, and bring them into the women's chambers." "But this, Apollonius," he said, "is plain even to a child; for since the gelding takes from them the power of sexual love, the women's chambers are thrown open to them, even though they should wish to sleep with the women." "And do you think," he said, "that loving, or consorting with women, has been cut out of them?" "Both," he said; "for if the part by which the body is goaded to frenzy is quenched, the love of it would come upon no one." But he, pausing a little, said: "Tomorrow, Damis, you shall learn that even eunuchs love, and that the desire which they admit through their eyes is not withered out of them, but remains warm and ready to kindle; for something must happen that will refute your argument. And if there were some human art, tyrannous and able to thrust such things out of the mind, I should not, I think, ever have set down eunuchs among those of chaste character, since they are forced into chastity and led by a violent art into not loving. For chastity is to be drawn and impelled and yet not be overcome by sexual things, but to abstain and to show oneself master of this frenzy."

Apollonius, taking up the word, said: "You have plainly described a return of the Heraclidae, and the gods are to be praised for their purpose, in that they helped a noble man going to his own in his return. But tell me this about the wise men: were they not once under Alexander, and brought to him, did they not philosophize to him about heaven?" "Those were the Oxydracae," he said; "and this nation is ever free and arrayed for war, and they claim to handle wisdom, though they know nothing useful. But the truly wise lie midway between the Hyphasis and the Ganges, a country Alexander never even came to—not, I think, fearing what was in it, but, I suppose, the sacred signs warned him off. And even if he had crossed the Hyphasis and been able to take the land about them, yet the tower in which they dwell he would never have mastered, not though he led ten thousand Achilles and thirty thousand Ajaxes; for they do not fight those who attack, but, being sacred and dear to the gods, drive them off by striking with celestial signs and thunderbolts. At any rate the Egyptian Heracles and Dionysus, who overran the Indian nation in arms, are said once to have marched against them and contrived engines and made trial of the place; but the wise men did nothing in resistance, but kept still, as it appeared to them; yet when the others drew near, fiery blasts thrust them back, and thunders rolling downward and falling upon their arms. There Heracles is said to have thrown away his shield, which was of gold, and the wise men have made it a dedication, both for the fame of Heracles and for the device on the shield; for Heracles himself is wrought there marking the bounds of Gadeira and making the mountains his pillars and drawing the Ocean inward—from which it is shown that not the Theban, but the Egyptian Heracles, came to Gadeira and became the bounder of the earth."

When they had drunk, the earth received them on couches which it strewed of itself. And when it was midnight, first they rose and hymned the ray aloft, as at noon, then they joined the king in all that he needed. Damis says that Apollonius was not present at what the king was earnest about, but supposes that the meeting was held concerning the secrets of his rule. So having sacrificed at daybreak, the king came to Apollonius and invited him to be his guest in the palace, saying he would send him back enviable to the Greeks. But Apollonius praised this, yet said he would not give himself to a man in no way like himself, and that, being abroad longer than was fitting, he was ashamed that his friends at home should seem to be slighted. When the king pressed him and now clung to him without dignity, Iarchas said: "The king wrongs the holy house in leading a man away from here against his will; and besides, being one of those with foreknowledge, this man knows that his meeting with you will not be for his good, nor perhaps will it have anything wholesome for you yourself.

And this too of his at Lacedaemon. A letter came from the emperor to the Lacedaemonians, bearing a rebuke to their council as men who outraged their freedom; and this was sent to them through the slanders of the governor of Greece. The Lacedaemonians were at a loss, and Sparta was at strife with herself whether to write deprecating the emperor's anger or scornfully. On this they made Apollonius their counsellor about the tone of the letter; and he, seeing them divided, came forward to their council and made this brief speech: "Palamedes discovered letters not only for writing, but also for knowing what one must not write." So he led the Lacedaemonians away from appearing either rash or cowardly.

Now Euphrates was already secretly envious of Apollonius, seeing the king attached to him more than those who come to the oracles are attached to them; and swelling beyond measure then, and raising his voice beyond his wont, he said: "We must not flatter men's impulses, nor be foolishly carried away with those who do anything contrary to the rein, but bring them into order, if indeed we are philosophers. For what ought to have been shown by deliberating whether it is fitting to do at all, you bid us discuss the manner in which it is to be done, not having yet learned whether deliberation is even in place. I bid Vitellius be overthrown, for I know the man to be foul and drunk with every wantonness; but you, whom I know to be a good man and pre-eminent in nobility, I say ought not to set right the affairs of Vitellius while not yet knowing your own. As for the outrages of monarchies, you need not learn them from me, for you have said them yourself; but you would know that youth leaping upon tyranny does something suited to it, for to be a tyrant is as natural to the young as to be drunk or to be in love; and a young man who has been a tyrant is not yet wicked, even if he seem murderous in the course of his tyranny, and cruel and wanton; but for an old man coming to tyranny the first charge is that he wished for such things. For even if he appear humane and orderly, men do not credit this to him, but to his age and to his being settled; and he will seem to have desired this long ago and to have erred while still young. And such errors lie close to misfortune, and close to cowardice; for a man seems either to have despaired of his own fortune, the design to be a tyrant being already in his mind, or to have given way to another who wished to be a tyrant, fearing him, no doubt, as a man. Let the matter of misfortune be passed over; but how will you escape the charge of cowardice, seeming as you do to have feared Nero, the most cowardly and idle of men? For the things which Vindex devised against him called you first, by Heracles. For you had an army, and the force you were leading against the Jews was the better fitted to punish Nero; for they have long ago revolted not only from the Romans but from all mankind. For men who have found out a life unsociable, and who share with men neither a common table nor libations nor prayers nor sacrifices, are further from us than Susa and Bactra and the Indians beyond them; so that it was not even reasonable to punish those who revolted, whom it were better not even to have acquired. But who would not have prayed to slay Nero with his own hand, a man all but drinking the blood of men and singing in the midst of slaughter? Yet my ears were pricked up toward the reports about you; and whenever anyone came from there saying that thirty thousand Jews had perished at your hands, and fifty thousand in the next battle, I took the newcomer aside and asked him measuredly, 'And the man? Nothing greater than this?' But since, making Vitellius an image of Nero, you march against him — what you have resolved, do, for these things too are noble; but for what comes after, let it be thus. To Romans the rule of the people is of great worth, and many of their possessions were gained under that polity. Put an end to monarchy, of which you have spoken such things, and give the Romans the power of the people, and to yourself the glory of having begun their freedom."

The letter to Demetrius ran thus: "Apollonius the philosopher to Demetrius the Cynic, greeting. I give you to King Titus as a teacher of the character of kingship; do you make my words true to him, and be to him, save anger, all things. Farewell."

said: "I know Nerva to be the most temperate of men, and the gentlest, and most suited to you, and a good ruler, but so cautious toward the weight of affairs that he even dreads honours. As for those about him—Rufus, I suppose, and Orfitus you mean—these men too are temperate, so far as I know, and slandered toward wealth, but sluggish to do even what is permitted, and would neither themselves conceive of innovations, nor join with another who had conceived them." The emperor, swelling with rage at what he heard, said: "So you have caught me out as an informer against them, that those whom I have found the foulest of men and leaping upon my own, you should say are good and sluggish? For I think those men too, being questioned about you, would say neither that you are a sorcerer, nor a reckless man, nor a boaster, nor a money-lover, nor one who thinks himself above the laws. So, you foul heads, you have leagued yourselves in wickedness. The accusation will convict everything; for I know no less of all your oaths, and for what, and when, and what you sacrificed, than if I had been present and shared in it." But Apollonius, not dismayed even at this, said: "It is shameful, sire, and not according to the laws, either to judge of what you have been persuaded, or to be persuaded of what you have not judged. But if it is so, allow me to begin my defence from this point: you think ill of me, sire, and wrong me more than the informer; for what he said he would teach you, you are persuaded of before hearing it." "Begin your defence from where you will," he said; "but I know both where I shall end, and from what point it is now fitting to begin."

So Damis, taking up the word, said: "These things we shall consider again, Apollonius; but as to what you should answer tomorrow to the king's offer, splendid as it is, it becomes you to have thought it out. For you will ask, perhaps, for nothing; but take care, and guard against this, that you do not seem to refuse what the king gives out of some other kind of pride, considering where on earth we are, and that we lie, as it were, in his hand. And we must guard against slanders, that we use disdain; and we must know that now indeed we have provision enough to send us to the Indians, but on our way back from there this would not suffice, and other could not be got." And with such art he sought to warm him—

While they were thus discoursing, the hymn came on with the flute, and Apollonius asked the king what the revel meant. "The Indians," he said, "sing counsels to the king, when he is about to sleep, that he may have good dreams and rise kindly and well-omened to his subjects." "And how, O king," he said, "are you disposed toward this? For it is you, I suppose, they pipe to." "I do not mock it," he said; "for one must accept it for the law's sake, though I need no counsel; for whatever the king does with measure and goodness, he will surely do as a favour to himself rather than to his subjects."

So the king went down to the village, for the law of the sages did not allow the king to be with them above one day; and Iarchas said to the messenger and to Damis: "We deem him worthy of the secrets here; let him come, and do you take care of the rest in the village." When Damis came, they sat down together, as was their custom, and gave Apollonius leave to ask; and he asked of what they thought the cosmos was composed. They said, "of elements." "Of four, then?" he said. "Not of four," said Iarchas, "but of five." "And what fifth could there be," he said, "besides water and air and earth and fire?" "The ether," he said, "which one must hold to be the begetting of the gods; for all that draws the air is mortal, but all that draws the ether is immortal and divine." Again he asked which of the elements came first into being, and Iarchas said: "All at once; for a living creature is not born part by part." "Am I to hold the cosmos a living creature?" he said. "If you judge soundly," he said; "for it brings all things to life of itself." "Shall we call it female," he said, "or of the male and opposite nature?" "Of both," he said; "for being joined with itself, it does both the part of mother and of father to the bringing-forth of life, and it has for itself a love hotter than any one thing has for another, which fits it together and holds it firm; nor is it strange that it should grow together with itself. And as the movement of a living creature is the work of hands and feet and of the mind within it, by which it is impelled, so let us hold that the parts of the cosmos too, through its mind, offer themselves fit for all things born and conceived. For the afflictions that come from droughts come according to that mind, whenever, justice having fallen out among men, they fare dishonourably; and this living creature is shepherded not by one hand but by many and unspeakable hands, which it uses, unbridled because of its greatness, yet moved obedient and easily led.
