Having spent some time at Sparta after Olympia, as the winter was ending, he came to Malea at the beginning of spring, to set out for Rome. As he purposed this, he had a dream of this kind: he thought a woman, very tall and very aged, embraced him and begged to be with him before he sailed to Italy, and said she was the nurse of Zeus, and she wore a crown holding all the fruits of earth and sea. Giving himself an account of the vision, he understood that he must first sail to Crete, which we hold to be the nurse of Zeus, since there he was tended at birth; and the crown perhaps signified another island too. There being at Malea many ships about to set out for Crete, he embarked on one sufficient for the company — and he called "the company" his companions and the slaves of his companions, for he did not overlook these either. Sailing to Cydonia and coasting to Cnossus, where the Labyrinth, which is shown there, once held, I think, the Minotaur, when his companions wished to see it, he allowed them this, but said that he himself would not be a spectator of the injustice of Minos. He went on to Gortyna out of longing for Ida. So going up and meeting with the theological lore there, he went also to the temple of Lebena; this is Asclepius', and as Asia resorts to Pergamum, so Crete resorted to this temple, and many of the Libyans too cross over to it, for it faces the Libyan sea about Phaestus, where the small stone keeps back the great sea. They say the temple was named Lebenaean because a headland runs out from it like a lion, as the chance shapes of rocks often show, and they tell a tale about the headland, that this was once one of the lions that drew Rhea's car. There, as Apollonius was once discoursing about noon — and he was discoursing to many men by whom the temple was served — an earthquake fell suddenly on Crete, and thunder sounded not from clouds but from the earth, and the sea withdrew perhaps seven stades. Most were afraid that the retreating sea would draw down the temple and carry them off; but Apollonius said: "Take courage; for the sea has brought forth land." They thought he meant the harmony of the elements, and that the sea would work no new mischief on the land; but a few days later some came from Cydonia and reported that on the day and at the noon when the sign from heaven occurred, an island rose out of the sea about the strait that flows between Thera and Crete. But leaving off length of words, let us come to his doings at Rome, which befell after those in Crete.

When Euphrates had said so much, Apollonius, seeing Dio assent to the opinion — for he showed this both by his nod and by his praise as the other spoke — said, "Do you, Dio, add anything to what has been said?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said; "in part the same, in part not the same. For that he would have been far better overthrowing Nero than setting right the affairs of the Jews, I think has been said by me too to you; but you seemed to make it a contest that Nero should never be overthrown, for he who set in good order the disorder of his affairs strengthened the man, no doubt, against all whom he was wickedly strong against. But the impulse against Vitellius I praise; for I hold it a greater thing than to put an end to an established tyranny not even to let one come to birth. As for democracy, I welcome it — for even if this polity is inferior to aristocracy, yet it is to be chosen by sober men above tyrannies and oligarchies — but I fear lest these tyrannies, having already made the Romans tractable, may make the change a hard one, and lest they prove unable either to live freely or to look up to democracy, like men who from darkness look at sudden light. Therefore I say that Vitellius must be thrust out of affairs, and let this be done as quickly and as well as may be; but it seems to me that you should prepare as if to make war, yet not proclaim war upon him, but punishment, unless he give up the empire; and when you have taken him — and this I think will be within your power even without effort — give the Romans the choice of their own polity, and if they choose democracy, grant it; for this will be greater for you than many tyrannies and many Olympiads, and everywhere you will be inscribed in the city, everywhere you will stand in bronze, and you will give us themes for discourse to which neither Harmodius nor Aristogeiton will be compared. But if they accept monarchy, to whom else but you will all vote the rule? For what you already hold and would surrender to the commonwealth, they will surely give to you rather than to another."

The inhabitants of Tarsus had at other times been vexed at Apollonius, both for his rebukes, since he made them strenuous, and because, being slack and luxurious, they could not endure even the force of his speech; but then they were so far overcome by the man that they held him their founder and the support of their city. For the emperor was sacrificing in public, and the city, gathering, made supplication about the greatest matters; and he said he would remember these things to his father and would himself be an ambassador for what they asked. But Apollonius, coming forward, said: "If I should convict some of these men as enemies to you and your father, and as having gone on embassies to Solyma about revolution, and as secret allies of your most open foes, what would they suffer?" "What else," he said, "than perish?" "Then is it not shameful," he said, "to demand punishments at once, but to give benefits late, and to make the one by yourself, but to refer the others to a sharing of judgement?" Overjoyed, the emperor said, "I grant the gifts; for my father will not be vexed at me for being overcome by truth and by you."

From this point began the outrage against the man: he cut off his beard and his hair, and bound him among the worst malefactors. As to the shearing, "Sire," he said, "I did not know I was in danger about my hair; but as to the bonds—if you hold me a sorcerer, how will you bind me? And if you bind me, how will you say I am a sorcerer?" "And I will not loose you," he said, "until you become water, or some beast, or a tree." "These things," he said, "not even if I could would I become, that I might never betray men who are in danger by no justice; but being such as I am, I will submit myself to all you do about this body, until I have defended the men." "And for you," he said, "who will be the defender?" "Time," he said, "and the breath of the gods, and the love of wisdom, with which I dwell."

—not to think it beneath him to take whatever the king gave. But Apollonius, as though helping him in his argument, said: "And will you neglect, Damis, the examples? Among which are these: that Aeschines, the son of Lysanias, went off to Dionysius in Sicily for the sake of money; that Plato is said to have measured Charybdis three times for the sake of Sicilian wealth; that Aristippus of Cyrene, and Helicon of Cyzicus, and Phyton of Rhegium, when he was in exile, sank themselves so deep into the treasures of Dionysius that they hardly came up again from there. And indeed they say that Eudoxus of Cnidus, having once come to Egypt, both confessed that he came for money and discoursed with the king about it; and, not to slander too many, that Speusippus the Athenian became so much a lover of money that he went revelling to Macedonia for the wedding of Cassander, having composed frigid verses, and sang these in public for money. But I hold, Damis, that the wise man runs more risk than seafarers and those who fight in arms; for envy advances upon him whether he is silent or speaks, whether he strains himself or relaxes, whether he passes anything by or approaches anyone, whether he addresses a man or does not address him. The man must be fenced about, and must know that the wise man, overcome by sloth or anger or love or fondness for drink, or acting more hastily than the moment required, might perhaps even find pardon; but he who subjects himself to money would neither be pardoned nor be anything but hated, as one who has gathered all vices together in himself. For he would not be overcome by money, unless he were first overcome by his belly and dress and wine and the being carried away to courtesans. And you, perhaps, think that to do wrong in Babylon is a lesser thing than to do wrong at Athens or Olympia or Delphi, and you do not consider that to a wise man Greece is everywhere, and that the wise man will neither hold nor reckon any place to be desert or barbarian, living as he does under the eyes of virtue, and looking upon few men, but being himself looked upon by ten thousand eyes. And if you were the companion of one of those athletes, Damis, who train for wrestling and the pancratium, would you think it right that he should be noble and good if he competed at the Olympia and went to Arcadia, and, by Zeus, if the Pythia or the Nemea were held, should take care of his body, since these contests are conspicuous and the lists are in a renowned part of Greece, but that, if Philip should hold an Olympic festival after taking cities, or his son Alexander hold a contest over his own victories, he should now prepare his body the worse and not be eager to win, since he will compete at Olynthus or in Macedonia or in Egypt, and not among Greeks and in the lists there?" By these words, Damis says, he was so affected that he covered his face for what he himself happened to have said, and begged Apollonius to pardon him, in that, not yet having understood him, he had ventured upon such counsel and persuasion. But he, restoring his courage, said: "Take heart; for I said these things not to rebuke you, but to sketch for you my own mind."

Having discoursed thus, they took their rest; and when day was breaking, the king himself came to the chamber in which Apollonius and his company slept, and feeling the bedstead, addressed the man, and asked him what he was thinking. "For surely," he said, "you are not asleep, drinking water and mocking wine." "Do you not think, then," he said, "that those who drink water sleep?" "They sleep," he said, "but a thin sleep, such as we may say sits on the very surface of their eyes, not on the mind." "On both," he said, "and perhaps more on the mind; for unless the mind be at rest, neither will the eyes receive sleep. At any rate the mad cannot even sleep through the leaping of the mind, but, as the thought goes off to one thing and another, they look up more fiercely and shamelessly, like the sleepless dragons. Since, then, O king," he said, "the work of sleep has been clearly interpreted, and what it shows to men, let us consider what the water-drinker will lack in sleep compared with the drunken man." "Do not quibble," said the king; "for if you suppose a drunken man, he will not sleep at all, for his mind, raving in revel, will whirl him and fill him with confusion. Indeed all who try to fall asleep from drunkenness seem to be sent up to the roof, and then again to be underground, and a whirling has fallen upon them, such as is said to befall Ixion. So I do not propose the drunken man, but one who has drunk of wine yet is sober, to consider how he will sleep, and how much better than the man without wine."

"And I do not know what example will suffice for the argument, great as it is and beyond conception; but let there be supposed a ship, such as the Egyptians frame and send out to our sea, giving Egyptian goods in exchange for Indian cargoes. For an ancient law concerning the Red Sea, which king Erythras laid down when he ruled that sea, that the Egyptians should not sail into it with a long ship, but should use one round vessel, leads the Egyptians to devise a craft equal to many of others'; and planking it about with all the joinings that compose a ship, and raising it with sides and a mast and fixing on it several cabins such as are on the decks, many pilots sail in this ship under the eldest and wisest, and many commanders at the prow, the best and most skilful sailors, leaping to the sails; and there is in this ship a part that bears arms also, for against the barbarians of the gulf, who lie on the right of the entrance, the ship must draw up in line when they sail out to plunder it. Let us hold that it is so with this cosmos too, viewing it after the figure of a voyage. For the first and most perfect seat must be given to the god who begets this living creature; the next to the gods who steer its parts; and let us accept the poets when they say that many gods are in heaven, many in the sea, many in springs and streams, many about the earth, and that there are some beneath the earth. But the place beneath the earth, if it exists, since they sing of it as full of horror and destruction, let us set apart from the cosmos.

Nero did not permit philosophising, but the philosophers seemed to him a meddlesome thing, and a cloak for divination; and once the coarse cloak was brought into court as a figure of divination. I pass over the rest, but Musonius the Babylonian, a man second only to Apollonius, was imprisoned for his wisdom, and remaining there was in danger, and would have died, so far as his jailer was concerned, had he not been very strong.

There was silence at this, and the king's face showed the struggle of his judgement, since, after dealing and acting in all things like an emperor, he seemed to be drawn away from this resolve. And Apollonius said: "You seem to me to err in unmaking a king about matters already resolved, falling into a chatter that is childish and more idle than the occasion. For if you were counsellors to me, who possessed power as great as his and was deliberating what good I might do men, the discourse would go forward with you — for the opinions of philosophers set right the philosophers among their hearers; but for men giving counsel to a consul, accustomed to rule, and to whom it is a thing prepared, once he falls from rule, to perish — what need to rebuke him, if he does not thrust away the gifts of fortune, but receives them as they come, and deliberates how he may use temperately what he has? Just as, then, if seeing an athlete fitted out with courage and stature and a frame harmonious for the purpose, walking through Arcadia already on his way to Olympia, we should come up and strengthen him against his adversaries, yet bid him, when he has won the Olympia, not to be proclaimed victor, nor to put his head beneath the wild-olive — we should be thought to talk nonsense, or to make sport of other men's toils — so, considering this man, and how great the spear-point about him, how great the bronze that flashes, how great the multitude of horses, and himself, how noble and temperate and fitted to hold what he purposes, let us send him to what he has set out for, speaking auspicious words to him and enjoining things more reverent than these. For you have not even considered this: that he is the father of two sons who already command armies, and whom, if he does not hand over the empire, he will have as bitterest foes; and what then remains but that he be at war with his own house? But if he takes up the empire, he will be tended by his own sons, and will be supported by them, and the sons by him, and he will use as his guards — no, by Zeus, not hired men, nor men forced, nor men feigning a kindly face, but his most intimate and dearest. For my part I care for no polity, for I live under the gods; but I do not think it right that the flock of mankind should perish for want of a herdsman just and temperate. For just as one man pre-eminent in virtue changes democracy so that it appears the rule of a single best man, so the rule of one man, looking to the advantage of all in common, is the people. 'You did not overthrow Nero,' he says. And did you, Euphrates? Or Dio? Or I? Yet no one rebukes us for this, nor thinks us cowards, if, when philosophic men have already brought down countless tyrannies, we were left behind in seeming to do something for freedom. And yet, so far as in me lay, I did set myself in array against Nero, having both maliciously argued and checked the most savage Tigellinus to his face; and what I did about the western regions to help Vindex was surely a fortifying against Nero. But neither for these things will I say that I overthrew the tyrant, nor will I hold you, because you did not do them, softer than befits philosophy. A philosophic man, then, will speak what comes into his mind, and will do it, I think, taking care not to say anything foolish or mad; but a consul who purposes to overthrow a tyrant needs first more counsel, that he may come at affairs from concealment; then a fitting pretext, that he may not seem to break his oath. For if against the very man who declared him general, and to whom he swore to counsel and do the best, he should mean to use arms, he must first surely make his defence to the gods, that he breaks his oath with holiness; and he needs more friends — for one ought not to do such things unfenced and unguarded — and money as much as possible, that he may win over the forces, and this when he sets upon a man possessed of all that is upon the earth. What delay there is about these things, what time! And these matters take as you will, for let us not come to a testing of what this man, as is likely, devised, but which fortune brought to pass for him without even his striving. But to this, what will you say? The man who yesterday ruled, and was crowned by the cities in the sanctuaries here, and transacted business splendidly and lavishly — this man you bid proclaim publicly today that he is henceforth a private man and came to empire out of madness? For just as, in carrying out what was resolved, he will set beside himself ready guards in whom he trusted when he devised it, so, in coming to change what was decided, he will have for an enemy the man thenceforth distrusted."

So many nations, they say, did Apollonius visit, being earnest and earnestly sought. The journeys that followed were many for the man, yet not so many as before, nor to other nations than those he knew; for about Egypt on the sea, when he had come down from Ethiopia, he spent a longer time, and about the Phoenicians and Cilicians and Ionians and Achaeans and Italians again, nowhere falling short of appearing the same. For though the knowing of oneself seems hard, I hold it harder still for the wise man to remain like himself; for he will not change those who are ill-born to the better unless he has first practised the not changing himself. About these things I have said enough in other discourses, teaching those who do not deal softly with them that the truly perfect man neither anything will change nor enslave. But that we may neither go into length of discourse, teaching in detail what was philosophized by him among each people, nor again seem to leap over an account which we hand down to those without experience of the man, not without labour, it seems good to me to go through the more serious of these, and all that will be held worthy of memory. Let us think them like the visits of the Asclepiads.

This is the preliminary contest of the defence, which took place between him and Domitian in private, such as Damis sets down. But those who have put these matters together maliciously say that he first made his defence, and was bound afterward, when indeed he was shorn; and they have fabricated a certain letter, composed in the Ionic manner, but unpleasant in its length, in which they would have Apollonius become a suppliant of Domitian, begging release from his bonds. But Apollonius renders his own will in the Ionic manner; yet a letter composed in the Ionic dialect I have never met with of Apollonius's, though I have collected very many of his; nor have I ever found long-windedness in the man in a letter, for they are all short and, as it were, from a Spartan despatch-staff. And besides, he left the court having won his case; and how then could he ever have been bound after the acquitting vote? But not yet the things in the court: let the matters concerning the shearing, and what he discoursed, be told first, for they are worth earnest attention.

When the eunuch came and summoned him to the king, "I will come," he said, "when my affairs with the gods are well." So having sacrificed and prayed, he went off, gazed at and admired for his appearance. When he came in, "I give you," said the king, "ten gifts, considering you such a man as none has yet come hither from the Greeks." And he, taking up the word, said: "I will not, O king, decline all of them, but one, which I choose in place of many tens, I will ask for eagerly"; and at the same time he went through the story of the Eretrians, taking it up from Datis. "I ask, then," he said, "that these wretched men be not cut off from their borders and their hill, but that they have to dwell in the measure of land which Darius allowed them; for it would be terrible, if, having fallen out of their own land, they should not even hold the land they have in its place." So the king, consenting, said: "The Eretrians, down to yesterday, were enemies of me and of my fathers, since they once took up arms against us, and were overlooked, that their race might be wiped out; but henceforth they shall be enrolled as friends, and a good man shall be their satrap, who will deal justly with the land. But why," he said, "will you not take the nine gifts?" "Because, O king," he said, "I have not yet gained friends here." "And do you yourself need nothing?" he asked. "The dried fruits," he said, "and the loaves, which feast me pleasantly and splendidly."

Apollonius, calling Damis, said: "The argument is against a clever man, and one well-trained in dialectic." "I see it," he said, "and this perhaps was what is meant by meeting a 'black-bottomed' fellow. But the argument he has spoken quite captivates me too; so it is time for you to wake and finish it." Apollonius, lifting up his head, said: "And indeed how much we who drink water have the advantage in sleeping more pleasantly, I will show, keeping to your own argument. For that the mind of the drunken is confused and they are more frenzied, you have clearly said, for we see those held by drunkenness thinking they see two moons and two suns; while those who have drunk less, even if quite sober, reckon none of these things, but are full of cheer and pleasure, which falls upon them often without any good fortune; and such men plead lawsuits though they have never yet spoken in court, and say they are rich though they have not a drachma within. These, O king, are frenzied conditions; for the very being pleased disturbs the mind, and I know many of those who think they fare very well not even able to sleep, but leaping out of sleep; and this would be a case of even good things bringing cares. There are also drugs of sleep contrived for men, by drinking or anointing which they sleep, stretched out as though dead, whence they rise with a kind of forgetfulness and are anywhere else rather than where they seem to be. That, then, what is drunk, or rather poured over the soul and body, brings on a sleep neither genuine nor proper, but either deep and half-dead or short and torn by what runs through it, even if it be sound, you will perhaps grant, unless you pursue contentiousness rather than reasoning. But my fellow-drinkers see things that are as they are, and things that are not they neither record to themselves nor imagine; nor have they ever seemed light, nor full of stupidity or silliness, nor more merry than is fitting, but they are composed and full of reason, like men at evening and when the market is full; for these do not nod, not though they study far into the night. For sleep does not thrust them out like a master pressing heavy upon the neck enslaved by wine, but they appear free and upright, and falling asleep they receive sleep with a pure soul, neither lifted from it by good fortunes nor leaping out of it through any misfortune. For the sober soul is well-measured toward both these things and overcome by neither passion, whence it sleeps most pleasantly and most painlessly, not starting out of sleep.

When the Indian had gone through this, Damis says he was beside himself with astonishment and cried aloud; for he would never have thought that an Indian man could come to such command of the Greek tongue, nor, even if he knew the tongue, could go through these things with such fluency and grace. And he praises his look and his smile and his not seeming to bring forth his opinions without divine help. And Apollonius too, who used his words gracefully and without din, yet improved, he says, after this Indian; and wherever he sat discoursing — and he did this often — he resembled Iarchas.

Philosophy being in such a state, he chanced to be approaching Rome, and a hundred and twenty stades distant he met Philolaus of Citium near the grove at Aricia. Philolaus was polished of tongue, but too soft to endure anything. He was withdrawing from Rome and himself seemed like a fugitive, and exhorted whatever philosopher he met to do the same. So accosting Apollonius, he bade him give way to the time, and not frequent Rome, since philosophising was in disrepute; and he told of what was being done there, often turning round lest someone behind should overhear him. "And you," he said, "having fastened to yourself a chorus of philosophers, go full of envy, not knowing those set at the gates by Nero, who will seize you and these men before you get within." "And what," said Apollonius, "Philolaus, do they say the emperor is busy about?" "He drives a chariot publicly," he said, "and sings as he comes forward into the Roman theatres, and lives with gladiators, and himself fights and slaughters." Apollonius took him up and said: "Do you think, my good man, there is any greater spectacle for educated men than to see a king disgrace himself? For man is the plaything of god, according to Plato's opinion; but a king who becomes the plaything of man and gives his own shame to the crowds for their delight — what discourses would he not provide to philosophers?" "By Zeus," said Philolaus, "if it could be done without danger; but if you are taken and perish, and Nero devours you raw, having seen nothing of what he does, your meeting with him will cost you much, and more than it cost Odysseus when he went to the Cyclops; for he lost many of his companions in his longing to see him, and was overcome by a strange and savage sight." But Apollonius said: "Do you think this man less blinded than the Cyclops, if he works such deeds?

The king, hearing this gladly, said, "If you had dwelt in my own soul, you could not have reported so clearly what I had in mind. I follow you, then, for I hold everything from you divine; and teach me all that a good king ought to do." And Apollonius said, "You ask me things not to be taught; for kingship is the greatest of human things, but not to be taught. Yet what seems to me that you would do soundly in doing, I will tell you. Hold not that wealth which is laid away — for how is this better than sand brought together from anywhere? — nor that which comes from men who lament their contributions; for gold is base and black when it comes from tears. You would use wealth best of kings by relieving those in need, and by making secure the wealth of those who possess much. Fear the power to do whatever you wish, for so you will use it more temperately. Do not cut the high ears of corn that overtop the rest — the saying of Aristotle is unjust — but rather root out disaffection, as thorns from the crops; and be terrible to those who plot revolution, not in punishing, but in being ready to punish. Let the law, O king, rule even you; for you will legislate more soberly if you do not despise the laws. Serve the gods more than before; for you have received great things from them, and pray for great things. The things that belong to your office, do as a king; the things of the body, as a private man. About dice and drunkenness and loves and the ill repute that goes with such things, what should I advise you, who they say did not approve them even in youth? You have two sons, O king, and noble ones, they say. Rule these above all, for their faults will surely bring reproach on you. Let there be too a threat against them, that you will not hand over the empire to them unless they remain good and noble men, that they may hold the empire not an inheritance but the prize of virtue. The pleasures that are at home in Rome — and they are many — it seems to me, O king, that you should check in measure, for it is hard to change a people to sobriety all at once, but one must little by little work rhythm into their minds, setting some things right openly and some in secret. From the freedmen and slaves whom your office gives you, let us take away luxury, training them to think the more humbly in proportion as they are the slaves of a greater master. What remains but to speak about the governors who go out to the nations? — not those whom you yourself will send, for you will give the offices by merit, but those who will obtain the rule by lot. Of these I say you must send each man suited to the nations he has drawn by lot, so far as the lot allows: men who Hellenize to rule Greeks, men who Romanize to rule those of like tongue and speech. And whence this came into my mind, I will tell you. In the time when I lived in the Peloponnese, the governor of Greece was a man who knew nothing of Greek affairs, and the Greeks understood nothing of his; so he both deceived and was deceived in most things, for his assessors and partners in the judgement in the courts trafficked in the lawsuits, having got the governor in their grip like a slave. These things came to my mind today, O king; but if anything else should occur to me, we shall come together again. Now do the things that belong to your office, lest you seem too idle to your subjects."

There was a youth uneducated in himself, but who educated birds and made them his housemates for wisdom's sake; and he taught them to chatter all that men do, and to pipe all that flutes do. Meeting him, Apollonius said, "What is your pursuit?" And when he went through the nightingales he had, and the blackbirds, and how he gave good tongue to the plovers, while his own voice appeared uneducated, "You seem to me," he said, "to corrupt the birds, first by not allowing them their own note, so sweet that not even the instruments of music could come to the imitation of it, and then by yourself, talking worst of all Greeks, making them your pupils in tonelessness. And you wear out your own house too, young man; for to one who looks at your attendants and how you are furnished, you appear of the delicate and not poor, and such men the informers drain, raising their tongues against them like goads. And what use will you make of your love of birds then? For not even by bringing the songs of all the nightingales will you scare them off when they press and lean on you, but you must pour out your substance and throw them gold, like the sops to dogs, and if they bark, give it again and again, and then yourself go hungry afterward and be in want. You need, then, some splendid turning and some change of your ways, lest, before you know it, you moult away your wealth, and, deserving rather to be wept over by birds than sung to, fare ill. The remedy of the change is not great; for there is in all cities a kind of men whom you do not yet know, but they are called teachers; to these giving a little of your substance you will safely possess the more, for they will teach you the rhetoric of the courts, and the art is easy. For if I saw you still a child, I would have counselled you to frequent the doors of philosophers and sophists and to fence your house with all wisdom; but since you are past the age for these things, learn at least to speak on your own behalf, reckoning that, if you had learned the more perfect things, you would have seemed like a man-at-arms and formidable, but having learned these you will have the equipment of the light-armed and slingers, for you might pelt the informers, as you do the dogs." The youth understood these things, and leaving the pastimes of the birds went to the teachers, by whom both his judgement and his tongue were strengthened.

The man having been bound two days, someone came to the prison saying that he had bought the right to approach him, and that he had come as a counsellor of his safety. This man was a Syracusan, the mind and tongue of Domitian, and was let down like the former one, but for more plausible ends. For the first came from afar, but this one, taking hold of present things, said: "O gods, who would have thought that Apollonius would be bound?" "He who bound me," he said; "for he would not, unless he had thought it, have bound me." "And who would ever have thought the ambrosial locks would be cut off?" "I," he said, "who wore them." "And how do you bear these things?" "As is fitting," he said, "for one who came to them neither willingly nor unwillingly." "And how does your leg hold out?" he said. "I do not know," he said, "for my mind is on other things." "And yet," he said, "the mind is with the part that pains." "Not at all," he said; "for the mind, at least in such a man, will either not feel pain, or will make the pain cease." "And what does the mind reflect upon?" "On this very thing," he said, "of not reflecting upon these matters." Again, calling up the locks and turning the talk to them, "You have profited, young man," he said, "by not being one of the Achaeans at Troy; for very much, I think, you would have lamented the locks of Achilles cut for Patroclus—if indeed they were cut—and would have fainted over them; for you who say you pity mine, which were grey and rough with neglect, what would you not have felt over those, dressed and golden?" Now this was said with a plot, that he might learn for what he grieved, and—by Zeus—whether he reviled the emperor for what he had suffered; but, cut short by what he heard, he said: "You are slandered to the emperor on many counts, and most of all on those for which Nerva and his party are in exile as wrongdoers; for some slanders have come to him also about the arguments in Ionia, which you spoke against him and hatefully; but he despises these, they say, since he is provoked toward greater things—though the man who slandered even those has gone high in repute." "What an Olympic victor you have described," he said, "if he says he lays hold of repute by being strong in slanders! And I understand that it is Euphrates, whom I know to be doing everything against me; and I have been wronged by him in other and greater things; for once, perceiving that I was about to go to the Naked Sages in Ethiopia, he set himself to slander me to them, and had I not understood the plot, I should perhaps have gone away without even seeing the men." The Syracusan, marvelling at the speech, said: "Then do you hold it greater than being slandered to the emperor, that you should seem to the Naked Sages not a good man, by the things Euphrates let down?" "By Zeus," he said; "for there I went to learn, but here I have come for the sake of teaching." "Teaching what?" he said. "That I am a noble and good man," he said; "but this the emperor does not yet know." "But it is possible," he said, "to set your own affairs well, by teaching him those things which, had you said them before coming here, you would not even have been bound." Understanding, then, that the Syracusan was driving him into talk like the emperor's, and thought that, weary of his bonds, he would say something false against the men, "My good man," he said, "if, having told Domitian the truth, I was bound, what shall I suffer if I do not tell the truth? For to him the truth seems worthy of bonds, but to me the falsehood does."

While they were talking thus with one another, a clamour of eunuchs and women together broke out from the palace. A eunuch had been caught lying with one of the king's concubines and doing all that adulterers do; and the keepers of the women's quarters were dragging him along, pulling him by the hair, in the way the king's slaves are dragged. When the eldest of the eunuchs said that he had long before perceived the man's love for the woman, and had forbidden him to converse with her or to touch her neck or hand, or to adorn her alone among those within, but that now he had even found him lying with her and playing the man toward the woman, Apollonius looked at Damis, as though the argument had been proved which they had discussed about even eunuchs loving; but the king said to those present: "It is shameful, gentlemen, that, with Apollonius present, we, and not he, should pronounce upon chastity. What, then, do you bid this man suffer, Apollonius?" "What else than to live?" he said, answering contrary to the opinion of all. The king, flushing, said: "Then is he not worthy of many deaths, creeping thus into my bed?" "But it was not for pardon, O king," he said, "that I said this, but for a punishment that will wear him away. For if he lives sick, and laying hold of the impossible, and neither food nor drink will please him, nor the spectacles that delight you and those with you, and his heart leaps as he often starts up from sleep—which they say happens most to those in love—what wasting will so consume him, what hunger so crush his entrails? And unless he be one of those who cling to life, he will himself, O king, one day beg you even to kill him, or will kill himself, lamenting much this present day, on which he did not die at once." Such, then, was this saying of Apollonius, and so wise and gentle, that the king remitted the death of the eunuch.

"And indeed the divination from dreams, which seems the most divine of human things, the soul beholds more easily when not befouled by wine, but receiving it undefiled and surveying it. At any rate the interpreters of visions, whom the poets call dream-readers, would not undertake to read any vision unless they first asked the time at which it was seen. For if it be at dawn and from the sleep about daybreak, they reckon it, since the soul prophesies soundly when it has cleansed itself of the wine; but if it be about the first sleep or midnight, when the soul is still sunk and befouled by the wine, they decline the reading, being wise. And that this is the judgment of the gods too, and that they set the oracular power in sober souls, I will show clearly. There was among the Greeks, O king, a man Amphiaraus, a seer." "I know," he said; "you mean, I suppose, the son of Oicles, whom the earth drew down alive as he returned from Thebes." "This man, O king," he said, "prophesying still in Attica, sends dreams to those who consult him; and the priests, taking the consultant, keep him from food for one day and from wine for three, that he may draw the oracles with a soul that shines through. But if wine were a good drug of sleep, the wise Amphiaraus would have bidden the consultants come to his shrine prepared the opposite way and full of wine, like amphorae. And I could tell of many famous oracles among Greeks and barbarians, in which the priest, having drawn water and not wine, utters the words from the tripod. Hold me too, then, god-borne, O king, and all who drink water; for we are nymph-possessed and bacchants of sobriety." "Will you make me too, then, Apollonius," he said, "a member of your company?" "If you will not seem vulgar to your subjects," he said; "for philosophy in a kingly man, if measured and somewhat relaxed, works a wondrous blend, as is shown in you, but if exact and overstrained, it appears both vulgar, O king, and humbler than your state, and the envious would even reckon it a kind of conceit."

When the others praised the discourse together with the voice, Apollonius asked again whether they held the sea or the land to be greater; and Iarchas said: "If the land be measured against the sea, it will be greater, for it holds the sea; but if it be viewed against the whole watery substance, we should declare the land the less, for the water bears it up too.

"Let him do," said Philolaus, "what he will; but you at least save these men." He said this in a louder voice and seemed to weep. Then Damis, fearing for the young men, lest they become worse than themselves through Philolaus' panic, drew Apollonius aside and said: "This hare will destroy the young men, filling all with trembling and faintheartedness." But Apollonius said: "Of many good things, which have often come to me from the gods even unprayed for, I should say I have enjoyed this present one most; for there has fallen out a test of the young men, which will sorely prove which of them are philosophers and which do something else rather than this." And at once the unsound among them were proved; for, led astray by Philolaus' words, some said they were sick, some that they had no provision for the journey, some that they longed for home, some that they were terrified by dreams; and Apollonius came down to eight followers from thirty-four who went with him to Rome. The rest fled, escaping both Nero and philosophy.

Euphrates said, "I consent to what has been resolved; for what more should I accomplish by trying to unteach it? But philosophy, O king — this last word I shall add — the philosophy that is according to nature, praise and welcome; but that which claims to invoke the gods, decline, for by lying much about the divine they puff us up with foolish things." This was said by him against Apollonius; but Apollonius, not at all moved, departed with his own acquaintances, having finished his business. And when Euphrates wished to say something more insolent about him, the king understood, and putting him off said, "Call in those who have business with the empire, and let the council resume its own form." So Euphrates, without knowing it, discredited himself, for he seemed to the king both envious and insolent; and his words on behalf of democracy he was thought to have spoken not as he believed, but in contradiction of Apollonius, because of the views the other held about empire. Yet the king did not cast him off, nor show any anger at this. And Dio he did not praise for siding with him, yet did not cease to love him; for he seemed pleasant in discourse and avoided wrangling, and showed a grace upon his words, such as breathes from the vapour about the sanctuaries, and he had besides the gift of improvising best of men. But Apollonius the king not only loved but submitted to him as he recounted ancient things, and told of the Indian Phraotes, and described the rivers and the beasts by which India is inhabited, and foretold all that the gods revealed about the empire. As he was setting out from Egypt, now settled and growing young again, he made Apollonius his companion of the road; but Apollonius did not think well of this, for he had not yet seen the whole of Egypt, nor had he come into discourse with the Naked Sages, being very eager to match the wisdom of Egypt against that of India. "Nor," he said, "have I drunk of the Nile where it begins." So the king, understanding that he was setting out for Ethiopia, said, "And of us will you keep no memory?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said, "if you remain a good king and keep memory of yourself."

Two accounts being told at Sardis, the one that the Pactolus once brought down gold-dust to Croesus, the other that the trees are older than the earth, the first he said was plausibly believed, for there were once sands of gold in Tmolus, and the rains carried them down, sweeping them into the Pactolus, but in time, as such things are wont, they failed, being washed away; but laughing at the other account, "You say," he said, "that the trees are older than the earth; but I, who have philosophized so long a time, have not yet found that the stars are older than the heaven" — teaching that nothing could come to be when that in which it grows is not.

The Syracusan, admiring him as one who out-philosophized, for he went off saying just this, departed from the prison; and Apollonius, looking at Damis, said: "Do you understand this Python?" "I understand," he said, "that he lurked and tried to draw you on; but what your 'Python' means to you, and what the sense of the name is, I do not know." "There was," he said, "a Python the Byzantine, a clever orator, they say, at persuading to evil; he, going as ambassador for Philip the son of Amyntas to the Greeks, about their enslavement, let the others be, but among the Athenians themselves—at the very time when they were strongest in oratory—declared that Philip was being wronged by them, and that the Athenians did dreadful things in freeing what was Greek. Python, flowing on copiously with these things, as they say—but Demosthenes of Paeania, alone contradicting him as he played the bold, set down the withstanding of him among his own labours. And I would never call my not being drawn into the things this man wished a labour of mine, but I said that he did the same as Python, since he came as the hireling of a tyrant and a counsellor of base things."

When he was once about to hunt the beasts in the parks, in which lions and bears and leopards are kept by the barbarians, the king asked Apollonius to be present with him at the hunt. But he said: "You forget, O king, that I am not present even when you sacrifice; and besides, it is no pleasure to attack beasts that have been tormented and enslaved against their own nature." And when the king asked him how he might rule firmly and securely, "By honouring many," he said, "but trusting few." Once, when the governor of Syria sent an embassy about two villages, I think, near the Zeugma, declaring that they had of old been subject to Antiochus and Seleucus, but now belonged to the king, being possessions of the Romans, and that the Arabians and Armenians did not trouble the villages, while the king, overstepping so great a tract of land, was enjoying their produce, as though they were his rather than the Romans', the king, withdrawing the ambassadors, said: "These villages, Apollonius, were granted to my forefathers by the kings I have named, for the feeding of the beasts, which, when caught among us, pass over into their land by way of the Euphrates; but they, as though forgetting this, lay hold of new and unjust claims. What, then, seems to you the meaning of the embassy?" "Moderate, O king," he said, "and fair, if they wish to obtain with your consent what they could hold even against your will, being within their own territory." And he added that one should not quarrel with the Romans over villages, of which private men perhaps possess larger, nor take up war even over great matters. When the king was ill, Apollonius, being present, discoursed so many and such divine things about the soul that the king revived and said to those present that Apollonius had wrought in him a freedom from care not only about his kingdom, but also about death.

Having discoursed thus—for day had now come—they went out. And Apollonius, understanding that the king must transact business with embassies and the like, said: "Do you, O king, attend to what befits your rule, but release me at this hour to the Sun, for I must say my accustomed prayer." "And may he hear you as you pray," he said, "for he will do a favour to all who rejoice in your wisdom; and I will await your return, for I have certain cases to judge, in which you will greatly profit me by being present."

In the midst of this discourse the messenger came before the sages, bringing Indians in need of help. And he led forward a woman entreating for her son, whom she said was sixteen years old and had been possessed by a demon for two years, and that the temper of the demon was mocking and lying. When one of the sages asked whence she said this, she said: "This son of mine is comely to look on, and the demon is in love with him and does not let him have his wits, nor suffer him to go to a teacher's or to an archer's, nor to be at home, but turns him aside into desert places; and the boy has not even his own voice, but speaks deep and hollow, as men do, and looks with other eyes than his own. And I weep over this and tear myself and admonish my son as is fitting, but he does not know me. And when I purposed this journey here — and I purposed it last year — the demon disclosed himself, using my son as his mouthpiece, and said that he was the ghost of a man who once died in war, and died loving his own wife; but when his wife outraged the marriage-bed by being wedded to another on the third day after he lay dead, he came thereby to hate the love of women, and passed over into this boy. And he promised, if I would not accuse him before you, to give the boy many good and excellent things. I was indeed moved by this, but he has now kept me off a long time and holds my house alone, with no moderate or true intent." So the sage asked again whether the boy were near, and she said no; "for I did much to make him come, but he threatens cliffs and chasms, and to kill my son for me, if I bring suit against him here." "Take heart," said the sage; "for he will not kill him when he has read this." And drawing a letter from his bosom he gave it to the woman; and the letter was addressed to the ghost, with threats and terrors.

So gathering those who were left — among whom was Menippus, who had had to do with the empusa, and Dioscorides the Egyptian, and Damis — he said: "I will not revile those who have left us, but rather will praise you, that you are men like myself; nor, if anyone has gone off in fear of Nero, will I count him a coward, but whoever proves stronger than this fear will be addressed by me as a philosopher, and I will teach him all I know. It seems to me, then, first to pray to the gods, by whom these things came into the mind of you and of them, and then to make them our guides; for apart from the gods we are nothing even in other matters. We must enter a city which rules so many parts of the inhabited world; how then could one enter it, unless they guided us? And that too with a tyranny so harsh established in it that it is not permitted to be wise. Let it seem foolish to no one to take courage on a road which many of the philosophers flee; for first I hold that nothing could become so terrible among men as to astound the wise man; and next I would not propose exercises of courage, unless they came with dangers. And besides, having traversed more of the earth than any man yet, I have seen very many beasts of Arabia and India; but this beast, which the many call a tyrant, I know neither how many heads it has, nor whether it is hook-clawed and saw-toothed. And yet this beast is said to be civic and to dwell in the heart of cities, but it is so much more savage than the mountain and forest beasts that lions and leopards are sometimes tamed by flattery and change their nature, while this one, exalted by those who fawn on it, grows more savage than itself and devours all. Of beasts you could not say that they ever feasted on their own mothers, but Nero is gorged with this food. And if these things were done by Orestes and Alcmaeon too, yet for them there was a pretext for the deed in their fathers — the one slain by his own wife, the other sold for a necklace; but this man, adopted by his mother to an old king and inheriting the rule, killed his mother by a shipwreck, contriving against her a boat by which she perished near the shore. If from these things anyone holds Nero terrible and on this account leaps away from philosophy, thinking it unsafe for himself to do anything to vex him, let him know that the terrible belongs to those who lay hold of temperance and wisdom — for to these the things from the gods are well — but let him count the doings of the insolent mere nonsense, as he does those of drunkards; for these too we hold foolish, but not terrible. Let us go then to Rome, if we are strong; for against the proclamations of Nero, by which he bars philosophy, we may say with Sophocles: 'For it was not Zeus who proclaimed this to me, nor the Muses and Apollo of discourse.' And it is likely that Nero himself knows these iambics, since he delights, they say, in tragedy." Here one, calling to mind the saying of Homer, that when the word fits warlike men they become one helmet and one shield, would, I think, find this very thing come to pass about these men; for, knit together by Apollonius' words, they were strong to die for philosophy and to appear better than those who had fled.

After this the king, having sacrificed in the temple, publicly proclaimed gifts to him. And Apollonius, as though he would ask for some, said, "And what gifts, O king, will you give?" "Ten now," he said, "and when I come to Rome, all that is mine." And Apollonius said, "Then I ought to spare what is yours as my own, and not waste now what will be laid up for me all together; but rather attend to these men, O king, for they seem to be in need." And he pointed to those about Euphrates. The king bade them ask with confidence; and Dio, blushing, said, "Reconcile me, O king, with Apollonius my teacher, concerning the things in which I seemed to contradict him, never before having contradicted the man." So the king, praising him, said, "This I asked yesterday, and it is granted; but ask for a gift." And Dio said, "Lasthenes is from Apamea among the Bithynian people, and while philosophizing with me he fell in love with the cloak and the soldier's life; this man, since he says he is again in love with the philosopher's mantle, release from his military service — he himself asks this. You will gratify me by making him a good man, and him by letting him live as he wishes." "Let him be released," he said; "and I give him the privileges of those who have served, since he loves wisdom and loves you." After him he turned to Euphrates, who had drawn up a letter about what he wished to ask. He held out the letter, as though for the king to read it by himself; but the king, wishing to give occasion against him, read it publicly before all; and it appeared that he was asking some things for himself, some for others, and of the gifts some were money, some in place of money. So Apollonius laughed and said, "Then it was you who counselled democracy, when you meant to ask a king for so much?"

When the governor of Syria was setting Antioch in faction and letting down suspicions among them, by which the city, holding assembly, was divided, and a mighty earthquake fell upon them, they cowered, and, as is wont in signs from heaven, they prayed for one another. So Apollonius, coming forward, said: "The god has become a plain reconciler of you, and you would not fall to faction again, fearing the same things." And he set them to the thought of what they would suffer, and that they would fear the same as one another.

Apollonius, then, discoursed many such things; but Damis says that he himself was at a loss about present matters, and saw no release of them, save such as have come to some, by their prayers, even from far harder straits, from the gods. A little before noon: "Tyanean,"—for he greatly rejoiced at this address—"what shall we suffer?" "What we have suffered," he said, "but nothing beyond, nor will anyone kill us." "And who," he said, "is so invulnerable? When will you be loosed?" "As far as it lies with the judge," he said, "today; but as far as it lies with me, this moment." And saying this he drew his leg out of the fetter, and said to Damis: "I have given you a proof of my own freedom—take heart." Then first, Damis says, he truly understood the nature of Apollonius, that it was divine and more than human; for without sacrificing—how, in a prison?—and without praying anything, or saying anything, he laughed at the fetter, and fitting his leg back again did the part of a prisoner.

When the king once showed him the tunnel under the Euphrates and said, "What does the wonder seem to you?" Apollonius, belittling the marvel, said: "It would be a wonder, O king, if you walked on foot through the river, being so deep and impassable." And when he showed him the walls at Ecbatana too, and said that these were the dwelling of the gods, "Of gods there is no dwelling at all," he said; "and whether of men, I do not know; for the city of the Lacedaemonians, O king, is built without walls." And indeed, when the king had given some judgment to villages and was priding himself before Apollonius that he had heard the case for two days, "You found justice slowly," he said. And when treasure once came in abundance from the subject country, the king opened his treasuries and showed the man the money, trying to lead him into a desire for wealth; but he, marvelling at none of what he saw, said: "These things, O king, are money to you, but to me they are chaff." "What, then," he said, "should I do to use them well?" "Use them," he said, "for you are a king."

When he returned, the day being now advanced, he asked what cases he had judged; and the king said: "Today I gave no judgment, for the sacred signs did not allow me." Apollonius, taking up the word, said: "Do you make these matters too dependent on omens, like your goings forth and your campaigns?" "Yes, by Zeus," he said; "for here too there is danger, if the judge be carried aside from the straight." It seemed to Apollonius that he spoke well, and he asked him again what case he was to judge: "For I see," he said, "that you are perplexed and at a loss how to vote." "I confess," he said, "that I am at a loss, whence I make you my counsellor. For a man sold to another land in which a treasure lay hidden, not yet revealed; and in time afterward the land, splitting open, disclosed a chest of gold, which the seller of the land says belongs rather to himself—for he would not have sold the land had he known beforehand that he had a fortune in it—while the buyer claims to have acquired what he found in his own land now. And the argument of both is just, and I should appear foolish if I bade them divide the gold, for even an old woman could so arbitrate." Apollonius, taking up the word, said: "That these two men are not philosophers their disputing about gold makes plain; but you would seem to me to judge best by considering thus—that the gods first care for those who philosophize with virtue, and second for those who are blameless and have never been thought to wrong anyone. To the philosophers they give to discern well things divine and human; to the otherwise good a sufficient livelihood, that they may not, in want of necessities, become unjust. It seems to me, then, O king, that you should weigh these men as in a balance and examine the life of each; for I do not think the gods would have taken even the land from the one, had he not been base, nor again given even what was under the land to the other, had he not been better than the seller." On the next day both came to be judged, and the seller was convicted of insolence and of having neglected the sacrifices which ought to be offered to the gods of the land, while the other appeared decent and most piously serving the gods. So the opinion of Apollonius prevailed, and the good man went away as one holding these things from the gods.

And there came also a lame man, already thirty years old, a mighty hunter of lions, upon whom a lion had fallen, so that he had dislocated his hip and was otherwise crippled in the leg. But when the hands of the sages stroked his hip, the young man came to walk upright. And another, who had a flux of the eyes, went away with all the light in them restored; and another, who was powerless in the hand, went away with the use of it. And a woman who had borne seven children with hard labour was healed thus through her husband's entreaty: he bade the husband, when his wife was in travail, to bring into the room where she bore a live hare under his cloak, and going round her to let the hare go at once; for the womb would be cast out together with the child, unless the hare were straightway carried out of doors.

So they approached the gates, and the guards asked nothing, but gazed at his appearance and marvelled; for his manner seemed holy and in no way like the begging sort. They put up at an inn near the gates, and as they were taking their supper, since it was now evening, a man came as if to a revel, drunk, with a voice not unpleasant; and he was going round Rome in a circle, singing Nero's songs, and hired for this, and whoever heard him carelessly, or did not pay the fee for the recital, he was permitted to carry off as guilty of impiety. He had a lyre too, and all the gear proper to lyre-playing, and he kept in a box a worn-out string that had been touched and stretched, which he said he had bought from Nero's lyre for two minae and would sell to no one, unless he were a lyre-singer of the best and contending at Pytho. So tuning up, as was his wont, and going through a short hymn of Nero's, he added songs, some from the Oresteia, some from the Antigone, some from wherever in the tragedies set by Nero, and bent his melodies as Nero twisted and ill-wrenched them. When they listened too languidly, he said they were doing Nero impiety and were enemies of the divine voice; but they paid no heed. When Menippus asked Apollonius how he heard him saying these things, "How," he said, "but as when he sang? Yet let us, Menippus, not be provoked at this, but giving the fee for the performance, let us let him sacrifice to the Muses of Nero.

Such, then, I found to be the matter of the quarrel that arose between Apollonius and Euphrates; and when the king had set out, they laid hold of one another openly — Euphrates with anger and abuse, Apollonius again philosophically and rather with refutation. As for all that he charged against Euphrates, as acting unbecomingly for philosophy, it is possible to learn from his letters to him, for they are many; but I must keep off the man, for I did not set out to slander him, but to hand down the life of Apollonius to those who do not yet know it. As for the story told about the cudgel — it is said that Euphrates raised it against Apollonius as he was speaking, but did not bring it down — most attribute this to the formidable nature of the man who was to be struck, but I to the reflection of the man who was to strike, through which he became stronger than an anger that had already won the day.

This too is worth remembering. A man was sacrificing to Earth for a treasure, and did not hesitate to pray about this even before Apollonius; and he, considering what kind of things the man loved, said, "I see a money-maker, and a clever one." "A wretched one, rather," he said, "for I have nothing but a little, not enough to feed my house." "You seem," he said, "to keep many and idle servants, for you do not appear yourself one of the unwise." And the man, weeping quietly, said, "I have four little daughters, and there is need of four dowries; and I have now some twenty thousand drachmas, but when they are divided among the daughters, they will seem to have got little, and I shall perish having nothing." Apollonius, feeling something for him, said, "I and Earth will take care of you, for they say you sacrifice to her." And saying this he went on to the suburbs, like those who buy crops; and seeing a place full of olives and pleased with the trees, since they were well-grown and great, and there being a little garden in it, in which were seen hives and flowers, he went into the little garden as if to inspect something greater, and after praying to Pandora went into the city. Going to the owner of the field, whose wealth had been got by the most lawless means, informing against the estates of the Phoenicians, he said, "Such-and-such a place — for how much did you buy it, and what has been spent by you on it?" And when the man said he had bought the field last year for fifteen thousand, and had not yet spent anything on it, he persuaded the man to sell it to him for twenty thousand, making the five thousand a windfall. Now the lover of the treasure did not yet understand the gift, but did not even think he had got equal value, and so much less, inasmuch as the twenty thousand, being in his hands, were his own, but the field instead of them would lie at the mercy of frosts and hail and the other things that destroy crops. But when he straightway found an amphora of three thousand darics about the very hive in the little garden, and the olive crop proved abundant when the rest of the land was not then fruitful, hymns were sung by him to the man, and all his house was full of suitors paying court to him.

The simpler sort of men refer these things to sorcerers; and they suffer this in many human affairs. For athletes need the art, and all contestants need it, through their craving to win; and it helps them nothing to victory, but the things they win by chance, these wretches, robbing themselves of them, reckon to this art; nor do even those of them who lose disbelieve it, for "if I had sacrificed this, and burned that incense, victory would not have escaped me"—such things they say and such they think. And the art frequents the doors of merchants too in the same way; for we should find these also reckoning the lucky strokes of trade to the sorcerer, and the unlucky to their own stinginess, and to not having sacrificed as much as they ought. And the art fastens most upon lovers; for being sick with so easily-misled a sickness as to discuss it even with old wives, they do nothing wonderful, I think, in going to these sophists and listening to such things from them—men who give them to carry a love-charm and stones, some from the secrets of the earth, some from the moon and stars, and all the spices that India cultivates; and brilliant sums of money they exact of them for these things, but they do nothing along with them. For if, the loved ones having felt something toward the lovers, or been led on by gifts, the love affair goes forward, the art is hymned as sufficient for all; but if the attempt fails, the reference is to what was left out—that one did not burn this incense, or sacrifice, or melt that—and this is great and impossible. The ways, then, by which they make portents of signs in the sky and many other things, and which have been written up by certain men who laughed broadly at the art—let it be declared by me too that the young should not even associate with those men, that they may not be accustomed even to jest at such things. Enough of this digression of the argument; for why should I lay hold further of a thing that is slandered both by nature and by law?

Having said many such things to the king, and finding him eager to do what he advised, and having had enough too of his fellowship with the magi, "Come, Damis," he said, "let us go to the Indians. For those who sailed to the Lotus-Eaters were carried away from their own ways by the food; but we, though we taste none of the things here, sit longer than is reasonable and fitting." "I too think this best," said Damis; "but since I had in mind the time you considered in the matter of the lioness, I was waiting for it to be fulfilled. It has not yet wholly run out, for it is now a year and four months with us; but if we were to set off now, would it be well?" "The king will not let us go, Damis," he said, "before the eighth month ends; for you see that he is good, and too good to rule over barbarians."

When the case had so ended, Apollonius came to the Indian and said: "Today, O king, is the third of the days in which you made me your guest, and at dawn tomorrow I must set out, following the law." "But the law," he said, "does not yet speak to you; for you may stay tomorrow too, since you came after midday." "I rejoice in your hospitality," he said, "for you seem even to quibble the law on my behalf." "I would I could break it," he said, "for your sake. But tell me this, Apollonius: the camels on which they say you ride, do they not bring you from Babylon?" "From there," he said, "Vardanes having given them." "Will they then be able to carry you on, having now come so many stadia from Babylon?" Apollonius kept silent; but Damis said: "This man, O king, does not yet understand about the journey, nor about the nations among which we yet are, but thinks that, since he will everywhere have you and Vardanes, to pass into India is child's play. But the truth about the camels he does not tell you, in what state they are; for they are so badly off that they are carried by us rather than carry us, and we need others. For if they collapse somewhere in a desert of India, we shall sit, he says, scaring the vultures and wolves from the camels, but no one will scare them from us, and we shall perish along with them." The king, taking up the word, said: "I will remedy this; for I will give you others—four, I think, you need—and the satrap over the Indus will send four others to Babylon. I have a herd of camels by the Indus, all white." "And will you not, O king," said Damis, "give a guide too?" "I will give the guide a camel," he said, "and provisions; and I will write to Iarchas, the eldest of the wise men, that he receive Apollonius as no worse than himself, and you as philosophers and followers of a divine man." And the Indian offered gold and precious stones and fine linens and countless such things; but Apollonius said that of gold he had enough, since Vardanes had secretly given it to the guide, but the linens he would take, since they resembled the cloak of the ancient and very Attic men. And taking up one of the stones, "O best of stones," he said, "how seasonably and not without divine help have I found you!"—having seen in it, I think, some secret and divine power. Damis and his company would not accept the gold either, but laid eager hold on the stones, to dedicate to the gods when they should return to their own homes.

And when a certain father said that sons had been born to him, but had died as soon as they began to drink wine, Iarchas took him up and said: "And it was better that they died; for they would not have escaped going mad, being sprung, as it seems, of too hot a seed. Those born of you, then, must abstain from wine; but that they may never even fall into a desire for wine — if a child should be born to you again, and one has been born seven days ago, as I see — you must watch the owl, the bird, where she nests, and snatching her eggs give them to the babe to chew, boiling them in moderation; for if it eats any of these before it tastes wine, a hatred of wine will be bred in it, and it will be most temperate, being tempered only by the heat that is in its nature." So filling themselves with these things and amazed at the men's wisdom in all matters, they asked very many discourses every day, and many they were themselves asked.

Thus far the man played the drunkard. But at daybreak Telesinus, the other of the consuls, calling Apollonius, said: "What is this garb?" He said it was pure and from nothing mortal. "And what is this wisdom?" "Inspiration," he said, "and how one should pray to the gods and sacrifice." "And is there anyone, philosopher, who does not know these things?" "Many," he said; "and if one knows them rightly, he would become far better than himself for hearing from a wiser man that what he knows, he knows well." When Telesinus heard this — for he chanced to be devout — the man came into his mind from what he had long heard about him, and he did not think fit to ask his name openly, lest he should still wish to be unknown, but led him back again to the discourse about the divine, for he had a turn for conversation; and as to a wise man he said: "What do you pray for when you approach the altars?" "I, for my part," he said, "pray that justice may prevail, that the laws be not broken, that the wise be poor, but the rest rich, yet without fraud." "Then," he said, "in asking so much do you think you will succeed?" "By Zeus," he said; "for I string all together into one prayer, and approaching the altars I pray thus: 'O gods, grant me what is due; if I am of the good men, I shall obtain more than I have asked, but if the gods rank me among the base, the opposite will come to me from them, and I shall not blame the gods if I am held worthy of evils, not being good.'" Telesinus was astounded at these words, and wishing to gratify him said: "Frequent all the temples, and it shall be written by me to the priests to receive you and to yield to you in your reforms." "And if you do not write," he said, "will they not receive me?" "By Zeus, no," he said; "for this is my office." "I rejoice," he said, "that being noble you hold a great office; but I would have you know this too of me: I delight to dwell in temples that are not firmly shut, and none of the gods refuses me, but they make me a sharer of their roof; let this be granted me, for the barbarians too allowed it." And Telesinus said: "The barbarians have anticipated a great praise of the Romans; for this I should wish said of us too." So he dwelt in the temples, shifting them and moving from one to another; and being blamed for this, he said: "Not even the gods dwell all the time in heaven, but go to Ethiopia, and go to Olympus and Athos; and I think it strange that the gods should go round all the nations of men, while men do not resort to all the gods. And yet masters who overlook their slaves will incur no blame, for perhaps they despise them as worthless; but slaves who do not by all means serve their masters would perish at their hands as accursed and god-hated chattels.

The philosophy of Dio seemed to Apollonius too rhetorical and contrived rather for delight; and so, setting him right, he says, "Charm with flute and lyre rather than with speech," and in many places of his letters to Dio he rebukes this demagoguery.

These things too I found worth recording of the man. Someone seemed to be in love with the statue of Aphrodite which stands naked in Cnidus, and made dedications to it, and said he would make more for the marriage. To Apollonius this seemed strange in any case; but since Cnidus did not refuse it, and they said the goddess would seem the more manifest if she were loved, it seemed good to the man to purge the sanctuary of this folly; and when the Cnidians asked him if he wished to set right anything of the sacrifices or prayers, "I will set right eyes," he said, "but let the ancestral customs of the sanctuary remain as they are." So calling the affected man, he asked him whether he believed in gods; and when he said that he so believed in gods as even to love them, and recalled the marriage which he thought he would celebrate, "You," he said, "the poets exalt, saying that Anchises and Peleus were wedded to goddesses; but about loving and being loved I know this: gods love gods, and men men, and beasts beasts, and in a word like loves like, for the begetting of true and kindred offspring; but a thing of one kind coming together with what is unlike is neither a wedlock nor a love. And if you considered the things of Ixion, you would not even come to the thought of loving what is not like. But he, made like a wheel, is bent through heaven; while you, unless you depart from the sanctuary, will perish over all the earth, with no power even to gainsay that the gods judged justly upon you." Thus the drunken folly was quenched, and the man who said he was in love went away, having sacrificed for pardon.

When Apollonius had shown himself to Damis and discoursed further, someone stood by about noon, signifying by word of mouth thus much: "The emperor releases you, Apollonius, from these bonds, on Aelian's counsel, and grants you to dwell in the free prison until the defence shall be; and you will perhaps make your defence on the fifth day." "Who then," he said, "will remove me hence?" "I," he said, "and follow me." And the men in the free prison, seeing him, all embraced him, as though he had returned when they did not even think it. For such longing as children have toward a father who sets himself to admonitions pleasant and measured to them, or who interprets the things of their time of life, the same these men had toward Apollonius, and acknowledged it; and he did not cease ever counselling them something.

When it seemed best at last to depart, and the king at length consented to let them go, Apollonius remembered the gifts which he had deferred until friends should be his, and said: "Most excellent king, I have done my host no service, and I owe wages to the magi; take care of them, therefore, and be zealous on my behalf for men who are wise and very well disposed toward you." Overjoyed, the king said: "Tomorrow I will show you these men enviable and judged worthy of great things; but since you need nothing of mine, at least permit these men to take money from me, and whatever they wish"—pointing to Damis and his company. And when they too turned away from the offer, "Do you see, O king," he said, "my hands, how many they are and how like to one another?" "But at least take a guide," said the king, "and camels to ride on, for the length of the road is too great to walk the whole of it." "Let this be, O king," he said; "for they say the road is impassable unless one rides thus, and besides, the animal is easily fed and simple to keep, where there is no fodder. And water too, I think, we must lay in and carry in skins, as we do the wine." "For three days," said the king, "the land is without water; after that there is great abundance of rivers and springs. You must travel by the road toward the Caucasus, for the supplies there are abundant and the land friendly." And when the king asked him what he would bring back to him from there, "A pleasing gift, O king," he said; "for if the company of those men makes me wiser, I shall come back to you better than I now am." The king embraced him as he said this, and "Come back," he said; "for the gift is great."

When they had stayed the next day too—for the Indian would not let them go—he gave them the letter to Iarchas, written thus: "King Phraotes to Iarchas his teacher and to those about him, greeting. Apollonius, a most wise man, holds you wiser than himself and comes to learn your lore; send him on, then, knowing all you know, for none of your teaching will be lost; for he speaks best of men and remembers. And let him see also the throne on which, when I sat, you gave me the kingdom, Iarchas my father. And those who follow him are worthy of praise too, that they are devoted to such a man. Farewell, and fare you all well."

In the dialectical converse both took part; but in the secret studies, by which they observed divination from the stars and were earnest about foreknowledge, and applied themselves to sacrifices and invocations in which the gods delight, Damis says that Apollonius alone shared the philosophy of Iarchas, and that from there he composed four books about divination by the stars, which Moeragenes also mentioned, and a book about sacrifices, and how one should sacrifice to each god fittingly and acceptably. As for the lore of the stars and all such divination, I hold it beyond the nature of man, and I do not even know whether anyone possesses it; but the work about sacrifices I found in many temples and many cities and many houses of wise men, and how should one interpret it, set down with such dignity and in the man's own ringing voice? Damis says too that Iarchas gave Apollonius seven rings named after the seven stars, which Apollonius wore one by one according to the names of the days.
