As he discoursed about the temples, the gods were the more served, and men came together to them, thinking to have more good things from the gods; and the man's meetings were not yet slandered, because they were earnestly attended publicly and openly spoken of to all; for he did not haunt doors, nor wear himself out about the powerful, but greeted those who came to him and discoursed to them as to the people.

As for his not coming again to the king, nor consorting with him after Egypt, though the king called him and wrote much about it, I wish to make clear how it came about. Nero had set Greece free, having taken a wiser resolve than was his wont, and the cities returned to Dorian and Attic ways, and all things grew young again in concord among the cities, which not even of old had Greece possessed. But Vespasian, when he came, took this from her, alleging factions and other things not deserving of so great a wrath. This seemed bitter, not only to those who suffered, but also to Apollonius, as beyond the character of his kingship; whence he wrote to the king thus: "Apollonius to the Emperor Vespasian, greeting. You have enslaved Greece, they say, and you think you have something more than Xerxes; but you have failed to see that you have less than Nero. For Nero, having it in his power, gave it up. Farewell." To the same: "Having shown yourself so ill-disposed toward the Greeks as to enslave free men, what need have you of my company? Farewell." To the same: "Nero in sport set the Greeks free, but you in earnest have enslaved them. Farewell." Such were the things that estranged Vespasian from Apollonius; but hearing that he ordered well all his rule thereafter, he was plainly glad, and thought it a good thing done for himself.

When earthquakes once held the cities on the left of the Hellespont, Egyptians and Chaldeans went begging about them for the gathering of money, that they might sacrifice ten-talent sacrifices to Earth and Poseidon, and the cities contributed, some from the common funds, some from their houses, subject to fear; but the men said that unless the silver were set out on tables they would not sacrifice on their behalf. So it seemed good to the man not to overlook the Hellespontines, and coming to the cities he drove out the ones who had made the calamities of others their treasure, and grasping the causes of the wraths, and sacrificing as was fitting to each, he prayed away the visitation at small cost, and the earth stood firm.

Calling Damis the next day, he said: "For me the matters of the defence will be on the appointed day; but you, go the road to Dicaearchia—for it is better to go on foot—and when you have greeted Demetrius, turn about by the sea where lies the island of Calypso, for there you will see me appear." "Alive," said Damis, "or what?" Apollonius, laughing, said: "As I think, alive; but as you think, restored to life." Damis says that he went off unwilling, neither despairing as of one to perish, nor of good hope as of one who would not perish; and that on the third day he came to Dicaearchia, and heard also about the storm which arose in those days—that a rainy wind, bursting upon the sea, sank some of the ships sailing there, and drove others off to Sicily and the strait—and that he understood then for what reason Apollonius had bidden him travel on foot.

Having set out from Taxila, and having gone a two days' journey, they came to the plain in which Porus is said to have fought Alexander, and in it they say they saw gates that shut in nothing, but were built for the sake of trophies. For upon them is set Alexander standing in a four-horse chariot, such as he stands over the satraps of Darius at Issus. And not far apart from one another two gates are said to be built, the one bearing Porus, the other Alexander, having met, I think, after the battle; for the one resembles a man greeting, the other one making obeisance.

Once, when their discourse was about foreknowledge, and Apollonius was devoted to this wisdom and turned most of his talk to it, Iarchas praised him and said: "Those who delight in divination, good Apollonius, become divine by it and work for the safety of men. For to discover by oneself what one would have to go to a god to find, and to foretell to others what they do not yet know — this I count the mark of one wholly blessed and of equal power with Apollo of Delphi. And since the art bids those who go to the god to be consulted come pure, or it will say to them, 'Depart from the temple,' it seems to me that the man who is to have foreknowledge must be sound in himself, and have neither stain clinging to his soul nor scars of sins stamped on his mind, but must prophesy purely, understanding himself and the tripod within his breast. For so he will deliver the oracles more clearly and more truly. Wherefore one need not marvel that you too have grasped the science, bearing so much ether in your soul.

When Demetrius, disposed towards him as I have said in the Corinthian account, came later to Rome and attended Apollonius, but launched himself against Nero, this was suspected to be the man's craft, and he himself seemed to have set Demetrius on to it, and much more when a gymnasium was built for Nero, the most wonderful of those there, and Nero himself and the great senate and the knighthood of Rome were keeping a white-letter day in it. For Demetrius came into the very gymnasium and went through a discourse against those who bathed, as enervated and defiling themselves, and showed that such things were a needless expense; and what helped him not to die at once was that Nero on that day sang most tunefully — and he sang in a tavern built onto the gymnasium, naked, with only a loincloth, like the most wanton of the tavern-keepers. Yet Demetrius did not escape danger for what he said, for Tigellinus, under whom was Nero's sword, drove him from Rome, as having razed the bath by what he said; and he secretly tracked Apollonius, watching for when he too should say something culpable and rash.

This too seemed a marvel of Apollonius in Egypt. A man was leading a tame lion by a leash, like a dog, and the lion fawned not only on the man who led it, but on whoever approached; and it begged in many of the cities, and was admitted even into the temples because it was clean — for it neither licked up the blood of the victims, nor sprang upon the flayed and dismembered offerings, but was fed on honey-cakes and bread and sweetmeats and boiled meats; and one might meet with it drinking wine too without departing from its nature. Coming to Apollonius as he sat in the temple, it whined at his knees and entreated him beyond all men, as most thought, for the sake of a fee; but Apollonius said, "The lion begs me to teach you whose soul of a man it has. It is Amasis, the king of Egypt about the Saite nome." And when the lion heard this, it roared piteously and mournfully, and lamented, crouching down, shedding tears. So Apollonius, stroking it, said, "It seems best to me to send the lion to Leontopolis, to be dedicated to the temple; for I do not think it right that a king, changed into the most kingly of beasts, should beg, like the poor among men." Thereupon the priests came together and sacrificed to Amasis, and adorning the beast with a collar and fillets escorted it into Egypt, piping and singing hymns and chanting over it.

When the emperor Domitian about this same time made a law that no eunuchs should be made and that no vines should be planted any longer, and that the vines already planted should be cut down, Apollonius, coming forward among the Ionians, said: "These ordinances are not for me, for I alone perhaps of men need neither things of love nor wine; but the most marvellous man has forgotten that, while sparing men, he is making a eunuch of the earth." Whence Ionia took courage to send an embassy to the emperor about vines, and to deprecate the law which ordered both that the earth be laid waste and that it be not planted.

What followed upon this Damis records from what he says he heard Apollonius tell both to Demetrius and to himself. A stripling from Messene in Arcadia, conspicuous for his beauty, came to Rome, and many loved him, but Domitian beyond all; and they loved him so, that they did not even fear to rival the emperor in love. But the stripling was temperate and spared his own beauty. Now if he had despised gold, or money, or horses, or such baits as draw on some loved ones, let us not praise him, for so a man ought to be prepared; but he, judged worthy of greater things than all together that the eyes of kings have drawn to themselves, did not hold himself worthy of what he was held worthy of. He was therefore bound, for this seemed good to his lover. And coming up to Apollonius, he seemed to wish to say something, but, having modesty as a counsellor of silence, did not yet take heart. So Apollonius, understanding, said: "You, not even at an age for wrongdoing, have been shut up, like us clever ones." "And I shall die too," he said; "for to be temperate is rated at death by the laws of our day." "And by those of Theseus's day too," he said; "for Hippolytus his own father destroyed for temperance." "And me too," he said, "my father has destroyed; for being an Arcadian from Messene, he did not have me taught the things of the Greeks, but sent me here to learn legal customs, and the emperor looked ill upon me as I came for these things." But Apollonius, as though not understanding what he said, said: "Tell me, stripling, the emperor does not, surely, hold you to be grey-eyed—though you are black-eyed, as I see—or crooked-nosed, though you have it squared like the well-trained Hermae, or your hair to be other than it is? But it is, I think, sun-touched and gleaming faintly; and your mouth too is so measured as to befit both silence and speech, and your neck so free and high-minded. What other of these things, then, will the emperor hold you to be, since you say you were looked upon ill by him?" "This very thing has destroyed me," he said; "for being led on to love me, he spares not the things he praises, but purposes to dishonour me, like those who love women." Apollonius, admiring him, passed over the question of what he thought of lying together, and whether this were shameful or not, and such questions, since he saw the Arcadian blushing and speaking with decorum; and he asked him thus: "Do you possess any slaves in Arcadia?" "By Zeus," he said, "many." "Of these, then," he said, "what do you hold yourself?" "Their master," he said, "for the laws make me so." "And ought slaves," he said, "to obey their masters, or to refuse what seems good to the lords of their body?" The youth, reflecting into what an answer he was being led round, said: "That the strength of tyrants is unconquerable and harsh, I know; for it is for this very reason that they wish to lord it over free men; but of my own body I am master, and will keep it inviolate." "How?" he said; "for the talk is of a lover who revels with a sword against your bloom." "I will rather offer my throat," he said, "for it is that the sword needs." Apollonius, praising him, said: "I see you are an Arcadian indeed." And of this stripling he makes mention also in a letter, and describes him far more pleasantly than I do here, praising his temperance; and to the man to whom he writes he says that this stripling did not even die at the tyrant's hands, but, marvelled at for his strength, sailed off to Malea, more to be envied among the Arcadians than those who win at the endurance of the lash among the Lacedaemonians.

Having crossed the river Hydraotes and passed many nations, they came to the Hyphasis; and thirty stadia from it they came upon altars on which was inscribed: "TO FATHER AMMON AND TO HERACLES THE BROTHER AND TO ATHENA PROVIDENCE AND TO OLYMPIAN ZEUS AND TO THE SAMOTHRACIAN CABEIRI AND TO THE INDIAN SUN AND TO DELPHIAN APOLLO." And they say there stands also a bronze pillar inscribed: "ALEXANDER STOOD HERE." Let us hold the altars to be Alexander's, honouring the limit of his own rule, but the pillar I think the Indians beyond the Hyphasis set up, glorying that Alexander did not advance further.

And jesting with Damis at the same time, he said: "And you, Assyrian, do you foreknow nothing, and that too while keeping company with such a man?" "By Zeus," said Damis, "the things at least that I need myself; for when I first met this Apollonius, and he seemed to me full of wisdom and cleverness and temperance and right endurance, and when I saw memory in him too, most learned and a slave to love of learning, something divine came over me; and joining him I thought I should seem wise instead of a layman and unwise, and learned instead of a barbarian, and that, following and studying with him, I should see the Indians and see you, and mingle with the Greeks, become a Greek through him. Now your matters, being about great things, you may count Delphi and Dodona and what you will; but mine, since it is Damis who foreknows them, and he foreknows only on his own behalf, let them be the foreknowledge of some begging old woman who prophesies about sheep and such things.

But he was neither plainly mocking nor anxious, like those guarding against some danger, but discoursed sufficiently on the matters before him, Telesinus joining him in philosophy, and other men who, though philosophy was in a dangerous case, did not think they would be in danger studying with him. He was suspected, as I said, and much more for what he said about a sign from heaven. For when there was an eclipse of the sun and thunder broke out — which seems least to happen in an eclipse — looking up to heaven he said: "There shall be something great, and there shall not." Those who chanced to be at the discourse could not yet construe the saying, but on the third day from the eclipse all understood it; for as Nero was dining, a thunderbolt fell upon the table and drove through the cup that was in his hands and not far from his mouth. His coming so near to being struck was what Apollonius meant by "something shall be done and shall not be done." Hearing this saying, Tigellinus came to fear the man as wise in things divine, and did not think fit to bring open charges against him, lest he should get some hidden harm from him, but watched him as he discoursed and as he was silent, and as he sat and walked, and what he ate and with whom, and whether he sacrificed or not, with all the eyes with which the government sees.

When he had had enough of Alexandria, he set out for Egypt and Ethiopia, to consort with the Naked Sages. Menippus, since he was now among the company of those who could discourse and was formidable in using frank speech, he left there as a match for Euphrates; and Dioscorides, seeing him not strongly disposed toward the journey, he excused from the road. The rest he gathered together — for after those who had left him about Aricia, more others had joined — and went through with them about the journey, beginning thus: "I have need, gentlemen, of an Olympic proclamation toward you. An Olympic proclamation would be of this kind. The Eleans train the athletes, when the Olympia come, for thirty days in Elis itself; and gathering them — as the Delphian does at the Pythia, and the Corinthian at the Isthmia — they say, 'Go to the stadium, and be men such as to conquer'; but the Eleans, when they go to Olympia, address the athletes thus: 'If you have toiled worthily of coming to Olympia, and have wrought nothing idle or ignoble, go with confidence; but those of you who have not so trained, depart wherever you wish.'" The disciples understood the saying, and about twenty remained with Menippus; the rest, ten, I think, in number, having prayed to the gods and sacrificed as it were the offerings for embarking on a voyage, went straight toward the pyramids mounted on camels, keeping the Nile on their right. In many places too the river was crossed by them for the study of all that is in it; for neither city nor temple nor any of the precincts throughout Egypt did they pass by in silence, but always learning and teaching some sacred discourses; and the ship which Apollonius boarded was like a sacred vessel.

This too they sing of the man in Tarsus. A dog had fallen, mad, upon a youth, and the bite carried the youth off into all the ways of dogs, for he barked and howled and ran on four feet, holding his hands to the running. When he had been sick thirty days, Apollonius, just come to Tarsus, stood by him, and bade them track out the dog which had done this; but they said they had neither met the dog, for he had been caught outside the wall while the youth was among the javelin-throwers, nor could they learn from the sick man what the dog was like, since he no longer even knew himself. So pausing, "Damis," he said, "the dog is white, shaggy, a sheep-dog, the size of an Amphilochian; he stands by such-and-such a spring, trembling, for he both desires the water and fears it. Bring me this dog to the bank of the river, where the wrestling-grounds are, only saying that he is called by me." When the dog was dragged by Damis, he cowered at the feet of Apollonius, weeping like a suppliant at the altars; and he tamed him still more and soothed him with his hand, and set the youth near, holding him himself; and that the great secret might not escape the many, he said: "The soul of Telephus the Mysian has passed into this youth, and the Fates wish the same for him." And saying this he bade the dog lick round the bite, that the very one who wounded might become the youth's healer again. Thereupon the youth turned to his father, and knew his mother, and addressed his fellows, and drank of the Cydnus; nor was the dog neglected either, but praying to the river over him too, he sent him through it. And the dog, when he had crossed the Cydnus, standing on the bank, gave tongue, which seldom happens with mad dogs, and laying back his ears wagged his tail, knowing that he was well; for water is a drug of madness, if the mad creature take courage at it. Such were the man's doings on behalf of sanctuaries and cities, and toward peoples and on their behalf, and on behalf of the dead or the sick, and toward the wise and the unwise, and toward kings, who made him a counsellor of virtue.

At this all the sages laughed; and when the laughter had settled, Iarchas led back to the discourse on divination, and said it had wrought many goods for men, but the greatest was the gift of medicine; for the wise sons of Asclepius would never have come to knowledge of it, had not Asclepius, being a son of Apollo, and composing, after his oracles and divinations, the drugs suited to diseases, handed them down to his own children and taught his followers which herbs to apply to moist sores and which to dry and parched ones, and the measures of liquid drugs by which dropsies are drained off and blood is staunched and consumptions are stayed and the like wasting diseases. And who shall take from divination the remedies for venoms and the use of the very venoms against many diseases? For men, it seems to me, would never without the foreknowing wisdom have dared to mix the most deadly of all drugs with those that save.

When a disease fell upon Rome, which the physicians call catarrh — from which arise coughs, and the voice goes ill for those who speak — the temples were full of men entreating the gods, since Nero's throat was swollen and his voice had gone husky. But Apollonius burst out against the folly of the multitude, yet rebuked no one, but even Menippus, provoked by such things, he made temperate and held back, bidding him pardon the gods if they delight in mimes of buffoons. When this saying was reported to Tigellinus, he sent men to bring him to the court, that he might defend himself against the charge of impiety to Nero; and an accuser was made ready against him who had already destroyed many and was full of such Olympiads, and he had a writing-tablet in his hands on which the charge was written, and shaking this like a sword against the man he said it was whetted and would destroy him. But when Tigellinus, unrolling the tablet, found in it no trace of a line, but lit upon a blank book, he was brought to the thought of a daimon. This too Domitian is later said to have suffered with regard to him. So taking Apollonius aside, he brought him into the secret court, in which this government tries the greatest matters in private, and removing all, pressed him with questions as to who he was. Apollonius mentioned his father and his country, and to what end he used wisdom, and said he used it to know the gods and to understand men; for to know another, he said, is harder than to know oneself. "The daimons," he said, "Apollonius, and the apparitions of phantoms, how do you refute them?" "As I do murderous and impious men," he said. This he said mocking at Tigellinus, since he was a teacher to Nero of all cruelty and wantonness. "Would you prophesy for me, if I asked?" he said. "How," he said, "since I am no prophet?" "And yet they say you are the one who said something great would be and would not be." "You heard truly," he said; "but do not set this down to divination, but rather to wisdom, which god reveals to wise men." "And why," he said, "do you not fear Nero?" "Because," he said, "the god who grants him to seem terrible has granted me to be without fear." "And what do you think of Nero?" he said. Apollonius said: "Better than you do; for you think him worthy of singing, but I worthy of silence." Astounded, Tigellinus said: "Go, having found sureties for your body." And Apollonius said: "And who will go surety for a body that no one will bind?" These things seemed to Tigellinus more than human and beyond a man, and as one careful not to war with a god, he said: "Go where you will; for you are too strong to be ruled by me.

And since this discourse too has been recorded by Damis, studied there concerning the beasts and springs and men told of in fable among the Indians, let it not be passed over by me either; for it would be a gain neither to believe nor to disbelieve all things. Apollonius asked: "Is there here a beast, the manticore?" And Iarchas said: "And what nature of this beast have you heard? For it is likely that something is told of its form too." "Great things and incredible are told," he said; "for they say it is four-footed, that its head is like a man's, but in size it is like a lion, and that the tail of this beast puts forth bristles a cubit long and thorny, which it shoots like arrows at those who hunt it." And when he asked also about the golden water which they say wells up from a spring, and about the stone which acts like the magnet, and about men who dwell underground, and pygmies again and shadow-foots, Iarchas took him up and said: "Of beasts or plants or springs, which you have seen on coming here, why should I tell you? For it is now for you to set them forth to others; but of a beast that shoots arrows, or springs of golden water, I have not yet heard here.

And this too is a marvel of Apollonius'. A girl seemed to have died in the hour of her marriage, and the bridegroom followed the bier, crying all that one cries over an unfulfilled marriage, and Rome mourned with him, for the girl belonged to a family of consular rank. Apollonius, chancing to be by at the grief, said: "Set down the bier, for I will stop your tears for the girl." And at once he asked what her name was. Most thought he would deliver a speech, such as those that rouse lamentations at funerals; but he did nothing but touch her and say something secretly, and woke the girl from her seeming death. The girl gave voice and went back to her father's house, as Alcestis, revived by Heracles, did. And when the girl's kin offered him a hundred and fifty thousand pieces, he said he gave them to the girl as a dowry. And whether he found a spark of the soul in her that had escaped those who tended her — for it is said that Zeus drizzled, and steam rose from her face — or whether he warmed and recovered the soul that had gone out, the apprehension of this has proved beyond words, not to me alone, but to those who chanced to be present.

"But concerning the stone that draws to itself and binds other stones, one must not disbelieve; for you may see the stone yourself and marvel at all that is in it. The largest is the size of this finger-nail" — and he pointed to his own thumb — "and it is conceived in the hollow earth, four fathoms deep; and there is so much breath in it that the earth swells and is rent in many places as the stone is conceived in it. To seek it out is permitted to none, for it flees away unless it be drawn up with a spell; but we alone, partly by deeds, partly by words, take up the pantarbe — for this is its name. By night it makes day appear, like fire, for it is fiery and ray-like; but if it be seen by day it strikes the eyes with countless flashings. The light within it is a breath of unspeakable strength, for it takes to itself everything near. Why do I say 'near'? You may sink as many stones as you wish anywhere in the rivers or in the sea, and not near one another but scattered and as it chanced; and the pantarbe, let down among them, gathers them all by the diffusion of its breath, and the stones lie beneath it in clusters, like a swarm.

About this time Musonius too was held in Nero's prisons, who they say was the most perfect of men in philosophy; and they did not converse openly with one another, since Musonius begged off this, lest both should be in danger, but held their meetings by letter, Menippus and Damis frequenting the prison. Leaving the letters that are not about great matters, we shall set down the necessary ones, from which one may discern something great. Apollonius to Musonius the philosopher, greeting. "I wish to come to you and share with you discourse and roof, that I may profit you somewhat — unless you disbelieve that Heracles once freed Theseus from Hades. Write what you wish. Farewell." Musonius to Apollonius the philosopher, greeting. "For what you intended, praise shall be laid up for you; but a man who has endured to make his defence and shown himself to do no wrong has saved himself. Farewell." Apollonius to Musonius the philosopher, greeting. "Socrates the Athenian, not willing to be freed by his own friends, came into court and died. Farewell." Musonius to Apollonius the philosopher, greeting.

And saying this he showed the stone itself and all it does. As for the pygmies, they dwell underground, and they lie beyond the Ganges, living in the manner that has been told by all. But shadow-footed men, or long-heads, or all that the writings of Scylax sing of these, neither live anywhere else on earth nor among the Indians.

"Socrates died because he did not prepare himself for a defence; but I will make my defence. Farewell." When Nero set out for Greece and publicly proclaimed that no one should philosophise at Rome, Apollonius turned to the western parts of the earth, which they say are bounded by the Pillars, to see the ebbings of the Ocean and Gadeira. For he heard too something about the philosophy of the men there, how far advanced they were in things divine; and all his acquaintances followed him, praising both the journey and the man.

The gold which the griffins dig up is in rocks spotted as it were with sparks by the drops of gold, which this beast quarries by the strength of its beak. For these beasts exist among the Indians and are held sacred to the Sun, and those who paint the Sun among the Indians yoke a team of four of them to his image; and in size and strength they are like lions, but with the advantage of their wings they set upon these very lions, and are mightier than elephants and dragons. They cannot yet fly far, but only as far as short-flighted birds; for they are not feathered as is natural to birds, but their feet are webbed with red membranes, so that they can wheel and fly and fight from aloft. The tiger alone is proof against them, since its swiftness makes it the equal of the winds.

And the phoenix, the bird that comes once in five hundred years to Egypt, flies during this time in India, and is one only, sprung from the sun's rays and shining with gold, in size and form like an eagle, and it settles in the nest which it makes for itself out of spices by the springs of the Nile. And what the Egyptians sing of it, that it comes to Egypt, the Indians also bear witness, adding to the tale that the phoenix, as it melts away in its nest, sings funeral hymns over itself. This too they say the swans do, who hear of it more wisely than the rest.

Such were the meetings Apollonius had with the sages, after he had spent four months there and gathered up all discourses both open and secret. When he wished to depart, they persuaded him to send back the guide and the camels to Phraotes with a letter, and themselves, giving him another guide and camels, escorted him on his way, counting both themselves and him happy. And greeting Apollonius, and saying that he would seem a god to the many, not only when dead but while living, they turned back to their place of meditation, often turning towards the man and showing that they parted from him unwillingly. And Apollonius, with the Ganges on his right and the Hyphasis on his left, went down to the sea, a journey of ten days from the holy hill. As they went down, many ostriches appeared, and many wild oxen, and many asses and lions and leopards and tigers, and a kind of ape different from those in the pepper-trees, for they were black and shaggy and dog-faced in their forms and equal to small men. Discoursing of what they saw, as was their wont, they came to the sea, on which were built small trading-towns, and in them lay at anchor passage-boats much like the Etruscan. The Red Sea is, he says, the deepest blue, and was named, as I said, after King Erythras, who gave that sea his own name.

Having come here, he sent the camels back to Iarchas with a letter: "Apollonius to Iarchas and the other sages, greeting. I came to you on foot, and you gave me the sea; but sharing with me the wisdom that is in you, you have given me to journey even through the heavens. I will remember these things among the Greeks, and will share discourse with you as though you were present, if I have not drunk of Tantalus in vain. Farewell, good philosophers.

He himself, embarking on a ship, was borne along by a smooth and favouring wind, marvelling at the mouth of the Hyphasis, how terribly it pours out through it; for at its end, as I said, it falls into rocky and narrow places and over crags, through which, breaking down into the sea by a single mouth, it seems dangerous to those who keep too close to the land.

They say they saw also the mouth of the Indus, and that upon it lies the city Patala, surrounded by the Indus, to which the fleet of Alexander came, over which Nearchus was set as admiral, no novice in sea-array. What Orthagoras has said of the Red Sea, that the Bear does not appear in it, nor do those who sail mark the south, and that the conspicuous stars shift from their proper order, Damis too thinks true, and one must believe that these things are said soundly and according to the heaven there. They make mention also of a small island named Biblus, on which the mussels and oysters and the like grow fast to the rocks, ten times the size of the Greek; and a pearl-stone too is caught there, in a white shell, holding the place of a heart in the oyster.

They say they put in also at Pegadae in the country of the Oreitae; and the Oreitae have rocks of bronze, and bronze sand, and the rivers carry down bronze dust. They count the land to be auriferous because of the nobility of its bronze.

They say they met also the Fish-eaters, whose city is Stobera; and these wear coats of the skins of the greatest fishes, and the flocks there are fishy and strange to eat, for the shepherds feed them on fish, as in Caria they feed them on figs. The Carmanians, an Indian race and gentle, pasture a sea so rich in fish that they do not even store the fish away, nor, like the Pontus, salt them, but sell a few of them and give back the most, still gasping, to the sea.

They say they sailed also to Balara; and Balara is a trading-town full of myrtles and palms, and they saw bays in it, and the place was watered by springs. Gardens of all kinds of edibles, and gardens of flowers, abound there, and there are harbours full of calm within it. Before this place lies a sacred island, called Selera, a hundred stades distant by the strait, and in it dwells a Nereid, a dread spirit; for she seizes many of those who sail, and does not even suffer ships to throw out a cable from the island.

It is worth while not to pass over the account of the other pearl-fishing either, since it did not seem childish to Apollonius, but is fashioned most pleasantly and is the most wonderful of the works of the sea. For the parts of the island that face the open sea have a boundless depth of sea, and it bears an oyster in a white shell full of fat, for it grows no stone at all. Watching for a calm, and themselves smoothing the sea — which the pouring of oil effects — one dives for the catch of the oyster, equipped in other respects like those who cut sponges, but he has also an iron tablet and an alabaster box of myrrh. Sitting beside the oyster, the Indian makes the myrrh a bait for it, and it opens and is made drunk by it; and pierced with a goad it spits out its juice, which he receives in the tablet hollowed into moulds. From this it turns to stone and is shaped, like the natural pearl; and the pearl is white blood from the Red Sea. The Arabians too, who dwell opposite, attack this fishing, they say. From there on the whole sea is full of beasts, and the sea-monsters herd in it, and the ships, as a defence against this, carry bells at stern and prow, and the sound frightens the beasts and does not let them come near the ships.

Having sailed down to the mouths of the Euphrates, they say they sailed up by it to Babylon, to Bardanes, and finding him such as they knew, came again to Ninus; and since Antioch was insolent after its wont and earnest about nothing Greek, they went down to the sea at Seleucia, and chancing upon a ship sailed to Cyprus, to Paphos, where stands the seat of Aphrodite, which being symbolically set up Apollonius admired; and having taught the priests much concerning the holiness of the temple, he sailed to Ionia, much admired and deemed worthy of great things among those who honour wisdom.
